passages.latin: Cum divina tua mens et numen, imperator Caesar, imperio potiretur orbis terrarum invictaque virtute cunctis hostibus stratis, triumpho victoriaque tua cives gloriarentur et gentes omnes subactae tuum spectarent nutum populusque Romanus et senatus liberatus timore amplissimis tuis cogitationibus consiliisque gubernaretur, non audebam, tantis occupationibus, de architectura scripta et magnis cogitationibus explicata edere, metuens ne non apto tempore interpellans subirem tui animi offensionem.
passages.translation: While your divine mind and inspiration, Emperor Caesar, held dominion over the world, and, once all enemies had been vanquished by your invincible valour, the citizens rejoiced in your triumph and victory, all subjugated nations awaited your signal, and the Roman people and the Senate, freed from fear, were guided by your profound reflections and counsel, I dared not, amidst such lofty occupations, publish my writings on architecture, composed after extensive meditations, fearing that, by interrupting you at an inopportune moment, I might incur your displeasure.

passages.latin: Cum vero attenderem te non solum de vita communi omnium curam publicaeque rei constitutione habere, sed etiam de opportunitate publicorum aedificiorum, ut civitas per te non solum provinciis esset aucta, verum etiam ut maiestas imperii publicorum aedificiorum egregias haberet auctoritates, non putavi praetermittendum quin primo quoque tempore de his rebus ea tibi ederem, ideo quod primum parenti tuo de eo fueram notus et eius virtutis studiosus. Cum autem concilium caelestium in sedibus inmortalitatis eum dedicavisset et imperium parentis in tuam potestatem transtulisset, idem studium meum in eius memoria permanens in te contulit favorem. Itaque cum M. Aurelio et P. Minidio et Gn. Cornelio ad apparationem ballistarum et scorpionum reliquorumque tormentorum refectionem fui praesto et cum eis commoda accepi, quae cum primo mihi tribuisti, recognitionem per sororis commendationem servasti.
passages.translation: But when I observed that you were not only concerned with the common life of all and with the ordering of the commonwealth, but also with the fitness of public buildings—so that the State was enlarged not only by your provinces, but also that the majesty of the empire might possess the eminent authority of its public buildings—I did not think it right to omit laying these matters before you at the earliest opportunity, the more so because I had first been known to your father and was an admirer of his virtue. But when the council of the heavenly powers had consecrated him among the seats of immortality and had transferred your father's empire into your power, that same devotion of mine, abiding in his memory, transferred my allegiance to you. And so, together with Marcus Aurelius, Publius Minidius and Gnaeus Cornelius, I was at hand for the preparation of ballistae and scorpiones and the repair of the other engines of war, and with them I received my emoluments, which, once you had first granted them to me, you continued to me by your sister's recommendation.

passages.latin: Cum ergo eo beneficio essem obligatus, ut ad exitum vitae non haberem inopiae timorem, haec tibi scribere coepi, quod animadverti multa te aedificavisse et nunc aedificare, reliquo quoque tempore et publicorum et privatorum aedificiorum, pro amplitudine rerum gestarum ut posteris memoriae traderentur, curam habiturum. Conscripsi praescriptiones terminatas, ut eas attendens et ante facta et futura qualia sint opera per te posses nota habere; namque his voluminibus aperui omnes disciplinae rationes.
passages.translation: Since this favor bound me to you and freed me from the fear of poverty for the rest of my life, I began to write these books for you. I had observed that you had built many works and were still building, and that you would continue to care for public and private buildings on a scale commensurate with your achievements, so that they might be handed down to posterity. I have set down precise rules so that, by attending to them, you may judge for yourself the quality of works already completed and of those yet to come; for in these volumes I have explained all the principles of the discipline.

passages.latin: Architecti est scientia pluribus disciplinis et variis eruditionibus ornata, cuius iudicio probantur omnia quae ab ceteris artibus perficiuntur opera. Ea nascitur ex fabrica et ratiocinatione. Fabrica est continuata ac trita usus meditatio, quae manibus perficit[ur] e materia cuiuscumque generis opus [est] ad propositum deformationis. Ratiocinatio autem est, quae res fabricatas sollertiae ac rationis pro portione demonstrare atque explicare potest.
passages.translation: The architect’s knowledge embraces many disciplines and varied forms of learning; by its judgment, all works accomplished by the other arts are assessed. It arises from fabrica and ratiocinatio. Fabrica is the continuous, practised exercise of making: through manual work and materials of whatever kind, it brings a work into being according to its intended design. Ratiocinatio, by contrast, enables one to demonstrate and explain constructed works according to the proper proportion of skill and reason.

passages.latin: Itaque architecti, qui sine litteris contenderant ut manibus essent exercitati, non potuerunt efficere ut haberent pro laboribus auctoritatem; qui autem ratiocinationibus et litteris solis confisi fuerunt, umbram non rem persecuti videntur. At qui utrumque perdidicerunt, uti omnibus armis ornati, citius cum auctoritate quod fuit propositum sunt adsecuti.
passages.translation: Therefore, architects who sought to train their hands without acquiring literary learning could not gain recognition commensurate with their labors; those who relied on reasoning and books alone seem to have pursued the shadow rather than the substance. Those, however, who thoroughly mastered both, equipped as though with every weapon, attained their aims more swiftly and with authority.

passages.latin: Cum in omnibus enim rebus, tum maxime etiam in architectura, haec duo insunt: quod significatur et quod significat. Significatur proposita res, de qua dicitur; hanc autem significat demonstratio rationibus doctrinarum explicata. Quare videtur utraque parte exercitatus esse debere qui se architectum profiteatur. Itaque eum etiam ingeniosum oportet esse et ad disciplinam docilem. Neque enim ingenium sine disciplina aut disciplina sine ingenio perfectum artificem potest efficere.
passages.translation: For in all things, and especially in architecture, two elements are present: what is signified and what signifies. What is signified is the proposed subject under discussion; what signifies it is a demonstration explained through the principles of the disciplines. Whoever professes to be an architect must therefore be trained in both. He must possess natural talent and be receptive to instruction, for neither talent without training nor training without talent can produce an accomplished practitioner.

passages.latin: Quae cur ita sint, haec sunt causae. Litteras architectum scire oportet, uti commentariis memoriam firmiorem efficere possit. Deinde graphidis scientiam habere, quo facilius exemplaribus pictis quam velit operis speciem deformare valeat. Geometria autem plura praesidia praestat architecturae, et primum ex euthygrammis circini tradit usum, ⟨regulaeque⟩ e quo maxime facilius aedificiorum in areis expediuntur descriptiones, normarumque et librationum et linearum directiones. Item per opticen in aedificiis ab certis regionibus caeli lumina recte ducuntur. Per arithmeticen vero sumptus aedificiorum consummantur, mensurarum rationes explicantur, difficilesque symmetriarum quaestiones geometricis rationibus et methodis inveniuntur.
passages.translation: The reasons for these requirements are as follows. The architect must be literate so that written notes may strengthen his memory. He must also know drawing, so that he can more easily represent the intended appearance of a work through drawings. Geometry provides architecture with many aids: first, it teaches the use of the straightedge and compasses, which facilitate the setting-out of buildings on their sites and the alignment of set squares, levels and lines. Optics enables light to be admitted correctly into buildings from particular quarters of the sky. Arithmetic is used to calculate construction costs, explain systems of measurement and resolve difficult questions of commensurability through geometrical reasoning and methods.

passages.latin: Historias autem plures novisse oportet, quod multa ornamenta saepe in operibus architecti designant, de quibus argumenti rationem, cur fecerint, quaerentibus reddere debent. Quemadmodum si quis statuas marmoreas muliebres stolatas, quae caryatides dicuntur, pro columnis in opere statuerit et insuper mutulos et coronas conlocaverit, percontantibus ita reddet rationem:
passages.translation: He must also know many historical narratives, because architects often include ornaments in their works and must explain the reasoning behind them to anyone who asks why they were used. Thus, if someone sets up marble statues of robed women, called caryatids, in place of columns, and places mutules and cornices above them, he will give the following explanation.

passages.latin: Non minus Lacones, Pausania Agesilae filio duce, Plataico proelio pauca manu infinitum numerum exercitus Persarum cum superavissent, acto cum gloria triumpho spoliorum et praedae, porticum Persicam ex manubiis, laudis et virtutis civium indicem, victoriae posteris pro tropaeo constituerunt. Ibique captivorum simulacra barbarico vestis ornatu, superbia meritis contumeliis punita, sustinentia tectum conlocaverunt, uti et hostes horrescerent timore eorum fortitudinis effectus, et cives id exemplum virtutis aspicientes gloria erecti ad defendendam libertatem essent parati. Itaque ex eo multi statuas Persicas sustinentes epistylia et ornamenta eorum conlocaverunt, et ita ex eo argumento varietates egregias auxerunt operibus. Item sunt aliae eiusdem generis historiae, quarum notitiam architectos tenere oporteat.
passages.translation: No less the Laconians, led by Pausanias, the son of Agesilaus, having defeated an immense Persian army with a small force in the battle of Plataea, having celebrated a glorious triumph of spoils and booty, erected a Persian portico from the proceeds of the spoils, a token of the praise and virtue of the citizens, and a trophy of victory for posterity. And there they placed the effigies of captives adorned with barbarian clothing, their pride punished with deserved insults, supporting a roof, so that both the enemies might shudder with fear at the effects of their fortitude, and the citizens, beholding that example of virtue, might be raised in glory and ready to defend their liberty. Therefore from it many placed Persian statues supporting their epistyles and ornaments, and thus from that argument they increased excellent varieties in their works. Likewise there are other stories of the same kind, of which architects should keep a knowledge.

passages.latin: Philosophia vero perficit architectum animo magno et uti non sit adrogans, sed potius facilis, aequus et fidelis, sine avaritia; quod est maximum. Nullum enim opus vere sine fide et castitate fieri potest. Ne sit cupidus neque in muneribus accipiendis habeat animum occupatum, sed cum gravitate suam tueatur dignitatem bonam famam habendo. Et haec enim philosophia praescribit.
passages.translation: Philosophy gives the architect breadth of mind and teaches him to be neither arrogant nor greedy, but approachable, fair and trustworthy. Above all, no work can be properly carried out without good faith and integrity. He should not be covetous or preoccupied with accepting gifts, but should uphold his dignity with seriousness and maintain a good reputation. These are the precepts of philosophy.

passages.latin: Musicen autem sciat oportet, uti canonicam rationem et mathematicam notam habeat, praeterea ballistarum, catapultarum scorpionum temperaturas possit recte facere. In capitulis enim dextra ac sinistra sunt foramina hemitoniorum, per quae tenduntur suculis et vectibus e nervo torti funes, qui non praecluduntur nec praeligantur nisi sonitus ad artificis aures certos et aequales fecerint. Bracchia enim, quae in eas tentiones includuntur, cum extenduntur, aequaliter et pariter utraque plagam mittere debent. Quodsi non homotona fuerint, inpedient directam telorum missionem.
passages.translation: He must know music so that he understands harmonic and mathematical principles and can correctly adjust the tensions of ballistae, catapults and scorpions. In their frames, on the right and left, are openings for the hemitonia, through which twisted sinew cords are tensioned by winches and levers. These are not secured until they produce clear and equal sounds to the craftsman’s ear. The two arms inserted into these torsion bundles must deliver their impulse equally when drawn back; if they are not tuned alike, they will prevent a straight discharge of the missiles.

passages.latin: Item theatris vasa aerea, quae in cellis sub gradibus mathematica ratione conlocantur, sonitûm ex discrimine, quae Graeci ἠχεῖα appellant, ad symphonias musicas sive concentus componuntur, divisa in circinatione diatessaron et diapente et diapason ad disdiapason, uti vox scaenici sonitu conveniens in dispositionibus tactu cum offenderit, aucta cum incremento clarior et suavior ad spectatorum perveniat aures. Hydraulicas quoque machinas et cetera quae sunt similia his organis sine musicis rationibus efficere nemo poterit.
passages.translation: Likewise, in theaters bronze vessels, which the Greeks call echea, are placed in niches beneath the seating according to mathematical principles and tuned to musical intervals. Arranged around the theater according to fourths, fifths, octaves and double octaves, they receive the actor’s voice and reinforce it by resonance, so that it reaches the spectators’ ears more clearly and pleasantly. Hydraulic organs and other similar instruments likewise cannot be constructed without knowledge of musical principles.

passages.latin: Disciplinam vero medicinae novisse oportet propter inclinationem caeli, quae Graeci κλίματα dicunt, et aeris et locorum qui sunt salubres aut pestilentes, aquarumque usus. Sine his enim rationibus nulla salubris habitatio fieri potest. Iura quoque nota habeat oportet ea quae necessaria sunt aedificiis ⟨locis⟩ communibus parietum ad ambitum stillicidiorum et cloacarum luminum, item aquarum ductiones. Et cetera quae eiusmodi sunt nota oportet sint architectis, uti ante caveant quam instituant aedificia, ne controversiae factis operibus patribus familiarum relinquantur, et ut legibus scribendis prudentia cavere possit et locatori et conductori. Namque si lex perite fuerit scripta, erit ut sine captione uterque ab utroque liberetur.
passages.translation: The architect must also know medicine, because of the inclinations of the sky, which the Greeks call klimata, the qualities of the air, the healthfulness or unhealthfulness of places and the uses of water. Without this knowledge no healthy dwelling can be built. He must understand the legal provisions needed for buildings: party walls, boundaries, rainwater runoff, drains, rights of light and water supply. Architects must know these matters before construction begins, so that disputes are not left to householders after the work is complete and so that carefully drafted contracts protect both parties. If a contract is expertly drawn up, each can discharge his obligations to the other without deception or prejudice.

passages.latin: Cum ergo tanta haec disciplina sit condecorata et abundans eruditionibus variis ac pluribus, non puto posse ⟨se⟩ iuste repente profiteri architectos nisi qui ab aetate puerili his gradibus disciplinarum scandendo, scientia plerarumque litterarum et artium nutriti pervenerint ad summum templum architecturae.
passages.translation: Since this discipline is enriched by so many different branches of learning, I do not think anyone can rightly profess to be an architect without having climbed the steps of those disciplines from childhood, nourished by knowledge of letters and arts, until reaching the highest sanctuary of architecture.

passages.latin: At fortasse mirum videbitur inperitis, hominis posse naturam tantum numerum doctrinarum perdiscere et memoria continere. Cum autem animadverterint omnes disciplinas inter se coniunctionem rerum et communicationem habere, fieri posse faciliter credent. Encyclios enim disciplina uti corpus unum ex his membris est composita. Itaque qui a teneris aetatibus eruditionibus variis instruuntur, omnibus litteris agnoscunt easdem notas communicationemque omnium disciplinarum, et ea re facilius omnia cognoscunt. Ideoque de veteribus architectis Pytheos, qui Prieni aedem Minervae nobiliter est architectatus, ait in suis commentariis architectum omnibus artibus et doctrinis plus oportere posse facere quam qui singulas res suis industriis et exercitationibus ad summam claritatem perduxerunt. Id autem re non expeditur.
passages.translation: Those unfamiliar with the subject may find it surprising that a person can learn so many disciplines thoroughly and retain them in memory. Once they recognize that the disciplines are connected and share their subject matter, however, they will readily believe it possible. Encyclopedic education is composed of these members as a single body. Those instructed in varied learning from an early age therefore recognize the same characteristics throughout the branches of knowledge and the connections among them, and so learn more easily. Thus Pytheus, one of the ancient architects, who designed the celebrated temple of Minerva at Priene, states in his commentaries that an architect ought to be able to accomplish more in all the arts and disciplines than those who have brought a single field to the highest distinction through their own diligence and practice. This, however, cannot be achieved in reality.

passages.latin: Non enim debet nec potest esse architectus grammaticus uti fuerat Aristarchus, sed non agrammatus, nec musicus ut Aristoxenus, sed non amusos, nec pictor ut Apelles, sed graphidos non inperitus, nec plastes quemadmodum Myron seu Polyclitus, sed rationis plasticae non ignarus, nec denuo medicus ut Hippocrates, sed non aniatrologetus, nec in ceteris doctrinis singulariter excellens, sed in îs non inperitus. Non enim in tantis rerum varietatibus elegantias singulares quisquam consequi potest, quod earum ratiocinationes cognoscere et percipere vix cadit in potestatem.
passages.translation: The architect neither needs nor is able to be a grammarian like Aristarchus, but he must not be illiterate; nor a musician like Aristoxenus, but he must not be ignorant of music; nor a painter like Apelles, but he must not be unskilled in drawing; nor a sculptor like Myron or Polyclitus, but he must know the principles of sculpture; nor a physician like Hippocrates, but he must not be ignorant of medicine. In the other disciplines too, he need not excel individually, but must have some knowledge of them. No one can attain exceptional refinement in such a variety of subjects, since even understanding and grasping their theoretical principles is scarcely within human capacity.

passages.latin: Nec tamen non tantum architecti non possunt in omnibus rebus habere summum effectum, sed etiam ipsi qui privatim proprietates tenent artium non efficiunt ut habeant omnes summum laudis principatum. Ergo si in singulis doctrinis singuli artifices neque omnes sed pauci aevo perpetuo nobilitatem vix sunt consecuti, quemadmodum potest architectus, qui pluribus artibus debet esse peritus, non id ipsum mirum et magnum facere ne quid ex his indigeat, sed etiam ut omnes artifices superet qui singulis doctrinis adsiduitatem cum industria summa praestiterunt.
passages.translation: Not only are architects unable to achieve the highest accomplishment in every field; even specialists in individual arts do not all attain the highest distinction. If, in each discipline, only a few practitioners have scarcely won lasting renown, how can an architect, who must be skilled in many arts, be expected to surpass all the specialists who have devoted their utmost diligence and sustained effort to a single subject? Is it not already a remarkable achievement that he should lack none of the knowledge he needs?

passages.latin: Igitur in hac re Pytheos errasse videtur quod non animadvertit ex duabus rebus singulas artes esse compositas, ex opere et eius ratiocinatione. Ex his autem unum proprium esse eorum qui singulis rebus sunt exercitati, id est operis effectus, alterum commune cum omnibus doctis, id est rationem, uti medicis et musicis et de venarum rythmo et pedum [motus], at si vulnus mederi aut aegrum eripere de periculo oportuerit, non accedet musicus, sed id opus proprium erit medici. Item in organo non medicus sed musicus modulabitur, ut aures suavem cantionibus recipiant iucunditatem.
passages.translation: Therefore, in this matter Pythius seems to have erred because he did not observe that the individual arts are composed of two things, from work and its reasoning. Of these, however, one is proper to those who are trained in each thing, that is, the effect of the work, the other is common to all learned men, that is, reasoning, as is the case with physicians and musicians concerning the rhythm of the veins and the movement of the foot. But if it is necessary to heal a wound or rescue a patient from danger, the musician will not come, but that will be the proper work of the physician. Likewise, the organ will be played not by the physician but by the musician, so that the ears may receive pleasure from the songs.

passages.latin: Similiter cum astrologis et musicis est disputatio communis de sympathia stellarum et symphoniarum in quadratis et trigonis diatessaron et diapente, a geometris [divisus] qui graece λόγος ὀπτικός appellatur, ceterisque omnibus doctrinis multae res vel omnes communes sunt dumtaxat ad disputandum. Operum vero ingressus, qui manu aut tractationibus ad elegantiam perducuntur, ipsorum sunt qui proprie una arte ad faciendum sunt instituti. Ergo satis abunde videtur fecisse qui ex singulis doctrinis partes et rationes earum mediocriter habet notas eas quae necessariae sunt ad architecturam, uti si quid de his rebus et artibus iudicare et probare opus fuerit ne deficiatur.
passages.translation: Similarly, astronomers and musicians share discussion of the correspondence between the stars and musical consonances, in squares and trines, and in the intervals of a fourth and a fifth; they share with geometers the theory of sight, which the Greeks call logos optikos. Many matters, or indeed all, are common to the disciplines at the level of theoretical discussion. The practical execution of works, however, brought to refinement by hand and skilled manipulation, belongs to those trained to practise a particular art. It is therefore amply sufficient for the architect to have a moderate knowledge of the parts and principles of each discipline that are necessary for architecture, so that he is not found wanting when required to judge and approve matters concerning them.

passages.latin: Quibus vero natura tantum tribuit sollertiae, acuminis, memoriae, ut possint geometriam, astrologiam, musicen ceterasque disciplinas penitus habere notas, praetereunt officia architectorum et efficiuntur mathematici. Itaque faciliter contra eas disciplinas disputare possunt, quod pluribus telis disciplinarum sunt armati. Hi autem inveniuntur raro, ut aliquando fuerunt Aristarchus Samius, Philolaus et Archytas Tarentini, Apollonius Pergaeus, Eratosthenes Cyrenaeus, Archimedes et Scopinas ab Syracusis, qui multas res ⟨mechanicas,⟩ organicas, gnomonicas numero naturalibusque rationibus inventas atque explicatas posteris reliquerunt.
passages.translation: Those whom nature has endowed with such skill, intellectual acuity and memory that they thoroughly master geometry, astronomy, music and the other disciplines go beyond the duties of architects and become mathematicians. They can readily discuss these disciplines, armed as they are with many intellectual weapons. Such people are rare: among them were Aristarchus of Samos, Philolaus and Archytas of Tarentum, Apollonius of Perga, Eratosthenes of Cyrene, and Archimedes and Scopinas of Syracuse. They left to posterity many mechanical and gnomonic inventions discovered and explained through calculation and the principles of nature.

passages.latin: Cum ergo talia ingenia ab naturali sollertia non passim cunctis gentibus sed paucis viris habere concedatur, officium vero architecti omnibus eruditionibus debeat esse exercitatum, et ratio propter amplitudinem rei permittat non iuxta necessitatem summas sed etiam mediocres scientias habere disciplinarum, peto, Caesar, et a te et ab îs, qui ea volumina sunt lecturi, ut, si quid parum ad regulam artis grammaticae fuerit explicatum, ignoscatur. Namque non uti summus philosophus nec rhetor disertus nec grammaticus summis rationibus artis exercitatus, sed ut architectus his litteris imbutus haec nisus sum scribere. De artis vero potestate quaeque insunt in ea ratiocinationes polliceor, uti spero, his voluminibus non modo aedificantibus sed etiam omnibus sapientibus cum maxima auctoritate me sine dubio praestaturum.
passages.translation: Since such gifts of natural ingenuity are granted only to a few people rather than to all peoples everywhere, and since an architect’s duties require training in all these branches of knowledge, the breadth of the subject reasonably permits a moderate rather than a supreme command of the disciplines needed for the work. I therefore ask you, Caesar, and those who will read these volumes to forgive anything expressed without strict observance of grammatical rules. I have attempted to write as an architect instructed in these studies, rather than as a great philosopher, an eloquent rhetorician or a grammarian thoroughly trained in the principles of the art. As for the powers of the art itself and the reasoning it involves, I undertake, as I hope, to establish my authority in these volumes beyond doubt, for the benefit of builders and of all learned readers.

passages.latin: Architectura autem constat ex ordinatione, quae graece τάξις dicitur, et ex dispositione, hanc autem Graeci διάθεσιν vocitant, et eurythmia et symmetria et decore et distributione, quae graece οἰκονομία dicitur.
passages.translation: Architecture rests upon Order (ordinatio), which the Greeks call τάξις; Arrangement (dispositio), which they term διάθεσιν; and further upon Eurythmy, Symmetry, Propriety (decor), and Economy (distributio), which in Greek is called οἰκονομία.

passages.latin: Ordinatio est modica membrorum operis commoditas separatim universeque proportionis ad symmetriam comparatio. Haec componitur ex quantitate, quae graece ποσότης dicitur. Quantitas autem est modulorum ex ipsius operis e singulisque membrorum partibus sumptio universi operis conveniens effectui. Dispositio autem est rerum apta conlocatio elegansque compositionibus effectus operis cum qualitate. Species dispositionis, quae graece dicuntur ἰδέαι, sunt hae: ichnographia, orthographia, scaenographia. Ichnographia est circini regulaeque modice continens usus, e qua capiuntur formarum in solis arearum descriptiones. Orthographia autem est erecta frontis imago modiceque picta rationibus operis futuri figura. Item scaenographia est frontis et laterum abscedentium adumbratio ad circinique centrum omnium linearum responsus. Hae nascuntur ex cogitatione et inventione. Cogitatio est cura, studii plena et industriae vigilantiaeque, effectus propositi cum voluptate. Inventio autem est quaestionum obscurarum explicatio ratioque novae rei vigore mobili reperta. Hae sunt terminationes dispositionum.
passages.translation: Order is the balanced adjustment of the individual members of the work taken separately, and, for the work as a whole, the comparison of the proportion with a view to a symmetrical result. It is composed of quantity, which in Greek is called ποσότης. Quantity, in turn, consists in taking the modules from the members of the work itself and, from the several parts of those members, producing the harmonious and fitting effect of the work as a whole. Arrangement, for its part, is the apt placement of the elements and the elegant effect of the work that results from their combinations according to its character. The kinds of arrangement, which in Greek are called ἰδέαι, are these: the ground plan (ichnographia), the elevation (orthographia), and the perspective (scaenographia). The ground plan is the measured use of compass and rule, by which the outlines of forms are set out upon the surfaces of the sites. The elevation is the upright image of the facade, drawn to scale as a figure of the work to come. Likewise, the perspective is the sketch of the facade together with its receding sides, with all the lines converging upon the center of a circle. These arise from reflection and invention. Reflection is the studious, industrious, and vigilant care devoted to the pleasurable accomplishment of a design. Invention, for its part, is the unravelling of obscure problems and the reasoned discovery of a new principle through a lively agility of mind. Such are the determinations of arrangement.

passages.latin: Eurythmia est venusta species commodusque in compositionibus membrorum aspectus. Haec efficitur cum membra operis convenientis sunt altitudinis ad latitudinem, latitudinis ad longitudinem, et ad summam omnia respondent suae symmetriae.
passages.translation: Eurythmy is a beautiful appearance and a graceful, becoming aspect in the composition of the members. This is achieved when the members of the work are of a height suited to their width, a width suited to their length, and, in sum, all correspond to their symmetry.

passages.latin: Item symmetria est ex ipsius operis membris conveniens consensus ex partibusque separatis ad universae figurae speciem ratae partis responsus. Uti in hominis corpore e cubito, pede, palmo, digito ceterisque particulis symmetros est eurythmiae qualitas, sic est in operum perfectionibus. Et primum in aedibus sacris aut e columnarum crassitudinibus aut triglypho aut etiam embatere, ballista e foramine ⟨capituli⟩, quod Graeci περίτρητον vocitant, navibus interscalmio, quae διάπηγμα dicitur, item ceterorum operum e membris invenitur symmetriarum ratiocinatio.
passages.translation: Symmetria is the fitting correspondence among the members of a work and the relationship of its separate parts, measured by a determined unit, to the appearance of the whole. Just as the human body has commensurable relations among forearm, foot, palm, finger and other members, so do completed buildings. In sacred temples the measure is taken from the diameter of a column, a triglyph or an embater; in a ballista, from the opening of its capital, which the Greeks call peritreton; in ships, from the spacing between thole-pins, called dipegma. In other works too, the system of commensurability is derived from their members.

passages.latin: Decor autem est emendatus operis aspectus probatis rebus compositi cum auctoritate. Is perficitur statione, quod graece θεματισμῷ dicitur, seu consuetudine aut natura. Statione, cum Iovi Fulguri et Caelo et Soli et Lunae aedificia sub divo hypaethraque constituentur; horum enim deorum et species et effectus in aperto mundo atque lucenti praesentes videmus. Minervae et Marti et Herculi aedes doricae fient; his enim diis propter virtutem sine deliciis aedificia constitui decet. Veneri, Florae, Proserpinae, fontium nymphis corinthio genere constitutae aptas videbuntur habere proprietates, quod his diis propter teneritatem graciliora et florida foliisque et volutis ornata opera facta augere videbuntur iustum decorem. Iunoni, Dianae, Libero Patri ceterisque diis qui eadem sunt similitudine si aedes ionicae construentur, habita erit ratio mediocritatis, quod et ab severo more doricorum et ab teneritate corinthiorum temperabitur earum institutio proprietatis.
passages.translation: Decorum, in turn, is the faultless appearance of a work composed, with authority, of approved elements. It is achieved by prescription—which in Greek is called θεματισμός, by usage, or by nature. By prescription, when temples to Jupiter the Lightning-bringer, to the Heaven, the Sun, and the Moon are erected in the open air and unroofed (hypaethral); for of these gods we behold the semblance and the active power present before us in the open and resplendent sky. The temples of Minerva, Mars, and Hercules will be made Doric, since to these gods, on account of their valour, it befits that buildings be raised without refinements. For Venus, Flora, Proserpina, the Spring (Fons), and the Water-Nymphs (Lymphae), temples built in the Corinthian manner will be seen to possess fitting qualities, since to these deities, on account of their gentleness, works that are more slender and florid—adorned with leaves and volutes—will seem to enhance their due grace. If temples are made Ionic for Juno, Diana, Father Liber, and the other gods of like nature, a due moderation will be observed, for the establishment of their character will temper both the severe manner of the Doric and the delicacy of the Corinthian.

passages.latin: Ad consuetudinem autem decor sic exprimitur, cum aedificiis interioribus magnificis item vestibula convenientia et elegantia erunt facta. Si enim interiora prospectus habuerint elegantes, aditus autem humiles et inhonestos, non erunt cum decore. Item si doricis epistyliis in coronis denticuli sculpentur aut in pulvinatis columnis ex ionicis epistyliis [capitulis] exprimentur triglyphi, translatis ex alia ratione proprietatibus in aliud genus operis offendetur aspectus, aliis ante ordinis consuetudinibus institutus.
passages.translation: Propriety according to custom is achieved when magnificent interiors are accompanied by fitting and elegant vestibules. If the interiors offer elegant views but the entrances are low and undistinguished, the building will lack propriety. Likewise, if dentils are carved in the cornices of Doric entablatures, or triglyphs are introduced into Ionic entablatures with cushion-capital columns, the transfer of features from one system to another kind of work will offend the eye, because the established conventions of the orders are different.

passages.latin: Naturalis autem decor sic erit, si primum omnibus templis saluberrimae regiones aquarumque fontes in îs locis idonei eligentur in quibus fana constituantur, deinde maxime Aesculapio, Saluti, ut eorum deorum quorum plurimi medicinis aegri curari videntur. Cum enim ex pestilenti in salubrem locum corpora aegra translata fuerint et e fontibus salubribus aquarum usus subministrabuntur, celerius convalescent. Ita efficietur uti ex natura loci maiores auctasque cum dignitate divinitas excipiat opiniones. Item naturae decor erit, si cubiculis et bybliothecis ab oriente lumina capiuntur, balneis et hibernaculis ab occidente hiberno, pinacothecis et quibus certis luminibus opus est partibus a septentrione, quod ea caeli regio neque exclaratur neque obscuratur solis cursu sed est certa inmutabilis die perpetuo.
passages.translation: Propriety according to nature is achieved, first, by choosing the healthiest regions and suitable springs of water for the places where sanctuaries are established, especially those of Aesculapius and Salus, through whose healing arts many sick people appear to recover. When the sick are transferred from an unhealthy place to a healthy one and supplied with water from wholesome springs, they recover more quickly. The nature of the place thus enhances the deity’s reputation and dignity. Natural propriety also requires bedrooms and libraries to receive light from the east, baths and winter rooms from the winter sunset, and picture galleries and rooms needing steady light from the north, since that quarter is neither brightened nor darkened by the sun’s course but remains constant throughout the day.

passages.latin: Distributio autem est copiarum locique commoda dispensatio parcaque in operibus sumptus ratione temperatio. Haec ita observabitur, si primum architectus ea non quaeret, quae non poterunt inveniri aut parari nisi magno. Namque non omnibus locis harenae fossiciae nec caementorum nec abietis nec sappinorum nec marmoris copia est, sed aliud alio loco nascitur, quorum comportationes difficiles sunt et sumptuosae. Utendum autem est, ubi non est harena fossicia, fluviatica aut marina lota; inopiae quoque abietis aut sappinorum vitabuntur utendo cupresso, populo, ulmo, pinu; reliquaque his similiter erunt explicanda.
passages.translation: Distributio is the suitable allocation of materials and ground and the prudent, economical control of expenditure. It is observed when the architect does not seek materials that can be obtained only with great difficulty. Pit sand, rubble stone, fir, sappinus timber and marble are not abundant everywhere: different materials occur in different places, and their transport can be difficult and costly. Where pit sand is unavailable, river sand or washed sea sand should be used. A shortage of fir or sappinus can be met by using cypress, poplar, elm, pine and other similar timbers.

passages.latin: Alter gradus erit distributionis, cum ad usum patrum familiarum et ad pecuniae copiam aut ad eloquentiae dignitatem aedificia apte disponentur. Namque aliter urbanas domos oportere constitui videtur, aliter quibus ex possessionibus rusticis influunt fructus, non item feneratoribus, aliter beatis et delicatis, potentibus vero, quorum cogitationibus respublica gubernatur, ad usum conlocabuntur; et omnino faciendae sunt aptae omnibus personis aedificiorum distributiones.
passages.translation: A second aspect of distributio concerns arranging buildings to suit the needs of householders, their financial resources and the standing associated with eloquence. Town houses call for one arrangement, the houses of those who receive produce from rural estates for another; moneylenders require another, the wealthy and refined another, and those whose deliberations govern the commonwealth another. The arrangement of buildings must, in every case, suit the people for whom they are intended.

passages.latin: Partes ipsius architecturae sunt tres: aedificatio, gnomonice, machinatio. Aedificatio autem divisa est bipertito, e quibus una est moenium et communium operum in publicis locis conlocatio, altera est privatorum aedificiorum explicatio. Publicorum autem distributiones sunt tres, e quibus est una defensionis, altera religionis, tertia opportunitatis. Defensionis est murorum turriumque et portarum ratio ad hostium impetus perpetuo repellendos excogitata; religionis deorum inmortalium fanorum aediumque sacrarum conlocatio; opportunitatis communium locorum ad usum publicum dispositio, uti portus, fora, porticus, balinea, theatra, ambulationes ceteraque quae isdem rationibus in publicis locis designantur.
passages.translation: The parts of architecture proper are three: construction, the making of sundials, and mechanics. Construction, in turn, is divided into two branches: the first is the laying-out of city walls and of works for common use in public places, the second the raising of private buildings. Public works admit of three classes: the first concerns defense, the second religion, and the third convenience. To defense belongs the design of walls, towers, and gates, devised to repel the assaults of enemies in perpetuity; to religion, the placing of shrines and sacred temples to the immortal gods; to convenience, the provision of common spaces for public use—such as harbors, fora, colonnades, baths, theaters, promenades, and the other works laid out on the same principles in public places.

passages.latin: Haec autem ita fieri debent, ut habeatur ratio firmitatis, utilitatis, venustatis. Firmitatis erit habita ratio, cum fuerit fundamentorum ad solidum depressio, quaque e materia, copiarum sine avaritia diligens electio; utilitatis autem, ⟨cum fuerit⟩ emendata et sine inpeditione usus locorum dispositio et ad regiones sui cuiusque generis apta et commoda distributio; venustatis vero, cum fuerit operis species grata et elegans membrorumque commensus iustas habeat symmetriarum ratiocinationes.
passages.translation: These constructions must be achieved in such a way that solidity (firmitas), utility (utilitas), and beauty (venustas) are taken into account. Solidity will have been considered when the excavation of the foundations is deepened to firm ground (solidum) and when a diligent selection of materials is made from among those available, without sparing any expense (sine avaritia); utility, when the arrangement of the spaces is impeccable and presents no impediments to their use, and when the distribution of each type of building is suitable, comfortable, and properly oriented to its region; and beauty, when the appearance of the work is pleasing and elegant, and when the proportion of the members maintains a just calculation of symmetries (symmetriarum ratiocinationes).

passages.latin: In ipsis vero moenibus ea erunt principia. Primum electio loci saluberrimi. Is autem erit excelsus et non nebulosus, non pruinosus regionesque caeli spectans neque aestuosas neque frigidas sed temperatas, deinde si vitabitur palustris vicinitas. Cum enim aurae matutinae cum sole oriente ad oppidum pervenient et his ortae nebulae adiungentur spiritusque bestiarum palustrium venenatos cum nebula mixtos in habitatorum corpora flatu spargent, efficient locum pestilentem. Item si secundum mare erunt moenia spectabuntque ad meridiem aut occidentem non erunt salubria, quod per aestatem caelum meridianum sole exoriente calescit, meridie ardet, item quod spectat ad occidentem, sole exorto tepescit, meridie calet, vespere fervet.
passages.translation: But for the city walls themselves the governing principles will be these. First comes the choice of a thoroughly healthy site: one that is elevated, free from mist and frost, facing quarters of the sky that are neither sweltering nor cold but temperate, and, further, removed from the neighborhood of marshes. For when the morning breezes reach the town at sunrise, bringing with them the mists that have gathered and, mingled with those mists, the poisonous exhalations of the marsh creatures, and scatter them by their breath into the bodies of the inhabitants, they render the place pestilential. Likewise, walls set along the coast and facing south or west will be unhealthy; for in summer the southern sky grows warm at sunrise and burns at midday, while a westward aspect grows warm at sunrise, is hot at midday, and blazes in the evening.

passages.latin: Igitur mutationibus caloris et refrigerationis corpora quae in his locis sunt vitiantur. Hoc autem licet animadvertere etiam ex îs quae non sunt animalia. In cellis enim vinariis tectis lumina nemo capit a meridie nec ab occidente sed a septentrione, quod ea regio nullo tempore mutationes recipit sed est firma perpetuo et inmutabilis. Ideo etiam ea granaria quae ad solis cursum spectant bonitatem cito mutant, obsoniaque et poma quae non in ea parte caeli ponuntur quae est aversa a solis cursu, non diu servantur.
passages.translation: Therefore, the bodies that are in these places are spoiled by changes in heat and cooling. This may be observed even from those that are not animals. For in roofed wine cellars no one receives light from the south or from the west, but from the north, because that region at no time receives changes, but is permanently fixed and unchangeable. Therefore also those granaries that look towards the course of the sun quickly change their quality, and food and fruits that are not placed in that part of the sky that is turned away from the course of the sun are not preserved for long.

passages.latin: Nam semper calor cum excoquit e rebus firmitatem et vaporibus fervidis eripit exsugendo naturales virtutes, dissolvit eas et fervore mollescentes efficit inbecillas. Ut etiam in ferro animadvertimus, quod quamvis natura sit durum, in fornacibus ab ignis vapore percalefactum ita mollescit uti in omne genus formae faciliter fabricetur, et idem cum molle et candens refrigeretur, tinctum frigida redurescit et restituitur in antiquam proprietatem.
passages.translation: For heat bakes the moisture out of all things and, snatching it away in rising vapors, deprives them of their natural strength; it dissolves them and, melting them by its warmth, renders them weak and soft. As we also observe in iron, that although it is hard by nature, when heated in furnaces by the vapors of fire it softens so much that it can be easily fashioned into every kind of form, and the same thing, when cooled while soft and red-hot, hardens when cold and is restored to its former properties.

passages.latin: Licet etiam considerare haec ita esse ex eo quod aestate non solum in pestilentibus locis sed etiam in salubribus omnia corpora calore fiant inbecilla, et per hiemem etiam quae pestilentissimae sint regiones efficiantur salubres. Ideo quod a refrigerationibus solidantur. non minus etiam quae ab frigidis regionibus corpora traducuntur in calidas, non possunt durare sed dissolvuntur, quae autem ex calidis locis sub septentrionum regiones frigidas, non modo non laborant inmutatione loci valetudinibus sed etiam confirmantur.
passages.translation: It is also possible to consider that this is so from the fact that in summer, not only in pestilent places but also in healthy ones, all bodies become weak from the heat, and during winter even the most pestilent regions become healthy. For this reason, when bodies are transferred from cold to warm ones, they cannot last but are dissolved, but those which come from warm places to cold regions of the north, not only do not suffer from the change of place, but are even strengthened.

passages.latin: Quare cavendum esse videtur in moenibus conlocandis ab îs regionibus quae caloribus flatus ad corpora hominum possunt spargere. Namque e principiis, quae Graeci στοιχεῖα appellant, ut omnia corpora sunt composita, id est e calore et umore, terreno et aere, et ita mixtionibus naturali temperatura figurantur omnium animalium in mundo generatim qualitates.
passages.translation: Therefore, it seems that one must be careful in placing walls away from those regions that can spread hot winds to human bodies. For just as all bodies are composed of the principles that the Greeks call stoicheia, that is, of heat and moisture, of earth and air, so the qualities of all animals in the world are generally formed by natural mixtures of temperature.

passages.latin: ergo in quibus ⟨vis⟩ corporibus cum exsuperat e principiis calor, tunc interficit dissolvitque cetera fervore. haec autem vitia efficit fervidum ab certis partibus caelum, cum insidit in apertas venas plus quam patitur e mixtionibus naturali temperatura corpus. item si umor occupavit corporum venas inparesque eas fecit, cetera principia liquido corrupta diluuntur et dissolvuntur compositionibus virtutes. item haec e refrigerationibus umoris ventorum et aurarum infunduntur vitia corporibus. non minus aeris etiamque terreni in corpore naturalis compositio augendo aut minuendo infirmat cetera principia, terrena cibi plenitate, aer gravitate caeli.
passages.translation: In any body where heat predominates over the other principles, its excessive warmth destroys and dissolves them. An overheated climate produces these defects when it enters the open veins beyond what the body’s natural balance can bear. If moisture fills the veins in excess, the other principles are weakened as though diluted, and the strength of their composition is dissolved. Cold moisture in winds and breezes likewise introduces these disorders. An increase or decrease in the natural proportions of air and earth also weakens the other principles: the earthy element through excessive food, and the airy element through the oppressive condition of the atmosphere.

passages.latin: Sed si qui voluerit diligentius haec sensu percipere, animadvertat attendatque naturas avium et piscium et terrestrium animalium, et ita considerabit discrimina temperaturae. Aliam enim mixtionem habet genus avium, aliam piscium, longe aliter terrestrium natura. Volucres minus habent terreni, minus umoris, caloris temperate, aeris multum. Igitur levioribus principiis compositae facilius in aeris impetum nituntur. Aquatiles autem piscium naturae quod temperatae sunt a calido plurimumque ex aeris et terreni ⟨principiis⟩ sunt compositae sed umoris habent oppido quam paulum, quo minus habent e principiis umoris in corpore, facilius in umore perdurant, itaque cum ad terram perducuntur, animam cum aqua relinquunt. Item terrestria quod e principiis ab aere caloreque sunt temperata minusque habent terreni plurimumque umoris, quod abundant umidae partes, non diu possunt in aqua vitam tueri.
passages.translation: But if anyone wishes to perceive these things more carefully with his senses, let him observe and pay attention to the natures of birds and fish and terrestrial animals, and thus he will consider the differences in elemental composition. For the genus of birds has one mixture, that of fish another, and the nature of terrestrial animals is very different. Birds have less of the earth, less of the moisture, and temperate heat, and much of the air. Therefore, being composed of lighter principles, they more easily rely on the force of the air. But the aquatic natures of fish, because they are temperate from the heat and are composed of both air and earth, but have little moisture, because they have less of the moisture principles in their bodies, they more easily persist in moisture, and therefore when they are brought to land, they yield up their vital breath with the water. Likewise, terrestrial animals, because they are temperate from the principles of air and heat, have less of the earth and much of the moisture, because their moist parts abound, cannot long maintain life in water.

passages.latin: Ergo si haec ita videntur quemadmodum proposuimus, et e principiis animalium corpora composita sensu percipimus et e superationibus aut defectionibus ea laborare dissolvique iudicamus, non dubitamus quin diligentius quaeri oporteat uti temperatissimas caeli regiones eligamus, cum quaerenda fuerit in moenium conlocationibus salubritas.
passages.translation: Therefore, if these things appear as we have proposed, and we judge that they suffer and are dissolved from excesses or defects, we do not doubt that it is necessary to seek more carefully how to choose the most temperate regions of the sky, since healthiness must be sought in the placement of walls.

passages.latin: Itaque etiam atque etiam veterem revocandam censeo rationem. Maiores enim pecoribus immolatis, quae pascebantur in îs locis, quibus aut oppida aut castra stativa constituebantur, inspiciebant iocinera, et si erant livida et vitiosa primo, alia immolabant dubitantes, utrum morbo an pabuli vitio laesa essent. Cum pluribus experti erant et probaverant integram et solidam naturam iocinerum ex aqua et pabulo, ibi constituebant munitiones; si autem vitiosa inveniebant, iudicio transferebant item humanis corporibus pestilentem futuram nascentem in his locis aquae cibique copiam, et ita transmigrabant et mutabant regiones quaerentes omnibus rebus salubritatem.
passages.translation: Again and again I think the old reason should be recalled. For the ancients examined the livers of the sacrificed cattle which were grazing in those places where towns or permanent camps were established, and if they were livid and defective at first, they sacrificed others, doubting whether they were damaged by disease or by the defect of the fodder. When they had tried many and had proved the intact and solid nature of the livers from water and fodder, they established fortifications there; but if they found them defective, they transferred the judgment to human bodies, and the future abundance of water and food growing in these places would be pestilent, and so they migrated and changed regions, seeking health in all things.

passages.latin: Hoc autem fieri, uti pabulo ciboque salubres proprietates terrae videantur, licet animadvertere et cognoscere ex agris Cretensium, qui sunt circa Pothereum flumen, quod est Cretae inter duas civitates Gnoson et Gortynam. Dextra enim et sinistra eius fluminis pascuntur pecora; sed ex his quae pascuntur proxime Gnoson si * * * quae autem ex altera parte proxime Gortynam, non habent apparentem splenem. Unde etiam medici quaerentes de ea re invenerunt in his locis herbam, quam pecora rodendo inminuerunt lienes. Ita eam herbam colligendo curant lienosos hoc medicamento, quod etiam Cretenses ἄσπληνον vocitant. Ex eo licet scire cibo atque aqua proprietates locorum naturaliter pestilentes aut salubres esse.
passages.translation: The properties of the land as revealed through fodder and food may be observed in the Cretan fields around the river Pothereus, between Knossos and Gortyna. Cattle graze on both banks. Those near Knossos […] whereas those on the other side near Gortyna have no visible spleen. Investigating this, physicians found a local plant whose consumption by the cattle reduced their spleens. They therefore collected it to treat patients with diseases of the spleen; the Cretans call the remedy asplenon (ἄσπληνον). Food and water thus reveal whether a place’s natural properties are healthy or unhealthy.

passages.latin: Item si in paludibus moenia constituta erunt, quae paludes secundum mare fuerint, spectabuntque ad septentrionem aut inter septentrionem et orientem, eaeque paludes excelsiores fuerint quam litus marinum, ratione videbuntur esse constituta. Fossis enim ductis fit aquae exitus ad litus, et mare tempestatibus actum in paludes redundantia motionibus concitata marisque mixtionibus non patitur bestiarum palustrium genera ibi nasci, quaeque de superioribus locis natando proxime litus perveniunt, inconsueta salsitudine necantur. Exemplar autem huius rei Gallicae paludes possunt esse quae circum ⟨cingunt⟩ Altinum, Ravennam, Aquileiam aliaque quae in eiusmodi locis municipia sunt proxima paludibus, quod his rationibus habent incredibilem salubritatem.
passages.translation: Likewise, if walls are built in marshes, which marshes are next to the sea, and face north or between north and east, and those marshes are higher than the seashore, they will seem to have been built for a reason. For by digging ditches, the water is brought to the shore, and the sea, increased by storms, overflowing into the marshes, agitated by the movements and mixtures of the sea, does not allow the kinds of marsh animals to be born there, and those that swim from higher places to reach the shore are killed by the unusual salinity. An example of this can be the marshes of Gaul which are around Altinus, Ravenna, Aquileia and others which are in such places towns close to the marshes, because for these reasons they have an incredible salubrious effect.

passages.latin: Quibus autem insidentes sunt paludes et non habent exitus profluentes neque per flumina neque per fossas, uti Pomptinae, stando putescunt et umores graves et pestilentes in îs locis emittunt. Item in Apulia oppidum Salpia vetus, quod Diomedes ab Troia rediens constituit sive quemadmodum nonnulli scripserunt Elpias Rhodius, in eiusmodi locis fuerat conlocatum, ex quo incolae quotannis aegrotando laborantes aliquando pervenerunt ad M. Hostilium ab eoque publice petentes impetraverunt ut is idoneum locum ad moenia transferenda conquireret eligeretque. Tunc is moratus non est, sed statim rationibus doctissime quaesitis secundum mare mercatus est possessionem loco salubri ab senatuque populoque Romano petît ut liceret transferre oppidum, constituitque moenia et areas divisit nummoque sestertio singulis municipibus mancipio dedit. His confectis lacum aperuit in mare et portum e lacu municipio perfecit. Itaque nunc Salpini quattuor milia passus progressi ab oppido veteri habitant in salubri loco.
passages.translation: Marshes that remain stagnant and have no outlet through rivers or ditches, such as the Pontine Marshes, become putrid and emit heavy, unhealthy vapors. Old Salpia in Apulia, founded by Diomedes on his return from Troy or, according to other writers, by Elpias of Rhodes, stood in such a place. Its inhabitants, afflicted by illness every year, eventually appealed to Marcus Hostilius and obtained his agreement to seek a suitable site for moving the town. He acted without delay: after careful investigation he purchased land in a healthy place by the sea, obtained permission from the Roman Senate and people, built the walls, divided the building plots and conveyed each plot to a citizen for one sestertius. He then opened the lake to the sea and made it a harbour for the town. The people of Salpia now live in a healthy place, four Roman miles from the old town.

passages.latin: Cum ergo his rationibus erit salubritatis moenium conlocandorum explicatio regiones[que] electae fuerint fructibus ad alendam civitatem copiosae et viarum munitiones aut opportunitates fluminum seu per portus marinae subvectionis habuerit ad moenia comportationes expeditas, tunc turrium murorumque fundamenta sic sunt facienda uti fodiantur, si queat inveniri, ad solidum et in solido, quantum ex amplitudine operis pro ratione videatur, crassitudine ampliore quam parietum qui supra terram sunt futuri, et ea impleantur quam solidissima structura.
passages.translation: When, therefore, the healthiness of the site for the walls has been secured on these principles, and a region has been chosen abounding in produce to feed the city, and the road network—or the advantage of a river, or the access of a sea-port—has provided ready means of transport to the walls, then the foundations of the towers and walls are to be laid in the following manner. Let them be dug down, if firm ground can be reached, to solid bottom and set within the solid, to a depth proportionate to the scale of the work, and made of a greater thickness than the walls that are to rise above the ground; and let the trenches be filled with the most solid masonry that can be laid.

passages.latin: Item turres sunt proiciendae in exteriorem partem, uti cum ad murum hostis impetu velit adpropinquare, a turribus dextra ac sinistra lateribus apertis telis vulnerentur. Curandumque maxime videtur ut non facilis aditus sit ad oppugnandum murum, sed ita circumdandum ad loca praecipitia et excogitandum uti portarum itinera non sint directa sed scaeva. Namque cum ita factum fuerit, tum dextrum latus accedentibus quod scuto non erit tectum proximum erit muro. Conlocanda autem oppida sunt non quadrata nec procurrentibus angulis sed circinationibus, uti hostis ex pluribus locis conspiciatur. In quibus enim anguli procurrunt, difficiliter defenditur, quod angulus magis hostem tuetur quam civem.
passages.translation: Likewise, the towers must be projected beyond the outer face of the wall, so that when an enemy seeks to press an assault against it, he may be wounded by missiles from the towers on his right and left, his flanks lying exposed. Above all, care must be taken that there be no easy approach for storming the wall; rather, the ground about the towers should be so disposed that the way to the gates runs not straight but obliquely, bearing to the left. For when this is done, the right side of those advancing—the side not covered by the shield—will lie nearest the wall. Towns ought to be laid out not as a square, nor with projecting angles, but in a rounded circuit, so that the enemy may be observed from several points; for where angles project, defense is difficult, since the angle shields the enemy rather than the townsman.

passages.latin: Crassitudinem autem muri ita faciendam censeo uti armati homines supra obviam venientes alius alium sine inpeditione praeterire possint. dum in crassitudine perpetuae taleae oleagineae ustilatae quam creberrime instruantur, uti utraeque muri frontes inter se, quemadmodum fibulis, his taleis conligatae aeternam habeant firmitatem. Namque ei materiae nec caries nec tempestates nec vetustas potest nocere, sed ea et in terra obruta et in aqua conlocata permanet sine vitiis utilis sempiterno. Itaque non solum in muro sed etiam in substructionibus quique parietes murali crassitudine erunt faciundi hac ratione religati non cito vitiabuntur.
passages.translation: I hold that the thickness of the wall should be such that armed men meeting upon it can pass one another without hindrance; and within that thickness let continuous tie-beams of charred olive-wood be set as closely as possible, so that the two faces of the wall, bound together by these beams as if by clamps, may possess lasting strength. For no decay, no tempest, and no lapse of time can harm that material; rather, whether buried in the earth or set in water, it endures sound and serviceable for ever. And so, not only in the walls but also in the substructures, and in any partitions built to the thickness of a wall, whatever is bound together in this manner will not soon fall into decay.

passages.latin: Intervalla autem turrium ita sunt facienda ut ne longius sit alia ab alia sagittae missionis, uti si qua oppugnetur, tum a turribus quae erunt dextra sinistra scorpionibus reliquisque telorum missionibus hostes reiciantur. Etiamque contra interiores ⟨partes⟩ turrium dividendus est murus intervallis tam magnis quam erunt turres, ut itinera sint interioribus partibus turrium contignata, neque ea ferro fixa. Hostis enim si quam partem muri occupaverit, qui repugnabunt rescindent et si celeriter administraverint, non patientur reliquas partes turrium murique hostem penetrare, nisi se voluerit praecipitare.
passages.translation: The intervals between the towers should be so arranged that no one tower stands further from the next than a bowshot, so that if any point is besieged, the enemy may be driven off by scorpions and other missiles from the towers to right and left. Opposite the lower part of the towers the wall should likewise be interrupted by gaps as wide as the towers themselves, and the passages across these gaps, within the towers, should be floored with timber that is not fastened with iron. For should the enemy seize any part of the wall, the defenders will cut away these timbers; and if they act quickly, they will not suffer the enemy to penetrate the remaining towers and stretches of wall—unless he is willing to fling himself headlong.

passages.latin: Turres itaque rotundae aut polygonoe sunt faciendae. Quadratas enim machinae celerius dissipant, quod angulos arietes tundendo frangunt; in rotundationibus autem, uti cuneos ad centrum adigendo, laedere non possunt. Item munitiones muri turriumque aggeribus coniunctae maxime sunt tutiores, quod neque arietes neque suffossiones neque machinae ceterae eis valent nocere.
passages.translation: The towers, therefore, should be built round or polygonal; for siege-engines dismantle square towers the more readily, since the rams shatter the corners by their battering, whereas in rounded forms, driving the stones towards the center as if with wedges, they can do no harm. Likewise, fortifications of wall and towers joined with earthworks are by far the safest, since neither rams nor mining nor the other engines have power to injure them.

passages.latin: Sed non in omnibus locis est aggeris ratio facienda, nisi quibus extra murum ex alto loco plano pede accessus fuerit ad moenia oppugnanda. Itaque in eiusmodi locis primum fossae sunt faciendae latitudinibus et altitudinibus quam amplissimis, deinde fundamentum muri deprimendum est infra alveum fossae et id extruendum est ea crassitudine ut opus terrenum facile sustineatur.
passages.translation: A rampart, however, need not be raised in every place, but only where, outside the wall, there is level approach from higher ground for an assault upon it. In such places, first let ditches be dug as broad and deep as possible; then let the foundation of the wall be sunk within the bed of the ditch and built of such a thickness that it may readily bear the weight of the earthwork.

passages.latin: Item interiore parte substructionis fundamentum distans ab exteriore introrsus amplo spatio, ita uti cohortes possint quemadmodum in acie instructae ad defendendum supra latitudinem aggeris consistere. Cum autem fundamenta ita distantia inter se fuerint constituta, tunc inter ea alia transversa, coniuncta exteriori et interiori fundamento, pectinatim disposita, quemadmodum serrae dentes solent esse, conlocentur. Cum enim sic erit factum, tunc ita oneris terreni magnitudo distributa in parvas partes neque universa pondere premens ⟨non⟩ poterit ulla ratione extrudere muri substructiones.
passages.translation: On the inner side of the substructure, likewise, let a further foundation be laid at a generous distance from the outer, so that cohorts may take their stand upon the breadth of the rampart, drawn up as if in line of battle to defend it. And when the two foundations have been set thus apart, let other foundations be laid between them, joining the outer to the inner and arranged comb-wise, after the manner of the teeth of a saw. For when this is done, the great mass of earth, distributed into small portions and no longer bearing down with its whole weight, will by no means be able to thrust out the substructures of the wall.

passages.latin: De ipso autem muro e qua materia struatur aut perficiatur, ideo non est praefiniendum, quod in omnibus locis quas optamus copias, eas non possumus habere. Sed ubi sunt saxa quadrata sive silex seu caementum aut coctus later sive crudus, his erit utendum. Non enim uti Babylone abundantes liquido bitumine pro calce et harena ex cocto latere factum habent murum, sic item possunt omnes regiones seu locorum proprietates habere tantas eiusdem generis utilitates, uti ex his comparationibus ad aeternitatem perfectus habeatur sine vitio murus.
passages.translation: As to the material of which the wall is to be built or finished, no fixed rule can be laid down, since we cannot everywhere command the resources we should wish. But wherever there are squared stones, or flint, or rubble, or fired or unfired brick, these are to be used. For not every region or locality can possess advantages of the same kind in such measure as Babylon, which, abounding in liquid bitumen in place of lime and sand, has its wall built of fired brick; yet from such resources as each affords, a wall may be made faultless and enduring for all time.

passages.latin: Moenibus circumdatis sequuntur intra murum arearum divisiones platearumque et angiportûm ad caeli regionem directiones. Dirigentur haec autem recte, si exclusi erunt ex angiportis venti prudenter. Qui si frigidi sunt, laedunt; si calidi, vitiant; si umidi, nocent. Quare vitandum videtur hoc vitium et avertendum ne fiat quod in multis civitatibus usu solet venire. Quemadmodum in insula Lesbo oppidum Mytilenae magnificenter est aedificatum et eleganter, sed positum non prudenter. In qua civitate Auster cum flat, homines aegrotant; cum Corus, tussiunt; cum Septentrio, restituuntur in salubritatem, sed in angiportis et plateis non possunt consistere propter vehementiam frigoris.
passages.translation: Once the walls have been built, there follow, within them, the apportionment of the building plots and the laying-out of the streets and lanes according to the quarters of the sky. These will be rightly directed if the winds are prudently excluded from the lanes; for if they are cold they are hurtful, if hot they enervate, if damp they are noxious. This fault, then, must be avoided, and care taken lest there befall what commonly happens in many cities. At Mytilene, for instance, in the island of Lesbos, the town is built with magnificence and elegance, but sited without prudence: in that city, when the south wind blows the people fall ill; when the north-west wind blows they cough; and when the north wind blows they are restored to health, yet cannot linger in the lanes and streets because of the sharpness of the cold.

passages.latin: Ventus autem est aeris fluens unda cum certa motus redundantia. Nascitur, cum fervor offendit umorem et impetus spiritus factionis exprimit vim flatus. Id autem verum esse ex aeolis aereis licet aspicere et de latentibus caeli rationibus artificiosis rerum inventionibus divinitatis exprimere veritatem. Fiunt enim aeoli pilae aereae cavae, — hae habent punctum angustissimum—quae aqua infunduntur conlocanturque ad ignem; et antequam calescant, non habent ullum spiritum, simul autem ut fervere coeperint, efficiunt ad ignem vehementem flatum. Ita scire et iudicare licet e parvo brevissimoque spectaculo de magnis et inmanibus caeli ventorumque naturae rationibus.
passages.translation: Wind is a flowing wave of air with a certain excess of motion. It arises when heat meets moisture and the impulse generated in producing breath forces out the power of the blast. This can be observed in bronze aeolipiles, through ingenious devices that reveal the truth of the hidden workings of the heavens. Hollow bronze spheres are made with a very narrow opening, filled with water and set beside a fire. Before they grow hot they give off no breath; as soon as they begin to boil, they produce a violent blast towards the fire. From a small and very brief demonstration, one may thus learn and judge the great and immense principles governing the heavens and the nature of the winds.

passages.latin: ⟨Venti autem si ex habitationibus⟩ exclusi fuerint, non solum efficient corporibus valentibus locum salubrem, sed etiam si qui morbi ex aliis vitiis forte nascentur, qui in ceteris ⟨minus⟩ salubribus locis habent curationes medicinae contrariae, in his propter exclusiones ventorum temperatura expeditius curabuntur. Vitia autem sunt, quae difficulter curantur in regionibus, quae sunt supra scriptae, haec: gravitudo arteriace, tussis, pleuritis, pthisis, sanguinis eiectio et cetera, quae non detractionibus sed adiectionibus curantur. Haec ideo difficulter medicantur, primum quod ex frigoribus concipiuntur, deinde quod defatigatis morbo viribus eorum aer agitatus est ⟨molestus; namque ubi⟩ ventorum agitationibus extenuatur, a vitiosis corporibus detrahit sucum et efficit ea exiliora. Contra vero lenis et crassus aer, qui perflatus non habet neque crebras redundantias, propter inmotam stabilitatem adiciendo ad membra eorum alit eos et reficit, qui in his sunt inpliciti morbis.
passages.translation: If the winds are excluded from dwellings, they will not only make the place healthy for sound bodies; should diseases happen to arise from other causes, which in other, less healthy places require contrary medical treatment, they will be cured more readily here through the temperate conditions produced by excluding the winds. The ailments difficult to cure in the regions described above are heaviness of the windpipe, cough, pleurisy, consumption, the spitting of blood, and the others treated by additions rather than subtractions. They are difficult to treat first because they arise from cold, and then because moving air troubles those whose strength has been exhausted by disease: where the air is thinned by the agitation of the winds, it draws moisture from diseased bodies and makes them more wasted. Mild, dense air, by contrast, free from draughts and frequent surges, by its unmoving stability nourishes and restores the limbs of those afflicted by these diseases.

passages.latin: Nonnullis placuit esse ventos quattuor: ab oriente aequinoctiali Solanum, a meridie Austrum, ab occidente aequinoctiali Favonium, ab septentrionali Septentrionem. Sed qui diligentius perquisierunt tradiderunt eos esse octo, maxime quidem Andronicus Cyrrestes, qui etiam exemplum conlocavit Athenis turrem marmoream octagonon et in singulis lateribus octagoni singulorum ventorum imagines excalptas contra suos cuiusque flatus designavit, supraque eam turrim metam marmoream perfecit et insuper Tritonem aereum conlocavit dextra manu virgam porrigentem, et ita est machinatus uti vento circumageretur et semper contra flatum consisteret supraque imaginem flantis venti indicem virgam teneret.
passages.translation: Archaeological note — Bk. 1.6 (the winds and the Tower of the Winds). The layout of the city, Vitruvius says, must orient the streets by the winds: along the lines dividing the eight winds —Solanus (E), Auster (S), Favonius (W), Septentrio (N) and, at the corners, Eurus (SE), Africus (SW), Caurus or Corus (NW), and Aquilo (NE)— so that no street channels the wind against the houses. Against those who counted only four winds, Vitruvius praises those who recognized eight, and cites as a living witness Andronicus of Cyrrhus, who raised at Athens an octagonal marble tower with a figure of each wind on its face and, at the apex, a bronze Triton turning to point to the quarter from which the wind blew. This is the Tower of the Winds (Horologion) in the Roman Agora of Athens (c. 50 BCE), of Pentelic marble, with nine sundials and a water-clock within: one of the very few buildings of classical antiquity to survive almost intact —and one that links this chapter to the gnomonics of Book IX.

passages.latin: Itaque sunt conlocati inter Solanum et Austrum ab oriente hiberno Eurus, inter Austrum et Favonium ab occidente hiberno Africus, inter Favonium et Septentrionem Caurus, quem plures vocant Corum, inter Septentrionem et Solanum Aquilo. Hoc modo videtur esse expressum uti pateat numerus et nomina et partes unde flatus certi ventorum spirent. Quod cum ita exploratum habeatur, ut inveniantur regiones et ortus eorum sic erit ratiocinandum.
passages.translation: Thus Eurus lies between Solanus and Auster, blowing from the winter sunrise; Africus lies between Auster and Favonius, from the winter sunset; Caurus, which many call Corus, lies between Favonius and Septentrio; and Aquilo lies between Septentrio and Solanus. This defines the number and names of the winds and the quarters from which they blow. With that established, the following method will determine their directions and points of origin.

passages.latin: Conlocetur ad libellam marmoreum amusium mediis moenibus, aut locus ita expoliatur ad regulam et libellam ut amusium non desideretur, supraque eius loci centrum medium conlocetur aeneus gnomon indagator umbrae, qui graece σκιαθήρας dicitur. Huius antemeridiana circiter hora quinta sumenda est extrema gnomonis umbra et puncto signanda, deinde circino diducto ad punctum quod est gnomonis umbrae longitudinis signum, ex eoque a centro circumagenda linea rotundationis. Itemque observanda postmeridiana istius gnomonis crescens umbra, et cum tetigerit circinationis lineam et fecerit parem antemeridianae umbrae postmeridianam, signanda puncto.
passages.translation: Let a marble plane be set level in the center of the city, or let the ground be smoothed with a straightedge and level so that a marble plane is unnecessary. Place a bronze gnomon, a shadow-tracer, at its center. At about the fifth hour of the morning mark the tip of the gnomon’s shadow. With the compasses opened from the center to that mark, describe a circle. Then observe the growing shadow in the afternoon; when it touches the circle and equals the length of the morning shadow, mark that point as well.

passages.latin: Ex his duobus signis circino decusatim describendum, et per decusationem et medium centrum linea perducenda ad extremum, ut habeatur meridiana et septentrionalis regio. Tum postea sumenda est sexta decima pars circinationis lineae totius rotundationis, centrumque conlocandum in meridiana linea qua tangit circinationem, et signandum dextra ac sinistra in circinatione et meridiana et septentrionali parte. Tunc ex signis his quattuor per centrum medium decusatim lineae ab extremis ad extremas circinationes perducendae. Ita Austri et Septentrionis habebitur octavae partis designatio. Reliquae partes dextra ac sinistra tres et tres aequales his distribuendae sunt in tota rotundatione, ut aequales divisiones octo ventorum designatae sint in descriptione. Tum per angulos inter duas ventorum regiones et platearum et angiportorum videntur deberi dirigi descriptiones.
passages.translation: From the two shadow-marks draw intersecting arcs with the compasses. Through their intersection and the center draw a line to the circumference, establishing south and north. Take one-sixteenth of the entire circumference and, with the compasses centered where the meridian meets it, mark that distance on either side at both the southern and northern ends. From the four marks draw intersecting lines through the center from one side of the circle to the other. This defines one-eighth of the circle for Auster and one-eighth for Septentrio. Divide the remaining regions into three equal sectors on either side, completing the eight wind divisions. The lines of streets and lanes should run along the angles between two wind regions.

passages.latin: His enim rationibus et ea divisione exclusa erit ex habitationibus et vicis ventorum vis molesta. Cum enim plateae contra directos ventos erunt conformatae, ex aperto caeli spatio impetus ac flatus frequens conclusus in faucibus angiportorum vehementioribus viribus pervagabitur. Quas ob res convertendae sunt ab regionibus ventorum directiones vicorum, uti advenientes ad angulos insularum frangantur repulsique dissipentur.
passages.translation: These principles and this division keep the troublesome force of the winds out of dwellings and streets. When streets face directly into the winds, the gusts from the open sky are confined in the narrow mouths of the lanes and pass through with greater force. The directions of the streets must therefore be turned away from the wind regions, so that incoming currents strike the corners of the blocks and are broken, repelled and dispersed.

passages.latin: Fortasse mirabuntur î, qui multa ventorum nomina noverunt, quod a nobis expositi sunt tantum octo esse venti. Si autem animadverterint orbis terrae circumitionem per solis cursum et umbras gnomonis aequinoctialis ex inclinatione caeli ab Eratosthene Cyrenaeo rationibus mathematicis et geometricis methodis esse inventam ducentorum quinquaginta duûm milium stadiûm, quae fiunt passus trecenties et decies quinquies centena milia, huius autem octava pars, quam ventus tenere videtur, est triciens nongenta triginta septem milia et passus quingenti, non debebunt mirari, si in tam magno spatio unus ventus vagando inclinationibus et recessionibus varietates mutatione flatus faciat.
passages.translation: Perhaps those acquainted with many names of winds will be surprised that we have set down only eight. But if they observe that the circuit of the earth's globe, by the course of the sun, the shadows of the equinoctial gnomon, and the inclination of the heavens, was found by Eratosthenes of Cyrene through mathematical reckoning and geometrical method to be two hundred and fifty-two thousand stadia, which make thirty-one million five hundred thousand paces, and that the eighth part of this, which a single wind appears to occupy, is three million, nine hundred and thirty-seven thousand five hundred paces. They will not be surprised that, in so vast a space of the earth, a single wind, ranging with its inclinations and retreats, gives rise to varieties and shifts of breezes.
