passages.latin: itaque dextra et sinistra austrum leuconotus et altanus flare solet, ⟨circa⟩ africum libonotus et subvesperus, circa favonium argestes et certis temporibus etesiae, ad latera cauri circius et corus, circa septentrionem thracias et gallicus, dextra ac sinistra aquilonem supernas et caecias, circa solanum carbas et certo tempore ornithiae, euri vero medias partes tenentis in extremis euricircias et volturnus. sunt autem et alia plura nomina flatusque ventorum e locis aut fluminibus aut montium procellis tracta,
passages.translation: On either side of Auster usually blow Leuconotus and Altanus; on either side of Africus, Libonotus and Subvesperus; around Favonius, Argestes and, at certain seasons, the Etesiae; beside Caurus, Circias and Corus; around Septentrio, Thracias and Gallicus; beside Aquilo, Supernas and Caecias; around Solanus, Carbas and, at a particular season, the Ornithiae; and on the outer sides of Eurus, Eurocircias and Volturnus. Many other names and winds also derive from places, rivers or mountain storms.

passages.latin: Praeterea aurae matutinae, qua sol cum emergit de subterranea parte versando pulsat aeris umorem et impetu scandendo praeurens exprimit aurarum antelucano impetu flatus. Qui cum exorto sole permanserunt, Euri venti tenent partes, et ea re quod ex auris procreatur, ab Graecis εὖρος videtur esse appellatus, crastinusque dies propter auras matutinas αὔριον fertur esse vocitatus. Sunt autem nonnulli qui negant Eratosthenem potuisse veram mensuram orbis terrae colligere. Quae sive est certa sive non vera, non potest nostra scriptura non veras habere terminationes regionum unde spiritus ventorum oriuntur.
passages.translation: Moreover, there are the morning breezes; for the sun, as it emerges from beneath the earth, strikes the moisture of the air in its turning and, rising with force, draws out the breath of the dawning breezes. Those that linger on after the sun has risen belong to the quarter of Eurus; and because this wind is begotten of the breezes (aurae), it seems to have taken from the Greeks the name Euros, and the morrow likewise is called aurion from these same morning breezes. Now there are some who deny that Eratosthenes could have arrived at a true measure of the earth's circumference. Yet whether his reckoning be exact or not, our treatise cannot fail to set down the true bounds of the regions from which the winds arise.

passages.latin: Ergo si ita est, tantum erit uti non certam mensurae rationem, sed aut maiores impetus aut minores habeant singuli venti. Quoniam haec a nobis sunt breviter exposita, ut facilius intellegatur, visum est mihi in extremo volumine formas, sive uti Graeci dicunt, σχήματα duo explicare: unum ita deformatum ut appareat unde certi ventorum spiritus oriantur, alterum quemadmodum ab impetu eorum aversis directionibus vicorum et platearum evitentur nocentes flatus. Erit autem in exaequata planitie centrum ubi est littera A, gnomonis autem antemeridiana umbra ubi est B; et a centro ubi est A, diducto circino ad id signum umbrae ubi est B, circumagatur linea rotundationis. Reposito autem gnomone ubi antea fuerat, expectanda est dum decrescat faciatque iterum crescendo parem antemeridianae umbrae postmeridianam tangatque lineam rotundationis ubi erit littera C. Tunc a signo ubi est B et a signo ubi est C, circino decusatim describatur ubi erit D; deinde per decusationem et centrum ubi est A perducatur linea ad extremum, in qua linea erunt litterae E et F. Haec linea erit index meridianae et septentrionalis regionis.
passages.translation: If, then, this is so, the only difference will be that each several wind has a force now greater, now less, while the method of measurement itself remains fixed. Since these matters have been briefly set forth by us, I have thought it well, that they may be the more easily understood, to append at the end of this book two figures—or, as the Greeks call them, schemata: the one drawn so as to show plainly from which quarters the several winds arise; the other, how their harmful blasts may be turned aside by setting the lines of the streets and quarters away from their force. The procedure is as follows. On a leveled surface let the center be marked with the letter A, and the tip of the gnomon's morning shadow with the letter B; then, opening the compasses from the center A to the shadow-mark B, describe the line of the circumference. Setting the gnomon back in its former place, one must wait until the shadow shortens and then lengthens again, until the afternoon shadow equals the morning shadow and touches the circumference at the point that shall be the letter C. Then from the marks B and C, with the compasses, strike two arcs crossing at the point that shall be D; and through the intersection D and the center let a line be carried to the circumference, upon which line shall be the letters E and F. This line will be the indicator of the southern and northern quarters.

passages.latin: Tunc circino totius rotundationis sumenda est pars XVI, circinique centrum ponendum est in meridiana linea, qua tangit rotundationem, ubi est littera E, et signandum dextra sinistra, ubi erunt litterae G H. Item in septentrionali parte centrum circini ponendum in rotundationis et septentrionali linea, ubi est littera F, et signandum dextra ac sinistra, ubi sunt litterae I et K, et ab G ad K et ab H ad I per centrum lineae perducendae. Ita quod erit spatium ab G ad H, erit spatium venti austri et partis meridianae; item quod erit spatium ab I ad K, erit septentrionis. Reliquae partes dextra ter ac sinistra ter dividendae sunt aequaliter, quae sunt ad orientem, in quibus litterae L M, et ab occidente, in quibus sunt litterae N et O. Ab M ad O et ab L ad N perducendae sunt lineae decusatim. Et ita erunt aequaliter ventorum octo spatia in circumitione. Quae cum ita descripta erunt, in singulis angulis octagoni, cum a meridie incipiemus, inter eurum et austrum in angulo erit littera G, inter austrum et africum H, inter africum et favonium N, inter favonium et caurum O, inter caurum et septentrionem K, inter septentrionem et aquilonem I, inter aquilonem et solanum L, inter solanum et eurum M. Ita his confectis inter angulos octagoni gnomon ponatur, et ita dirigantur angiportorum divisiones.
passages.translation: Next, a sixteenth part of the whole circumference is to be taken with the compasses. Setting the compass-point on the meridian line where it meets the circle at the southern end, marked with the letter E, make two marks to right and left, where the letters G and H shall be placed; likewise, at the northern end, marked with the letter F, set the compass-point and make marks to right and left, where the letters I and K shall fall; then draw lines through the center, from G to K and from H to I. Thus the space from G to H will be the sector of the South wind (Auster) and the meridian quarter, and the space from I to K that of the North wind (Septentrio). The remaining parts—three on the right and three on the left—are to be divided equally: to the east, where the letters L and M stand; and to the west, where the letters N and O stand. From M to O and from L to N let lines be drawn through the center. Thus there will be eight equal spaces for the winds around the circumference. When the diagram is so drawn, the angles of the octagon, beginning from the south, will be these: the letter G at the angle between Eurus and Auster; H between Auster and Africus; N between Africus and Favonius; O between Favonius and Caurus; K between Caurus and Septentrio; I between Septentrio and Aquilo; L between Aquilo and Solanus; and M between Solanus and Eurus. When these are completed, a chord is set between the angles of the octagon, and so the divisions of the lanes and streets are directed.

passages.latin: Divisis angiportis et plateis constitutis arearum electio ad opportunitatem et usum communem civitatis est explicanda aedibus sacris, foro reliquisque locis communibus. Et si erunt moenia secundum mare, area ubi forum constituatur eligenda proxime portum, sin autem mediterraneo, in oppido medio. Aedibus vero sacris, quorum deorum maxime in tutela civitas videtur esse, et Iovi et Iunoni et Minervae in excelsissimo loco unde moenium maxima pars conspiciatur areae distribuantur. Mercurio autem in foro, aut etiam ut Isidi et Serapi in emporio, Apollini Patrique Libero secundum theatrum, Herculi in quibus civitatibus non sunt gymnasia neque amphitheatra ad circum, Marti extra urbem sed ad campum, itemque Veneri ad portum. Id autem etiam Etruscis haruspicibus disciplinarum scripturis ita est dedicatum: extra murum Veneris, Volcani, Martis fana ideo conlocari uti non insuescat in urbe adulescentibus seu matribus familiarum veneria libido, Volcanique vi e moenibus religionibus et sacrificiis evocata ab timore incendiorum aedificia videantur liberari. Martis vero divinitas cum sit extra moenia dedicata, non erit inter cives armigera dissensio, sed ab hostibus ea defensa belli periculo conservabit.
passages.translation: Once the lanes and streets have been laid out, sites must be chosen for sacred temples, the forum and other public places, with regard to the city’s convenience and common use. In a coastal town the forum should be near the harbour; in an inland town, at its center. Temples of the gods under whose special protection the city stands, such as Jupiter, Juno and Minerva, should occupy the highest place, from which most of the walls can be seen. Mercury’s temple belongs in the forum or trading center, as do those of Isis and Serapis; Apollo’s and Father Liber’s near the theater; Hercules’s near the circus in towns without gymnasia or amphitheatres; Mars’s outside the city beside the exercise ground; and Venus’s likewise near the harbour. Etruscan haruspical writings prescribe that the shrines of Venus, Vulcan and Mars stand outside the walls, so that erotic passion does not become habitual among the young and the matrons, and so that Vulcan’s power, summoned beyond the walls through rites and sacrifices, appears to free buildings from fear of fire. Mars’s divinity, consecrated outside the walls, is to prevent armed discord among the citizens and defend the city from its enemies.

passages.latin: Item Cereri extra urbem loco, quo ⟨non quolibet⟩ nomine semper homines nisi per sacrificium necesse habeant adire; cum religione, caste sanctisque moribus is locus debet tueri. Ceterisque diis ad sacrificiorum rationes aptae templis areae sunt distribuendae. De ipsis autem aedibus sacris faciundis et de earum symmetriis in tertio et quarto volumine reddam rationes, quia in secundo visum est mihi primum de materiae copiis, quae in aedificiis sunt parandae, quibus sint virtutibus et quem habeant usum, exponere, ⟨deinde⟩ commensus aedificiorum et ordines et genera singula symmetriarum peragere et in singulis voluminibus explicare.
passages.translation: Likewise, Ceres is to have a site outside the city, in a place to which people need not go for any ordinary reason, but only for sacrifice. That place must be maintained with religion, chastity and holy customs. Suitable sites for the temples of the other gods are to be assigned according to the requirements of their sacrifices. I shall explain the construction of the sacred temples themselves and their systems of symmetria in the third and fourth volumes. In the second, I have thought it appropriate first to set out the supplies of materials to be prepared for building, their qualities and their uses; afterwards I shall examine the commensurations of buildings, the orders and each type of symmetria, explaining them in their respective volumes.

passages.latin: Dinocrates architectus cogitationibus et sollertia fretus, cum Alexander rerum potiretur, profectus est e Macedonia ad exercitum regiae cupidus commendationis. Is e patria a propinquis et amicis tulit ad primos ordines et purpuratos litteras ut aditus haberet faciliores, ab eisque exceptus humane petît uti quamprimum ad Alexandrum perduceretur. Cum polliciti essent, tardiores fuerunt idoneum tempus expectantes. Itaque Dinocrates ab his se existimans ludi ab se petît praesidium. Fuerat enim amplissima statura, facie grata, forma dignitateque summa. His igitur naturae muneribus confisus vestimenta posuit in hospitio et oleo corpus perunxit caputque coronavit populea fronde, laevum umerum pelle leonina texit, dextraque clavam tenens incessit contra tribunal regis ius dicentis.
passages.translation: Dinocrates the architect, trusting in his ideas and ingenuity, left Macedonia for the army while Alexander was in power, eager to win the king’s favor. He brought letters from relatives and friends at home to the leading officers and courtiers, hoping to gain easier access. They received him kindly, and he asked to be brought before Alexander as soon as possible. Although they promised to do so, they delayed while waiting for a suitable occasion. Thinking that they were making a fool of him, Dinocrates sought a resource within himself. He was very tall, with a pleasing face and an impressive, dignified physique. Trusting in these natural gifts, he left his clothes at the inn, anointed his body with oil, crowned his head with poplar leaves, draped a lion’s skin over his left shoulder and, holding a club in his right hand, advanced towards the tribunal where the king was administering justice.

passages.latin: Novitas populum cum avertisset, conspexit eum Alexander. Admirans ei iussit locum dari ut accederet, interrogavitque quis esset. At ille: «Dinocrates», inquit, «architectus Macedo, qui ad te cogitationes et formas adfero dignas tuae claritati. Namque Athon montem formavi in statuae virilis figuram, cuius manu laeva designavi civitatis amplissimae moenia, dextera pateram quae exciperet omnium fluminum quae sunt in eo monte aquam, ut inde in mare profunderetur».
passages.translation: The unusual sight drew the crowd’s attention, and Alexander saw him. Astonished, he ordered room to be made for him to approach and asked who he was. “Dinocrates,” he replied, “a Macedonian architect, bringing you ideas and designs worthy of your glory. I have designed Mount Athos in the form of a male statue: in its left hand I have represented the walls of a very large city, and in its right a patera, a ritual bowl, to receive the water of all the mountain’s rivers and pour it into the sea.

passages.latin: Delectatus Alexander ratione formae statim quaesiit, si essent agri circa qui possent frumentaria ratione eam civitatem tueri. Cum invenisset non posse nisi transmarinis subvectionibus, «Dinocrates», inquit, «attendo egregiam formae compositionem et ea delector, sed animadverto si qui deduxerit eo loci coloniam fore ut iudicium eius vituperetur. Ut enim natus infans sine nutricis lacte non potest ali neque ad vitae crescentis gradus perduci, sic civitas sine agris et eorum fructibus in moenibus affluentibus non potest crescere nec sine abundantia cibi frequentiam habere populumque sine copia tueri. Itaque quemadmodum formationem puto probandam, sic iudico locum inprobandum, teque volo esse mecum, quod tua opera sum usurus».
passages.translation: Delighted by the account of the design, Alexander immediately asked whether there was farmland nearby capable of supplying the city with grain. Learning that it could be sustained only by supplies brought from overseas, he said: “Dinocrates, I appreciate the excellence of your design and take pleasure in it, but anyone who founded a colony there would, I see, be criticized for his judgment. Just as a newborn child cannot be nourished without its nurse’s milk or develop through the stages of growing life, so a city cannot grow without farmland and its produce flowing into its walls, maintain a numerous population without abundant food, or sustain its people without supplies. I therefore approve the design but reject the site. Nevertheless, I want you to remain with me, for I shall make use of your services.

passages.latin: Ex eo Dinocrates ab rege non discessit et in Aegyptum est eum persecutus. Ibi Alexander cum animadvertisset portum naturaliter tutum, emporium egregium, campos circa totam Aegyptum frumentarios, inmanis fluminis Nili magnas utilitates, iussit eum suo nomine civitatem Alexandriam constituere. Ita Dinocrates a facie dignitateque corporis commendatus ad eam nobilitatem pervenit. Mihi autem, imperator, staturam non tribuit natura, faciem deformavit aetas, valetudo detraxit vires. Itaque quoniam ab his praesidiis sum desertus, per auxilia scientiae scriptaque ut spero perveniam ad commendationem.
passages.translation: From then on Dinocrates did not leave the king and followed him to Egypt. There, when Alexander had observed a naturally safe harbor, an excellent emporium, corn fields around the whole of Egypt, and the great benefits of the immense river Nile, he ordered him to found the city of Alexandria in his own name. Thus Dinocrates, commended by his face and dignity of body, attained that nobility. But to me, emperor, nature has not given stature, age has disfigured my face, and illness has sapped my strength. Therefore, since I am deserted by these protections, I hope to attain commendation through the aids of science and writings.

passages.latin: Cum autem ⟨quae⟩ primo volumine de officio architecturae terminationibusque artis perscripsi, item de moenibus et intra moenia arearum divisionibus, insequatur ordo de aedibus sacris et publicis aedificiis itemque privatis quibus proportionibus et symmetriis debeant esse uti explicentur, non putavi ante ponendum nisi prius de materiae copiis, e quibus conlatis aedificia structuris et materiationibus perficiuntur, quas habeant in usu virtutes exposuissem quibusque rerum natura e principiis essent temperatae dixissem. Sed antequam naturales res incipiam explicare, de aedificiorum rationibus unde initia ceperint et uti creverint eorum inventiones ante ponam, et insequar ingressus eorum, qui antiquitates rerum naturae et initia humanitatis et inventiones perquisitas scriptorum praeceptis dedicaverunt. Itaque quemadmodum ab his sum institutus exponam.
passages.translation: In the first book I described the architect’s duties and the boundaries of the art, as well as city walls and the division of building plots within them. The next subject in order would be the proportions and commensurabilities required for sacred, public and private buildings. Before that, however, I thought it necessary to explain the properties in use of the materials assembled to complete buildings in masonry and timber, and the natural principles of which those materials are composed. Before discussing their nature, I shall first describe the beginnings of building and the development of its inventions. I shall follow those writers who investigated the early history of nature, the beginnings of human society and its inventions, and committed their precepts to writing. I shall explain these matters as I have learned them from those authors.

passages.latin: Homines vetere more ut ferae in silvis et speluncis et nemoribus nascebantur ciboque agresti vescendo vitam exigebant. Interea quodam in loco ab tempestatibus et ventis densae crebritatibus arbores agitatae et inter se terentes ramos ignem excitaverunt, et eius flamma vehementi perterriti qui circa eum locum fuerunt sunt fugati. postea re quieta propius accedentes cum animadvertissent commoditatem esse magnam corporibus ignis teporem, ligna adicientes et îs conservantes alios adducebant et nutu monstrantes ostendebant quas haberent ex eo utilitates. In eo hominum congressu cum profundebantur aliter ⟨atque aliter⟩ e spiritu voces, cotidiana consuetudine vocabula ut obtigerant constituerunt, deinde significando res saepius in usu ex eventu fari fortuito coeperunt et ita sermones inter se procreaverunt.
passages.translation: In the earliest ages of the world, men were born like the wild beasts in forests, caves, and groves, and passed their lives feeding upon wild fare. Meanwhile, in a certain place, trees densely crowded and tossed by storms and winds, and rubbing their branches one against another, kindled fire; and those who were about that place, terrified by the fierce flame, were put to flight. Afterwards, when it had grown quiet, drawing nearer they perceived that the warmth of the fire was of great comfort to their bodies; and, adding wood and so keeping it alive, they brought others to it, and by signs made plain what advantages they had from it. In that gathering of men, as their voices were uttered in differing ways with the breath, they established by daily use words as chance had brought them; then, signifying the things in more frequent use, they came by chance to speak, and thus speech was born among them.

passages.latin: Ergo cum propter ignis inventionem conventus initio apud homines et concilium et convictus esset natus, et in unum locum plures convenirent habentes ab natura praemium praeter reliqua animalia ut non proni sed erecti ambularent mundique et astrorum magnificentiam aspicerent, item manibus et articulis quam vellent rem faciliter tractarent, coeperunt in eo coetu alii de fronde facere tecta, alii speluncas fodere sub montibus, nonnulli hirundinum nidos et aedificationes earum imitantes de luto et virgulis facere loca quae subirent. Tunc observantes aliena tecta et adicientes suis cogitationibus res novas, efficiebant in dies meliora genera casarum.
passages.translation: The discovery of fire thus first gave rise to gatherings, deliberation and communal life, and brought more people together in one place. Nature had given them an advantage over the other animals: they walked upright rather than bent towards the ground, could contemplate the magnificence of the world and stars, and could handle whatever they wished with their hands and fingers. In that gathering some began to make shelters from foliage, others to dig caves beneath hills, and others, imitating swallows and their nests, to build places of mud and twigs in which to shelter. By observing one another’s dwellings and adding new ideas of their own, they made better kinds of huts each day.

passages.latin: Cum essent autem homines imitabili docilique natura, cotidie inventionibus gloriantes alius alii ostendebant aedificiorum effectus, et ita exercentes ingenia certationibus in dies melioribus iudiciis efficiebantur. Primumque furcis erectis et virgulis interpositis luto parietes texerunt. Alii luteas glaebas arefacientes struebant parietes, materia eos iugumentantes, vitandoque imbres et aestus tegebant harundinibus et fronde. Posteaquam per hibernas tempestates tecta non potuerunt imbres sustinere, fastigia facientes, luto inducto proclinatis tectis stillicidia deducebant.
passages.translation: But since they were of an imitative and teachable nature, daily glorying in their inventions, they pointed out to one another the results of their building; and thus, sharpening their wits in rivalry, they grew day by day of sounder judgment. At first, with forked stakes set up and twigs laid between, they wove their walls with mud. Others built walls of lumps of dried clay, binding them together with timber, and, to keep off the rains and the heat, they covered them with reeds and leaves. Afterwards, when the roofs could not withstand the rains through the winter storms, they made gables, and, overlaying them with mud, carried off the drippings by the sloping roofs.

passages.latin: Haec autem ex îs, quae supra scriptae sunt, originibus instituta esse possumus sic animadvertere, quod ad hunc diem nationibus exteris ex his rebus aedificia constituuntur, uti Gallia, Hispania, Lusitania, Aquitania, scandulis robusteis aut stramentis. Apud nationem Colchorum in Ponto, propter silvarum abundantiam, arboribus perpetuis planis dextra ac sinistra in terra positis, spatio inter eas relicto quanto arborum longitudines patiuntur, conlocantur in extremis partibus earum supra alterae transversae, quae circumcludunt medium spatium habitationis. Tum insuper alternis trabibus ex quattuor partibus angulos iugumentantes et ita parietes arboribus statuentes ad perpendiculum imarum educunt ad altitudinem turres, intervallaque, quae relinquuntur propter crassitudinem materiae, schidiis et luto obstruunt. Item tecta, recidentes ad extremos ⟨angulos⟩ transtra, traiciunt gradatim contrahentes, et ita ex quattuor partibus ad altitudinem educunt medio metas, quas fronde et luto tegentes efficiunt barbarico more testudinata turrium tecta.
passages.translation: From what has been said above we may see that these things were originally established as has been described, since to this day the buildings of foreign nations are made of such materials: in Gaul, Spain, Lusitania, and Aquitaine, roofed with oak shingles or with thatch. Among the Colchians in Pontus, where forests abound, whole trees are laid flat upon the ground to right and to left, a space being left between them as wide as the length of the trees allows; and upon the outer ends of these, others are laid across, so enclosing the dwelling-space within. Then, binding together the four corners with beams laid alternately, and raising the walls of tree-trunks set plumb above the lower ones, they carry up towers to a height; and the gaps that are left, by reason of the thickness of the timber, they stop with chips and mud. The roofs, drawing in by degrees from the extreme angles, they raise pyramid-fashion; and these they cover with foliage and mud, thus fashioning, after the barbarian manner, the testudinate (covered) roofs of their towers.

passages.latin: Phryges vero, qui campestribus locis sunt habitantes, propter inopiam silvarum egentes materiae, eligunt tumulos naturales eosque medios fossura detegentes et itinera perfodientes dilatant spatia, quantum natura loci patitur. Insuper autem stipites inter se religantes metas efficiunt, quas harundinibus et sarmentis tegentes exaggerant supra habitationes e terra maximos grumos. Ita hiemes calidissimas, aestates frigidissimas efficiunt tectorum rationes. Nonnulli ex ulva palustri componunt tuguria tecta. Apud ceteras quoque gentes ex cannula pari similique ratione casarum perficiuntur constitutiones. Non minus etiam Massiliae animadvertere possumus sine tegulis, subacta cum paleis terra, tecta. Athenis Areopagi antiquitatis exemplar ad hoc tempus luto tectum; item in Capitolio commonefacere potest et significare mores vetustatis Romuli casa et in arce sacrorum stramentis tecta.
passages.translation: The Phrygians, who dwell in the plains and, for want of timber through the scarcity of forests, choose natural hillocks; these they cleave down the middle with trenches, hollow out passages, and enlarge the space within as far as the nature of the site allows. Over them they set a framework of logs tied together, which they cover with reeds and brushwood, and heap great mounds of earth above their dwellings. Thus they make their houses very warm in winter and very cool in summer. Some build their huts of marsh sedge. Among other peoples too, and in certain places, dwellings are raised upon the same and like principles. No less may one observe at Massilia roofs without tiles, made of earth kneaded with straw. At Athens, the Areopagus, a relic of antiquity, is to this day roofed with mud; and on the Capitol, the hut of Romulus and the thatched roofs of the shrines upon the citadel can still signify and recall the customs of antiquity.

passages.latin: Ita his signis de antiquis inventionibus aedificiorum sic ea fuisse ratiocinantes possumus iudicare. Cum autem cotidie faciendo tritiores manus ad aedificandum perfecissent et sollertia ingenia exercendo per consuetudinem ad artes pervenissent, tum etiam industria in animis eorum adiecta perfecit ut qui fuerunt in his studiosiores fabros esse se profiterentur. Cum ergo haec ita fuerint primo constituta et natura non solum sensibus ornavisset gentes quemadmodum reliqua animalia, sed etiam cogitationibus et consiliis armavisset mentes et subiecisset cetera animalia sub potestate, tunc vero ex fabricationibus aedificiorum gradatim progressi ad ceteras artes et disciplinas, e fera agrestique vita ad mansuetam perduxerunt humanitatem.
passages.translation: From these tokens, then, we may judge that the building-inventions of the ancients were of this kind, and so reason concerning them. And as, by daily practice, men’s hands grew more skilled in building, and as by exercising their wits they attained through habit to the arts, then industry, added to their minds, brought it about that those who were the more diligent in such things should claim to be craftsmen. Since, therefore, these things were thus first established, and since nature had not only endowed mankind with the senses, as it had the other animals, but had also armed their minds with thought and judgment, and had set the other animals beneath their dominion, they advanced by degrees from the building of houses to the other arts and disciplines, and led humanity from a wild and rustic life to a gentler civilization.

passages.latin: Tum autem struentes animose et aevo prospicientes maioribus cogitationibus ex varietate artium natis, non casas sed etiam domos fundatas et latericiis parietibus aut e lapide structas materiaque et tegula tectas perficere coeperunt; deinde observationibus studiorum e vagantibus iudiciis et incertis ad certas symmetriarum perduxerunt rationes. Posteaquam animadverterunt profusos esse partus naturae et abundantem materiae copiam ad aedificationes ab ea comparatam, tractando nutrierunt et auctam per artes ornaverunt voluptatibus elegantiam vitae. Igitur de his rebus, quae sunt in aedificiis ad usum idoneae, quibusque sunt qualitatibus et quas habeant virtutes, ut potuero, dicam.
passages.translation: Then, schooling their minds and looking forward to greater conceptions born of the variety of the arts, they began to build, not huts, but houses with foundations, with walls of brick or stone, and roofed with timber and tiles; and next, by careful observation, they were led from wavering and uncertain notions to fixed rules of symmetry. When they perceived that nature had brought forth her materials in abundance, and had furnished a plentiful store for building, they tended these with care, and, enlarging them through the arts, adorned the elegance of life with its pleasures. I shall therefore speak, as best I can, of those things which are fit for use in building, with what properties they are endowed, and how they possess their excellences.

passages.latin: Sed si qui de ordine huius libri disputare voluerit, quod putaverit eum primum institui oportuisse, ne putet me erravisse, sic reddam rationem. Cum corpus architecturae scriberem, primo volumine putavi quibus eruditionibus et disciplinis esset ornata ⟨oportere⟩ exponere, finireque terminationibus eius species et e quibus rebus esset nata dicere. ergo in primo de artis officio itemque quid oporteat esse in architecto, ibi pronuntiavi., in hoc de naturalibus materiae rebus, quem habeant usum, disputabo. Namque hic liber non profitetur unde architectura nascatur, sed unde origines aedificiorum sunt institutae et quibus rationibus enutritae et progressae sint gradatim ad hanc finitionem.
passages.translation: But should anyone wish to dispute the order of this book, thinking that it ought to have been placed first, lest he suppose that I have erred, I will render my reason thus. When I was writing the body of architecture, I thought in the first volume to set forth with what branches of learning and disciplines it is adorned, to define its departments, and to say from what things it has sprung; and there I declared what an architect ought to be. In the first, therefore, I treat of the duty of the art; in this, of the natural properties of materials, and what use they have. For this book does not profess to show whence architecture is born, but whence the origins of building were established, and by what means they were fostered and advanced by degrees to their present condition.

passages.latin: Ergo ita suo ordine et loco huius erit voluminis constitutio. Nunc revertar ad propositum et de copiis, quae aptae sunt aedificiorum perfectionibus, quemadmodum videantur esse ab natura rerum procreatae quibusque mixtionibus principiorum congressus temperentur, ne obscura sed perspicua legentibus sint, ratiocinabor. Namque nulla materiarum genera neque corpora neque res sine principiorum coetu nasci neque subici intellectui possunt, neque aliter natura rerum praeceptis physicorum veras patitur habere explicationes, nisi causae, quae insunt in his rebus, quemadmodum et quid ita sint, subtilibus rationibus habeant demonstrationes.
passages.translation: This volume, then, will have its constitution in its own order and place. Now I shall return to my purpose and reason concerning the materials suitable for the perfecting of buildings: how they appear to have been brought forth by the nature of things, and by what minglings of their first principles their combinations are tempered; and I shall make this not obscure but clear to my readers. For no kinds of matter, no bodies, no things can come into being without a concurrence of first principles, nor be brought within the understanding; nor, otherwise, can the precepts of the physicists touching the nature of things have true explanations, unless the causes inherent in these things—how and why they are as they are—be demonstrated by subtle reasoning.

passages.latin: Thales primum aquam putavit omnium rerum esse principium. Heraclitus Ephesius, qui propter obscuritatem scriptorum a Graecis σκοτεινὸς est appellatus, ignem. Democritus, quique est eum secutus, Epicurus, atomos, quas nostri insecabilia corpora, nonnulli individua vocitaverunt. Pythagoreorum vero disciplina adiecit ad aquam et ignem aera et terrenum. Ergo Democritus, etsi non proprie res nominavit sed tantum individua corpora proposuit, ideo ea ipsa dixisse videtur, quod ea cum sint disiuncta nec laeduntur nec interitionem recipiunt nec sectionibus dividuntur, sed sempiterno aevo perpetuo infinitam retinent in se soliditatem.
passages.translation: Thales first held water to be the principle of all things. Heraclitus of Ephesus, whom the Greeks called skoteinos (σκοτεινός) because of the obscurity of his writings, held fire to be that principle. Democritus and his follower Epicurus proposed atoms, which some Latin writers call indivisible bodies and others individual particles. The Pythagorean school added air and earth to water and fire. Democritus, although he did not name the substances individually but proposed indivisible bodies, seems to have held that these bodies, being separate, cannot be damaged, destroyed or divided by cutting, but retain an inexhaustible solidity throughout eternity.

passages.latin: Ex his ergo congruentibus, cum res omnes coire nascique videantur, et hae in infinitis generibus rerum naturae sint disparatae, putavi oportere de varietatibus et discriminibus usus earum, quasque haberent in aedificiis qualitates, exponere; uti, cum fuerint notae, non habeant qui aedificare cogitant errorem, sed aptas ad usum copias aedificiis comparent.
passages.translation: Since all things appear to arise from combinations of these principles, yet occur in infinitely different forms in nature, I thought it necessary to explain the varieties of materials, the differences in their uses and their qualities in buildings. With that knowledge, those planning to build can avoid error and obtain materials suited to the work.

passages.latin: Itaque primum de lateribus, qua de terra duci eos oporteat, dicam. Non enim de harenoso neque calculoso luto neque sabulone soluto sunt ducendi, quod ex his generibus cum sint ducti primum fiunt graves, deinde cum ab imbribus in parietibus sparguntur, dilabuntur et dissolvuntur, paleaeque in his non cohaerescunt propter asperitatem. Faciendi autem sunt ex terra albida cretosa sive de rubrica aut etiam masculo sabulone. Haec enim genera propter levitatem habent firmitatem et non sunt in opere ponderosa et faciliter aggerantur.
passages.translation: I shall first discuss bricks and the earth from which they should be molded. They should not be made from sandy or gravelly clay or loose sand: bricks of these materials are heavy, break up and dissolve when rain strikes the walls, and do not bind well with straw because of their roughness. They should instead be made from whitish clayey earth, red earth or coarse, firm sand. These materials combine lightness with strength, add little weight to the work and are readily laid up.

passages.latin: Ducendi autem sunt per vernum tempus et autumnale, ut uno tenore siccescant. Qui enim per solstitium parantur, ideo vitiosi fiunt, quod summum corium sol acriter cum praecoquit, efficit ut videatur aridum, interior autem sit non siccus. Et cum postea siccescendo se contrahit, perrumpit ea quae erant arida. Ita rimosi facti efficiuntur inbecilli. Maxime autem utiliores erunt, si ante biennium fuerint ducti; namque non ante possunt penitus siccescere. Itaque cum recentes et non aridi sunt structi, tectorio inducto rigidoque obsolidate, permanente ipsi sidentes non possunt eandem altitudinem, qua est tectorium, tenere, contractioneque moti non haerent cum eo, sed ab coniunctione eius disparantur. Igitur tectoria ab structura seiuncta, propter tenuitatem per se stare non possunt, sed franguntur, ipsique parietes fortuito sidentes vitiantur. Ideo etiam Uticenses laterem, si sit aridus et ante quinquennium ductus, cum arbitrio magistratus fuerit ita probatus, tunc utuntur in parietum structuris.
passages.translation: Bricks should be molded in spring or autumn so that they dry evenly. Those made at midsummer are defective because the sun rapidly bakes their outer skin, making it appear dry while the interior remains moist. As the interior later contracts in drying, it breaks through the dry surface, leaving the bricks cracked and weak. Bricks are most useful if molded two years before use, since they cannot dry thoroughly sooner. If fresh, undried bricks are built into a wall and coated with plaster that then sets hard, the bricks continue to settle and cannot retain the plaster’s height. Their shrinkage separates them from it; the plaster, detached from the masonry and too thin to support itself, breaks, while the settling walls are also damaged. For this reason the people of Utica use bricks in walls only after they have dried for five years and have been approved by a magistrate’s inspection.

passages.latin: fiunt autem laterum genera tria. unum quod graece Lydium appellatur, id est quo nostri utuntur, longum sesquipede, latum pede. ceteris duobus Graecorum aedificia struuntur. ex his unum πεντάδωρον, alterum τετράδωρον dicitur. δῶρον autem Graeci appellant palmum, quod munerum datio graece δῶρον appellatur, id autem semper geritur per manus palmum. ita quod est quoquoversus quinque palmorum pentadoron, quod quattuor tetradoron dicitur, et quae sunt publica opera πεντάδωρον, quae privata τετράδωρον struuntur.
passages.translation: Now there are three kinds of bricks. One which is called Lydian in Greek, that is, which our people use, is a foot and a half long and a foot wide. With the other two Greek buildings are built. Of these one is called pentadoron, the other tetradoron. But the Greeks call doron a palm, because the giving of gifts is called doron in Greek, and this is always done with the palm of the hand. So that which is five palms in each direction is called pentadoron, that which is four is called tetradoron, and which are public works are built pentadoron, and which are private tetradoron.

passages.latin: fiunt autem cum his lateribus semilateria, quae cum struuntur, una parte lateribus ordines, altera semilateres ponuntur. ergo ex utraque parte ad lineam cum struuntur, alternis coriis parietes alligantur et medii lateres supra coagmenta conlocati et firmitatem et speciem faciunt utraque parte non invenustam. Est autem in Hispania ulteriore civitas Maxilua, et Callet, et in Asia Pitane, ubi lateres cum sunt ducti et arefacti, proiecti natant in aqua. natare autem eos posse ideo videtur quod terra est de qua ducuntur pumicosa. ita cum est levis, aere solidata non recipit in se nec combibit liquorem. igitur levi raraque cum sit proprietate, quocumque pondere fuerit cogitur ab rerum natura quemadmodum pumex uti ab aqua sustineatur. sic autem magnas habent utilitates, quod neque in aedificationibus sunt onerosi, et cum non patiantur penetrare in corpus umidam potestatem, a tempestatibus non dissolvuntur.
passages.translation: Half-bricks are made along with these bricks. In laying them, courses of full bricks are placed on one face and half-bricks on the other. With both faces built to the line and the courses alternating, the walls are bonded: the middle of a brick lies over the joint below, giving both strength and an attractive appearance on each face. At Maxilua and Callet in Further Spain, and at Pitane in Asia, bricks, once molded and dried, float when thrown into water. This appears to be because the earth from which they are made is pumice-like: light and consolidated with air, it neither admits nor absorbs water. Being naturally light and porous, yet resistant to moisture entering their substance, such bricks are supported by water like pumice, whatever their total weight. They have great advantages: they do not burden buildings, and storms do not dissolve them.

passages.latin: In caementiciis autem structuris primum est de harena quaerendum, ut ea sit idonea ad materiem miscendam neque habeat terram commixtam. Genera autem harenae fossiciae sunt haec: nigra, cana, rubra, carbunculus. Ex his quae in manu confricata fecerit stridorem, erit optima; quae autem terrosa fuerit, non habebit asperitatem. Item si in vestimentum candidum ea coniecta fuerit, postea excussa vel icta id non inquinarit neque ibi terra subsiderit, erit idonea.
passages.translation: For rubble masonry, the first requirement is sand suitable for mixing mortar and free from earth. The kinds of pit sand are black, gray, red and carbunculus. The best sand makes a gritty sound when rubbed in the hand; sand mixed with earth lacks that roughness. If sand is thrown onto a white cloth and shaken off, leaving neither a stain nor a deposit of earth, it is suitable.

passages.latin: Sin autem non erunt harenaria, unde fodiatur, tum de fluminibus aut e glarea erit excernenda, non minus etiam de litore marino. Sed ea in structuris haec habet vitia: difficulter siccescit, neque onerari se continenter paries patitur, nisi intermissionibus requiescat, neque concamerationes recipit. Marina autem hoc amplius, quod etiam parietes, cum in îs tectoria facta fuerint, remittente se salsugine eorum dissolvuntur.
passages.translation: But if there are no sand pits from which it can be dug, sand must be sifted from rivers or gravel, and likewise from the seashore. In masonry it has these defects: it dries with difficulty, the wall cannot tolerate continuous loading unless it rests at intervals, and it cannot support vaults. Sea sand has the further disadvantage that walls, after they have been plastered, break down as their salinity is released.

passages.latin: fossiciae vero celeriter in structuris siccescunt, et tectoria permanent, et concamerationes patiuntur, sed eae quae sunt de harenariis recentes. si enim exemptae diutius iacent, ab sole et luna et pruina concoctae resolvuntur et fiunt terrosae. ita cum in structuram coiciuntur, non possunt continere caementa, sed ea ruunt et labuntur oneraque parietes non possunt sustinere. recentes autem fossiciae cum in structuris tantas habeant virtutes, eae in tectoriis ideo non sunt utiles quod pinguitudini eius calx commixta propter vehementiam non potest sine rimis inarescere. fluviatica vero, propter macritatem uti signinum, liaculorum subactionibus in tectorio recipit soliditatem.
passages.translation: Pit sand, by contrast, dries quickly in masonry, allows plaster to remain sound and supports vaulting, provided it is fresh from the pit. If left exposed too long, sun, moon and frost break it down and make it earthy. Used in masonry in that condition, it cannot bind the rubble: the stones fall and slip, and the walls cannot carry their loads. Although fresh pit sand has these advantages in masonry, it is unsuitable for plaster because its rich texture, mixed with lime, dries too vigorously to avoid cracking. River sand, by contrast, because of its leaner texture, acquires a firm surface in plaster under the action of polishing tools, as does signinum.

passages.latin: De harenae copiis cum habeatur explicatum, tum etiam de calce diligentia est adhibenda, uti de albo saxo aut silice coquatur; et quae erit ex spisso et duriore, erit utilis in structura, quae autem ex fistuloso, in tectoriis. Cum ea erit extincta, tunc materia ita misceatur, ut, si erit fossicia, tres harenae et una calcis infundatur; si autem fluviatica aut marina, duo harenae, una calcis coiciatur. Ita enim erit iusta ratio mixtionis temperaturae. Etiam in fluviatica aut marina si qui testam tunsam et succretam ex tertia parte adiecerit, efficiet materiae temperaturam ad usum meliorem.
passages.translation: Having explained the supplies of sand, I must also discuss lime, which should be burned from white stone or silex. Lime from dense, harder stone is useful in masonry; lime from porous stone is useful in plaster. Once the lime has been slaked, mix the mortar in these proportions: three parts sand to one part lime when pit sand is used, or two parts sand to one part lime when river or sea sand is used. These give the correct balance of the mixture. Adding one-third of crushed and sifted potsherd to river- or sea-sand mortar improves its composition for use.

passages.latin: Quare autem cum recipit aquam et harenam calx, tunc confirmat structuram, haec esse causa videtur, quod e principiis, uti cetera corpora, ita et saxa sunt temperata. Et quae plus habent aeris, sunt tenera; quae aquae, lenta sunt ab umore; quae terrae, dura; quae ignis, fragiliora. Itaque ex his saxa si, antequam coquantur, contusa minute mixta harenae in structuram coiciantur, non solidescunt nec eam poterunt continere. Cum vero coniecta in fornacem ignis vehementi fervore correpta amiserint pristinae soliditatis virtutem, tunc exustis atque exhaustis eorum viribus relinquuntur patentibus foraminibus et inanibus.
passages.translation: The reason why lime, on receiving water and sand, strengthens masonry appears to be that stones, like other bodies, are compounded from the elements. Those containing more air are soft; those containing more water are pliant through moisture; those containing more earth are hard; those containing more fire are more brittle. If such stones, before firing, are finely crushed, mixed with sand and put into masonry, they do not set and cannot hold it together. When placed in a kiln and seized by the violent heat of the fire, however, they lose the strength of their original solidity: their powers are burned out and exhausted, leaving open pores and voids.

passages.latin: (Ideo autem, quo pondere saxa coiciuntur in fornacem, cum eximuntur, non possunt ad id respondere, sed cum expenduntur, permanente ea magnitudine, excocto liquore circiter tertia parte ponderis inminuta esse inveniuntur.) Ergo liquor, qui est in eius lapidis corpore, et aer cum exustus et ereptus fuerit, habueritque in se residuum calorem latentem, prius quem ex ignis vi recepit, intinctus in aqua, umore penetrante in foraminum raritates, confervescit et ita refrigeratus reicit ex calcis corpore fervorem. Igitur cum patent foramina eorum et raritates, harenae mixtionem in se corripiunt et ita cohaerescunt siccescendoque cum caementis coeunt et efficiunt structurarum soliditatem.
passages.translation: (Thus stones cannot weigh the same when removed from the kiln as when put into it: weighed after firing, they are found to have lost approximately one-third of their weight, while retaining the same volume, because their liquid has been driven off.) Once the liquid and air in the stone have been burned out and removed, the latent heat remaining in it, previously received from the force of the fire, causes it to seethe when immersed in water, as moisture penetrates the open pores. On cooling in this way, it expels the heat from the substance of the lime. Its pores and voids, now open, take up the sand mixture and cohere; as they dry, they bind with the rubble and produce the solidity of the masonry.

passages.latin: Est etiam genus pulveris quod efficit naturaliter res admirandas. nascitur in regionibus Baianis in agris municipiorum quae sunt circa Vesuvium montem. quod commixtum cum calce et caemento non modo ceteris aedificiis praestat firmitates, sed etiam moles cum struuntur in mari, sub aqua solidescunt. hoc autem fieri hac ratione videtur quod sub his montibus et terrae ferventes sunt et fontes crebri, qui non essent, si non in imo haberent aut e sulphure aut alumine aut bitumine ardentes maximos ignes. igitur penitus ignis et flammae vapor per intervenia permanans et ardens efficit levem eam terram, et ibi quod nascitur tofus exsurgens est sine liquore. ergo cum tres res consimili ratione ignis vehementia foratae in unam pervenerint mixtionem, repente recepto liquore una cohaerescunt et celeriter umore duratae solidantur, neque eas fluctus neque vis aquae potest dissolvere.
passages.translation: There is also a kind of powder that naturally produces remarkable effects. It occurs in the region of Baiae and around the towns near Mount Vesuvius. Mixed with lime and rubble, it strengthens ordinary buildings and even causes harbour works built in the sea to harden under water. This appears to happen because beneath those mountains lie hot earth and numerous springs, which could not exist without great subterranean fires burning in sulphur, alum or bitumen. The fire and heat of the flame pass through the interstices, burning and lightening the earth; the tuff formed there is likewise free from liquid. When three substances similarly altered by intense fire are brought into one mixture and suddenly receive water, they cohere and harden rapidly through moisture, so that neither waves nor the force of water can break them down.

passages.latin: ardores autem esse in his locis etiam haec res potest indicare quod in montibus Cumanorum Baianis sunt loca sudationibus excavata, in quibus vapor fervidus ab imo nascens ignis vehementia perforat eam terram per eamque manando in his locis oritur et ita sudationum egregias efficit utilitates. non minus etiam memorantur antiquitus crevisse ardores et abundavisse sub Vesuvio monte et inde evomuisse circa agros flammam. ideoque tunc quae spongia sive pumex Pompeianus vocatur excocto ex alio genere lapidis in hanc redacta esse videtur generis qualitatem.
passages.translation: The existence of heat in these places is also shown by the chambers excavated for sweat baths in the hills of Cumae and Baiae. Hot vapor rising from below penetrates the earth through the force of fire, flows through it and emerges in the chambers, making them very effective for sweating. It is also recorded that in ancient times heat increased beneath Vesuvius and that flames spread from it over the surrounding countryside. What is called sponge-stone or Pompeian pumice therefore appears to have been transformed by burning from another kind of stone into its present character.

passages.latin: id autem genus spongiae quod inde eximitur non in omnibus locis nascitur, nisi circum Aetnam et collibus Mysiae quae a Graecis κατακεκαυμένη nominatur et si quae eiusdem modi sunt locorum proprietates. si ergo in his locis aquarum ferventes inveniuntur fontes et montibus excavatis calidi vapores, ipsaque loca ab antiquis memorantur pervagantes in agris habuisse ardores, videtur esse certum ab ignis vehementia ex tofo terraque, quemadmodum in fornacibus ex calce, ita ex his ereptum esse liquorem.
passages.translation: But that kind of sponge which is taken from there does not grow in all places, except around Etna and the hills of Mysia which the Greeks call κατακεκαυμένη and if there are any properties of the same kind in the places. Therefore if in these places boiling springs of water are found and hot vapors are found in excavated mountains, and if in the same places ancient people are mentioned as having had burnings pervading the fields, it seems certain that the liquid was extracted from the tuff and earth by the force of the fire, just as in kilns from lime, so from these.

passages.latin: igitur dissimilibus et disparibus rebus correptis et in udam potestatem conlatis, calida umoris ieiunitas aqua repente satiata latenti calore confervescit et vehementer efficit ea coire celeriterque communibus corporibus unam soliditatis percipere virtutem. Relinquetur desideratio, quoniam item sunt in Etruria ex aqua calida crebri fontes, quid ita non etiam ibi nascitur pulvis, e quo eadem ratione sub aqua structura solidescat. itaque visum est antequam desideraretur de his rebus quemadmodum esse videantur exponere.
passages.translation: When these unlike substances are brought together, their hot, moisture-starved material is suddenly supplied with water. Their latent heat causes the mixture to seethe, binds the components strongly together and quickly gives them a single, solid character. A question remains: since Etruria also has many hot springs, why does it not produce a powder that enables masonry to harden under water in the same way? I have therefore thought it appropriate to explain the matter before the question is asked.

passages.latin: omnibus locis et regionibus non eadem genera terrae nec lapides nascuntur, sed nonnulla sunt terrena, alia sabulosa itemque glareosa, aliis locis harenosa non minus materia, et omnino dissimili disparique genere in regionum varietatibus qualitates insunt in terra. maxime autem id sic licet considerare quod qua mons Appenninus regiones Italiae Etruriaeque circa cingit, prope in omnibus locis non desunt fossicia harenaria, trans Appenninum vero quae pars est ad Adriaticum mare, nulla inveniuntur, item Achaia Asia omnino trans mare nec nominantur quidem. igitur non in omnibus locis quibus effervent aquae calidae crebri fontes, eaedem opportunitates possunt similiter concurrere, sed omnia uti natura rerum constituit, non ad voluptatem hominum sed ut fortuito disparata procreantur.
passages.translation: The same kinds of soil and stone do not occur in every region. Some soils are earthy, others sandy or gravelly; elsewhere there are sand and soft tuff. Across different regions the earth has unlike and diverse qualities. This is especially evident where the Apennines enclose the regions of Italy and Etruria: sand pits are found almost everywhere on that side, while on the Adriatic side none are found; nor are they mentioned in Achaia, Asia and the lands across the sea. The same favorable conditions therefore do not necessarily coincide wherever hot springs abound. Nature produces things in diverse ways, as circumstance determines, rather than to suit human wishes.

passages.latin: ergo quibus locis non sunt terrosi montes sed genere materiae, est autem materiae potestas mollior quam tofus, solidior quam terra ignis vis per eius venas egrediens adurit eam. quod est molle et tenerum exurit, quod autem asperum relinquit. quo penitus ab imo vehementia vaporis adusto, nonnullis locis procreatur id genus harenae, quod dicitur carbunculus itaque uti Campania exusta terra cinis, sic in Etruria excocta materia efficitur carbunculus. utraque autem sunt egregia in structuris, sed alia in terrenis aedificiis alia etiam in maritimis molibus habent virtutem..
passages.translation: Where there are no earthy mountains but soft tuff, fire issuing through its veins burns away the softer parts and leaves the harder residue. Thus, just as burned earth in Campania becomes volcanic ash, burned tuff in Etruria becomes carbunculus sand. Both are excellent in masonry, but one works in buildings on land while the other also serves in structures built in the sea. The material involved is softer than tuff but more solid than earth; when thoroughly burned by subterranean heat, it produces in some places the kind of sand called carbunculus.

passages.latin: De calce et harena quibus varietatibus sint et quas habeant virtutes dixi. sequitur ordo de lapidicinis explicare, de quibus et quadrata saxa et caementorum ad aedificia eximuntur copiae et comparantur. haec autem inveniuntur esse disparibus et dissimilibus virtutibus. sunt enim aliae molles, uti sunt circa urbem Rubrae Pallenses Fidenates Albanae, aliae temperatae, uti Tiburtinae Amiterninae Soractinae et quae sunt his generibus, nonnullae durae, uti siliceae. sunt etiam alia genera plura, uti in Campania rubrûm et nigrûm tofûm, in Umbria et Piceno et in Venetia albus, quod etiam serra dentata uti lignum secatur.
passages.translation: I have discussed the varieties of lime and sand and their properties. Next come the stone quarries from which ashlar and rubble for buildings are cut and prepared. Their properties differ. Some stones are soft, such as the red stones near Rome and those of Pallene, Fidenae and the Alban district; others are intermediate, such as those of Tibur, Amiternum and Soracte; others, such as hard silex, are very hard. There are many further kinds, including red and black tuffs in Campania, and stones in Umbria, Picenum and Venetia, some of which can be cut with a toothed saw like timber.

passages.latin: sed haec omnia quae mollia sunt hanc habent utilitatem quod ex his saxa cum sunt exempta in opere faciliter tractantur. et si sunt in locis tectis, sustineant laborem, si autem in apertis et patentibus, gelicidiis et pruina congesta friantur et dissolvuntur. item secundum oram maritimam ab salsugine exesa diffluunt neque perferunt aestus. Tiburtina vero et quae eodem genere sunt omnia sufferunt et ab oneribus et a tempestatibus iniurias, sed ab igni non possunt esse tuta simulque sunt ab eo tacta dissiliunt et dissipantur, ideo quod temperatura naturali parvo sunt umore itemque non multum habent terreni sed aeris plurimum et ignis. igitur cum et umor et terrenum in his minus inest, tum etiam ignis, tactu et vi vaporis ex his aere fugato, penitus insequens interveniorum vacuitates occupans fervescit et efficit a suis ardentia corporibus ⟨carbonibus⟩ similia.
passages.translation: Soft stones are easily worked when freshly quarried. Under cover they serve well, but in exposed places frost and hoarfrost cause them to crumble and dissolve. Near the sea, salt also eats into them, and they do not withstand intense heat. Travertine and stones of the same kind withstand both loads and weather, but are unsafe in fire: once heated they crack and disintegrate. Their natural composition contains little moisture or earth and much air and fire. With moisture and earth scarce, heat expels the air, fills the intervening voids, and makes the stone itself burn like the bodies already on fire.

passages.latin: sunt vero item lapidicinae complures in finibus Tarquiniensium, quae dicuntur Anicianae, colore quemadmodum Albanae, quarum officinae maxime sunt circa lacum Vulsiniensem, item praefectura Statonensi. haec autem habent infinitas virtutes. neque enim his gelicidiorum tempestas neque ignis tactus potest nocere, sed est firma et ad vetustatem ideo permanens quod parum habet e naturae mixtione aeris et ignis, umoris autem temperate plurimumque terreni. ita spissis comparationibus solidata neque ab tempestatibus neque ab ignis vehementia nocetur.
passages.translation: There are also many stones in the territory of the Tarquinians, which are called Anician, in color like the Alban, whose quarries are principally around Lake Volsini, as well as in the prefecture of Staton. These have infinite virtues. For neither the storm of frost nor the touch of fire can harm them, but they are strong and durable because they have little of the natural mixture of air and fire, but a moderate and very earthy moisture. Thus, solidified by thick layers, they are not harmed by the violence of storms or fire.

passages.latin: id autem maxime iudicare licet e monumentis quae sunt circa municipium Ferenti ex his facta lapidicinis. namque habent et statuas amplas factas egregie et minora sigilla floresque et acanthos eleganter scalptos. quae cum sint vetusta, sic apparent recentia uti si sint modo facta. non minus etiam fabri aerarii de his lapidicinis in aeris flatura formis comparatis habent ex his ad aes fundendum maximas utilitates. quae si prope urbem essent, dignum esset ut ex his officinis omnia opera perficerentur.
passages.translation: This may be judged especially from monuments made of these stones around Ferentium. They include large statues excellently executed, smaller figures, flowers and acanthus leaves skilfully carved. Although old, they appear as fresh as if made recently. Bronze-workers also find the stones very useful when prepared as molds for casting bronze. If these quarries were near Rome, it would be appropriate to use their stone for all building works.

passages.latin: cum ergo propter propinquitatem necessitas cogat ex Rubris lapidicinis et Pallensibus et quae sunt urbi proximae copiis uti, si qui voluerit sine vitiis perficere, ita erit praeparandum. cum aedificandum fuerit, ante biennium ea saxa non hieme sed aestate eximantur, et iacentia permaneant in locis patentibus. quae autem eo biennio a tempestatibus tacta laesa fuerint, ea in fundamenta coiciantur. cetera quae non erunt vitiata, ab natura rerum probata durare poterunt supra terram aedificata. nec solum ea in quadratis lapidibus sunt observanda sed etiam in caementiciis structuris.
passages.translation: Since, therefore, necessity compels us to use the resources of Rubri and Pallensi, and those which are near the city, if anyone wishes to complete it without defects, this is how it should be prepared. When it is to be built, let those stones be taken out two years before, not in winter but in summer, and let them remain lying in open places. But those which have been damaged by storms during those two years, let them be cast into the foundations. The rest, which will not be defective, will be able to last built above ground, as proven by the nature of things. And not only should these be observed in square stones, but also in rubble masonry.

passages.latin: Structurarum genera sunt haec, reticulatum quo nunc omnes utuntur, et antiquum quod incertum dicitur. ex his venustius est reticulatum, sed ad rimas faciendas ideo paratum quod in omnes partes dissoluta habet cubilia et coagmenta. incerta vero caementa alia super alia sedentia inter seque imbricata non speciosam sed firmiorem quam reticulata praestant structuram.
passages.translation: Archaeological note — II.8, masonry bonds. Vitruvius contrasts two arrangements of wall facing: reticulatum, customary in his time, and the older incertum. He considers the former more elegant (venustius), though more prone to cracking because of the arrangement of beds and joints; the latter he judges less handsome but stronger. Vitruvian terminology has decisively influenced modern archaeological nomenclature, although that classification should not be projected without qualification on to every phase of Roman construction. Opus incertum uses irregular pieces visible in the facing; opus reticulatum arranges cubilia with their faces forming a diagonal network. Later or combined techniques, such as brick facings and so-called opus mixtum, belong to developments beyond the passage’s immediate description. Vitruvius subsequently compares these fabrics with Greek procedures, including emplekton and the use of transverse elements (διάτονοι).

passages.latin: utraque autem ex minutissimis sunt instruenda, uti materia ex calce et harena crebriter parietes satiati diutius contineantur. molli enim et rara potestate cum sint, exsiccant sugendo e materia sucum. cum autem superarit et abundarit copia calcis et harenae, paries plus habens umoris non cito fiet evanidus, sed ab his continetur. simul autem umida potestas e materia per caementorum raritatem fuerit exsucta calxque ab harena discedat et dissolvatur, item caementa non possunt cum his cohaerere, sed in vetustatem parietes efficiunt ruinosos.
passages.translation: Both kinds should be built with very small stones, so that abundant mortar of lime and sand saturates the walls and holds them together longer. Soft, porous stones dry out by drawing moisture from the mortar. If lime and sand are plentiful, the wall retains more moisture and does not quickly weaken. But once the pores of the stones have absorbed the mortar’s moisture, the lime separates from the sand and disintegrates; the rubble can no longer adhere, and the walls become ruinous with age.

passages.latin: id autem licet animadvertere etiam de nonnullis monumentis, quae circa urbem facta sunt e marmore seu lapidibus quadratis intrinsecusque medio calcata structuris, vetustate evanida facta materia caementorumque exsucta raritate, proruunt et coagmentorum ab ruina dissolutis iuncturis dissipantur.
passages.translation: This can be observed in monuments near Rome whose outer faces were made of marble or ashlar, with a rubble core packed between them. As the mortar weakens with age and the porous rubble dries it out, the monuments collapse; the joints of their facing stones loosen and the work breaks apart.

passages.latin: quodsi qui noluerit in id vitium incidere, medio cavo servato secundum orthostatas, intrinsecus ex rubro saxo quadrato aut ex testa aut ex silicibus ordinariis struat bipedales parietes, et cum his ansis ferreis et plumbo frontes vinctae sint. ita enim non acervatim sed ordine structum opus poterit esse sine vitio sempiternum, quod cubilia et coagmenta eorum inter se sedentia et iuncturis alligata non protrudent opus neque orthostatas inter se religatos labi patiuntur.
passages.translation: To avoid this defect, leave the space behind the facing stones and build inner walls two feet thick of squared red stone, fired brick or ordinary hard stone. Tie the inner work to the outer faces with iron clamps secured with lead. Built in regular courses rather than loose heaps, the work can remain sound: the beds and bonded joints keep the masonry from thrusting out, while the connected facing stones prevent it from slipping.

passages.latin: Itaque non est contemnenda Graecorum structura. non enim utuntur e molli caemento structura polita, sed cum discesserunt a quadrato, ponunt de silice seu lapide duro ordinaria, et ita uti latericia struentes alligant eorum alternis coriis coagmenta, et sic maxime ad aeternitatem firmas perficiunt virtutes. haec autem duobus generibus struuntur. ex his unum isodomum, alterum pseudisodomum appellatur.
passages.translation: Greek masonry should therefore not be disparaged. The Greeks do not make a carefully finished facing of soft rubble: when not using ashlar, they build with ordinary hard stone, laying it like brick and bonding the joints in alternating courses. They thus achieve lasting strength. They build this masonry in two forms, one called isodomon and the other pseudisodomon.

passages.latin: isodomum dicitur cum omnia coria aequa crassitudine fuerint structa, pseudisodomum cum inpares et inaequales ordines coriorum diriguntur. ea utraque sunt ideo firma, primum quod ipsa caementa sunt spissa et solida proprietate neque de materia possunt exsugere liquorem sed conservant eam in suo umore ad summam vetustatem, ipsaque eorum cubilia primum plana et librata posita non patiuntur ruere materiam, sed perpetua parietum crassitudine religata continent ad summam vetustatem.
passages.translation: Masonry is called isodomon when every course has the same height, and pseudisodomon when the courses differ in height. Both are strong because their dense, solid stones do not draw liquid from the mortar but preserve its moisture. Their beds, laid flat and level, prevent the mortar from slipping, while the continuous thickness and bonding of the walls hold the work securely together.

passages.latin: altera est quam ἔμπλεκτον appellant, qua etiam nostri rustici utuntur. quorum frontes poliuntur, reliqua ita uti sunt nata cum materia conlocata alternis alligant coagmentis. sed nostri celeritati studentes, erecta conlocantes frontibus serviunt et in medio farciunt fractis separatim cum materia caementis. ita tres suscitantur in ea structura crustae, duae frontium et una media farturae. Graeci vero non ita, sed plana conlocantes et longitudines eorum alternis in crassitudinem instruentes, non media farciunt sed e suis frontatis perpetuam et unam crassitudinem parietum consolidant. praeterea interponunt singulos crassitudine perpetua utraque parte frontatos, quos διάτονοι appellant, qui maxime religando confirmant parietum soliditatem.
passages.translation: Another kind, called emplekton, is also used by our country builders. Its faces are dressed, while the stones within are left in their natural state and bonded with mortar in alternating courses. Our builders, pursuing speed, set the facings upright and fill the middle separately with rubble and mortar, producing three distinct layers: two outer faces and an inner filling. The Greeks instead lay their stones flat and alternate their lengths through the thickness. They do not merely fill the middle but make one continuous thickness from face to face. They also insert stones that run through the full thickness and project at both faces, called diatonoi; these ties greatly strengthen the walls.

passages.latin: itaque si qui voluerit ex his commentariis animadvertere et eligere genus structurae, perpetuitatis poterit rationem habere. non enim quae sunt e molli caemento subtili facie venustatis, non eae possunt esse in vetustate non ruinosae. itaque cum arbitri communium parietum sumuntur, non aestimant eos quanti facti fuerint, sed cum ex tabulis inveniunt eorum locationes, pretia praeteritorum annorum singulorum deducunt octogesimas et ita ex reliqua summa ⟨pro rata⟩ parte reddi pro his parietibus sententiam pronuntiant eos non posse plus quam annos LXXX durare.
passages.translation: Anyone wishing to examine these observations and select a kind of masonry can therefore take account of its durability. Walls built from soft rubble, however finely finished, cannot remain free from decay as they age. Accordingly, when valuers assess party walls, they do not simply allow their original cost: after establishing the date of the contract from the records, they deduct one-eightieth of the price for each year that has elapsed and award the appropriate proportion of the remainder. Their assessment assumes that such walls cannot endure for more than eighty years.

passages.latin: De latericiis vero dummodo ad perpendiculum sint stantes nihil deducitur, sed quanti fuerint olim facti, tanti esse semper aestimantur. itaque nonnullis civitatibus et publica opera et privatas domos etiam regias e latere structas licet videre, et primum Athenis murum qui spectat ad Hymettum montem et Pentelensem, item Patris in aede Iovis et Herculis latericias cellas, cum circa lapidea in aede epistylia sint et columnae, in Italia Arretio vetustum egregie factum murum, Trallibus domus regibus Attalicis facta quae ad habitandum semper datur ei qui civitatis gerit sacerdotium. item Lacedaemone e quibusdam parietibus etiam picturae excisae intersectis lateribus inclusae sunt in ligneis formis et in comitium ad ornatum aedilitatis Varronis et Murenae fuerunt adlatae.
passages.translation: In brick walls, provided they remain plumb, no deduction is made: they are always valued at their original cost. In some cities public works, private houses and royal palaces can therefore be seen built of brick. Examples include the Athenian wall facing Hymettus and Pentelicus; the brick cellae in the temples of Jupiter and Hercules at Patras, with stone columns and architraves around them; the ancient, excellently built wall at Arretium in Italy; and the house at Tralles built for the Attalid kings, assigned as a residence to whoever holds the city’s priesthood. At Sparta, paintings were cut out of brick walls, enclosed in wooden frames and brought to the Comitium to adorn the aedileship of Varro and Murena.

passages.latin: Croesi domus, quam Sardiani civibus ad requiescendum aetatis otio, seniorum collegio gerusiam dedicaverunt. item Halicarnasso potentissimi regis Mausoli domus cum Proconnensio marmore omnia haberet ornata, parietes habet latere structos, qui ad hoc tempus egregiam praestant firmitatem ita tectoriis operibus expoliti uti vitri perluciditatem videantur habere. neque is rex ab inopia id fecit. infinitis enim vectigalibus erat fartus, quod imperabat Cariae toti.
passages.translation: The house of Croesus, which the people of Sardis assigned to the citizens of their city to rest in the leisure of their age, to the college of elders. Likewise, the house of the most powerful king Mausolus at Halicarnassus, although it was adorned with Proconnesian marble, has walls built of brick, which for this time show excellent strength, so polished by the works of painting that they seem to have the translucency of glass. Nor did that king do this from want. For he was enriched by immense revenues, since he ruled all Caria.

passages.latin: acumen autem eius et sollertiam ad aedificia paranda sic licet considerare. cum esset enim natus Mylasis et animadvertisset Halicarnasso locum naturaliter esse munitum idoneum portum emporiumque utile, ibi sibi domum constituit. is autem locus est theatri curvaturae similis. itaque in imo secundum portum forum est constitutum. per mediam autem altitudinis curvaturam praecinctionemque platea ampla latitudine facta, in qua media Mausoleum ita egregiis operibus est factum ut in septem spectaculis nominetur. in summa arce media Martis fanum habens statuam colossicam acrolithon nobili manu Leocharis factam. hanc autem statuam alii Leocharis alii Timothei putant esse. in cornu autem summo dextro Veneris et Mercurii fanum ad ipsum Salmacidis fontem.
passages.translation: His judgment and skill in planning buildings may be understood as follows. Born at Mylasa, he observed that Halicarnassus offered natural defenses, a suitable trading center and a useful harbour, and established his residence there. The site curves like a theater. At its lowest part, beside the harbour, he laid out the forum; halfway up the curving slope he made a broad street, with the Mausoleum at its center, a work of such distinction that it was numbered among the Seven Wonders. At the center of the summit stood the temple of Mars with a colossal acrolithic statue, attributed by some to Leochares and by others to Timotheus. On the right-hand height stood the temple of Venus and Mercury, near the spring of Salmacis.

passages.latin: is autem falsa opinione putatur venerio morbo inplicare eos qui ex eo biberint. sed haec opinio quare per orbem terrae falso rumore sit pervagata non pigebit exponere. non enim quod dicitur molles et inpudicos ex ea aqua fieri, id potest esse, sed est eius fontis potestas perlucida saporque egregius. cum autem Melas et Areuanias ab Argis et Troezene coloniam communem eo loci deduxerunt, barbaros Caras et Lelegas eiecerunt. Hi autem ad montes fugati inter se congregantes discurrebant et ibi latrocinia facientes crudeliter eos vastabant. postea de colonis unus ad eum fontem propter bonitatem aquae quaestus causa tabernam omnibus copiis instruxit eamque exercendo eos barbaros allectabat. ita singillatim decurrentes et ad coetus convenientes e duro feroque more commutati in Graecorum consuetudinem et suavitatem sua voluntate reducebantur. ergo ea aqua non inpudico morbi vitio sed humanitatis dulcedine mollitis animis barbarorum eam famam est adepta.
passages.translation: It is falsely believed that this spring causes an effeminate condition in those who drink from it. I shall explain how that mistaken report spread. Its water cannot produce the softness and immodesty alleged: it is clear and excellent to taste. When Melas and Arevanias brought a joint colony from Argos and Troezen, they expelled the local Carians and Leleges. Driven into the mountains, these people gathered in bands, raided the settlers and devastated the district. One colonist later built a tavern beside the spring, attracted by the water’s quality, and by conducting his business drew the local people to it. Coming first singly and then in groups, they gradually exchanged their harsh customs for the gentler ways of the Greeks. The water acquired its reputation not by causing a bodily disease but by softening their dispositions through the civilising appeal of human society.

passages.latin: Relinquitur nunc quoniam ad explicationem moenium eorum sum invectus, ut tota uti sunt definiam. quemadmodum enim in dextra parte fanum est Veneris et fons supra scriptus, ita in sinistro cornu regia domus, quam rex Mausolus ad suam rationem conlocavit. conspicitur enim ex ea ad dextram partem forum et portus moeniumque tota finitio, sub sinistram secretus sub moenibus latens portus ita ut nemo possit quid in eo geratur aspicere nec scire,
passages.translation: Since I have been led to describe the city, it remains to set out its overall arrangement. Just as the temple of Venus and the spring described above stand on the right, the royal palace stands on the left. Mausolus placed it to serve his own purposes: to the right it commands a view of the forum, the harbour and the whole circuit of the walls; to the left lies a harbour concealed beneath the walls, where no one else could see or know what was being done.

passages.latin: at rex ipse de sua domo remigibus et militibus sine ullo sciente quae opus essent imperaret. itaque post mortem Mausoli Artemisia uxore eius regnante Rhodii indignantes mulierem imperare civitatibus Cariae totius, armata classe profecti sunt uti id regnum occuparent. tum Artemisiae cum esset id renuntiatum, in eo portu abstrusam classem celatis remigibus et epibatis comparatis, reliquos autem cives in muro esse iussit. cum autem Rhodii ornata classe in portum maiorem exposuissent, plausum iussit ab muro his dare pollicerique se oppidum tradituros. qui cum penetravissent intra murum relictis navibus inanibus, Artemisia repente fossa facta in pelagum eduxit classem ex portu minore et ita invecta est in maiorem. expositis autem militibus classem Rhodiorum inanem abduxit in altum. ita Rhodii non habentes quo se reciperent, in medio conclusi in ipso foro sunt trucidati.
passages.translation: From his own house the king could direct the rowers and soldiers without anyone else knowing what was required. After Mausolus’s death, when his wife Artemisia ruled, the Rhodians, indignant that a woman should govern all the cities of Caria, sailed with an armed fleet to seize the kingdom. Informed of their approach, Artemisia ordered her own fleet concealed in the smaller harbour, with rowers and marines ready, while the other citizens occupied the walls. When the Rhodians entered the larger harbour, she had the citizens salute them from the walls and promise to surrender the town. The Rhodians left their ships empty and entered within the walls. Artemisia then brought her fleet out of the smaller harbour through the opening to the sea and round into the larger harbour. Landing her soldiers, she seized the empty Rhodian ships and took them out to sea. With no route of retreat, the Rhodians were surrounded and killed in the forum.

passages.latin: ita Artemisia in navibus Rhodiorum suis militibus et remigibus inpositis Rhodum est profecta.
