Rhodii autem cum prospexissent suas naves laureatas venire, opinantes cives victores reverti hostes receperunt. tum Artemisia Rhodo capta principibus occisis tropaeum in urbe Rhodo suae victoriae constituit aeneasque duas statuas fecit unam Rhodiorum civitatis alteram suae imaginis. eam ita figuravit Rhodiorum civitati stigmata inponentem. id autem postea ⟨tollere⟩ Rhodii religione inpediti quod nefas est tropaea dedicata removeri, circa eum locum aedificium struxerunt et id electa Graia statione texerunt ne qui posset aspicere, et id ἄβατον vocitari iusserunt.
passages.translation: Artemisia then sailed to Rhodes in the Rhodians’ ships with her own soldiers and rowers aboard. Seeing their ships arrive crowned with laurel, the Rhodians thought their victorious citizens were returning and admitted the enemy. After taking Rhodes and killing its leaders, Artemisia erected a trophy of her victory and two bronze statues: one representing the city of Rhodes and the other herself. She represented herself branding the Rhodian city. The Rhodians later refrained from removing the monument for religious reasons, since a dedicated trophy could not lawfully be taken away. They built an enclosure around the place and screened it so that no one could look upon it, ordering it to be called the abaton (ἄβατον), the inaccessible precinct.

passages.latin: Cum ergo tam magna potentia reges non contempserint latericiorum parietum structuras, quibus ex vectigalibus et praeda saepius licitum fuerat non modo caementicio aut quadrato saxo sed etiam marmoreo habere, non puto oportere inprobare quae sunt e latericia structura facta aedificia, dummodo recte sint tecta. sed id genus quid ita populo Romano in urbe fieri non oporteat exponam, quaeque sunt eius rei causae et rationes non praetermittam.
passages.translation: Since powerful kings did not disdain brick walls, although their revenues and spoils allowed them to use rubble, ashlar or even marble, I do not think brick buildings should be rejected, provided they are properly roofed. I shall explain why the Roman people do not use such walls in the city, and shall set out the causes and reasons.

passages.latin: leges publicae non patiuntur maiores crassitudines quam sesquipedales constitui loco communi. ceteri autem parietes, ne spatia angustiora fierent, eadem crassitudine conlocantur. latericii vero nisi diplinthii aut triplinthii fuerint, sesquipedali crassitudine non possunt plus quam unam sustinere contignationem. in ea autem maiestate urbis et civium infinita frequentia innumerabiles habitationes opus est explicare. ergo cum recipere non possint areae planatae tantam multitudinem ad habitandum in urbe, ad auxilium altitudinis aedificiorum res ipsa coegit devenire. itaque pilis lapideis structuris testaceis parietibus caementiciis altitudines extructae contignationibus crebris coaxatae cenaculorum ad summas utilitates perficiunt despectationes. ergo moenibus e contignationibus areis alto spatio multiplicatis populus Romanus egregias habet sine inpeditione habitationes.
passages.translation: Public regulations do not allow party walls thicker than a foot and a half, and other walls are built to the same thickness to avoid narrowing the available space. Yet brick walls of that thickness cannot support more than one story unless they are two or three bricks thick. The greatness of Rome and the immense number of its citizens require countless dwellings. Since the ground area cannot accommodate so many people, necessity has forced recourse to building upwards. Stone piers, fired-brick masonry and rubble walls, raised high and joined by frequent timber floors, provide useful upper-story dwellings. By multiplying floor space vertically, the Roman people obtain ample housing without obstructing the ground.

passages.latin: Quoniam ergo explicata ratio est quid ita in urbe propter necessitatem angustiarum non patiuntur esse latericios parietes, cum extra urbem opus erit his uti, ⟨ut sint⟩ sine vitiis ad vetustatem sic erit faciendum. summis parietibus structura testacea sub tegula subiciatur altitudine circiter sesquipedali, habeatque proiecturas coronarum. ita vitari poterunt quae solent in his fieri vitia. cum enim in tecto tegulae fuerint fractae aut a ventis deiectae, qua possint ex imbribus aquae perpluere, non patietur lorica testacea laedi laterem, sed proiectura coronarum reiciet extra perpendiculum stillas et ea ratione servaverit integras parietum latericiorum structuras.
passages.translation: Having explained why restricted sites prevent the use of brick walls in Rome, I shall describe how to make them durable where they are used outside the city. At the tops of the walls, beneath the roof tiles, build a fired-brick course about a foot and a half high, with projecting cornices. This prevents the usual damage: if roof tiles break or are displaced by wind and rainwater enters, the fired-brick protection prevents it from harming the unfired bricks. The projecting cornice throws the drops beyond the face of the wall and preserves the brick masonry intact.

passages.latin: De ipsa autem testa, si sit optima seu vitiosa ad structuram, statim nemo potest iudicare, quod in tempestatibus et aestate in tecto cum est conlocata, tunc, si est firma, probatur; namque quae non fuerit ex creta bona aut parum erit cocta, ibi se ostendet esse vitiosam gelicidiis et pruina tacta. Ergo quae non in tectis poterit pati laborem, ea non potest in structura oneri ferendo esse firma. Quare maxime ex veteribus tegulis tecta ⟨et ex vetere testa⟩ structi parietes firmitatem poterunt habere.
passages.translation: No one can immediately judge whether a fired brick is good or bad for masonry. Its strength is tested by exposure to weather and age when used on a roof. If it is made from unsuitable clay or insufficiently fired, frost reveals its weakness. A material that cannot endure service on a roof cannot be strong enough to bear a load in masonry. Walls made of old, tested roof tiles will therefore be especially strong.

passages.latin: craticii vero velim quidem ne inventi essent. quantum enim celeritate et loci laxamento prosunt, tanto maiori et communi sunt calamitati, quod ad incendia uti faces sunt parati. itaque satius esse videtur inpensa testaceorum in sumptu quam compendio craticiorum esse in periculo. etiamque in tectoriis operibus rimas hi faciunt arrectariorum et transversariorum dispositione. cum enim linuntur, recipientes umorem turgescunt, deinde siccescendo contrahuntur et ita extenuati disrumpunt tectoriorum soliditatem. sed quoniam nonnullos celeritas aut inopia aut in pendenti loco dissaeptio cogit, sic erit faciundum. solum substruatur [aliae], ut sit intactum ab rudere et pavimento. obruta enim in his cum sunt, vetustate marcida fiunt, deinde subsidentia proclinantur et disrumpunt speciem tectoriorum. De parietibus et apparitione generatim materiae eorum, quibus sint virtutibus et vitiis quemadmodum potui exposui, de contignationibus autem et copiis earum, quibus comparentur ut ad vetustatem non sint infirmae, uti natura rerum monstrat explicabo.
passages.translation: I wish timber-framed partition walls had never been invented. Their speed of construction and saving of space are outweighed by the greater and more general danger they create, for they are ready-made torches for a fire. It is better to incur the expense of fired-brick walls than to save money through timber framing and live in danger. Such framing also cracks the plaster along the upright and cross-members: when plastered, the timbers absorb moisture and swell, then shrink as they dry and break the plaster’s cohesion. Where speed, lack of resources or the need for a partition on an upper floor makes timber framing necessary, its base should be built up so that the timbers do not touch the rubble bedding or floor pavement. If buried in those layers, they decay with age, settle, lean and break the plaster surface. I have explained wall construction, its materials and their strengths and weaknesses as well as I can. I shall now discuss timber floors and the supplies used for them, explaining the natural properties needed for durability.

passages.latin: Materies caedenda est a primo autumno ad id tempus quod erit antequam flare incipiat favonius. vere enim omnes arbores fiunt praegnantes et omnes suae proprietatis virtutem efferunt in frondem anniversariosque fructus. cum ergo inanes et tumidae temporum necessitate eorum fuerint, vanae fiunt et raritatibus inbecillae, uti etiam corpora muliebria cum conceperint, fetus a partu non iudicantur integra, neque in venalibus ea cum sunt praegnantia praestantur sana, ideo quod in corpore praeseminatio crescens ex omnibus cibi potestatibus detrahit alimentum in se, et quo firmior efficitur ad maturitatem partus, eo minus patitur esse solidum id ipsum ex quo procreatur. itaque edito fetu quod prius in aliud genus incrementi detrahebatur cum disparatione procreationis est liberatum, inanibus et patentibus venis in se recipiens lambendo sucum etiam solidescit et redit in pristinam naturae firmitatem.
passages.translation: Timber should be felled from the beginning of autumn until before Favonius starts to blow. In spring, all trees become, as it were, pregnant and direct their natural strength into foliage and annual fruit. Drained and swollen by the demands of the season, they become porous and weak. The same comparison is made with women’s bodies: after conception they are not considered unimpaired until delivery, nor are they warranted as healthy in sales while pregnant, because the growing foetus drew nourishment from the body and weakened the source from which it developed. After delivery, nourishment was no longer diverted into another growing body; the open veins again took up sustenance, restoring solidity and the former natural strength.

passages.latin: eadem ratione autumnali tempore maturitate fructuum flaccescente fronde, ex terra recipientes caudices arborum in se sucum recuperantur et restituuntur in antiquam soliditatem. at vero aeris hiberni vis comprimit et consolidat eas per id ut supra scriptum est tempus. ergo si ea ratione et eo tempore quod est supra scriptum caeditur materies, erit tempestiva.
passages.translation: For the same reason, in the autumn season, when the leaves of the fruit ripen and fall, the trees, receiving sap from the earth through their roots, are recovered and restored to their former solidity. But the force of the winter air compresses and consolidates them for the time mentioned above. Therefore, if the material is cut down for that reason and at the time mentioned above, it will be in season.

passages.latin: caedi autem ita oportet uti incidatur arboris crassitudo ad mediam medullam, et relinquatur, uti per eam exsiccescat stillando sucus. ita qui inest in his inutilis liquor effluens per torulum non patietur emori in eo saniem nec corrumpi materiae aequalitatem. tum autem cum sicca et sine stillis erit arbor, deiciatur et ita erit optima in usu.
passages.translation: The tree should first be cut through to the middle of its pith and left standing so that the sap can drain through the cut. The useless liquid within can then flow out rather than decay and damage the timber. When the tree is dry and no longer dripping, it should be felled; it will then be in the best condition for use.

passages.latin: hoc autem ita esse licet animum advertere etiam de arbustis. ea enim cum suo quoque tempore ad imum perforata castrantur, profundunt e medullis quem habent in se superantem et vitiosum per foramina liquorem, et ita siccescendo recipiunt in se diuturnitatem. qui autem non habent ex arboribus exitus umores intra concrescentes putrescunt et efficiunt inanes eas et vitiosas. ergo si stantes et vivae siccescendo non senescunt, sine dubio cum eae ad materiam deiciuntur, cum ea ratione curatae fuerint, habere poterunt magnas in aedificiis ad vetustatem utilitates.
passages.translation: The same can be observed in trees: when pierced at the base in the proper season, they discharge through the openings the excessive, harmful sap in their pith, and drying in this way increases their longevity. Liquids that have no outlet, by contrast, putrefy within the tree and leave it hollow and defective. If trees left standing and alive resist decay when drained in this manner, then timber felled for use, once so treated, can undoubtedly provide great durability in buildings.

passages.latin: Hae autem inter se discrepantes et dissimiles habent virtutes, uti robur ulmus populus cupressus abies ceteraque quae maxime in aedificiis sunt idonea. namque non potest id robur quod abies, nec cupressus quod ulmus, nec cetera easdem habent inter se natura rerum similitates, sed singula genera principiorum proprietatibus comparata alios alii generis praestant in operibus effectus.
passages.translation: But they have virtues that are different and dissimilar from each other, such as the oak, the elm, the poplar, the cypress, the fir, and the others that are most suitable for buildings. For the oak cannot be the same as the fir, nor the cypress as the elm, nor the others have the same natural similarities between themselves, but each kind of principle has properties comparable to those of another kind in works.

passages.latin: et primum abies aeris habens plurimum et ignis minimumque umoris et terreni levioribus rerum natura e potestatibus comparata non est ponderosa. itaque rigore naturali contenta non cito flectitur ab onere, sed directa permanet in contignatione. sed ea quod habet in se plus caloris, procreat et alit cariem ab eaque vitiatur, etiamque ideo celeriter accenditur quod quae inest in eo corpore aeris raritas, ut est patens accipit ignem et ita vehementem ex se mittit flammam.
passages.translation: Fir contains much air and fire but little moisture and earth, so its lighter constituent principles make it relatively light. Its natural rigidity prevents it from bending readily under a load, and it remains straight in floor framing. Because it contains more heat, however, it breeds and nourishes decay and is damaged by it. It also catches fire quickly: its porous, air-filled substance readily admits fire and gives out an intense flame.

passages.latin: ex ea autem antequam est excisa quae pars est proxima terrae per radices recipiens ex proximitate umorem enodis et liquida efficitur. quae vero est superior, vehementia caloris eductis in aera per nodos ramis, praecisa alte circiter pedes XX et perdolata propter nodationis duritiem dicitur esse fusterna. ima autem cum excisa quadrifluviis disparatur eiecto torulo ex eadem arbore ad intestina opera comparatur et ⟨ab⟩ infima fusterna sappinea vocatur.
passages.translation: In the uncut tree, the part nearest the ground receives moisture through the roots and is relatively free from knots and full of sap. In the upper part, heat draws branches out through knots into the air; cut at about twenty feet and hewn, this knotty timber is called fusterna. The lower part, when cut and split into four, has the central round core removed and is prepared for interior joinery; this is called sappinea, in distinction from the lower part of the fusterna.

passages.latin: contra vero quercus terrenis principiorum satietatibus abundans parumque habens umoris et aeris et ignis, cum in terrenis operibus obruitur, infinitam habet aeternitatem. ex eo cum tangitur umore non habens foraminum raritates propter spissitatem non potest in corpus recipere liquorem, sed fugiens ab umore resistit et torquetur et efficit in quibus est operibus ea rimosa.
passages.translation: Oak, by contrast, contains much earth and little moisture, air or fire, and lasts indefinitely when buried in earthworks. When exposed to moisture, its dense texture and lack of open pores prevent it from absorbing liquid. Resisting moisture, it twists and causes cracks in the work in which it is used.

passages.latin: aesculus vero quod est omnibus principiis temperata, habet in aedificiis magnas utilitates, sed ea, cum in umore conlocatur, recipiens penitus per foramina liquorem eiecto aere et igni operatione umidae potestatis vitiatur. cerrus [quercus] fagus quod pariter habent mixtionem umoris et ignis et terreni, aeris plurimum, per huius raritates umores penitus recipiendo celeriter marcescunt. populus alba et nigra, item salix tilia cum non sint dura terreni mixtione, propter raritatem sunt candida et in sculpturis commodam praestant tractabilitatem vitex ignis et aeris habendo satietatem, umoris temperate, parum autem terreni, habens leviore temperatura comparata egregiam habere videtur in usu rigiditatem..
passages.translation: Aesculus, with a balanced mixture of the elements, is very useful in buildings. In damp conditions, however, its pores admit water as air and fire are expelled, and moisture causes it to decay. Cerrus, a kind of oak, and beech, containing balanced amounts of moisture, fire and earth but much air, are porous and quickly decay when thoroughly wetted. White and black poplar, willow, lime and vitex contain much fire and air, moderate moisture and little earth; their light composition gives them useful rigidity. Because they are not hardened by much earth, they remain soft and readily workable for carving.

passages.latin: alnus autem, quae proxima fluminum ripis procreatur et minime materies utilis videtur, habet in se egregias rationes. etenim est aere et igni plurimo temperata, non multum terreno, umore paulo. itaque in palustribus locis infra fundamenta aedificiorum palationibus crebre fixa, recipiens in se quod minus habet in corpore liquoris, permanet inmortalis ad aeternitatem et sustinet inmania pondera structurae et sine vitiis conservat. ita quae non potest extra terram paulum tempus durare, ea in umore obruta permanet ad diuturnitatem.
passages.translation: Alder, which grows beside rivers and appears of little use as timber, has remarkable properties. It contains much air and fire, little earth and little moisture. Driven densely as piles beneath foundations in marshy places, it takes up the liquid lacking in its substance and remains durable, carrying enormous masonry loads without damage. Timber that lasts only a short time out of the ground can thus endure for a long time when buried in moisture.

passages.latin: est autem maxime id considerare Ravennae, quod ibi omnia opera et publica et privata sub fundamentis eius generis habeant palos. ulmus vero et fraxinus maximos habent umores minimumque aeris et ignis, terreni temperate ⟨ea e⟩ mixtione comparatae. sunt in operibus cum fabricantur lentae et ab pondere umoris non habent rigorem et celeriter pandant. simul autem vetustate sunt aridae factae aut in agro perfecto qui est eis liquor stantes emoriuntur, fiunt duriores et in commissuris et coagmentationibus ab lentitudine firmas recipiunt catenationes.
passages.translation: This is particularly evident at Ravenna, where all public and private buildings have alder piles beneath their foundations. Elm and ash contain much moisture, little air and fire, and a moderate amount of earth. When used green they are flexible, and their moisture makes them lack rigidity and bend readily under load. Once dried by age, or drained of their sap while standing, they become harder; their pliancy makes them effective in joints and connections.

passages.latin: item carpinus quod est minima ignis et terreni mixtione, aeris autem et umoris summa continetur temperatura, non est fragilis sed habet utilissimam tractabilitatem. itaque Graeci quod ex ea materia iuga iumentis comparant, quod apud eos iuga ζυγά
passages.translation: vocitantur, item ζυγίην eam appellant. non minus est admirandum de cupresso et pinu, quod eae habentes umoris abundantiam aequamque ceterorum mixtionem, propter umoris satietatem in operibus solent esse pandae, sed in vetustatem sine vitiis conservantur, quod is liquor qui inest penitus in corporibus earum habet amarum saporem, qui propter acritudinem non patitur penetrare cariem neque eas bestiolas quae sunt nocentes. ideoque quae ex his generibus opera constituuntur permanent ad aeternam diuturnitatem.

passages.latin: item cedrus et iuniperus easdem habent virtutes et utilitates, sed quemadmodum ex cupressu et pinu resina, ex cedro oleum quod cedrium dicitur nascitur, quo reliquae res cum sunt unctae, uti etiam libri, a tineis et carie non laeduntur. arboris autem eius sunt similes cupresseae foliaturae, materies vena directa. Ephesi in aede simulacrum Dianae, ex ea lacunaria et ibi et in ceteris nobilibus fanis propter aeternitatem sunt facta. nascuntur autem eae arbores maxime Cretae et Africae et nonnullis Syriae regionibus.
passages.translation: Cedar and juniper have similar properties and uses. Just as cypress and pine yield resin, cedar produces an oil called cedrium; objects such as books, when anointed with it, are protected from moths and decay. The tree’s foliage resembles cypress, and its timber is straight-grained. At Ephesus the temple’s statue of Diana was made from it, as were the coffered ceilings there and in other celebrated sanctuaries, because of its durability. These trees grow principally in Crete, Africa and parts of Syria.

passages.latin: Larix vero, qui non est notus nisi îs municipalibus, qui sunt circa ripam fluminis Padi et litora maris Hadriani, non solum ab suci vehementi amaritate ab carie aut tinea non nocetur, sed etiam flammam ex igni non recipit, nec ipse per se potest ardere, nisi uti saxum in fornace ad calcem coquendam aliis lignis uratur; nec tamen tunc flammam recipit nec carbonem remittit, sed longo spatio tarde comburitur. ⟨Namque ea materies,⟩ quod est minima ignis et aeris e principiis temperatura, umore autem et terreno est spisse solidata, non habet spatia foraminum, qua possit ignis penetrare, reicitque eius vim nec patitur ab eo sibi cito noceri, propterque pondus ab aqua non sustinetur, sed cum portatur, aut in navibus aut supra abiegnas rates conlocatur.
passages.translation: Larch is known only to the townspeople near the Po and the Adriatic coast. The intense bitterness of its sap protects it from decay and insects; the account also states that it does not catch flame or burn by itself unless burned with other wood, like stone in a lime kiln. Even then it does not take flame or yield charcoal but is slowly consumed over a long time. Its composition contains very little fire and air and is densely consolidated with moisture and earth, leaving no open pores through which fire can penetrate. It therefore resists fire and is not quickly damaged. Because of its weight it does not float, and must be carried in boats or placed on rafts of fir.

passages.latin: Ea autem materies quemadmodum sit inventa est causa cognoscere. divus Caesar cum exercitum habuisset circa Alpes imperavissetque municipiis praestare commeatus ibique esset castellum munitum quod vocaretur Larignum, tunc qui in eo fuerunt naturali munitione confisi noluerunt imperio parere. itaque imperator copias iussit admoveri. erat autem ante eius castelli portam turris ex hac materia alternis trabibus transversis uti pyra inter se composita alte, uti possent de summo sudibus et lapidibus accedentes repellere. tunc vero cum animadversum est alia eos tela praeter sudes non habere neque posse longius a muro propter pondus iaculari, imperatum est fasciculos ex virgis alligatos et faces ardentes ad eam munitionem accedentes mittere. itaque celeriter milites congesserunt.
passages.translation: The reason this timber became known was as follows. When the deified Caesar was campaigning near the Alps and had ordered the towns to supply provisions, the inhabitants of a fortified place called Larignum refused, trusting in its natural defenses. He ordered his forces forward. Before its gate stood a tower built of this timber, with beams laid crosswise like a funeral pyre, from whose top the defenders repelled attackers with stakes and stones. Seeing that they had only stakes, too heavy to be thrown far from the wall, Caesar ordered bundles of brushwood and burning torches to be thrown against the fortification. The soldiers quickly collected them.

passages.latin: posteaquam flamma circa illam materiam virgas comprehendisset, ad caelum sublata effecit opinionem uti videretur iam tota moles concidisse. cum autem ea per se extincta esset et re quieta turris intacta apparuisset, admirans Caesar iussit extra telorum missionem eos circumvallari. itaque timore coacti oppidani cum se dedidissent, quaesitum unde essent ea ligna quae ab igni non laederentur. tunc ei demonstraverunt eas arbores, quarum in his locis maximae sunt copiae. et ideo id castellum Larignum item materies larigna est appellata. haec autem per Padum Ravennam deportatur, in colonia Fanestri Pisauri Anconae reliquisque quae sunt in ea regione municipiis praebetur. cuius materies si esset facultas adportationibus ad urbem, maximae haberentur in aedificiis utilitates, et si non in omne, certe tabulae in subgrundiis circum insulas si essent ex ea conlocatae, ab traiectionis incendiorum aedificia periculo liberarentur, quod eae neque flammam nec carbonem possunt recipere nec facere per se.
passages.translation: The flame caught the brushwood around the tower and rose into the sky, giving the impression that the whole structure would collapse. When the fire burned itself out, however, the tower appeared intact. Astonished, Caesar ordered the place surrounded beyond missile range. The townspeople, intimidated, surrendered, and he asked where the timber that resisted the fire came from. They showed him the trees, abundant in the district. Just as the fort was called Larignum, the timber was called larigna. It is transported down the Po to Ravenna and supplied to the colony at Fanum, to Pisaurum, Ancona and other nearby towns. If it could readily be transported to Rome, it would be very useful in buildings. Even if not used throughout, boards of it set under the eaves around blocks of houses could protect buildings against spreading fires, since the timber, according to the account, neither catches flame nor ignites by itself.

passages.latin: sunt autem eae arbores foliis similibus pini, materies earum prolixa, tractabilis ad intestinum opus non minus quam sappinea, habetque resinam liquidam mellis Attici colore quae etiam medetur pthisicis. De singulis generibus quibus proprietatibus e natura rerum videantur esse comparatae quibusque procreantur rationibus exposui. insequitur animadversio quid ita quae in urbe supernas dicitur abies deterior est, quae infernas egregios in aedificiis ad diuturnitatem praestat usus, et de his rebus, quemadmodum videantur e locorum proprietatibus habere vitia aut virtutes, uti ea sint considerantibus apertiora exponere.
passages.translation: These trees have foliage resembling pine, long timbers as workable for interior joinery as sappinea, and a liquid resin the color of Attic honey, which is also used against consumption. I have explained the different kinds of timber, the properties nature gives them and the reasons for their development. It remains to consider why the fir known at Rome as supernas is inferior, while infernas is particularly durable in buildings. I shall explain more clearly how the characteristics of their places of growth give them strengths or weaknesses.

passages.latin: montis Appennini primae radices ab Tyrrenico mari inter Alpis et extremas Etruriae regiones oriuntur. eius vero montis iugum se circumagens et media curvatura prope tangens oras maris Hadriani pertingit circumitionibus contra fretum. itaque citerior eius curvatura quae vergit ad Etruriae Campaniaeque regiones apricis est potestatibus. namque impetus habet perpetuos ad solis cursum. ulterior autem quae est proclinata ad superum mare, septentrionali regioni subiecta continetur umbrosis et opacis perpetuitatibus. itaque quae in ea parte nascuntur arbores umida potestate nutritae non solum ipsae augentur amplissimis magnitudinibus, sed earum quoque venae umoris copia repletae turgentes liquoris abundantia saturantur. cum autem excisae et dolatae vitalem potestatem amiserunt, venarum rigore permanente siccescendo propter raritatem fiunt inanes et evanidae, ideoque in aedificiis non possunt habere diuturnitatem.
passages.translation: The first foothills of the Apennines rise from the Tyrrhenian Sea between the Alps and the outer regions of Etruria. The ridge curves through Italy, approaches the Adriatic coast in its central bend and continues towards the strait. Its nearer slope, facing Etruria and Campania, lies in sunlight and remains exposed to the sun’s course. The farther slope, facing the upper sea, looks north and is continually shaded. Trees growing there, nourished by moisture, become very large, and their veins swell with abundant sap. Once felled and hewn, they lose their vital force; as the veins stiffen and dry, their porous substance becomes weak and insubstantial. Such timber therefore lacks durability in buildings.

passages.latin: quae autem ad solis cursum spectantibus locis procreantur, non habentes interveniorum raritates siccitatibus exsuctae solidantur, quia sol non modo ex terra lambendo sed etiam ex arboribus educit umores. itaque quae sunt in apricis regionibus spissis venarum crebritatibus solidatae, raritatemque non habentes ex umore cum in materiem perdolantur, reddunt magnas utilitates ad vetustatem. ideo infernates, quod ex apricis locis adportantur, meliores sunt quam quae ab opacis de supernatibus advehuntur.
passages.translation: Trees growing on slopes exposed to the sun, by contrast, lack those moisture-filled voids. Dried and consolidated by the sun, which draws moisture from both earth and trees, they develop a dense structure. Hewn into timber, they provide great durability. Infernas fir is therefore better than supernas because it comes from sunny places, whereas supernas comes from shaded ones.

passages.latin: Quantum animo considerare potui, de copiis quae sunt necessariae in aedificiorum comparationibus et quibus temperaturis e rerum natura principiorum habere videantur mixtionem quaeque insunt in singulis generibus virtutes et vitia, uti non sint ignota aedificantibus exposui. ita qui potuerint eorum praeceptorum sequi praescriptiones erunt prudentiores, singulorumque generum usum eligere poterunt in operibus. ergo quoniam de apparitionibus est explicatum, in ceteris voluminibus de ipsis aedificiis exponetur, et primum de deorum inmortalium aedibus sacris et de earum symmetriis et proportionibus, uti ordo postulat, insequenti perscribam.
passages.translation: I have explained, as far as I could judge, the supplies needed in building, the mixtures of natural principles that compose them, and the strengths and weaknesses of each kind, so that builders may understand them. Those who follow these precepts will be better able to choose the appropriate use of each material. Having dealt with the preparations, I shall explain the buildings themselves in the following books, beginning, as the order requires, with the sacred temples of the immortal gods and their symmetriae and proportions.

passages.latin: Delphicus Apollo Socratem omnium sapientissimum Pythiae responsis est professus. Is autem memoratur prudenter doctissimeque dixisse, oportuisse hominum pectora fenestrata et aperta esse, uti non occultos haberent sensus sed patentes ad considerandum. Utinam vero rerum natura sententiam eius secuta explicata et apparentia ea constituisset! Si enim ita fuisset, non solum laudes aut vitia animorum ad manum aspicerentur, sed etiam disciplinarum scientiae sub oculorum consideratione subiectae non incertis iudiciis probarentur, sed et doctis et scientibus auctoritas egregia et stabilis adderetur ipsique artifices pellicerent sua prudentia, ⟨qui, etiam⟩si non pecunia sint copiosi seu vetustate officinarum habuerint notitiam aut etiam gratia forensi et eloquentia, cum fuerint parati, pro industria studiorum auctoritates possent habere, ut eis, quod profitentur scire, id crederetur. Igitur quoniam haec non ita, sed uti natura rerum voluit, sunt constituta, non efficitur, ut possint homines obscuratis sub pectoribus ingeniis scientias artificiorum penitus latentes, quemadmodum sint, iudicare.
passages.translation: The Delphic Apollo, through the responses of the Pythia, proclaimed Socrates the wisest of all men. Socrates is remembered as having said, with prudence and great learning, that men’s breasts ought to have been fitted with windows and left open, so that their thoughts would not remain hidden but be exposed to examination. Would that nature had followed his judgment and made them manifest and visible! Then not only would the merits or faults of minds be seen at a glance, but the knowledge of the various disciplines, placed before the eyes for examination, would not be exposed to uncertain judgments. The learned and knowledgeable would receive firm and lasting authority, and craftsmen themselves would attract confidence through their understanding: even if they were not wealthy, known through the long standing of their workshops, or furnished with favor in the forum and eloquence, their preparation would win authority commensurate with their diligent studies, so that people would believe that they knew what they professed to know. Since things are constituted otherwise, as nature willed, and men’s talents remain concealed within their breasts, people cannot judge the knowledge peculiar to each art, which lies deeply hidden.

passages.latin: Maxime autem id animadvertere possumus ab antiquis statuariis et pictoribus, quod ex his, qui dignitatis notas et commendationis gratiam habuerunt, aeterna memoria ad posteritatem sunt permanentes, uti Myron, Polycletus, Phidias, Lysippus ceterique, qui nobilitatem ex arte sunt consecuti. Namque ut civitatibus magnis aut regibus aut civibus nobilibus opera fecerunt, ita id sunt adepti. At qui non minore studio et ingenio sollertiaque fuerunt nobilibus et humili fortuna civibus non minus egregie perfecta fecerunt opera, nullam memoriam sunt adsecuti, quod hi non ab industria neque artis sollertia sed a felicitate fuerunt deserti, ut Hegias Atheniensis, Chion Corinthius, Myagrus Phocaeus, Pharax Ephesius, Boedas Byzantius etiamque alii plures. Non minus item pictores, uti Aristomenes Thasius, Polycles et Androcydes ⟨Cyzice⟩ni, Theo Magnes ceterique, quos neque industria neque artis studium neque sollertia defecit, sed aut rei familiaris exiguitas aut inbecillitas fortunae seu in ambitione certationis contrariorum superatio obstitit eorum dignitati.
passages.translation: This can be seen above all in the sculptors and painters of old. Those who enjoyed marks of distinction and the favor of recommendation remain in everlasting memory among posterity—Myron, Polyclitus, Phidias, Lysippus and the others who won renown through their art. They achieved it because they made works for great cities, kings or noble citizens. Others, with no less zeal, talent and skill, made works no less admirably finished for citizens both noble and of modest means, yet obtained no remembrance: they were forsaken not by diligence or artistic skill, but by good fortune. Such were Hegias of Athens, Chion of Corinth, Myagrus of Phocaea, Pharax of Ephesus, Boedas of Byzantium and many more. Likewise among painters there were Aristomenes of Thasos, Polycles and Androcydes of Cyzicus, Theon of Magnesia and the others, who lacked neither diligence, artistic commitment nor skill, but whose standing was obstructed by a small patrimony, adverse fortune or the superiority of rivals in the competition for distinction.

passages.latin: Nec tamen est admirandum, si propter ignotitiam artis virtutes obscurantur, sed maxime indignandum, cum etiam saepe eblandiatur gratia conviviorum a veris iudiciis falsam probationem. Ergo, uti Socrati placuit, si ita sensus et sententiae scientiaeque disciplinis auctae perspicuae et perlucidae fuissent, non gratia neque ambitio valeret, sed si qui veris certisque laboribus doctrinarum pervenissent ad scientiam summam, eis ultro opera traderentur. Quoniam autem ea non sunt inlustria neque apparentia in aspectu, ut putamus oportuisse, et animadverto potius indoctos quam doctos gratia superare, non esse certandum iudicans cum indoctis ambitione, potius his praeceptis editis ostendam nostrae scientiae virtutem.
passages.translation: It is no wonder that merit is obscured through ignorance of the art; but it is especially a cause for indignation when favor won at banquets often coaxes a false approval from true judgment. As Socrates wished, had perceptions, opinions and knowledge enriched by the disciplines been clear and transparent, neither favor nor ambition would prevail: works would be entrusted spontaneously to those who had attained the highest knowledge through genuine and sound scholarly labor. Since these things are neither manifest nor visible, as we think they ought to be, and I observe that the unlearned more often surpass the learned through favor, I judge that I should not compete with the unlearned in ambition. I shall instead show the worth of our knowledge by publishing these precepts.

passages.latin: Itaque, imperator, in primo volumine tibi de arte et quas habeat ea virtutes quibusque disciplinis oporteat esse auctum architectum exposui, et subieci causas quid ita earum oporteat eum esse peritum, rationesque summae architecturae partitione distribui finitionibusque terminavi. deinde quod erat primum et necessarium, de moenibus quemadmodum eligantur loci salubres ratiocinationibus explicui, ventique qui sint et e quibus <regionibus> singuli spirant deformationibus grammicis ostendi, platearumque et vicorum uti emendate fiant distributiones in moenibus docui et ita finitionem primo volumine constitui. item in secundo de materia quas habeat in operibus utilitates et quibus virtutibus e natura rerum est comparata peregi. nunc in tertio de deorum inmortalium aedibus sacris dicam et uti oportet perscriptas exponam.
passages.translation: Accordingly, Emperor, in the first book I set forth for you what the art is, what virtues it possesses, and in what disciplines the architect ought to be trained; I added the reasons why he must be skilled in them, distributed the whole of architecture by a division, and defined it by definitions. Then, treating what was first and most necessary, I explained by reasoned argument how, in laying out city walls, to choose healthy sites; I showed by linear diagrams which the winds are and from what regions each blows; I taught how the streets and lanes within the walls may be correctly laid out, and so brought the first book to a close. In the second I dealt with materials—what advantages they afford in works, and with what qualities Nature has endowed them. Now, in the third, I shall speak of the sacred temples of the immortal gods and set them forth, as is fitting, in full detail.

passages.latin: Aedium compositio constat ex symmetria, cuius rationem diligentissime architecti tenere debent. ea autem paritur a proportione, quae graece ἀναλογία dicitur. proportio est ratae partis membrorum in omni opere totiusque commodulatio, ex qua ratio efficitur symmetriarum. namque non potest aedis ulla sine symmetria atque proportione rationem habere compositionis, nisi uti hominis bene figurati <> membrorum habuerit exactam rationem.
passages.translation: The composition of temples depends on symmetria, whose principles architects must observe with the greatest care. Symmetria arises from proportion, which the Greeks call analogia (ἀναλογία). Proportion is the commensuration of the members and the whole of a work with a determined part as their common measure; from it the system of commensurability is established. No temple can have a coherent composition without symmetria and proportion, unless its members stand in an exact relationship comparable to that of a well-formed human body.

passages.latin: Corpus enim hominis ita natura composuit, uti os capitis a mento ad frontem summam et radices imas capilli esset decimae partis, item manus pansa ab articulo ad extremum medium digitum tantundem, caput a mento ad summum verticem octavae, cum cervicibus imis ab summo pectore ad imas radices capillorum sextae, ⟨a medio pectore⟩ ad summum verticem quartae. Ipsius autem oris altitudinis tertia est pars ab imo mento ad imas nares, nasum ab imis naribus ad finem mediûm superciliorum tantundem, ab ea fine ad imas radices capilli frons efficitur item tertiae partis. Pes vero altitudinis corporis sextae, cubitum quartae, pectus item quartae. Reliqua quoque membra suas habent commensus proportiones, quibus etiam antiqui pictores et statuarii nobiles usi magnas et infinitas laudes sunt adsecuti.
passages.translation: For nature has so composed the human body that the face, from the chin to the top of the forehead at the roots of the hair, is a tenth part of the stature; the outstretched hand, from the wrist to the tip of the middle finger, as much again. The head, from the chin to the crown, is an eighth part; from the top of the breast, including the neck, to the roots of the hair, a sixth; and from the middle of the breast to the crown, a fourth. Of the height of the face itself, a third runs from the base of the chin to the underside of the nose; the nose, from its base to the line of the brows, as much again; and thence to the roots of the hair the forehead is formed, likewise a third. The foot is a sixth part of the body's height; the forearm a fourth; and the breast likewise a fourth. The other members too have their proportions of commensurability, of which the ancient painters and the celebrated sculptors availed themselves to win great and boundless praise.

passages.latin: similiter vero sacrarum aedium membra ad universam totius magnitudinis summam ex partibus singulis convenientissimum debent habere commensus responsum.
passages.translation: item corporis centrum medium naturaliter est umbilicus. namque si homo conlocatus fuerit supinus manibus et pedibus pansis circinique conlocatum centrum in umbilico eius, circumagendo rotundationem utrarumque manuum et pedum digiti linea tangentur. non minus quemadmodum schema rotundationis in corpore efficitur, item quadrata designatio in eo invenietur. nam si a pedibus imis ad summum caput mensum erit eaque mensura relata fuerit ad manus pansas, invenietur eadem latitudo uti altitudo, quemadmodum areae quae ad normam sunt quadratae.

passages.latin: ergo si ita natura composuit corpus hominis uti proportionibus membra ad summam figurationem eius respondeant, cum causa constituisse videntur antiqui ut etiam in operum perfectionibus singulorum membrorum ad universam figurae speciem habeant commensus exactionem. igitur cum in omnibus operibus ordines traderent, <> maxime in aedibus deorum, <⟨quod eorum⟩> operum et laudes et culpae aeternae solent permanere.
passages.translation: Therefore, if nature has so composed the human body that its members answer proportionally to the whole figure, the ancients seem to have established with good reason that in the execution of works too each of the members should keep an exact commensurability with the aspect of the whole figure. And so, though they handed down orders of proportion for works of every kind, they did so above all in the temples of the gods, whose merits and faults are wont to endure for ever.

passages.latin: Nec minus mensurarum rationes, quae in omnibus operibus videntur necessariae esse, ex corporis membris collegerunt, uti digitum, palmum, pedem, cubitum, et eas distribuerunt in perfectum numerum, quem Graeci τέλειον dicunt. Perfectum autem antiqui instituerunt numerum qui decem dicitur; namque ex manibus digitorum numero [ab palmo pes] est inventus. Si autem in utrisque palmis ex articulis ab natura decem sunt perfecti, etiam Platoni placuit esse eum numerum ea re perfectum, quod ex ⟨X⟩ singularibus rebus, quae μονάδες apud Graecos dicuntur, perficitur decusis. Simul autem undecim aut duodecim sunt facti, quod superaverint, non possunt esse perfecti, donec ad alterum decusis perveniant; singulares enim res particulae sunt eius numeri.
passages.translation: They also derived from the members of the body the units of measure required in every work—the finger, palm, foot and cubit—and distributed them according to the perfect number, which the Greeks call teleion (τέλειον). The ancients established ten as the perfect number, for it was discovered from the number of fingers on the hands. Since the fingers articulated in both hands amount by nature to ten, Plato too considered ten perfect because the decad is completed from ten single units, called monades (μονάδες) by the Greeks. Once eleven or twelve is reached, however, the excess cannot be perfect until the second decad is attained; single units are particles of that number.

passages.latin: Mathematici vero contra disputantes ea re perfectum dixerunt esse numerum qui sex dicitur, quod is numerus habet partitiones eorum rationibus sex numero convenientes sic: sextantem unum, trientes duo, semissem tria, besem quem δίμοιρον dicunt quattuor, quintarium quem πεντάμοιρον dicunt quinque, perfectum sex. Cum ad duplicationem crescat, supra sex adiecto asse ἔφεκτον; cum facta sunt octo, quod est tertia adiecta, tertiarium alterum, qui ἐπίτριτος dicitur; dimidia adiecta cum facta sunt novem, sesquialterum, qui ἡμιόλιος appellatur; duabus partibus additis et decusis facto bes alterum, quem ἐπιδίμοιρον vocitant; in undecim numero quod adiecti sunt quinque, quintarium, quem ἐπίπεμπτον dicunt; duodecim autem, quod ex duobus numeris simplicibus est effectus, διπλάσιονα.
passages.translation: The mathematicians, arguing the contrary, called six the perfect number because its constituent divisions correspond to it: a sixth is one, a third two and a half three; two-thirds, called dimoiron (δίμοιρον), are four; five-sixths, called pentamoiron (πεντάμοιρον), are five; and the complete number is six. In the progression beyond six, adding one produces seven, the ephekton (ἔφεκτον); adding a third produces eight, the epitritos (ἐπίτριτος); adding a half produces nine, the sesquialter or hemiolios (ἡμιόλιος); adding two-thirds produces ten, the epidimoiron (ἐπιδίμοιρον); adding five produces eleven, the epipempton (ἐπίπεμπτον); and twelve, made from two complete sixes, is diplasion (διπλάσιον), the double.

passages.latin: Non minus etiam, quod pes hominis altitudinis sextam habet partem, (ita etiam, ex eo quod perficitur pedum numero corporis ⟨altitudo, veteribus columnis basis scapi elata⟩ sexies altitudines terminavit) eum perfectum constituerunt, cubitumque animadverterunt ex sex palmis constare digitisque XXIIII. Ex eo etiam videntur civitates Graecorum fecisse, quemadmodum cubitus est sex palmorum, in drachma, qua nummo uterentur, aereos signatos uti asses ex aequo sex, quos obolos appellant, quadrantesque obolorum, quae alii dichalca, nonnulli trichalca dicunt, pro digitis viginti quattuor in drachma constituisse.
passages.translation: They also regarded six as perfect because the human foot is a sixth of the body’s height (the body’s height is completed by six foot-lengths; likewise, in ancient columns, the height of the shaft with its base was determined as sixfold). They observed that the cubit comprises six palms and twenty-four fingers. The Greek cities appear to have followed the same pattern: just as the cubit contains six palms, they established six equally valued bronze pieces, like asses, in the drachma which they used as currency, calling them obols; quarter-obols, called dichalca by some and trichalca by others, numbered twenty-four to the drachma, corresponding to the fingers.

passages.latin: Nostri autem primo fecerunt ⟨perfectum⟩ antiquum numerum et in denario denos aeris constituerunt, et ea re compositio nominis ad hodiernum diem denarium retinet. Etiamque quarta pars quod efficiebatur ex duobus assibus et tertio semisse, sestertium vocitaverunt. Postea autem quam animadverterunt utrosque numeros esse perfectos, et sex et decem, utrosque in unum coiecerunt et fecerunt perfectissimum decusis sexis. Huius autem rei auctorem invenerunt pedem. E cubito enim cum dempti sunt palmi duo, relinquitur pes quattuor palmorum, palmus autem habet quattuor digitos. Ita efficitur, ut habeat pes sedecim digitos et totidem asses aeracius denarius.
passages.translation: Our own people, on the other hand, first adopted the ancient perfect number and fixed ten bronze asses to the denarius; and hence the composition of the name preserves to this day the 'denarius.' And the quarter part, which was made up of two asses and a semis, they called the sestertius. But afterwards, observing that both numbers were perfect—six and ten—they combined them into one and formed the most perfect number, sixteen. Of this they found the foot to be the author: for, when two palms are taken from the cubit, there remains the foot of four palms, and the palm has four fingers; so it comes about that the foot has sixteen fingers, and the denarius as many bronze asses.

passages.latin: Ergo si convenit ex articulis hominis numerum inventum esse et ex membris separatis ad universam corporis speciem ratae partis commensus fieri responsum, relinquitur ut suspiciamus eos qui etiam aedes deorum inmortalium constituentes ita membra operum ordinaverunt ut proportionibus et symmetriis separatae atque universae convenientes efficerentur eorum distributiones.
passages.translation: Therefore, if it is agreed that number was found from the joints of the human body, and that between the several members and the whole aspect of the body there is a correspondence of commensurability according to a determined part, it remains for us to admire those who, in building the temples of the immortal gods also, so ordered the members of their works that, taken severally and together, they might be made concordant in their proportions and symmetries throughout the distribution of the whole edifice.

passages.latin: Aedium autem principia sunt e quibus constat figurarum aspectus. ea primum in antis, quod graece ναὸς ἐν παραστάσιν dicitur, deinde prostylos, amphiprostylos, peripteros, pseudodipteros, <dipteros,> hypaethros. horum exprimuntur formationes his rationibus.
passages.translation: Archaeological note — III.2, temple types. Vitruvius classifies temples by the arrangement of their columns: in antis (naos en parastasin), prostyle, amphiprostyle, peripteral, pseudodipteral, dipteral and hypaethral. Archaeology illustrates each type: Vitruvius himself exemplifies the in antis temple, with two columns between the antae, by the “Three Fortunes” near Rome’s Colline Gate; the peripteral scheme, with six columns at the front and eleven on each side, is that of the canonical Greek temple; the pseudodipteral arrangement, octastyle with a single row where a double row could stand, is exemplified by the temple of Diana at Magnesia, by Hermogenes of Alabanda, and that of Apollo, by Menesthes; the dipteral, with its double colonnade, and the hypaethral, decastyle and open to the sky, complete the sequence. The pseudoperipteral type—columns engaged in the cella wall to simulate a peripteral arrangement, defined by Vitruvius in 4.8—was the most widespread in the Roman world. Its best-preserved examples are the temple of Portunus in the Forum Boarium, Ionic and dating to the late second century BC, and above all the Maison Carrée at Nîmes, a Corinthian hexastyle prostyle temple of around AD 2, the world’s best-preserved Roman temple.

passages.latin: in antis erit aedes, cum habebit in fronte antas parietum qui cellam circumcludunt, et inter antas in medio columnas duas, supraque fastigium symmetria ea conlocatum quae in hoc libro fuerit perscripta. huius autem exemplar erit ad tres Fortunas ex tribus quod est proxime portam Collinam.
passages.translation: A temple is in antis when the front has the antae of the walls enclosing the cella, with two columns between them and a pediment above, arranged according to the symmetria prescribed in this book. Of the three temples at the Three Fortunes, the one nearest the Colline Gate provides an example.

passages.latin: prostylos omnia habet quemadmodum in antis, columnas autem contra antas angulares duas, supraque epistylia quemadmodum et in antis, et dextra ac sinistra in versuris singula. huius exemplar est in insula Tiberina in aede Iovis et Fauni.
passages.translation: The prostyle has all the features of the in antis temple, but with two corner columns opposite the antae and architraves above, as in the in antis, with a single architrave return on each side, right and left. An example stands on Tiber Island, in the temple of Jupiter and Faunus.

passages.latin: amphiprostylos omnia habet ea quae prostylos, praetereaque habet in postico ad eundem modum columnas et fastigium.
passages.translation: The amphiprostyle has all that the prostyle has, and besides, at the rear, columns and a pediment arranged in the same way.

passages.latin: Peripteros autem erit, quae habebit in fronte et postico senas columnas, in lateribus cum angularibus undenas. Ita autem sint hae columnae conlocatae, ut intercolumnii latitudinis intervallum sit a parietibus circum ad extremos ordines columnarum, habeatque ambulationem circa cellam aedis, quemadmodum est sine postico in porticu Metelli Iovis Statoris Hermodori et Mariana Honoris et Virtutis a Mucio facta.
passages.translation: A peripteral temple has six columns at the front and rear, and eleven on each side including the corner columns. Arrange them so that a space equal to one intercolumniation separates the walls from the outer rows of columns all around, providing a walk around the cella. The examples, without a rear part in the adopted wording, are the temple of Jupiter Stator by Hermodorus in the Portico of Metellus and Marius’s temple of Honor and Virtue, built by Mucius.

passages.latin: Pseudodipteros autem sic conlocatur, ut in fronte et postico sint columnae octonae, in lateribus cum angularibus quinae denae. Sint autem parietes cellae contra quaternas columnas medianas in fronte et postico. Ita duorum intercolumniorum et imae crassitudinis columnae spatium erit ab parietibus circa ad extremos ordines columnarum. Huius exemplar Romae non est, sed Magnesiae Dianae Hermogenis Alabandei et Apollinis a Menesthe facta.
passages.translation: The pseudodipteral is arranged with eight columns at the front and rear, and fifteen on each side including the corner columns. The cella walls stand opposite the four central columns at the front and rear. A space of two intercolumniations plus the lower column diameter thus lies between the walls and the outer rows of columns all around. There is no example at Rome, but there is the temple of Diana at Magnesia, the work of Hermogenes of Alabanda, and that of Apollo, built by Menesthes.

passages.latin: dipteros autem octastylos et pronao et postico, sed circa aedem duplices habet ordines columnarum, uti est aedis Quirini dorica et Ephesi Dianae ionica a Chersiphrone constituta.
passages.translation: The dipteral is octastyle both in the pronaos and at the rear, but about the temple it has double rows of columns—as is the temple of Quirinus, of the Doric order, and that of Diana at Ephesus, of the Ionic order, built by Chersiphron.

passages.latin: hypaethros vero decastylos est in pronao et postico. reliqua omnia eadem habet quae dipteros, sed interiore parte columnas in altitudine duplices, remotas a parietibus ad circumitionem ut porticus peristyliorum. medium autem sub divo est sine tecto. Aditus valvarum ex utraque parte in pronao et postico. huius item exemplar Romae non est, sed Athenis octastylos ex templo Olympio.
passages.translation: The hypaethral temple is decastyle in the pronaos and at the rear. In all other respects it resembles the dipteral, but inside it has columns in two tiers, set away from the walls to provide a circuit like the porticoes of peristyles. The center is open to the sky and unroofed. There are doorways at both ends, in the pronaos and at the rear. There is no example at Rome; at Athens the text gives the octastyle temple of Olympian Zeus.

passages.latin: Species autem aedium sunt quinque, quarum ea sunt vocabula: pycnostylos, id est crebris columnis, systylos paulo remissioribus, diastylos amplius quam oportet inter se diductis, araeostylos spatiis intercolumniorum patentibus rare, eustylos intervallorum iusta distributione.
passages.translation: There are five kinds of temples, whose names are these: pycnostyle, with closely set columns; systyle, with somewhat greater spacing; diastyle, with the columns farther apart than is fitting; araeostyle, with wide and sparse intercolumniations; and eustyle, with a just distribution of the intervals.

passages.latin: ergo pycnostylos est cuius intercolumnio unius et dimidiatae columnae crassitudo interponi potest, quemadmodum est divi Iulii et in Caesaris foro Veneris et si quae aliae sic sunt compositae. item systylos est in qua duarum columnarum crassitudo in intercolumnio poterit conlocari, et spirarum plinthides aeque magnae sint ei spatio quod fuerit inter duas plinthides, quemadmodum est Fortunae Equestris ad theatrum lapideum reliquaeque quae eisdem rationibus sunt compositae.
passages.translation: Thus the pycnostyle is that in whose intercolumniation the thickness of one and a half columns can be inserted, as in the temple of the Divine Julius, that of Venus in Caesar's forum, and any others composed in this way. The systyle, in turn, is that in whose intercolumniation the thickness of two columns can be placed, and in which the plinths of the bases are as large as the space that lies between two plinths, as in the temple of Fortuna Equestris, near the stone theater, and the rest composed on the same principles.

passages.latin: haec utraque genera vitiosum habent usum. matres enim familiarum cum ad supplicationem gradibus ascendunt, non possunt per intercolumnia amplexae adire nisi ordines fecerint, item valvarum aspectus abstruditur columnarum crebritate ipsaque signa obscurantur, item circa aedem propter angustias inpediuntur ambulationes.
passages.translation: Both these kinds have a faulty use. For the matrons, when they mount the steps in supplication, cannot pass through the intercolumniations arm in arm, but only in single file; moreover, the view of the doors is obstructed by the crowding of the columns, and the statues themselves are darkened; and likewise, owing to the narrowness, the walks around the temple are impeded.

passages.latin: diastyli autem haec erit compositio, cum trium columnarum crassitudinem intercolumnio interponere possumus, tamquam est Apollinis et Dianae aedis. haec dispositio hanc habet difficultatem quod epistylia propter intervallorum magnitudinem franguntur.
passages.translation: The arrangement of the diastyle will be this: when we can interpose in the intercolumniation the thickness of three columns, as in the temple of Apollo and Diana. This disposition has the drawback that the architraves break on account of the great width of the intervals.

passages.latin: In araeostylis autem nec lapideis nec marmoreis epistyliis uti datur, sed inponendae de materia trabes perpetuae. Et ipsarum aedium species sunt varicae, barycephalae, humiles, latae, ornanturque signis fictilibus aut aereis inauratis earum fastigia tuscanico more, uti est ad Circum Maximum Cereris et Herculis Pompeiani, item Capitolii.
passages.translation: In araeostyles it is not possible to use architraves of stone or marble; instead, continuous timber beams must be laid on. The very aspect of such temples is splayed, top-heavy, low and broad, and their pediments are adorned with figures of terracotta or gilded bronze, in the Tuscan manner—as in the temple of Ceres near the Circus Maximus, that of Hercules Pompeianus, and the Capitol.

passages.latin: Reddenda nunc est eustyli ratio, quae maxime probabilis et ad usum et ad speciem et ad firmitatem rationes habet explicatas. namque facienda sunt in intervallis spatia duarum columnarum et quartae partis columnae crassitudinis, mediumque intercolumnium unum quod erit in fronte, alterum quod in postico, trium columnarum crassitudine. sic enim habebit et figurationis aspectum venustum et aditus usum sine inpeditionibus et circa cellam ambulatio auctoritatem.
passages.translation: It now remains to set forth the method of the eustyle, which is the most commendable and has the principles of use, appearance, and stability fully worked out. For in the intervals there must be made spaces of two and a quarter column-thicknesses, and a single central intercolumniation—one at the front and one at the rear—of three column-thicknesses. For thus it will have at once a graceful aspect in its figure, a convenient and unhindered approach, and a dignity in the walk about the cella.

passages.latin: huius autem rei ratio explicabitur sic. frons loci quae in aede constituta fuerit, si tetrastylos facienda fuerit, dividatur in partes XI S praeter crepidines et proiecturas spirarum, si sex erit columnarum, in partes XVIII. si octastylos constituetur, dividatur in XXIV et semissem. item ex his partibus sive tetrastyli sive hexastyli sive octastyli una pars sumatur eaque erit modulus. cuius moduli unus erit crassitudinis columnarum. intercolumnia singula, praeter media, modulorum duorum et moduli quartae partis. mediana in fronte et postico singula ternûm modulorum. ipsarum columnarum altitudo modulorum VIIII et dimidiae moduli partis. ita ex ea divisione intercolumnia altitudinesque columnarum habebunt iustam rationem.
passages.translation: The method of this will be explained as follows. The front of the site laid out for the temple, if it is to be tetrastyle, let it be divided into 11½ parts, excluding the crepidines (steps or platform margins) and the projections of the column bases; if it is of six columns, into 18 parts; if octastyle is to be set out, into 24½. Then, from these parts—whether of a tetrastyle, a hexastyle, or an octastyle—let one be taken, and that will be the module. The thickness of the columns will be one module. The intercolumniations, except the central ones, will each be two and a quarter modules; the central ones, at front and rear, three modules each. The height of the columns themselves will be nine and a half modules. Thus, by this division, the intercolumniations and the heights of the columns will keep a just proportion.

passages.latin: huius exemplar Romae nullum habemus, sed in Asia Teo hexastylon Liberi Patris. Eas autem symmetrias constituit Hermogenes, qui etiam primus invenit octastylon pseudodipterive rationem. ex dipteri enim aedis symmetria distulit interiores ordines columnarum XXXIV eaque ratione sumptus operasque compendii fecit. is in medio ambulationi laxamentum egregie circa cellam fecit, de aspectuque nihil inminuit sed sine desiderio supervacuorum conservavit auctoritatem totius operis distributione.
passages.translation: Of this we have no example at Rome, but in Asia the hexastyle of Father Liber at Teos. These symmetries were established by Hermogenes, who was also the first to devise the method of the octastyle pseudodipteral. For from the symmetry of the dipteral temple he removed the inner rows of columns, thirty-four in number, and by this means he saved expense and labor. In the middle he made an admirable open ambulatory about the cella, and in no way diminished the appearance; rather, without any want of the superfluous, he preserved the dignity of the whole work in its distribution.

passages.latin: Pteromatos enim ratio et columnarum circum aedem dispositio ideo est inventa, ut aspectus propter asperitatem intercolumniorum habeat auctoritatem, praeterea, si ex ⟨improviso⟩ imbrium aquae vis occupaverit et intercluserit hominum multitudinem, ut habeat in aede circaque cellam cum laxamento liberam moram. Haec autem ut explicantur in pseudodipteris aedium dispositionibus! Quare videtur acuta magnaque sollertia effectus operum Hermogenes fecisse reliquisseque fontes, unde posteri possent haurire disciplinarum rationes.
passages.translation: For the principle of the pteroma and the arrangement of columns about the temple was devised so that the appearance might have dignity through the relief created by the intercolumniations, and further, that if a sudden downpour of rain should overtake and shut in a throng of people, they might have within the temple and about the cella an ample and free place to wait. All this is worked out thus in the arrangements of pseudodipteral temples. Wherefore Hermogenes seems to have acted with keen and great sagacity in the execution of his works, and to have left springs from which posterity might draw the principles of the disciplines.

passages.latin: Aedibus araeostylis columnae sic sunt faciendae uti crassitudines earum sint partis octavae ad altitudines. item in diastylo dimetienda est altitudo columnae in partes octo et dimidiam et unius partis columnae crassitudo conlocetur. in systylo altitudo dividatur in novem et dimidiam partem et ex eis una ad crassitudinem columnae detur. item in pycnostylo dividenda est altitudo in ⟨partes⟩ decem et eius una pars facienda est columnae crassitudo. eustyli autem aedis columnae, uti systyli, in novem partes altitudo dividatur et dimidiam partem et eius una pars constituatur in crassitudine imi scapi. ita habebitur pro rata parte intercolumniorum ratio.
passages.translation: In araeostyle temples the columns are to be made so that their thickness is an eighth part of their height. Likewise in the diastyle, let the height of the column be divided into eight and a half parts, and let the thickness of the column be one part. In the systyle, let the height be divided into nine and a half parts, and of these let one be given to the thickness of the column. Likewise in the pycnostyle, the height is to be divided into ten, and one part of it made the thickness of the column. In the eustyle temple, as in the systyle, let the height be divided into nine and a half parts, and let one of them be fixed as the thickness of the lower shaft. Thus the proportion will be had according to the kind of intercolumniation.

passages.latin: quemadmodum enim crescunt spatia inter columnas, proportionibus adaugendae sunt crassitudines scaporum. namque si in araeostylo nona aut decima pars crassitudinis fuerit, tenuis et exilis apparebit, ideo quod per latitudinem intercolumniorum aer consumit et inminuit aspectu scaporum crassitudinem; contra vero pycnostylis, si octava pars crassitudinis fuerit, propter crebritatem et angustias intercolumniorum tumidam et invenustam efficiet speciem. itaque generis operis oportet persequi symmetrias. etiamque angulares columnae crassiores faciendae sunt ex sua diametro quinquagesima parte, quod eae ab aere circumciduntur et graciliores videntur esse aspicientibus. ergo quod oculus fallit, ratiocinatione est exaequandum.
passages.translation: For as the spaces between the columns increase, the thicknesses of the shafts must be enlarged in proportion. For if in the araeostyle the thickness were a ninth or a tenth part, the column will appear thin and slender, because through the width of the intercolumniations the air consumes and diminishes the diameter of their thickness to the view. Contrariwise, in pycnostyles, if the thickness were an eighth part, on account of the frequency and narrowness of the intercolumniations it will produce a swollen and graceless appearance. One must therefore pursue the symmetries proper to each kind of work. Moreover, the corner columns are to be made thicker by a fiftieth part of their diameter, because they are cut round by the air and appear more slender to those who behold them. Therefore what the eye deceives must be redressed by calculation.

passages.latin: contracturae autem in summis columnarum hypotracheliis ita faciendae videntur uti si columna sit ab minimo ad pedes quinos denos, ima crassitudo dividatur in partes sex et earum partium quinque summa constituatur. item quae erit ab quindecim pedibus ad pedes viginti, scapus imus in partes sex et semissem dividatur earumque partium quinque et semisse superior crassitudo columnae fiat. item quae erunt a pedibus viginti ad pedes triginta, scapus imus dividatur in partes septem earumque sex summa contractura perficiatur. quae autem ab triginta pedibus ad quadraginta alta erit, ima dividatur in partes septem et dimidiam, ex his sex et dimidiam in summo habeat contracturae rationem. quae erunt ab quadraginta pedibus ad quinquaginta, item dividendae sunt in octo partes et earum septem in summo scapo sub capitulo contrahantur. item si quae altiores erunt, eadem ratione pro rata constituantur contracturae.
passages.translation: The diminution at the tops of columns, in the hypotrachelia, should be made as follows. For a column up to fifteen feet high, divide the lower diameter into six parts and make the upper diameter five of them. For a column from fifteen to twenty feet, divide the lower shaft into six and a half parts and make the upper diameter five and a half. For columns from twenty to thirty feet, divide the lower shaft into seven parts and complete the upper diminution with six. For a column from thirty to forty feet high, divide the lower diameter into seven and a half parts and give the top six and a half. For columns from forty to fifty feet, divide the lower diameter into eight parts and diminish the top of the shaft, below the capital, to seven. For taller columns, establish the diminution proportionally by the same principle.

passages.latin: haec autem propter altitudinis intervallum, scandentis oculi species, adiciuntur crassitudinibus temperaturae. venustates enim persequitur visus, cuius si non blandimur voluptati proportione et modulorum adiectionibus, uti quod fallitur temperatione adaugeatur, vastus et invenustus conspicientibus remittetur aspectus. de adiectione quae adicitur in mediis columnis, quae apud Graecos ἔντασις appellatur, in extremo libro erit forma et ratio eius quemadmodum mollis et conveniens efficiatur subscripta.
passages.translation: These compensating adjustments are added to the thicknesses on account of the interval of height, as the eye ascends. For sight pursues beauty, and if we do not flatter its pleasure by proportion and by additions of modules—so that what deceives may be augmented by compensation—the aspect will be rendered coarse and graceless to beholders. As for the addition made in the middle of the columns, which among the Greeks is called entasis (ἔντασις), at the end of the book its form and method will be set down, showing how it is made soft and fitting.

passages.latin: Fundationes eorum operum fodiantur, si queat inveniri, ad solidum et in solido, quantum ex amplitudine operis pro ratione videbitur, extruaturque structura totum solum quam solidissima. Supraque terram parietes extruantur sub columnas dimidio crassiores quam columnae sunt futurae, uti firmiora sint inferiora superioribus; quae stereobates appellantur, nam excipiunt onera. Spirarumque proiecturae non procedant extra solidum; item supra parietis ad eundem modum crassitudo servanda est. Intervalla autem concamaranda aut solidanda festucationibus, uti distineantur.
passages.translation: The foundations of these works must be dug, if solid ground can be found, down to and into it, to a depth proportionate to the magnitude of the work; the whole foundation area must be built up with masonry as solid as possible. Above ground, raise walls beneath the columns one-half thicker than the columns are to be, so that the lower parts are stronger than the upper. These are called stereobates, since they receive the loads. The projections of the bases must not extend beyond the solid support; the wall thickness must likewise be maintained above. The spaces between must be vaulted or consolidated by ramming, so that they are held apart.

passages.latin: sin autem solidum non invenietur, sed locus erit congesticius ad imum aut paluster, tunc is locus fodiatur exinaniaturque et palis alneis aut oleagineis aut robusteis ustilatis configatur, sublicaque machinis adigatur quam creberrime, carbonibusque expleantur intervalla palorum et tunc structuris solidissimis fundamenta impleantur. extructis autem fundamentis ad libramentum stylobatae sunt conlocandi.
passages.translation: If solid ground cannot be found, and the site consists of fill down to the bottom or is marshy, dig out and empty the place. Drive in charred stakes of alder, olive or oak, using machines to set the piles as closely together as possible; fill the spaces between them with charcoal, then fill the foundations with exceptionally solid masonry. Once the foundations have been constructed, set the stylobates level.

passages.latin: supra stylobatas columnae disponendae quemadmodum supra scriptum est, sive in pycnostylo quemadmodum pycnostyla, sive systylo aut diastylo aut eustylo quemadmodum supra scripta sunt et constituta. in araeostylis enim libertas est quantum cuique libet constituendi. sed ita columnae in peripteris conlocentur uti quot intercolumnia sunt in fronte, totidem bis intercolumnia fiant in lateribus. ita enim erit duplex longitudo operis ad latitudinem. namque qui columnarum duplicationes fecerunt erravisse videntur, quod unum intercolumnium in longitudine plus quam oporteat procurrere videtur.
passages.translation: On the stylobates arrange the columns as prescribed above for the pycnostyle, systyle, diastyle or eustyle. In araeostyles there is freedom to establish whatever spacing one wishes. In peripteral temples, however, arrange the columns so that the sides have twice as many intercolumniations as the front; the length of the work will thus be twice its breadth. Those who doubled the number of columns appear to have erred, because the length extends one intercolumniation farther than it should.

passages.latin: Gradus in fronte constituendi ita sunt, uti sint semper inpares; namque cum dextro pede primus gradus ascendatur, item in summo templo primus erit ponendus. Crassitudines autem eorum graduum ita finiendas censeo, ut neque crassiores dextante nec tenuiores dodrante sint conlocatae; sic enim durus non erit ascensus. Retractiones autem graduum nec minus quam sesquipedales nec plus quam bipedales faciendae videntur. Item si circa aedem gradus futuri sunt, ad eundem modum fieri debent.
passages.translation: The steps at the front must always be odd in number: since the first step is mounted with the right foot, the same foot must be placed first at the top of the temple. I consider that the risers should be no higher than a dextans and no lower than a dodrans, that is, five-sixths and three-quarters of a foot respectively, so that the ascent is not difficult. The treads should be no less than one and a half feet and no more than two feet. Steps around the temple must be made in the same way.

passages.latin: sin autem circa aedem ex tribus lateribus podium faciendum erit, id constituatur uti quadrae spirae trunci coronae lysis ad ipsum stylobatam qui erit sub columnarum spiris conveniant. stylobatam ita oportet exaequari uti habeat per medium adiectionem per scamillos inpares. si enim ad libellam dirigetur, alveolatum oculo videbitur. hoc autem ut scamilli ad id convenientes fiant, item in extremo libro forma et demonstratio erit descripta.
passages.translation: If a podium is to be built around three sides of the temple, its plinths, bases, dado blocks, cornices and lysis molding must correspond to the stylobate beneath the column bases. The stylobate should be leveled with a rise at its center by means of scamilli impares; if it is set strictly level, it will appear hollow to the eye. A figure and demonstration of how the scamilli are to be adapted for this purpose will likewise be drawn at the end of the book.

passages.latin: His perfectis in suis locis spirae conlocentur, eaeque ad symmetriam sic perficiantur, uti crassitudo cum plintho sit columnae ex dimidia crassitudine proiecturamque, quam Graeci ἐκφοράν vocitant, habeant S extantem: ita tum lata et longa erit columnae crassitudinis unius et dimidiae.
passages.translation: When these parts are complete, set the column bases in position and proportion them so that their height, including the plinth, is half the column’s diameter. They are to have the projection called ekphora (ἐκφορά) in Greek of […]; their overall width and length will thus be one and a half column diameters.

passages.latin: altitudo eius si atticurges erit, ita dividatur ut superior pars tertia parte sit crassitudinis columnae, reliquum plintho relinquatur. dempta plintho reliquum dividatur in partes quattuor fiatque superior torus quartae, reliquae tres aequaliter dividantur et una sit inferior torus, altera pars cum suis quadris scotia, quam Graeci τροχίλον dicunt.
passages.translation: If the base is Attic, divide its height so that the upper part is one-third of the column diameter, leaving the remainder for the plinth. Excluding the plinth, divide what remains into four parts and make the upper torus one part. Divide the other three equally between the lower torus and the scotia with its fillets, which the Greeks call trochilus (τροχίλος).

passages.latin: sin autem ionicae erunt faciendae, symmetriae earum sic erunt constituendae uti latitudo spirae quoqueversus sit columnae crassitudinis adiecta ⟨e⟩ crassitudine quarta et octava, altitudo ita uti atticurges, item et eius plinthos, reliquumque praeter plinthum, quod erit tertia pars crassitudinis columnae, dividatur in partes septem. inde trium partium torus qui est in summo, reliquae quattuor partes dividendae sunt aequaliter et una pars fiat cum suis astragalis et supercilio superior trochilus, altera pars inferiori trochilo relinquatur, sed inferior maior apparebit ideo quod habebit ad extremam plinthum proiecturam. astragali faciendi sunt octavae partis trochili. proiectura erit spirae pars octava et sexta decuma pars crassitudinis columnae.
passages.translation: But if Ionic bases are to be made, their symmetries are to be established thus: that the width of the base, in every direction, be the thickness of the column plus a quarter and an eighth of that thickness. The height, as in the Attic, and likewise its plinth; and the remainder, apart from the plinth—which will be a third of the column's thickness—let it be divided into seven parts. Of these, three for the torus that is at the top; let the remaining four be divided equally, and let one part, with its astragals and its fillet, be made the upper trochilus, and the other part left for the lower trochilus. But the lower will appear larger, because it will have its projection out to the edge of the plinth. The astragals are to be made of an eighth part of the trochilus; the projection will be an eighth plus a sixteenth of the column’s diameter.

passages.latin: Spiris perfectis et conlocatis columnae sunt medianae in pronao et postico ad perpendiculum medii centri conlocandae, angulares autem quaeque e regione earum futurae sunt in lateribus aedis dextra ac sinistra, uti partes interiores, quae ad parietes cellae spectant, ad perpendiculum latus habeant conlocatum, exteriores autem partes †uti dicant se earum contracturam. Sic enim erunt figurae compositionis aedium contractura eius tali ratione exactae.
passages.translation: When the bases have been completed and set in place, position the central columns of the pronaos and the rear part plumb through their central axes. The corner columns and those aligned with them along the temple’s right and left sides must have their inner faces, towards the cella walls, set vertically, while their outer faces †show their diminution†.
