I too should wish the subject of our studies to permit such expansiveness, so that greater length might enhance the authority of these teachings; but this is less straightforward than one might suppose. Architecture cannot be written about in the same way as history or poetry. History holds the reader’s attention through the prospect of varied new events; poetry, through its meters, rhythms, elegant arrangement of words and speeches assigned to different characters, carries the reader’s attention smoothly to the conclusion of the work.

passages.latin: id autem in architecturae conscriptionibus non potest fieri, quod vocabula ex artis propria necessitate concepta inconsueto sermone obiciunt sensibus obscuritatem. cum ergo ea per se non sint aperta nec pateant eorum in consuetudine nomina, tum etiam praeceptorum late vagantes scripturae, si non contrahentur, ut paucis et perlucidis sententiis explicentur, frequentia multitudineque sermonis inpediente incertas legentium efficient cogitationes. itaque occultas nominationes commensusque e membris operum pronuntians, ut memoriae tradantur, breviter exponam. sic enim expeditius ea recipere poterunt mentes.
passages.translation: Architectural writing cannot achieve the same effect, because the technical vocabulary required by the art is unfamiliar and difficult for readers. If the exposition also wanders at length instead of being compressed into a few clear statements, the quantity of words will confuse their understanding. I shall therefore explain unfamiliar terms and the measured relationships of architectural members briefly, so that they can be remembered and more readily understood.

passages.latin: non minus cum animadvertissem distentam occupationibus civitatem publicis et privatis negotiis, paucis iudicavi scribendum, uti angusto spatio vacuitatis ea legentes breviter percipere possent. Etiamque Pythagorae quique eius haeresim fuerunt secuti placuit cybicis rationibus praecepta in voluminibus scribere, constitueruntque cybum CCXVI versus eosque non plus tres in una conscriptione oportere esse putaverunt.
passages.translation: Seeing also that the citizens were occupied with public and private affairs, I judged that I should write briefly, so that they could grasp my subject during their limited leisure. Pythagoras and the followers of his school likewise chose to set down their precepts in books on a cubic principle: they made one cube consist of 216 verses and thought that no more than three such units should appear in a single composition.

passages.latin: Cybus autem est corpus ex lateribus aequali latitudine planitiarum perquadratum. is cum est iactus, quam in partem incubuit dum est intactus inmotam habet stabilitatem, uti sunt etiam tesserae quas in alveo ludentes iaciunt. hanc autem similitudinem ex eo sumpsisse videntur quod is numerus versuum uti cybus in quemcumque sensum insederit, inmotam efficiat ibi memoriae stabilitatem. Graeci quoque poetae comici interponentes e choro canticum diviserunt spatia fabularum. ita partes cybica ratione facientes intercapedinibus levant actorum pronuntiationes.
passages.translation: A cube is a solid bounded by equal square faces. When thrown, it remains stable on whichever face it rests, provided it is left untouched, like the dice cast by players into a gaming tray. The comparison seems to have been adopted because this number of verses, once established in the mind as a cube rests on a face, would give memory a similar stability. Greek comic poets also divided their plays by inserting songs for the chorus. By organizing the parts on a cubic principle, they relieved the actors’ delivery with intervals.

passages.latin: Cum ergo haec naturali modo sint a maioribus observata animoque advertam inusitatas et obscuras multis res esse mihi scribendas, quo facilius ad sensus legentium pervenire possint, brevibus voluminibus iudicavi scribere. ita enim expedita erunt ad intellegendum. eorumque ordinationes institui uti non sint quaerentibus separatim colligenda, sed e corpore uno et in singulis voluminibus generum haberent explicationes. itaque, Caesar, tertio et quarto volumine aedium sacrarum rationes exposui, hoc libro publicorum locorum expediam dispositiones. primumque forum uti oporteat constitui dicam, quod in eo et publicarum et privatarum rerum rationes per magistratus gubernantur.
passages.translation: Since our predecessors observed these principles in a natural way, and since I must discuss matters unfamiliar and obscure to many readers, I have chosen to write short books that make them easier to understand. I have arranged the material so that readers need not gather it from separate sources: the work forms a single body, with each book explaining a particular class of subjects. Thus, Caesar, after setting out the principles of sacred buildings in the third and fourth books, I shall explain the arrangement of public places in this one. I shall begin with the forum, where magistrates administer public and private affairs.

passages.latin: Graeci in quadrato amplissimis et duplicibus porticibus fora constituunt crebrisque columnis et lapideis aut marmoreis epistyliis adornant et supra ambulationes in contignationibus faciunt. Italiae vero urbibus non eadem est ratione faciendum, ideo quod a maioribus consuetudo tradita est gladiatoria munera in foro dari.
passages.translation: The Greeks raised large double porticoes in the agora and adorned them with closely set columns and with epistyles of stone or marble, and above they made walkways over the floors. But in the cities of Italy this should not be done in the same way, because it is a custom handed down by the ancestors to give gladiatorial shows in the forum.

passages.latin: igitur circum spectacula spatiosiora intercolumnia distribuantur circaque in porticibus argentariae tabernae maenianaque superioribus coaxationibus conlocentur, quae et ad usum et ad vectigalia publica recte erunt disposita. Magnitudines autem ad copiam hominum oportet fieri, ne parvum spatium sit ad usum aut ne propter inopiam populi vastum forum videatur. latitudo autem ita finiatur uti longitudo in tres partes cum divisa fuerit, ex his duae partes ei dentur. ita enim erit oblonga eius formatio et ad spectaculorum rationem utilis dispositio.
passages.translation: Therefore the spaces between the columns around the area used for spectacles should be wider. Bankers’ shops should be arranged in the surrounding porticoes, with viewing galleries on the upper floors, so that the whole serves its intended uses and provides public revenue.

passages.latin: columnae superiores quarta parte minores quam inferiores sunt constituendae, propterea quod oneri ferendo quae sunt inferiora firmiora debent esse quam superiora, non minus quod etiam nascentium oportet imitari naturam, ut in arboribus teretibus, abiete cupresso pinu, e quibus nulla non crassior est ab radicibus, dein decrescendo progreditur in altitudinem naturali contractura peraequata nascens ad cacumen. ergo si natura nascentium ita postulat, recte est constitutum et altitudinibus et crassitudinibus superiora inferiorum fieri contractiora.
passages.translation: The upper columns should be one-quarter smaller than the lower ones. The members carrying the load below must be stronger, and the arrangement should also follow the growth of trees: fir, cypress and pine are thicker at the roots and narrow naturally toward the top. Since this is the pattern of growth, the upper members are appropriately reduced in both height and thickness.

passages.latin: Basilicarum loca adiuncta foris quam calidissimis partibus oportet constitui, ut per hiemem sine molestia tempestatium se conferre in eas negotiatores possint. Earumque latitudines ne minus quam ex tertia, ne plus ex dimidia longitudinis constituantur, nisi si loci natura inpedierit et aliter coegerit symmetriam commutari. Sin autem locus erit amplior in longitudine, chalcidica in extremis constituantur, uti sunt in Iulia Aquiliana.
passages.translation: The sites of the basilicas, adjoined to the fora, should be established on the warmest sides, so that in winter the merchants may resort to them without the annoyance of storms. Their widths should be set at no less than a third and no more than half of their length, unless the nature of the site prevents it and compels the symmetry to be otherwise altered. But if the site is more ample in length, let chalcidica be placed at the ends, as they are in the Julia Aquiliana.

passages.latin: Columnae basilicarum tam altae, quam porticus latae fuerint, faciendae videntur; porticus, quam medium spatium futurum est, ex tertia finiatur. Columnae superiores minores quam inferiores, uti supra scriptum est, constituantur. Pluteum, quod fuerit inter superiores et inferiores columnas, item quarta parte minus, quam superiores columnae fuerint, oportere fieri videtur, uti supra basilicae contignationem ambulantes ab negotiatoribus ne conspiciantur. Epistylia, zophora, coronae ex symmetriis columnarum, uti in tertio libro diximus, explicentur.
passages.translation: The columns of the basilicas appear to be as tall as the width of the portico; the gallery, which will be the space in between, should be completed from the third level. The upper columns should be smaller than the lower ones, as described above. The shelf, which was between the upper and lower columns, also a quarter shorter than the upper columns, seems to have been necessary so as not to be seen by the merchants walking on the basilica floor. The architraves (epistylia), friezes (zophora), and cornices are set out according to the symmetries of the columns, as we said in the third book.

passages.latin: Non minus summam dignitatem et venustatem possunt habere comparationes basilicarum quo genere Coloniae Iuliae Fanestri conlocavi curavique faciendam, cuius proportiones et symmetriae sic sunt constitutae. mediana testudo inter columnas est longa pedes CXX, lata pedes LX. porticus eius circa testudinem inter parietes et columnas lata pedes XX. columnae altitudinibus perpetuis cum capitulis pedes L, crassitudinibus quinûm, habentes post se parastaticas altas pedes XX, latas pedes II S, crassas I S, quae sustinent trabes in quibus invehuntur porticuum contignationes. supraque eas aliae parastaticae pedum XVIII, latae binûm, crassae pedem, quae excipiunt item trabes sustinentes cantherium et porticûm, quae sunt summissa infra testudinem, tecta.
passages.translation: No less can comparisons of the basilicas of the kind I have placed and taken care to build in the Colonia Julia Fanestri, the proportions and symmetries of which are thus established. The central hall (testudo) between the columns is 120 feet long, 60 feet wide. Its portico around the dome between the walls and columns is 20 feet wide. The columns are of continuous heights with capitals of 50 feet, five feet thick, having behind them parastatics 20 feet high, 25 feet wide, and 15 feet thick, which support the beams on which the floors of the porticoes are carried. And above them other parastatics 18 feet, two feet wide, and a foot thick, which also accommodate the beams supporting the cantherium and the roofs of the porticoes, which are lowered below the dome.

passages.latin: reliqua spatia inter parastaticarum et columnarum trabes per intercolumnia luminibus sunt relicta. columnae sunt in latitudine testudinis cum angularibus dextra ac sinistra quaternae, in longitudine quae est foro proxima cum isdem angularibus octo, ex altera parte cum angularibus VI, ideo quod mediae duae in ea parte non sunt positae ne inpediant aspectus pronai aedis Augusti, quae est in medio latere parietis basilicae conlocata spectans medium forum et aedem Iovis,
passages.translation: The remaining spaces, between the beams of the pilasters and those of the columns, are left open through the intercolumniations to admit light. Across the width of the nave (testudo) the columns are four on each side, counting the corner ones, right and left; along the long side nearest the forum, eight with the same corner columns; and on the other side, six, because the two central columns were not set on that side, so as not to block the view of the pronaos of the temple of Augustus, which stands in the middle of the basilica’s side wall, facing the center of the forum and the temple of Jupiter.

passages.latin: item tribunal quod est in ea aede hemicycli schematis minoris curvatura formatum. eius autem hemicycli in fronte est intervallum pedes XLVI, introrsus curvatura pedes XV, uti qui apud magistratus starent negotiantes in basilica ne inpedirent. supra columnas ex tribus tignis bipedalibus compactis trabes sunt circa conlocatae. eaeque ab tertiis columnis quae sunt in interiore parte revertuntur ad antas quae a pronao procurrunt dextraque et sinistra hemicyclium tangunt.
passages.translation: Likewise, the tribunal in that hall is formed with the curvature of a hemicycle of a lesser segment. The front of this hemicycle is forty-six feet across, and its curvature inward fifteen feet, so that those who stood before the magistrates might not obstruct those doing business in the basilica. Above the columns, beams made of three two-foot timbers joined together are placed around; and these, from the third columns which are on the inner side, return to the antae that run forward from the pronaos and touch the hemicycle on the right and left.

passages.latin: supra trabes contra capitula ex fulmentis dispositae pilae sunt conlocatae altae pedes III, latae quoqueversus quaternis. supra eas ex duobus tignis bipedalibus trabes everganeae circa sunt conlocatae. quibus insuper transtra cum capreolis columnarum contra corpora et antas et parietes pronai conlocata sustinent unum culmen perpetuae basilicae, alterum a medio supra pronaum aedis.
passages.translation: Above the beams, opposite the capitals and set upon brackets, piers (pilae) are placed, three feet high and four feet wide each way. Upon these, made of two two-foot timbers, beams are laid running round about. And upon these, the cross-beams with the struts (capreoli) of the columns, set against the shafts, the antae and the walls of the pronaos, support two ridge-beams: one running the whole length of the basilica, the other rising from the center over the pronaos of the temple.

passages.latin: ita fastigiorum duplex pectinata dispositio extrinsecus tecti et interioris altae testudinis praestat speciem venustam. item sublata epistyliorum ornamenta et pluteorum columnarumque superiorum distributio operosam detrahit molestiam sumptusque inminuit ex magna parte summam. ipsae vero columnae in altitudine perpetua sub trabes testudinis perductae et magnificentiam inpensae et auctoritatem operi adaugere videntur.
passages.translation: Thus the double arrangement of the roof-pediments, so produced, presents a beautiful appearance both on the exterior of the roof and within the high vaulted nave (testudo). Moreover, the omission of the ornaments of the architraves (epistylia), together with the arrangement of the parapets (plutei) and the upper columns, removes laborious work and greatly reduces the total cost. And the columns themselves, carried up in continuous height to the beams of the vault, seem to add magnificence to the outlay and authority to the work.

passages.latin: Aerarium, carcer, curia foro sunt coniungenda, sed ita uti magnitudo ⟨ac⟩ symmetriae eorum foro respondeant. maxime quidem curia in primis est facienda ad dignitatem municipii sive civitatis. et si quadrata erit, quantum habuerit latitudinis dimidia addita constituatur altitudo, sin autem oblonga fuerit, longitudo et latitudo componatur et summae compositae, eius dimidia pars sub lacunariis altitudini detur.
passages.translation: The treasury, the prison, and the senate-house (curia) should adjoin the forum, but so that the magnitude of their symmetry answers to the forum. Above all the curia is to be built in keeping with the dignity of the municipality or city. If it is square, let its height be established by adding to its width the half of that width; but if it is oblong, let its length and width be added together, and of that total sum let the half be given to the height, up to the coffered ceiling.

passages.latin: praeterea praecingendi sunt parietes medii coronis ex intestino opere aut albario ad dimidiam partem altitudinis. quae si non erunt, vox ibi disputantium elata in altitudinem intellectui non poterit esse audientibus. cum autem coronis praecincti parietes erunt, vox ab imis, morata priusquam in aera elata dissipabitur, auribus erit intellecta.
passages.translation: Furthermore, the walls are to be girded at mid-height by cornices of joinery (intestinum opus) or of stucco (albarium). For if these are lacking, the voice of those debating, rising into the height, cannot be understood by the listeners. But when the walls are girded with cornices, the voice, held back from below before it rises into the air and is dissipated, will be understood by the ears.

passages.latin: Cum forum constitutum fuerit, tum deorum inmortalium diebus festis ludorum spectationibus eligendus est locus theatro quam saluberrimus, uti in primo libro de salubritatibus in moenium conlocationibus est scriptum. per ludos enim cum coniugibus et liberis persedentes delectationibus detinentur et corpora propter voluptatem inmota patentes habent venas, in quas insidunt aurarum flatus, qui si a regionibus palustribus aut aliis regionibus vitiosis advenient, nocentes spiritus corporibus infundent. itaque si curiosius eligetur locus theatro, vitabuntur vitia.
passages.translation: Once the forum was established, then, in anticipation of the festivals of the immortal gods, a place as wholesome as possible should be chosen for the theater, as is written in the first book concerning the healthfulness of settlements within the walls. For during the games, those who sit with their wives and children are seized by pleasure, and their bodies are immobile because of it, and their veins are open, through which gusts of wind enter, which, if they come from marshy or other vicious regions, infuse their bodies with harmful spirits. Therefore, if the place for the theater is chosen with greater care, defects will be avoided.

passages.latin: etiamque providendum est ne impetus habeat a meridie. sol enim cum implet eius rotunditatem, aer conclusus curvatura neque habens potestatem vagandi versando confervescit et candens adurit excoquitque et inminuit e corporibus umores. ideo maxime vitandae sunt his rebus vitiosae regiones et eligendae salubres.
passages.translation: Care must also be taken that the hall does not receive the southern exposure. For when the sun fills the chamber with its heat, the air enclosed in the vault, having no way to circulate, boils and consumes with its vapor the sturdy parts of the bodies.

passages.latin: fundamentorum autem, si in montibus fuerint, facilior erit ratio, sed si necessitas coegerit in plano aut palustri loco ea constitui, solidationes substructionesque ita erunt faciendae, quemadmodum de fundationibus aedium sacrarum in tertio libro est scriptum. insuper fundamenta lapideis et marmoreis copiis gradationes ab substructione fieri debent.
passages.translation: But the arrangement of the foundations, if they are in the mountains, will be easier; but if necessity compels them to be established on a plain or in a marshy place, the consolidations and substructures will be made in the same way as is written about the foundations of the sacred buildings in the third book. Moreover, the foundations must be of stone and the steps of marble for the substructure.

passages.latin: praecinctiones ad altitudines theatrorum pro rata parte faciendae videntur, neque altiores quam quanta praecinctionis itineris sit latitudo. si enim excelsiores fuerint, repellent et eicient e superiore parte vocem nec patientur in sedibus suis, quae sunt supra praecinctiones, verborum casus certa significatione ad aures pervenire. et ad summam ita est gubernandum uti linea cum ad imum gradum et ad summum extenta fuerit, omnia cacumina graduum angulosque tangat. ita vox non inpedietur.
passages.translation: The praecinctiones (belts) should be made in proportion to the height of the theaters, and no higher than the width of the passage of the praecinctio; for if they were too high, they would drive the voice upward and would not let the endings of words reach with clarity the ears of those seated above the praecinctiones. In sum, it must be so governed that, when a line is drawn from the lowest step to the highest, it touches all the summits and angles of the steps: thus the voice will not be hindered.

passages.latin: aditus complures et spatiosos oportet disponere, nec coniunctos superiores inferioribus sed ex omnibus locis perpetuos et directos sine inversuris faciendos, uti cum populus dimittatur de spectaculis, ne comprimatur, sed habeat ex omnibus locis exitus separatos sine inpeditione. Etiam diligenter est animadvertendum ne sit locus surdus, sed ut in eo vox quam clarissime vagari possit. hoc vero fieri ita poterit, si locus electus fuerit ubi non inpediatur resonantia.
passages.translation: It is necessary to provide several spacious entrances, and not to connect the upper and lower ones, but to make them continuous and direct from all areas without any obstacles, so that when people leave the performances, they should not be cramped, but have separate exits from all areas without obstruction. Care must also be taken to ensure that it is not a soundproof space, but that the voice can travel through it as clearly as possible. This can only be achieved if a location has been chosen where echoes are not lingering.

passages.latin: vox autem est spiritus fluens aeris, e tactu sensibilis auditu. ea movetur circulorum rotundationibus infinitis, uti si in stantem aquam lapide inmisso nascantur innumerabiles undarum circuli crescentes, a centro quam latissime possint et vagantes, nisi angustia loci interpellaverit aut aliqua offensio quae non patitur designationes earum undarum ad exitus pervenire. itaque cum interpellentur offensionibus, primae redundantes insequentium disturbant designationes.
passages.translation: But the voice is like a flowing breath of air, and it is truly perceptible to the ear. It moves through the endless roar of the circles, as if a stone were thrown into stagnant water; countless circles of waves are born, growing from the center as wide as they can, and wandering, unless the narrowness of the place interrupts them or some offense prevents the designs of these waves from reaching their outlet. And so, when they are interrupted by offenses, the first overflow of the following ones disturbs their designs.

passages.latin: eadem ratione vox item ad circinum efficit motiones, sed in aqua circuli planitiae in latitudine moventur, vox et in latitudine progreditur et altitudinem gradatim scandit. igitur ut in aqua undarum designationibus, item in voce cum offensio nulla primam undam interpellaverit, non disturbat secundam nec insequentes, sed omnes sine resonantia perveniunt ad imorum et ad summorum aures.
passages.translation: In the same way, the voice makes its movements as if traced by a compass (ad circinum). But whereas in water the circles move in breadth over the flat surface, the voice advances at once in breadth and ascends gradually in height. Therefore, as with the waves on the surface of water, so with the voice: when the first wave meets no obstacle, it does not impede the second or the third, but all reach, without resonance, the ears of those below and those above.

passages.latin: ergo veteres architecti naturae vestigia persecuti indagationibus vocis scandentis theatrorum perfecerunt gradationes, et quaesierunt per canonicam mathematicorum et musicam rationem ut quaecumque vox esset in scaena, clarior et suavior ad spectatorum perveniret aures. uti enim organa aeneis lamminis aut corneis ἠχεῖα ad chordarum sonitûm claritatem perficiuntur, sic theatrorum per harmonicen ad augendam vocem ratiocinationes ab antiquis sunt constitutae.
passages.translation: Therefore, the ancient architects, following the steps of nature, investigating the rising sound of theaters, completed the gradations, and sought, through the canonical method of mathematics and music, that whatever voice was on the stage, it should reach the ears of the spectators in a clear and sweet manner. For just as organs are made of brass plates or ox horns for the clarity of the heart's sound, so the ancients established the reasoning of theaters to augment the voice through harmonics.

passages.latin: Harmonice autem est musica litteratura obscura et difficilis, maxime quidem quibus graecae litterae non sunt notae. quam si volumus explicare, necesse est etiam graecis verbis uti, quod nonnulla eorum latinas non habent appellationes. itaque ut potuero quam apertissime ex Aristoxeni scripturis interpretabor et eius diagramma subscribam finitionesque sonituum designabo, uti qui diligentius attenderit facilius percipere possit.
passages.translation: Harmonic theory is a difficult and obscure branch of learning, especially for those unfamiliar with Greek. To explain it, we must use Greek terms, since some have no Latin equivalents. I shall therefore interpret the writings of Aristoxenus as clearly as I can and set out his diagram and the limits of the notes, so that attentive readers may understand them more readily.

passages.latin: vox enim mutationibus cum flectitur alias fit acuta alias gravis, duobusque modis movetur, e quibus unus effectus habet continuatos, alter distantes. continuata vox neque in finitionibus consistit neque in loco ullo, efficitque terminationes non apparentes, intervalla autem media apparentia, uti sermone cum dicamus sol lux flos vox. nunc enim nec unde incipit nec ubi desinit intellegitur, sed quod ex acuta facta est gravis et ex gravi acuta, apparet auribus. per distantiam autem e contrario. namque cum flectitur inmutatione vox statuit se in alicuius sonitus finitione, deinde in alterius, et id ultro citro crebre faciendo ⟨non⟩ constans apparet sensibus, uti in cantionibus cum flectentes vocem varietatem facimus modulationis. itaque intervallis ea cum versatur, et unde initium fecit et ubi desiit apparet in sonorum patentibus finitionibus, medianis autem patentia intervallis obscurantur.
passages.translation: As the voice changes inflection, it becomes high or low and moves in two ways: continuously or by distinct intervals. Continuous movement settles at no fixed pitch; its boundaries are imperceptible, although the intervening movement is audible, as when we say sol, lux, flos, vox in ordinary speech. We do not identify its precise starting and stopping points, but the ear hears the change from high to low and from low to high. Movement by intervals is different. The voice settles at one definite pitch, then another, and repeatedly passes between them, as in singing when changes of pitch produce melodic variety. The beginnings and endings are then perceptible at the clearly defined notes, while the intervening passage is obscured by the intervals.

passages.latin: Genera vero sunt modulationum tria, primum quod Graeci nominant ἁρμονίην, secundum χρῶμα, tertium διάτονον. est autem harmoniae modulatio ab arte concepta, et ea re cantio eius maxime gravem et egregiam habet auctoritatem. chroma subtili sollertia ac crebritate modulorum suaviorem habet delectationem. diatoni vero quod naturalis est, facilior est intervallorum distantia. in his tribus generibus dissimiles sunt tetrachordorum dispositiones, quod harmonia [tetrachordorum] et tonos et dihesis habet binas. dihesis autem est toni pars quarta, ita in hemitonio duae diheses sunt conlocatae. chromati duo hemitonia in ordine sunt composita, tertium trium hemitoniorum est intervallum; dia⟨tono⟩ toni duo sunt continuati, tertium hemitonium finit tetrachordi magnitudinem. ita in tribus generibus tetrachorda ex duobus tonis et hemitonio sunt peraequata, sed ipsa cum separatim uniuscuiusque generis finibus considerantur, dissimilem habent intervallorum designationem.
passages.translation: There are three genera of melody: the first, called harmonia by the Greeks, is the enharmonic; the second is chroma, the chromatic; and the third is the diatonic. The enharmonic is an artistic construction whose melody has a particularly grave and distinguished character. The chromatic offers a gentler pleasure through the subtle skill and closeness of its steps. The diatonic is natural and its intervals are easier to grasp. The tetrachords are divided differently in the three genera. The enharmonic contains two whole tones and two dieses; a diesis is one-quarter of a tone, so two dieses make a semitone. The chromatic has two successive semitones and a third interval of three semitones. The diatonic has two successive whole tones, with a final semitone completing the tetrachord. Each genus therefore spans two tones and a semitone, although the division of that span differs.

passages.latin: igitur intervalla tonorum et hemitoniorum et ⟨diheseon⟩ tetrachordorum in voce divisit natura finîtque terminationes eorum mensuris intervallorum quantitate, modisque certis distantibus constituit qualitates, quibus etiam artifices qui organa fabricant ex natura constitutis utendo comparant ad concentus convenientes eorum perfectiones.
passages.translation: Nature has divided the voice into the intervals of tones, semitones and dieses within the tetrachords, fixing their limits by the size of the intervals and establishing distinct qualities at definite distances. Instrument makers use these natural divisions to bring their finished instruments into consonance.

passages.latin: Sonitus, qui graece φθόγγοι dicuntur, in unoquoque genere sunt X et VIII, e quibus VIII sunt in tribus generibus perpetui et stantes, reliqui X cum communiter modulantur sunt vagantes. stantes autem sunt qui inter mobiles [sunt] interpositi, continent tetrachordi coniunctionem et e generum discriminibus suis finibus sunt permanentes, appellantur autem sic, proslambanomenos, hypate hypaton, hypate meson, mese, nete synhemmenon, paramese, nete diezeugmenon, nete hyperbolaeon. mobiles autem sunt qui in tetrachordo inter inmotos dispositi in generibus ex locis loca mutant, vocabula autem habent haec, parhypate hypaton, lichanos hypaton, parhypate meson, lichanos meson, trite synhemmenon, <paranete synhemmenon,> trite diezeugmenon, paranete diezeugmenon, trite hyperbolaeon, paranete hyperbolaeon.
passages.translation: The notes, called phthongoi (φθόγγοι) in Greek, number eighteen in each genus. Eight remain fixed in all three genera; the other ten are movable when the genera are considered together. The fixed notes, interposed among the movable ones, maintain the connection of the tetrachords and retain their positions as the genera change. Their names are proslambanomenos, hypate hypaton, hypate meson, mese, nete synhemmenon, paramese, nete diezeugmenon and nete hyperbolaeon. The movable notes occupy positions between the fixed notes within a tetrachord and change their places with the genus. They are parhypate hypaton, lichanos hypaton, parhypate meson, lichanos meson, trite synhemmenon, ⟨paranete synhemmenon⟩, trite diezeugmenon, paranete diezeugmenon, trite hyperbolaeon and paranete hyperbolaeon.

passages.latin: ei autem qua moventur, recipiunt virtutes alias, intervalla enim et distantias habent crescentes. itaque parhypate, quae in harmonia distat ab hypate <dimidium> hemitonium, in chroma transmutata habet hemitonium. quae lichanos in harmonia dicitur, ab hypate distat hemitonium, in chroma translata progreditur duo hemitonia, in diatono distat ab hypate tria hemitonia. ita X sonitus propter translationes in generibus efficiunt triplicem modulationum varietatem.
passages.translation: The movable notes acquire different properties as their intervals and distances increase. Thus parhypate, which in the enharmonic lies half a semitone above hypate, lies a semitone above it in the chromatic. Lichanos is a semitone above hypate in the enharmonic, two semitones above it in the chromatic, and three in the diatonic. Through their changes of position in the genera, these ten notes produce three different arrangements of melody.

passages.latin: Tetrachorda autem sunt quinque: primum gravissimum, quod graece dicitur ὕπατον, secundum medianum, quod appellatur μέσον, tertium coniunctum, quod συνημμένον dicitur, quartum disiunctum, quod διεζευγμένον nominatur, quintum, quod est acutissimum, graece ὑπερβόλαιον dicitur. Concentus, quos natura hominis modulari potest, graece quae συμφωνίαι dicuntur, sunt sex: diatessaron, diapente, diapason, et disdiatessaron, et disdiapente, et disdiapason.
passages.translation: There are five tetrachords: the lowest, called hypaton (ὕπατον); the middle, meson (μέσον); the conjunct, synhemmenon (συνημμένον); the disjunct, diezeugmenon (διεζευγμένον); and the highest, hyperbolaion (ὑπερβόλαιον). The consonances that the human voice can produce, called symphonies (συμφωνίαι) in Greek, are six: diatessaron, diapente, diapason, disdiatessaron, disdiapente and disdiapason.

passages.latin: ideoque et a numero nomina ceperunt, quod cum vox constiterit in una sonorum finitione ab eaque se flectens mutaverit et pervenerit in quartam terminationem, appellatur diatessaron, in quintam diapente [in sextam diapason, in octavam et dimidiam diapason et diatessaron, in nonam et dimidiam diapason diapente, in XII disdiapason].
passages.translation: These consonances take their names from number. When the voice starts at a definite note and moves to the fourth position, the interval is called diatessaron; when it reaches the fifth, diapente. [The following numerical sequence is excluded from the constituted Latin text: at the sixth, diapason; at the eighth and a half, diapason and diatessaron; at the ninth and a half, diapason and diapente; at the twelfth, disdiapason.]

passages.latin: non enim inter duo intervalla, cum chordarum sonitus aut vocis cantus factus fuerit, nec inter tria aut sex aut septem possunt consonantiae fieri, sed uti supra scriptum est, diatessaron et diapente et ex ordine ad disdiapason convenientiae ex natura vocis congruentis habent finitiones, et ei concentus procreantur ex coniunctione sonituum [qui graece φθόγγοι dicuntur].
passages.translation: Consonance does not arise at the second or third interval, or at the sixth or seventh, whether produced by strings or by the singing voice. Rather, as explained above, the fourth and fifth and the sequence extending to the double octave have limits determined by the natural agreement of the voice. These consonances arise from the combination of notes [called phthongoi in Greek].

passages.latin: Ita ex his indagationibus mathematicis rationibus fiant vasa aerea pro ratione magnitudinis theatri eaque ita fabricentur ut cum tangantur, sonitum facere possint inter se diatessaron diapente et ex ordine ad disdiapason. postea inter sedes theatri constitutis cellis, ratione musica ibi conlocentur ita uti nullum parietem tangant circaque habeant locum vacuum et ab summo capite spatium, ponanturque inversa et habeant in parte quae spectat ad scaenam suppositos cuneos ne minus altos semipede, contraque eas cellas relinquantur aperturae inferiorum graduum cubilibus longae pedes duo, altae semipede.
passages.translation: On these principles, bronze vessels should be made by mathematical calculation in proportion to the size of the theater. They must be fashioned so that, when struck, they sound in relation to one another at a fourth, a fifth and successively up to the double octave. Vaulted chambers should then be built among the seats and the vessels placed in them according to musical principles. Each vessel must touch none of the surrounding walls and must have free space around it and above. Set the vessels upside down, supported on wedges at least half a foot high on the side facing the stage. Opposite the chambers, leave openings in the beds of the lower seating steps, two feet long and half a foot high.

passages.latin: designationes autem eorum, quibus in locis constituantur, sic explicentur. si non erit ampla magnitudine theatrum, media altitudinis transversa regio designetur et in ea tredecim cellae duodecim aequalibus intervallis distantes confornicentur, uti ea echea quae supra scripta sunt ad neten hyperbolaeon sonantia in cellis, quae sunt in cornibus extremis, utraque parte prima conlocentur, secunda ab extremis diatessaron ad neten diezeugmenon, tertia diatessaron ad paramesen, quarta ad neten synhemmenon, quinta diatessaron ad mesen, sexta diatessaron ad hypaten meson, in medio unum diatessaron ad hypaten hypaton.
passages.translation: Their positions should be laid out as follows. In a theater of modest size, mark a transverse line halfway up the seating and construct thirteen vaulted chambers along it, separated by twelve equal intervals. On each side, place first in the outermost chamber a vessel sounding nete hyperbolaeon. In the next chamber inward, place one a fourth away, sounding nete diezeugmenon; in the third, one a fourth away at paramese; in the fourth, one at nete synhemmenon; in the fifth, one a fourth away at mese; and in the sixth, one a fourth away at hypate meson. In the central chamber, place a single vessel a fourth away at hypate hypaton.

passages.latin: ita hac ratiocinatione vox a scaena uti ab centro profusa se circumagens tactuque feriens singulorum vasorum cava excitaverit auctam claritatem et concentu convenientem sibi consonantiam. sin autem amplior erit magnitudo theatri, tunc altitudo dividatur in partes IIII, uti tres efficiantur regiones cellarum transverse designatae, una harmoniae, altera chromatos, tertia diatoni. et ab imo quae erit prima, ea ex harmonia conlocetur ita uti in minore theatro supra scriptum est.
passages.translation: With this arrangement, the voice spreading from the stage as from a center strikes the hollow of each vessel and acquires greater clarity, producing through resonance a consonance in harmony with itself. In a larger theater, divide the height of the seating into four parts and arrange three transverse rows of chambers: one for the enharmonic genus, another for the chromatic and the third for the diatonic.

passages.latin: in mediana autem prima in extremis cornibus ad chromaticen hyperbolaeon habentia sonitum ponantur, in secundis ab his diatessaron ad chromaticen diezeugmenon, in tertiis ad chromaticen synhemmenon, quartis diatessaron ad chromaticen meson, quintis diatessaron ad chromaticen hypaton, sextis ad paramesen, quod et ad chromaticen hyperbolaeon diapente et ad chromaticen synhemmenon diatessaron habet consonantiae communitatem.
passages.translation: In the middle row, place at each outer end a vessel sounding chromatic hyperbolaeon. Place in the second chamber a vessel a fourth away at chromatic diezeugmenon; in the third, one at chromatic synhemmenon; in the fourth, one a fourth away at chromatic meson; in the fifth, one a fourth away at chromatic hypaton; and in the sixth, one at paramese. This last note has a fifth in common with chromatic hyperbolaeon and a fourth with chromatic synhemmenon.

passages.latin: in medio nihil est conlocandum, ideo quod sonitûm nulla alia qualitas in chromatico genere symphoniae consonantiam potest habere. in summa vero divisione et regione cellarum in cornibus primis ad diatonon hyperbolaeon fabricata vasa sonitu ponantur, in secundis diatessaron ad diatonon <diezeugmenon>, tertiis ad diatonon synhemmenon, quartis diatessaron ad diatonon meson, quintis diatessaron ad diatonon hypaton, sextis diatessaron ad proslambanomenon, in medio ad mesen, quod ea et ad proslambanomenon diapason et ad diatonon hypaton diapente habet symphoniarum communitates.
passages.translation: Nothing should be placed in the central chamber, since no other pitch in the chromatic genus can form the required consonance. In the upper row, place at the outer ends vessels sounding diatonic hyperbolaeon; in the second chambers, a fourth away at diatonic ⟨diezeugmenon⟩; in the third, at diatonic synhemmenon; in the fourth, a fourth away at diatonic meson; in the fifth, a fourth away at diatonic hypaton; and in the sixth, a fourth away at proslambanomenos. In the middle, place a vessel at mese, which forms an octave with proslambanomenos and a fifth with diatonic hypaton.

passages.latin: haec autem si qui voluerit ad perfectum facile perducere, animadvertat in extremo libro diagramma musica ratione designatum, quod Aristoxenus magno vigore et industria generatim divisis modulationibus constitutum reliquit. de quo si qui ratiocinationibus his attenderit, ad [naturas vocis et] audientium delectationes facilius valuerit theatrorum efficere perfectiones.
passages.translation: Anyone wishing to carry this arrangement through accurately should consult the musical diagram at the end of this book, which Aristoxenus established with great care and effort by distinguishing the melodic genera. Attention to that diagram and these calculations will make it easier to complete theaters that give pleasure to their listeners.

passages.latin: Dicet aliquis forte multa theatra quotannis Romae facta esse neque ullam rationem harum rerum in his fuisse, sed errabit in eo, quod omnia publica lignea theatra tabulationes habent complures, quas necesse est sonare. hoc vero licet animadvertere etiam ab citharoedis, qui superiore tono cum volunt canere, avertunt se ad scaenae valvas et ita recipiunt ab earum auxilio consonantiam vocis. cum autem ex solidis rebus theatra constituuntur, id est ex structura caementorum, lapide, marmore, quae sonare non possunt, tunc echeis hae rationes sunt explicandae.
passages.translation: Someone may object that many theaters are built in Rome each year without any provision of this kind. The objection overlooks the many boarded surfaces in public wooden theaters, which necessarily resonate. The same effect can be observed in cithara players: when they wish to sing in a higher register, they turn toward the stage doors and obtain support for the resonance of their voices. When theaters are built of solid materials—rubble masonry, stone or marble—which do not resonate in this way, the system of sounding vessels must be employed.

passages.latin: sin autem quaeritur in quo theatro ea sint facta, Romae non possumus ostendere sed in Italiae regionibus et in pluribus Graecorum civitatibus, etiamque auctorem habemus Lucium Mummium, qui diruto theatro Corinthiorum ea aenea Romam deportavit et de manubiis ad aedem Lunae dedicavit. multi etiam sollertes architecti, qui in oppidis non magnis theatra constituerunt, propter inopiam fictilibus doliis ita sonantibus electis hac ratiocinatione compositis perfecerunt utilissimos effectus.
passages.translation: If one asks in which theaters this arrangement has been used, we cannot point to an example at Rome, but there are examples in the regions of Italy and in many Greek cities. We also have the testimony of Lucius Mummius, who, after the destruction of the theater at Corinth, brought its bronze vessels to Rome and dedicated them from the spoils at the temple of Luna. Many resourceful architects working in small towns, unable to afford bronze, have selected earthenware jars with the appropriate tones and arranged them on these principles, obtaining highly useful results.

passages.latin: Ipsius autem theatri conformatio sic est facienda uti quam magna futura est perimetros imi, centro medio conlocato circumagatur linea rotundationis, in eaque quattuor scribantur trigona paribus lateribus ⟨quae paribus⟩ intervallis, extremam lineam circinationis tangant, quibus etiam in duodecim signorum caelestium <⟨astrologia⟩> astrologi ex musica convenientia astrorum ratiocinantur. ex his trigonis cuius latus fuerit proximum scaenae, ea regione qua praecidit curvaturam circinationis, ibi finiatur scaenae frons, et ab eo loco per centrum parallelos linea ducatur, quae disiungat proscaenii pulpitum et orchestrae regionem.
passages.translation: The configuration of the theater itself is to be made in such a way that, however large the perimeter will be, a line of the rounding (rotundatio) is described about the center placed in the middle, and four triangles are inscribed in it with equal sides and intervals, which touch the outermost line of the circumference, by which astrologers also reason from the concordance of the stars in the twelve celestial signs. From these triangles, the side of which is closest to the stage, in the region where it intersects the curvature of the circumference, the front of the stage is to end there, and from that place a parallel line is drawn through the center, which separates the stage platform of the proscenium and the region of the orchestra.

passages.latin: ita latius factum fuerit pulpitum quam Graecorum, quod omnes artifices in scaena dant operam, in orchestra autem senatorum sunt sedibus loca designata. et eius pulpiti altitudo sit ne plus pedum quinque, uti qui in orchestra sederint, spectare possint omnium agentium gestus. cunei spectaculorum in theatro ita dividantur uti anguli trigonorum, qui currunt circum curvaturam circinationis, dirigant ascensus scalasque inter cuneos ad primam praecinctionem, supra autem alternis itineribus superiores cunei medii dirigantur.
passages.translation: The stage-platform (pulpitum) should be made wider than that of the Greeks, because all the artists work on the stage. Places are designated for the seats of the senators in the orchestra. And the height of the stage platform should not exceed five feet, so that whoever sits in the orchestra can watch the movements of all the actors. The wedges of the spectacles in the theater should be divided in such a way that the corners of the triangles, which run around the curvature of the circumference, direct the ascents and stairs between the wedges to the first enclosure, and above all, the upper wedges in the middle should be directed by alternate routes.

passages.latin: Hi autem qui sunt in imo et dirigunt scalaria, erunt numero VII, reliqui quinque scaenae designabunt compositionem, et unus medius contra se valvas regias habere debet, et qui erunt dextra sinistra hospitaliorum designabunt compositionem, extremi duo spectabunt itinera versurarum. gradus spectaculorum ubi subsellia componantur ne minus alti sint palmopede, <ne plus pedem> et digitos sex, latitudines eorum ne plus pedes duo semis, ne minus pedes duo constituantur.
passages.translation: But those who are at the bottom and direct the stairs will be seven in number, the remaining five stages will designate the composition, and the one in the middle should have the royal doors opposite it, and those who will be on the right and left of the hospitals will designate the composition, the two outermost will watch the routes of the turns. The steps of the spectacles where the seats are arranged should be no less than a palm's breadth high, <no more than a foot> and six fingers, their widths should be no more than two and a half feet, no less than two feet.

passages.latin: tectum porticus quod futurum est in summa gradatione, cum scaenae altitudine libratum perficiatur, ideo quod vox crescens aequaliter ad summas gradationes et tectum perveniet. namque si non erit aequale, quo minus fuerit altum, vox praeripietur ad eam altitudinem quam perveniet primo.
passages.translation: The roof of the portico at the top of the seating should be level with the top of the stage building, so that the rising voice reaches the upper rows and the roof together. If these heights are unequal, the voice will be intercepted at the lower level it first encounters.

passages.latin: orchestra inter grados imos quod diametron habuerit, eius sexta pars sumatur, et in cornibus utrimque ad eius mensurae perpendiculum inferiores sedes praecidantur, et qua praecisio fuerit, ibi constituantur itinerum supercilia. ita enim satis altitudinem habebunt eorum confornicationes.
passages.translation: Take one-sixth of the diameter of the orchestra measured between the lowest seating tiers. At the two ends of the orchestra, cut back the lower seats vertically to this height and place the lintels of the passages at the resulting level. Their vaults will then have sufficient height.

passages.latin: scaenae longitudo ad orchestrae diametron duplex fieri debet. podii altitudo ab libramento pulpiti cum corona et lysi duodecumam orchestrae diametri. supra podium columnae cum capitulis et spiris altae quarta parte eiusdem diametri, epistylia et ornamenta earum columnarum altitudinis quinta parte. pluteum insuper cum unda et corona inferioris plutei dimidia parte. supra id pluteum columnae quarta parte minore altitudine sint quam inferiores, epistylium et ornamenta earum columnarum quinta parte. item si tertia episcenos futura erit, mediani plutei summum sit dimidia parte, columnae summae medianarum minus altae sint quarta parte, epistylia cum coronis earum columnarum item habeant altitudinis quintam partem.
passages.translation: The length of the stage building should be twice the diameter of the orchestra. The podium, including its crowning moldings, should rise one-twelfth of that diameter above the stage platform. The columns above it, including capitals and bases, should be one-quarter of the same diameter in height; their architraves and entablatures, one-fifth of the column height. The parapet above, including its cymatium and cornice, should be half the height of the lower parapet. The columns above this parapet should be one-quarter shorter than those below, with their entablatures one-fifth of their own height. If there is a third stage elevation, its upper parapet should be half the height of the middle parapet; the uppermost columns should be one-quarter shorter than the middle columns, and their architraves and cornices should likewise be one-fifth of the column height.

passages.latin: Nec tamen in omnibus theatris symmetriae ad omnes rationes et effectus possunt respondere, sed oportet architectum animadvertere quibus proportionibus necesse sit sequi symmetriam et quibus ad loci naturam aut magnitudinem operis temperari. sunt enim res quas et in pusillo et in magno theatro necesse est eadem magnitudine fieri propter usum, uti gradus diazomata pluteos itinera ascensus pulpita tribunalia et si qua alia intercurrunt ex quibus necessitas cogit discedere ab symmetria ne inpediatur usus. non minus si qua exiguitate copiarum, id est marmoris, materiae reliquarumque rerum quae parantur, in opere defuerint, paulum demere aut adicere, dum id ne nimium inprobe fiat sed cum sensu, non erit alienum. hoc autem erit si architectus erit usu peritus, praeterea ingenio mobili sollertiaque non fuerit viduatus.
passages.translation: Yet in all theaters symmetries cannot correspond to all reasons and effects, but the architect must observe with what proportions it is necessary to follow symmetry and with which to temper it to the nature of the place or the size of the work. For there are things which in both a small and a large theater it is necessary to make the same size for the sake of use, such as steps, diazomata, shelves, itinerant ascents, pulpits, tribunals, and if there are such things which intersect from which necessity compels a departure from symmetry lest use be hindered. Not less, if there is any scarcity of supplies, that is, of marble, materials, and other things which are prepared, in the work, a little should be taken away or added, provided that this is not done too improperly but with sense, it will not be out of place. This will be the case if the architect is skilled in use, and moreover is not deprived of mobile talent and skill.

passages.latin: Ipsae autem scaenae suas habent rationes explicitas ita uti mediae valvae ornatus habeant aulae regiae, dextra ac sinistra hospitalia, secundum autem spatia ad ornatus comparata, quae loca Graeci περιάκτοι dicunt ab eo quod machinae sunt in his locis versatiles trigonoe habentes singulares species ornationis, quae cum aut fabularum mutationes sunt futurae seu deorum adventus cum tonitribus repentinis, [ea] versentur mutentque speciem ornationis in frontes. secundum ea loca versurae sunt procurrentes, quae efficiunt una a foro, altera a peregre aditus in scaenam.
passages.translation: The scenes themselves have their own elaborate arrangements, such that the middle doors have decorations for the royal courts, the right doors for the hospitals, and the spaces for the decorations, which the Greeks call periaktos, from the fact that in these places there are machines, each with three kinds of decorations, which, when changes in the plays are to come or the arrival of the gods with sudden thunder, are turned and change the kind of decorations in front. According to these places, there are turnings that run forward, one forming the forum, the other the entrance to the stage.

passages.latin: genera autem sunt scaenarum tria, unum quod dicitur tragicum, alterum comicum, tertium satyricum. horum autem ornatus sunt inter se dissimili disparique ratione, quod tragicae deformantur columnis et fastigiis et signis reliquisque regalibus rebus, comicae autem aedificiorum privatorum et maenianorum habent speciem prospectusque fenestris dispositos imitatione, communium aedificiorum rationibus, satyricae vero ornantur arboribus speluncis montibus reliquisque agrestibus rebus in topeodis speciem deformati.
passages.translation: There are three kinds of scenes, one which is called tragic, the other comic, the third satirical. But the decorations of these are different from each other and in different ways, because the tragic ones are deformed with columns and pinnacles and standards and other royal things, while the comic ones have the appearance of private and walled buildings and have windows arranged in imitation of public buildings, while the satirical ones are decorated with trees, caves, mountains and other rural things deformed into the appearance of a landscape.

passages.latin: In Graecorum theatris non omnia isdem rationibus sunt facienda, quod primum in ima circinatione ut in latino trigonorum IIII, in eo quadratorum trium anguli circinationis lineam tangunt, et cuius quadrati latus est proximum scaenae praeciditque curvaturam circinationis, ea regione designatur finitio proscaenii. et ab ea regione ad extremam circinationem curvaturae parallelos linea designatur, in qua constituitur frons scaenae, per centrumque orchestrae proscaenii regioni parallelos linea describitur et qua secat circinationis lineas dextra ac sinistra in cornibus hemicycli centra signantur, et circino conlocato in dextra ab intervallo sinistro circumagitur circinatio ad proscaenii sinistram partem, item centro conlocato in sinistro cornu ab intervallo dextro circumagitur ad proscaenii dextram partem.
passages.translation: In Greek theaters, not everything should be done according to the same principles, because first, in the lower circle, as in the Latin trigon IV, the squares of the three corners touch the line of the circle, and the side of the plaza that is next to the stage and cuts the curvature of the circle, in that region, the end of the proscenium is designated. And from that region to the end of the circle, a line parallel to the curvature is drawn, in which the front of the stage is formed, and through the center of the orchestra, a line parallel to the proscenium region is described, and because it cuts the lines of the circle, the right and left lines are marked in the centers of the horns of the hemicycle. And having been placed on the right, from the left interval, the circle moves towards the left side of the proscenium; likewise, placed in the center of the left wing, it moves from the right interval towards the right side of the proscenium.

passages.latin: ita tribus centris hac descriptione ampliorem habent orchestram Graeci et scaenam recessiorem minoreque latitudine pulpitum, quod λογεῖον appellant, ideo quod ⟨apud⟩ eos tragici et comici actores in scaena peragunt, reliqui autem artifices suas per orchestram praestant actiones, itaque ex eo scaenici et thymelici graece separatim nominantur. eius logei altitudo non minus debet esse pedum X, non plus duodecim. gradationes scalarum inter cuneos et sedes contra quadratorum angulos dirigantur ad primam praecinctionem, a praecinctione inter eas iterum mediae dirigantur, et ad summam quotiens praecinguntur, altero tanto semper amplificantur.
passages.translation: Nomenclature note — Bk. 5.7.2 (the Greek stage). Technical terms retained with the Graecism and transliteration at first occurrence: orchestra (ὀρχήστρα), the circular space of the chorus; proscaenium / λογεῖον (logeîon), the raised platform of the actors; σκηνή (skené), the stage-building; παρασκήνια (paraskénia), its side-wings.

passages.latin: Cum haec omnia summa cura sollertiaque explicata sunt, tunc etiam diligentius est animadvertendum uti sit electus locus, in quo leniter adplicet se vox neque repulsa resiliens incertas auribus referat significationes. sunt enim nonnulli loci naturaliter inpedientes vocis motus, uti desonantes, qui graece dicuntur κατηχοῦντες, circumsonantes qui apud eos nominantur περιηχοῦντες, item resonantes qui dicuntur ἀντηχοῦντες, consonantesque quos appellant συνηχοῦντας. desonantes sunt in quibus vox prima cum est elata in altitudinem, offensa superioribus solidis corporibus repulsaque residens in imo opprimit insequentis vocis elationem,
passages.translation: When all this has been set out with the utmost care and skill, then still greater vigilance is needed to ensure that a site is chosen on which the voice settles gently and is not thrown back in such a way as to carry uncertain meanings to the ears. There are, indeed, places that by their nature hinder the movement of the voice: the dissonant, called in Greek κατηχοῦντες (katechountes); the circumsonant, which they name περιηχοῦντες (periechountes); the resonant, called ἀντηχοῦντες (antechountes); and the consonant, which they call συνηχοῦντες (synechountes). The dissonant are those in which the first voice, rising aloft, strikes solid bodies above and, driven back, settles below and smothers the rise of the voice that follows.

passages.latin: circumsonantes autem in quibus circumvagando coacta exsolvens in medio, sine extremis casibus sonans ibi extinguatur incerta verborum significatione, resonantes vero in quibus cum in solido tactu percussa resiliat, imagines exprimendo novissimos casus duplices faciat auditu. item consonantes sunt in quibus ab imis auxiliata cum incremento scandens egrediatur ad aures diserta verborum claritate. ita si in locorum electione fuerit diligens animadversio, emendatus erit prudentia ad utilitatem in theatris vocis effectus. formarum autem descriptiones inter se discriminibus his erunt notatae uti quae Graecorum habent usus ex quadratis designentur,, latina e paribus lateribus trigonorum. ita his praescriptionibus qui voluerit uti, emendatas efficiet theatrorum perfectiones.
passages.translation: The circumsonant are those in which the voice, forced to wander round, dissolves in the middle and, sounding there without its final syllables, dies away in an uncertain meaning of the words. The resonant are those in which, striking against a solid body, it rebounds and, forming echoes, doubles the last syllables to the ear. The consonant are those in which the voice, supported from below, rises with increasing strength and reaches the ears with distinct clarity of words. Thus, if due attention is given to the choice of site, prudence will secure, to good effect, the sound of the voice in theaters. The layouts of the plans will be marked by this difference between them: those designed from squares serve Greek usage; the Latin, from triangles of equal sides. Whoever chooses to follow these prescriptions will achieve theaters of finished perfection.

passages.latin: Post scaenam porticus sunt constituendae, uti cum imbres repentini ludos interpellaverint, habeat populus quo se recipiat ex theatro choragiaque laxamentum habeant ad comparandum. uti sunt porticus Pompeianae itemque Athenis porticus Eumenicae Patrisque Liberi fanum, et exeuntibus e theatro sinistra parte odeum, quod Themistocles columnis lapideis dispositis, navium malis et antemnis e spoliis Persicis pertexit, ideo autem etiam incensum Mithridatico bello rex Ariobarzanes restituit, Smyrnae Stratoniceum, Trallibus porticus ex utraque parte est scaenae supra stadium, ceterisque civitatibus quae diligentiores habuerunt architectos circa theatra sunt porticus et ambulationes.
passages.translation: Behind the stage, porticos are to be built, so that when sudden showers interrupt the games, the people may have a place to retreat from the theater and a place to rest while preparing for the festivities. Such are the porticos of Pompeii, and also in Athens the porticos of the Eumenes and the Parumontes and the temples of Liber, and on the left side of those leaving the theater, the ode, which Themistocles covered with stone columns, the masts of ships, and the antlers from the spoils of the Persians, and the same incense burner was restored by King Ariobarzanes during the Mithridatic war, the Stratoniceum at Smyrna, the porticos at Trallis on both sides of the stage above the stadium, and in other cities that have had more diligent architects, there are porticos and walks around the theaters.

passages.latin: quae videntur ita oportere conlocari uti duplices sint habeantque exteriores columnas doricas cum epistyliis et ornamentis ex ratione modulationis perfectas. latitudines autem earum ita oportere fieri videntur uti quanta altitudo columnae fuerit exterioris, tantam latitudinem habeant ab inferiore parte columnarum extremarum ad medias et a medianis ad parietes qui circumcludunt porticus ambulationes. medianae autem columnae quinta parte altiores sint quam exteriores, sed aut ionico aut corinthio genere deformentur.
passages.translation: which seem to be so placed that they are double and have exterior Doric columns with epistyles and ornaments perfect in proportion to the modulation. Their widths seem to be made so that the height of the exterior columns is such that they have as much width from the lower part of the outer columns to the middle ones and from the middle ones to the walls that enclose the portico walks. The middle columns, however, are to be a fifth higher than the exterior ones, but are to be shaped either in the Ionic or Corinthian style.

passages.latin: columnarum autem proportiones et symmetriae non erunt isdem rationibus quibus in aedibus sacris scripsi. aliam enim in deorum templis debent habere gravitatem, aliam in porticibus et ceteris operibus subtilitatem. itaque si dorici generis erunt columnae, dimetiantur earum altitudines cum capitulis in partes XV. ex eis partibus una constituatur et fiat modulus, ad cuius moduli rationem omnis operis erit explicatio. et in imo columnae crassitudo fiat duorum modulorum, intercolumnium quinque et moduli dimidia parte, altitudo columnae praeter capitulum XIIII modulorum, capituli altitudo moduli unius, latitudo modulorum duorum et moduli sextae partis. ceteri operis modulationes uti in aedibus sacris in libro IIII scriptum est ita perficiantur.
passages.translation: The proportions and commensurability of these columns do not follow the same rules as those prescribed for sacred buildings: temples require one degree of dignity, porticoes and other works another degree of slenderness. For Doric columns, divide their height, including the capitals, into fifteen parts. One part becomes the module governing the whole work. Make the lower diameter two modules and the intercolumniation five and a half. The shaft, excluding the capital, is fourteen modules high; the capital is one module high and two and one-sixth modules wide. Complete the remaining members according to the temple rules given in Book IV.

passages.latin: sin autem ionicae columnae fient, scapus praeter spiram et capitulum in octo et dimidiam partem dividatur et ex his una crassitudini columnae detur, <spira> cum plintho dimidia crassitudine constituatur, capituli ratio ita fiat uti in libro tertio est demonstratum. si corinthia erit, scapus et spira uti in ionica, capitulûm autem quemadmodum in quarto libro est scriptum, ita habeant rationem. stylobatisque adiectio quae fit per scamillos inpares, ex descriptione quae supra scripta est in libro tertio sumatur. epistylia coronae ceteraque omnia ad columnarum rationem ex scriptis voluminum superiorum explicentur.
passages.translation: If the columns are Ionic, divide the shaft, excluding the base and capital, into eight and a half parts, and assign one part to the column’s diameter. The base, including its plinth, should be half a diameter high; the capital should follow the proportions described in Book III. For Corinthian columns, the shaft and base should follow the Ionic proportions, and the capital those given in Book IV. The addition to the stylobate made by means of the scamilli inpares should follow the description in Book III. The architraves, cornices, and remaining members should be proportioned to the columns as explained in the preceding books.

passages.latin: Media vero spatia quae erunt subdiu inter porticus, adornanda viridibus videntur, quod hypaethroe ambulationes habent, magnam salubritatem, et primum oculorum quod ex viridibus subtilis et extenuatus aer propter motionem corporis influens perlimat speciem et ita auferens ex oculis umorem crassum, aciem tenuem et acutam speciem relinquit. praeterea cum corpus motionibus in ambulatione calescat, umores ex membris aer exsugendo inminuit plenitates extenuatque dissipando quod plus inest quam corpus potest sustinere.
passages.translation: The middle spaces, which will lie open to the sky between the porticoes, seem fit to be planted with greenery, because the walks of the hypaethroe have great health benefits, and first of all for the eyes, because the subtle and thin air flowing in from the greenery due to the movement of the body refines the appearance and, taking away the thick moisture from the eyes, leaves a thin and sharp appearance. Moreover, when the body is heated by the movements of walking, the air, by sucking the moisture from the limbs, diminishes the fullness and thins it by dissipating what is more in it than the body can bear.

passages.latin: hoc autem ita esse ex eo licet animadvertere, quod sub tectis cum sint aquarum fontes aut etiam sub terra palustris abundantia, ex his nullus surgit umor nebulosus, sed in apertis hypaethrisque locis cum sol oriens vapore tangat mundum, ex umidis et abundantibus excitat umores et eos conglobatos in altitudinem tollit. ergo si ita videtur uti in hypaethris locis ab aere umores ex corporibus exsugantur molestiores, quemadmodum ex terra per nebulas videntur, non puto dubium esse quin amplissimas et ornatissimas subdiu hypaethrusque conlocari oporteat in civitatibus ambulationes.
passages.translation: But this is so from the fact that, when there are springs of water under roofs or even an abundance of marshes under the ground, no misty moisture rises from these, but in open and humid places, when the rising sun touches the world with vapor, it stirs up the moisture from the moist and abundant places and carries the accumulated moisture to a height. Therefore, if it seems that in humid places the more troublesome moistures are sucked out of the bodies from the air, just as they are seen from the ground through mists, I do not think there is any doubt that the most spacious and most ornate promenades should be placed in cities under humid and humid conditions.

passages.latin: eae autem uti sint semper siccae et non lutosae, sic erit faciendum. fodiantur et exinaniantur quam altissime. dextra atque sinistra structiles cloacae fiant inque earum parietibus qui ad ambulationem spectaverint, tubuli instruantur inclinati fastigio cloacis. his perfectis compleantur ea loca carbonibus, deinde insuper sabulone eae ambulationes sternantur et exaequentur. ita propter carbonum raritatem naturalem et tubulorum in cloacas instructionem excipientur aquarum abundantiae, et ita siccae et sine umore perfectae fuerint ambulationes.
passages.translation: But that they may always be dry and not muddy, this is what must be done. They shall be dug and emptied as deep as possible. On the right and left, constructed sewers shall be made, and in their walls, which face the passage, pipes shall be laid out, inclined with a peak into the sewers. When these are completed, those places shall be filled with coal, then on top of that, those passages shall be spread out and leveled with sand. Thus, because of the natural scarcity of coal and the direction of the pipes into the sewers, abundance of water shall be taken care of, and thus the passages shall be dry and free from moisture.

passages.latin: Praeterea in his operibus thensauri sunt civitatibus in necessariis rebus a maioribus constituti. in conclusionibus enim reliqui omnes faciliores sunt apparatus quam lignorum. sal enim facile ante inportatur, frumenta publice privatimque expeditius congeruntur et si defit, holeribus carne seu leguminibus defenditur, aquae fossuris puteorum et de caelo repentinis tempestatibus ex tegulis excipiuntur. de lignatione quae maxime necessaria est ad cibum coquendum, difficilis et molesta est apparatio, quod et tarde comportatur et plus consumitur.
passages.translation: Furthermore, in these works, the cities have treasuries for the necessary things, established by their forebears against times of need; for in a siege all other supplies are more easily obtained than firewood. The rest are easier to prepare than for wood. For salt is easily brought in beforehand, grain is more expediently stored both publicly and privately, and if it is lacking, it is protected with vegetables, meat or legumes, water is collected from the roof tiles by digging wells and from sudden storms of the sky. The preparation of wood, which is most necessary for cooking food, is difficult and troublesome, because it is both slow to be brought in and consumed more.

passages.latin: in eiusmodi temporibus tunc eae ambulationes aperiuntur et mensurae tributim singulis capitibus designantur. ita duas res egregias hypaethroe ambulationes praestant, unam in pace salubritatis, alteram in bello salutis. ergo his rationibus ambulationum explicationes non solum post scaenam theatri sed etiam omnium deorum templis effectae magnas civitatibus praestare poterunt utilitates. Quoniam haec nobis satis videntur esse exposita, nunc insequentur balinearum dispositionum demonstrationes.
passages.translation: At such times, then, those walks are thrown open and measured spaces are allotted tribe by tribe. Thus, the walks of the hypaethro perform two excellent functions, one in peace of health, the other in war of safety. Therefore, with these reasons, the explanations of the walks, carried out not only behind the scenes in theaters but also in the temples of all the gods, will be able to perform great benefits for the cities. Since these seem to us to have been sufficiently explained, now there will follow demonstrations of the arrangements of the baths.

passages.latin: primum eligendus locus est quam calidissimus, id est aversus ab septentrione et aquilone. ipsa autem caldaria tepidariaque lumen habeant ab occidente hiberno, si autem natura loci inpedierit, utique a meridie, quod maxime tempus lavandi a meridiano ad vesperum est constitutum. et item est animadvertendum uti caldaria muliebria et virilia coniuncta et in isdem regionibus sint conlocata. sic enim efficietur ut vasaria et hypocausis communis sit eorum utrisque. aenea supra hypocausim tria sunt componenda, unum caldarium, alterum tepidarium, tertium frigidarium, et ita conlocanda uti ex tepidario in caldarium quantum aquae caldae exierit, influat
passages.translation: First, a place should be chosen that is as warm as possible, that is, facing away from the north and the north-east. The caldariums and tepidariums themselves should have light from the winter west, but if the nature of the place prevents this, then from the south, since the best time for bathing is from midday to evening. It should also be noted that the caldariums for women and men should be connected and placed in the same areas. For in this way it will be ensured that there is something common to both of them in the vases and hypocauses. Three bronze vessels should be arranged above the hypocauses, one caldarium, the other tepidarium, and the third frigidarium, and they should be placed in such a way that as much hot water as comes out of the tepidarium into the caldarium, it flows

passages.latin: suspensurae caldariorum ita sunt faciendae ut primum sesquipedalibus tegulis solum sternatur inclinatum ad hypocausim, uti pila cum mittatur non possit intro resistere sed rursus redeat ad praefurnium ipsa per se. ita flamma facilius pervagabitur sub suspensione. supraque laterculis besalibus pilae struantur ita dispositae uti bipedales tegulae possint supra esse conlocatae. altitudinem autem pilae habeant pedes duo eaeque struantur argilla cum capillo subacta, supraque conlocentur tegulae bipedales quae sustineant pavimentum.
passages.translation: The suspensions of the boilers are to be made in such a way that first the floor is laid with half-foot tiles inclined towards the hypocausis, so that when the ball is thrown in it cannot resist but returns to the pre-furnace by itself. In this way the flame will spread more easily under the suspension. Above this, the pillars (pilae) are raised with small bessal bricks, arranged so that two-foot tiles can be placed above. The height of the balls, however, should be two feet, and they should be laid with clay with hair pressed down, and above them are placed two-foot tiles that support the floor.

passages.latin: concamarationes vero si ex structura factae fuerint, erunt utiliores, sin autem contignationes fuerint, figlinum opus subiciatur, sed hoc ita erit faciendum. regulae ferreae aut arcus fiant eaeque uncinis ferreis ad contignationem suspendantur quam creberrimis, eaeque regulae sive arcus ita disponantur uti tegulae sine marginibus sedere in duabus invehique possint, et ita totae concamarationes in ferro nitentes sint perfectae. earumque camararum superiora coagmenta ex argilla cum capillo subacta liniantur, inferior autem pars, quae ad pavimentum spectat, primum testa cum calce trullizetur, deinde opere albario sive tectorio poliatur. eaeque camarae in caldariis si duplices factae fuerint, meliorem habebunt usum. non enim a vapore umor corrumpere poterit materiem contignationis, sed inter duas camaras vagabitur.
passages.translation: If the chambers are made of a structure, they will be more useful, but if they are floors, then pottery work should be placed under them, but this should be done in this way. Iron rules or arches should be made and they should be hung on iron hooks as thick as possible to the floor, and these rules or arches should be arranged so that the tiles can sit without edges on two and can be driven in, and thus the entire chambers should be perfect, shining in iron. And the upper joints of their chambers should be lined with clay with hair, but the lower part, which looks to the floor, should first be troweled with clay and lime, then polished with whitewash or plaster. And if these chambers in the boilers are made double, they will have a better use. For the moisture from the steam will not be able to corrupt the material of the floor, but will wander between the two chambers.

passages.latin: magnitudines autem balneorum videntur fieri pro copia hominum, <dummodo> sint ita compositae. quanta longitudo fuerit, tertia dempta, latitudo sit praeter scholam labri et alvei. labrum utique sub lumine faciundum videtur, ne stantes circum suis umbris obscurent lucem. scholas autem labrorum ita fieri oportet spatiosas uti cum priores occupaverint loca, circum expectantes reliqui recte stare possint. alvei autem latitudo inter parietem et pluteum ne minus sit pedes senos, ut gradus inferior inde auferat et pulvinus duos pedes.
passages.translation: The sizes of the baths seem to be made according to the number of people, <provided> they are arranged in such a way. Whatever the length is, subtract a third, the width is to be in addition to the width of the basin and the basin. The basin certainly seems to be made under the light, so that those standing around it do not obscure the light with their shadows. The basins, however, must be made so spacious that when the first have taken their places, the rest, looking around, can stand upright. The width of the basin between the wall and the shelf should not be less than six feet, so that the lower step takes away from it and the cushion two feet.

passages.latin: laconicum sudationesque sunt coniungendae tepidario, eaeque quam latae fuerint, tantam altitudinem habeant ad imam curvaturam hemisphaerii. mediumque lumen in hemisphaerio relinquatur ex eoque clipeum aeneum catenis pendeat, per cuius reductiones et demissiones perficietur sudationis temperatura. ipsumque ad circinum fieri oportere videtur, ut aequaliter a medio flammae vaporisque vis per curvaturae rotundationes pervagetur.
passages.translation: The laconic and the tepidariums are to be connected, and however wide they are, they should have as much height to the lowest curvature of the hemisphere. And a central lumen should be left in the hemisphere and from it a brass cup should hang with chains, by the reductions and lowerings of which the temperature of the sweating will be perfected. And it seems necessary to make it like a compass, so that the force of the flame and vapors from the middle should spread evenly through the roundings of the curvature.

passages.latin: Nunc mihi videtur, tametsi non sint italicae consuetudinis palaestrarum aedificationes, traditae tamen explicare et quemadmodum apud Graecos constituantur monstrare. in palaestris peristylia quadrata sive oblonga ita sunt facienda uti duorum stadiorum habeant ambulationis circumitionem, quod Graeci vocant δίαυλον, ex quibus tres porticus simplices disponantur, quarta quae ad meridianas regiones est conversa, duplex, uti cum tempestates ventosae sint, non possit aspergo in interiorem partem pervenire.
passages.translation: Now it seems to me that, even if they are not the buildings of the Italian custom of the gymnasiums, they should nevertheless explain the traditional ones and show how they are constructed among the Greeks. In the gymnasiums, square or oblong peristyles should be made so that they have a circumference of two stadia for walking, which the Greeks call δίαυλον, from which three simple porticos should be arranged, the fourth, which faces the southern regions, should be double, so that when there are windy storms, the spray cannot reach the inner part.
