passages.latin: constituantur autem in tribus porticibus exhedrae spatiosae, habentes sedes in quibus philosophi rhetores reliquique qui studiis delectantur sedentes disputare possint. in duplici autem porticu conlocentur haec membra. ephebeum in medio, hoc autem est exhedra amplissima cum sedibus, tertia parte longior sit quam lata. sub dextro coryceum, deinde proxime conisterium, a conisterio in versura porticus frigida lavatio, quam Graeci λουτρόν vocitant. ad sinistram ephebei elaeothesium, proxime autem elaeothesium <frigidarium>, ab eoque iter in propnigeum in versura porticus. proxima autem introrsus e regione frigidarii conlocetur concamerata sudatio longitudine duplex quam latitudo, quae habeat in versuris ex una parte laconicum ad eundem modum uti quam supra scriptum est, compositum, ex adverso laconici caldam lavationem. in palaestra peristylia, quemadmodum supra scriptum est, ita debent esse [perfecta] distributa.
passages.translation: In the three porticos, spacious rooms should be set up, with seats in which philosophers, rhetoricians, and others who delight in studies can sit and debate. In the double portico, these members should be placed. The ephebeum in the middle, which is the largest exedra with seats, which is one-third longer than it is wide. On the right, the coryceum, then next to it, the conisterium, from the conisterium, in the turn of the portico, a cold bath, which the Greeks call λουτρόν. On the left, the ephebeum, the elaeothesium, and next to it, the elaeothesium, and from there a path to the propnigeum, in the turn of the portico. But next to it, inward, opposite the frigidarium, a conchamarata sweating room should be placed, twice as long as it is wide, which should have a laconic bath on one side in the turns in the same way as written above, and a hot bath on the opposite side of the laconic bath. In the palaestra, the peristyle, as written above, should be distributed in this way.

passages.latin: extra autem disponantur porticus tres, una ex peristylo exeuntibus, duae dextra atque sinistra stadiatae, ex quibus una quae spectaverit ad septentrionem, perficiatur duplex amplissima latitudine, altera simplex ita factae uti in partibus quae fuerint circa parietes et quae erit ad columnas, margines habeant uti semitas non minus pedum denûm mediumque excavatum uti gradus sint in descensu marginibus sesquipedem ad planitiem, quae planities sit non minus pedes XII. ita qui vestiti ambulaverint circum in marginibus, non inpedientur ab unctis se exercentibus.
passages.translation: Outside, three porticos are to be arranged, one leading from the peristyle, and two on the right and left, of which one, which faces north, is to be completed as a double, with a very ample width, the other single, so made that in the parts which will be around the walls and which will be at the columns, the edges should be like paths of not less than ten feet and the middle should be excavated so that there are steps in the descent from the edges, one half-foot to the plain, which plain should be no less than twelve feet. Thus, those who walk around the edges dressed will not be hindered by the anointed exercising themselves.

passages.latin: haec autem porticus ξυστός apud Graecos vocitatur, quod athletae per hiberna tempora in tectis stadiis exercentur. proxime autem xystum et duplicem porticum designentur hypaethroe ambulationes, quas Graeci παραδρομίδες, nostri xysta appellant, in quas per hiemem ex xysto sereno caelo athletae prodeuntes exercentur. faciunda autem xysta sic videntur ut sint inter duas porticus silvae aut platanones et in his perficiantur inter arbores ambulationes ibique ex opere signino stationes. post xystum autem stadium ita figuratum ut possint hominum copiae cum laxamento athletas certantes spectare. Quae in moenibus necessaria videbantur esse ut apte disponantur, perscripsi.
passages.translation: This portico is called the ξυστός among the Greeks, because athletes exercise in covered stadia during the winter months. Next to the xystum and the double portico are designated the hypaethroe walks, which the Greeks call παραδρομίδας, ours xysta, in which athletes, coming out of the xystum in clear weather, exercise during the winter. The xystum is made in such a way that there are forests or plane trees between the two porticos and in these walks are made between the trees and there are stations according to the work I design. After the xystum is the stadium, so shaped that crowds of people can watch the athletes competing with ease. I have written down what seemed to be necessary in the walls to be arranged appropriately.

passages.latin: de opportunitate autem portuum non est praetermittendum, sed quibus rationibus tueantur naves in his ab tempestatibus explicandum. hi autem naturaliter si sint bene positi habeantque acroteria sive promunturia procurrentia, ex quibus introrsus curvaturae sive versurae ex loci natura fuerint conformatae, maximas utilitates videntur habere. circum enim porticus sive navalia sunt facienda sive ex porticibus aditus ad emporia, turresque ex utraque parte conlocandae, ex quibus catenae traduci per machinas possint.
passages.translation: The suitability of harbors must also be considered, together with the means of protecting ships from storms. Natural sites offer great advantages when projecting headlands form inward-curving bays or sheltered angles. Build porticoes or shipyards around them, with access from the porticoes to the trading facilities. Place towers on both sides of the entrance, from which chains can be drawn across by machinery.

passages.latin: Sin autem non naturalem locum neque idoneum ad tuendas ab tempestatibus naves habuerimus, ita videtur esse faciendum uti si nullum flumen in his locis inpedierit sed erit ex una parte statio, tunc ex altera parte structuris sive aggeribus expediantur progressus. et ita conformandae portuum conclusiones. eae autem structurae quae in aqua sunt futurae, videntur sic esse faciendae uti portetur pulvis a regionibus quae sunt a Cumis continuatae ad promunturium Minervae, isque misceatur uti in mortario duo ad unum respondeant.
passages.translation: If there is no natural site suitable for sheltering ships from storms, proceed as follows. Where no river obstructs the site and there is an anchorage on one side, extend masonry works or embankments from the other to form the harbor enclosure. For structures to be built in water, bring volcanic powder from the region extending from Cumae to the promontory of Minerva and mix it into mortar in a ratio of two parts powder to one part lime.

passages.latin: deinde tunc in eo loco qui definitus erit, arcae stipitibus robusteis et catenis inclusae in aquam demittendae destinandaeque firmiter, deinde inter ea extrastilis inferior pars sub aqua exaequanda et purganda, et caementis ex mortario, materia mixta quemadmodum supra scriptum est, ibi congerendum, doneque compleatur structurae spatium quod fuerit inter arcas. hoc autem munus naturale habent ea loca quae supra scripta sunt. Sin autem propter fluctus aut impetus aperti pelagi destinae arcas non potuerint continere, tunc ab ipsa terra sive crepidine pulvinus quam firmissime struatur, isque pulvinus exaequata struatur planitia minus quam dimidiae partis, reliquum quod est proxime litus, proclinatum latus habeat.
passages.translation: Then, in the place that will be determined, the caissons (arcae), framed with stout posts and chains, are to be lowered into the water and firmly placed, then the lower part inside the water is to be leveled and cleaned with the help of the ladles, and rubble and mortar, the material mixed as described above, are to be piled there, until the structure is completed, filling the space between the arks. Now, the places described above have this natural function. But if, due to waves or the force of the open sea, the arks cannot be contained, then a cushion is to be built as firmly as possible from the land itself or from the shore, and this cushion, when leveled, is to be built so that less than half of the surface is level, the remainder, which is closest to the shore, has a sloping side.

passages.latin: deinde ad ipsam aquam et latera pulvino circiter sesquipedales margines struantur aequilibres ex planitia quae est supra scripta, tunc proclinatio ea impleatur harena et exaequetur cum margine et planitia pulvini. deinde insuper eam exaequationem pila quam magna constituta fuerit ibi struatur, eaque cum erit extructa, relinquatur ne minus duos menses ut siccescat. tunc autem succidatur margo quae sustinet harenam. ita harena fluctibus subruta efficiet in mare pilae praecipitationem. hac ratione quotienscumque opus fuerit, in aquam poterit esse progressus.
passages.translation: Then, to the water itself and the sides of the cushion, margins of about one and a half feet are built, equal to the level described above. Then, that slope is filled with sand and made equal to the edge and level of the cushion. Then, on top of that leveling, a large pile is built there, and when it is built, it is left for at least two months to dry. Then, however, the edge that supports the sand is cut away. Thus, the sand, crushed by the waves, will cause the pile to precipitate into the sea. In this way, whenever necessary, it will be possible to advance into the water.

passages.latin: In quibus autem locis pulvis non nascitur, his rationibus erit faciendum uti arcae duplices relatis tabulis et catenis conligatae in eo loco qui finitus erit constituantur, et inter destinas creta in aeronibus ex ulva palustri factis calcetur. cum ita bene calcatum et quam densissime fuerit, tunc cocleis rotis tympanis conlocatis locus qui ea saeptione finitus fuerit exinaniatur sicceturque, et ibi inter saeptiones fundamenta fodiantur. si terrena erunt, usque ad solidum crassiora quam qui murus supra futurus erit, et tunc structura ex caementis calce et harena compleantur.
passages.translation: In places where pozzolana (pulvis) is not found, it will be necessary to do this by placing double caissons, tied together with burnt sticks and chains, in the place that will be finished, and between the designated places, chalk will be trampled in aerofoils made of marsh bulrush. When it has been trampled well and as densely as possible, then with augers and drum wheels placed, the place that will be finished with that partition will be emptied and dried, and there between the partitions the foundations will be dug. If they will be earthen, they will be emptied and dried until solid, thicker than the wall that will be above, and then the structure will be completed with rubble, lime, and sand.

passages.latin: sin autem mollis locus erit, palis ustilatis alneis aut oleagineis configantur et carbonibus compleantur, quemadmodum in theatrorum et muri fundationibus est scriptum. deinde tunc quadrato saxo murus ducatur iuncturis quam longissimis, uti maxime medii lapides coagmentis contineantur. tunc qui locus erit inter murum ruderatione sive structura compleatur. ita erit uti possit turris insuper aedificari.
passages.translation: But if the place is soft, it is to be driven with piles of charred alder or olive-wood and packed with charcoal, as is written in the foundations of theaters and walls. Then the wall is to be built with squared stone with the joints as long as possible, so that the middle stones are held together with mortar. Then whatever space there is between the wall is to be filled with rubble or masonry. It will be so that a tower can be built on top.

passages.latin: His perfectis navaliorum ea erit ratio ut constituantur spectantia maxime ad septentrionem. nam meridianae regiones propter aestus cariem tineam teredines reliquaque bestiarum nocentium genera procreant alendoque conservant, eaque aedificia minime sunt materianda propter incendia. de magnitudinibus autem finitio nulla debet esse, sed faciunda ad maximum navium modum, uti etsi maiores naves subductae fuerint, habeant cum laxamento ibi conlocationem. Quae necessaria ad utilitatem in civitatibus publicorum locorum succurrere mihi potuerunt, quemadmodum constituantur et perficiantur in hoc volumine scripsi, privatorum autem aedificiorum utilitates et eorum symmetrias insequenti volumine ratiocinabor
passages.translation: When these are completed, the plan for the shipyards will be to build those facing mainly to the north. For the southern regions, because of the heat, breed and nourish moths, beetles, and other kinds of harmful animals, and those buildings should be least materialized because of fires. There should be no limitation on the sizes, but the maximum size of the ships should be made, so that even if larger ships are removed, they can still be accommodated there with ease. I have written in this volume how these necessary utilities in the cities of public places can be of assistance to me, but I will discuss the utilities and their symmetries of private buildings in the following volume.

passages.latin: Aristippus philosophus Socraticus naufragio cum eiectus ad Rhodiensium litus animadvertisset geometrica schemata descripta, exclamavisse ad comites ita dicitur bene speremus, hominum enim vestigia video statimque in oppidum Rhodum contendit et recta gymnasium devenit, ibique de philosophia disputans muneribus est donatus, ut non tantum se ornaret sed etiam eis qui una fuerunt et vestitum et cetera quae opus essent ad victum praestaret. cum autem eius comites in patriam reverti voluissent interrogarentque eum quidnam vellet domum renuntiari, tunc ita mandavit dicere, eiusmodi possessiones et viatica liberis oportere parari quae etiam e naufragio una possent enatare.
passages.translation: Aristippus, the Socratic philosopher, shipwrecked and cast ashore on the coast of Rhodes, noticed geometrical figures drawn in the sand and is said to have cried out to his companions: “Let us be of good hope, for I see the traces of men.” He made at once for the city of Rhodes and went straight to the gymnasium, where, discoursing on philosophy, he was rewarded with gifts so generous that he could provide not only for himself but also for those who were with him, with clothing and everything else needed for life. When his companions wished to return home and asked what message he would have them carry back, he bade them say this: that children ought to be furnished with such possessions and such provisions for the journey as could swim ashore with them even from a shipwreck.

passages.latin: namque ea vera praesidia sunt vitae quibus neque fortunae tempestas iniqua neque publicarum rerum mutatio neque belli vastatio potest nocere. non minus eam sententiam augendo Theophrastus, hortando doctos potius esse quam pecuniae confidentes ita ponit, doctum ex omnibus solum neque in alienis locis peregrinum neque amissis familiaribus et necessariis inopem amicorum sed in omni civitate esse civem difficilesque fortunae sine timore posse despicere casus, at qui non doctrinarum sed felicitatis praesidiis putaret se esse vallatum, labidis itineribus vadentem non stabili sed infirma conflictari vita.
passages.translation: For these are the true safeguards of life: neither the adverse storms of fortune, nor upheavals in public affairs, nor the devastation of war can harm them. Theophrastus develops the same idea, urging people to become learned rather than to put their trust in wealth. The educated person alone is not a stranger in foreign lands or left without friends when family and companions are lost; in every city such a person is a citizen and can face the hazards of fortune without fear. By contrast, one who trusts in good luck rather than learning walks on slippery paths and struggles through a fragile, uncertain life.

passages.latin: Epicurus vero non dissimiliter ait pauca sapientibus fortunam tribuere, quae autem maxima et necessaria sunt, animi mentisque cogitationibus gubernari. haec ita etiam plures philosophi dixerunt. non minus poetae qui antiquas comoedias graece scripserunt, easdem sententias versibus in scaena pronuntiaverunt, ut Crates Chionides Aristophanes, maxime etiam cum his Alexis, qui Athenienses ait oportere ideo laudari quod omnium Graecorum leges cogunt parentes <ali> a liberis, Atheniensium non omnes nisi eos qui liberos artibus erudissent. omnia enim munera fortunae cum dantur ab ea faciliter adimuntur, disciplinae vero coniunctae cum animis nullo tempore deficiunt, sed permanent stabiliter ad summum exitum vitae.
passages.translation: Epicurus likewise says that fortune grants the wise relatively little, whereas the greatest and most necessary matters are governed by thought and judgment. Many other philosophers held the same view. The authors of ancient Greek comedy — Crates, Chionides, Aristophanes and, above all, Alexis — expressed similar ideas on stage. Alexis praises the Athenians because, whereas Greek laws generally require children to support their parents, the Athenians impose that duty only in respect of parents who have taught their children an art. Fortune may take away everything it has given; learning, once joined to the mind, remains steadfast to the end of life.

passages.latin: itaque ego maximas infinitasque parentibus ago atque habeo gratias, quod Atheniensium legem probantes me arte erudiendum curaverunt, et ea quae non potest esse probata sine litteratura encyclioque doctrinarum omnium disciplina. cum ergo et parentium cura et praeceptorum doctrinis auctas haberem copias disciplinarum, philologis et philotechnis rebus commentariorumque scripturis me delectans eas possessiones animo paravi, e quibus haec est fructuum summa, nullas plus habendi esse necessitates eamque esse proprietatem divitiarum maxime, nihil desiderare. sed forte nonnulli haec levia iudicantes putant eos esse sapientes qui pecunia sunt copiosi. itaque plerique ad id propositum contendentes audacia adhibita cum divitiis etiam notitiam sunt consecuti.
passages.translation: I therefore give and owe the greatest, indeed boundless, thanks to my parents, who, approving the law of the Athenians, took care that I should be trained in an art, and in one that cannot be mastered without letters and the encyclopedic education that embraces all the disciplines. Having thus enlarged my store of learning through my parents’ care and my teachers’ instruction, and delighting in literary and technical studies and in the writing of treatises, I acquired for my mind possessions whose chief fruit is this: that one has no need to possess more, and that the truest property of wealth is to desire nothing. Some, perhaps, think these things of little account and hold that the wise are those who abound in money. Many, therefore, pursuing that aim with boldness, have won notoriety together with riches.

passages.latin: ego autem, Caesar, non ad pecuniam parandam ex arte dedi studium, sed potius tenuitatem cum bona fama quam abundantiam cum infamia sequendam probavi. ideo notities parum est adsecuta. sed tamen his voluminibus editis, ut spero, etiam posteris ero notus. neque est mirandum quid ita pluribus sim ignotus. ceteri architecti rogant et ambiunt ut architectent, mihi autem a praeceptoribus est traditum rogatum non rogantem oportere suscipere curam, quod ingenuus color movetur pudore petendo rem suspiciosam. nam beneficium dantes non accipientes ambiuntur. quid enim putemus suspicari qui rogetur de patrimonio sumptus faciendos committere gratiae petentis, nisi praedae compendiique eius causa iudicet faciundum?.
passages.translation: I, however, Caesar, have not applied myself to making money by my art; I have preferred slender means with a good name to abundance with disrepute. For this reason I have gained little renown. Yet, now that these volumes are published, I hope to be known even to posterity. Nor should it surprise anyone that I am unknown to so many. Other architects solicit and canvass for commissions; but I was taught by my masters that one should undertake a charge when asked, not by asking, because a freeborn man’s complexion is changed by shame when he petitions for something that arouses suspicion. For it is those who confer a favor who are courted, not those who receive it. What, then, are we to suppose a man suspects when he is asked to entrust the spending of his patrimony to the goodwill of a petitioner, if not that the petitioner judges the work worth doing for his own plunder and profit?

passages.latin: itaque maiores primum a genere probatis operam tradebant architectis, deinde quaerebant si honeste essent educati, ingenuo pudori non audaciae protervitatis permittendum iudicantes. ipsi autem artifices non erudiebant nisi suos liberos aut cognatos et eos viros bonos instituebant, quibus tantarum rerum fidei pecuniae sine dubitatione permitterentur. Cum autem animadverto ab indoctis et inperitis tantae disciplinae magnitudinem iactari et ab îs qui non modo <> architecturae sed omnino ne fabricae quidem notitiam habent, non possum non laudare patres familiarum eos qui litteraturae fiducia confirmati per se aedificantes ita iudicant, si inperitis sit committendum, ipsos potius digniores esse ad suam voluntatem quam ad alienam pecuniae consumere summam.
passages.translation: Our predecessors therefore entrusted building works first to architects whose family standing had been tested, and then enquired whether they had received an honorable education. They judged that responsibility should rest with the restraint of a freeborn man, rather than the audacity of the shameless. Craftsmen themselves trained only their sons or relatives, forming them as upright men to whose integrity funds for important works could safely be entrusted. Yet when I see so great a discipline handled at the whim of the uneducated and inexperienced, including men who know neither architecture nor even the craft of building, I cannot but commend those householders who, trusting in their literary education, build for themselves. If the work must be entrusted to the inexperienced, they judge themselves more entitled to spend their money according to their own judgment than according to someone else’s.

passages.latin: itaque nemo artem ullam aliam conatur domi facere, uti sutrinam fullonicam aut ex ceteris quae sunt faciliores, nisi architecturam, ideo quod qui profitentur non arte vera sed falso nominantur architecti. quas ob res corpus architecturae rationesque eius putavi diligentissime conscribendas, opinans munus omnibus gentibus non ingratum futurum. igitur quoniam in quinto de opportunitate communium operum perscripsi, in hoc volumine privatorum aedificiorum ratiocinationes et commensus symmetriarum explicabo.
passages.translation: Thus no one attempts to practise any other art at home — shoemaking, fulling or any of the other easier crafts — except architecture, because those who profess it are called architects not by virtue of true art but falsely. For these reasons I judged that the body of architecture and its principles should be set down with the utmost care, believing that this would be a service not unwelcome to all peoples. Accordingly, since in the fifth book I have written of the fitness of public works, in this volume I shall set out the principles of private buildings and the commensurability of their proportions.

passages.latin: Haec autem ita erunt recte disposita, si primo animadversum fuerit quibus regionibus aut quibus inclinationibus mundi constituantur. namque aliter Aegypto, aliter Hispania, non eodem modo Ponto, dissimiliter Romae, item ceteris terrarum et regionum proprietatibus oportere videntur constitui genera aedificiorum, quod alia parte solis cursu premitur tellus, alia longe ab eo distat, alia per medium temperatur. igitur uti constitutio mundi ad terrae spatium inclinatione signiferi circuli et solis cursu disparibus qualitatibus naturaliter est conlocata, ad eundem modum etiam ad regionum rationes caelique varietates videntur aedificiorum debere dirigi conlocationes.
passages.translation: These buildings will be rightly disposed if attention is first paid to the regions and latitudes of the world in which they are set. For it seems that the kinds of building ought to be constituted in one way in Egypt, in another in Spain, not in the same way in Pontus, differently at Rome, and so on according to the properties of other lands and regions; for in one part the earth is oppressed by the course of the sun, in another it lies far from it, and in another it is tempered by an intermediate position. Therefore, just as the constitution of the heavens in relation to the extent of the earth is naturally disposed with unequal qualities by the inclination of the zodiac and the course of the sun, so the disposition of buildings ought likewise to be governed by the character of each region and the variety of its climate.

passages.latin: sub septentrione aedificia testudinata et maxime conclusa et non patentia sed conversa ad calidas partes oportere fieri videntur. contra autem sub impetu solis meridianis regionibus, quod premuntur a calore, patentiora conversaque ad septentrionem et aquilonem sunt faciunda. ita quod ultra natura laedit, arte erit emendandum. item reliquis regionibus ad eundem modum <debet> temperari, quemadmodum caelum est ad inclinationem mundi conlocatum.
passages.translation: In the north, it seems, buildings should be vaulted, closed in as much as possible rather than open, and turned towards the warm quarters. In southern regions, on the contrary, which lie under the full force of the sun and are oppressed by its heat, they should be built more open and turned towards the north and north-east. Thus what nature harms by excess must be corrected by art. In the other regions, too, buildings must be tempered in the same way, according to how the climate is disposed in relation to the inclination of the world.

passages.latin: Haec autem ex natura rerum sunt animadvertenda et consideranda atque etiam ex membris corporibusque gentium observanda. namque sol quibus locis mediocriter profundit vapores, in his conservat corpora temperata, quaeque proxime currendo deflagrat, eripit exurendo temperaturam umoris. contra vero refrigeratis regionibus, quod absunt a meridie longe, non exhauritur a caloribus umor, sed ex caelo roscidus aer in corpora fundens umorem efficit ampliores corporaturas vocisque sonitus graviores. ex eo quoque quae sub septentrionibus nutriuntur gentes inmanibus corporibus, candidis coloribus, directo capillo et rufo, oculis caesis, sanguine multo ab umoris plenitate caelique refrigerationibus sunt conformati.
passages.translation: These matters are to be observed and considered from the nature of things, and also studied in the limbs and bodies of peoples. For where the sun pours out its heat in moderation, it keeps bodies temperate; where it runs close and scorches, it burns away their due proportion of moisture; in cold regions, on the other hand, which lie far from the south, moisture is not drawn off by heat, but the dewy air, pouring moisture from the sky into bodies, produces larger frames and deeper voices. Hence, too, the peoples reared under the north are formed with huge bodies, fair complexions, straight red hair, gray-blue eyes and abundant blood, because of the fullness of moisture and the coldness of the climate;

passages.latin: qui autem sunt proximi ad axem meridianum subiectique solis cursui, brevioribus corporibus, colore fusco, crispo capillo, oculis nigris, cruribus validis, sanguine exiguo solis impetu perficiuntur. itaque etiam propter sanguinis exiguitatem timidiores sunt ferro resistere, sed ardores ac febres sufferunt sine timore, quod nutrita sunt eorum membra cum fervore. itemque corpora quae nascuntur sub septentrione a febri sunt timidiora et inbecilla, sanguinis autem abundantia ferro resistunt sine timore.
passages.translation: those, on the other hand, who live nearest to the southern pole and beneath the course of the sun are formed by its force with shorter bodies, dark complexions, curly hair, black eyes, strong legs and little blood. Hence, because of the scarcity of their blood, they are more afraid of resisting the sword, but they endure heat and fevers without fear, since their limbs have been nourished in heat; whereas bodies born under the north are more fearful of fever and weaker against it, but, owing to the abundance of their blood, they resist the sword without fear.

passages.latin: Non minus sonus vocis in generibus gentium dispares et varias habet qualitates, ideo quod terminatio orientis et occidentis circa terrae librationem, qua dividitur pars superior et inferior mundi, habere videtur libratam naturali modo circumitionem, quam etiam mathematici ὁρίζοντα dicunt. igitur cum id habemus certum ab imo sustinens, ab labro quod est in regione septentrionali, linea traiecta ad id quod est supra meridianum axem ab eoque altera obliqua in altitudinem ad summum cardinem qui est post stellas septentrionum, sine dubitatione animadvertemus ex eo esse schema trigonii mundo, uti organi quam σαμβύκη graeci dicunt.
passages.translation: No less does the sound of the voice have unequal and varied qualities among the different kinds of peoples, because the boundary of east and west around the level of the earth, by which the upper and lower parts of the world are divided, appears to have a circuit naturally leveled, which the mathematicians also call ὁρίζων, the horizon. Taking this as certain, if a line is drawn from the edge in the northern region to the edge above the southern axis, and from there another line obliquely upwards to the highest pole, behind the stars of the Bear, we shall perceive without doubt that the world thereby has the figure of a triangle, like that of the instrument the Greeks call σαμβύκη, the sambuca.

passages.latin: itaque quod est spatium proximum imo cardini ab axis linea in meridianis finibus, sub eo loco quae sunt nationes propter brevitatem altitudinis ad mundum sonitum vocis faciunt tenuem et acutissimum, uti in organo chorda quae est proxima angulo. secundum eam autem reliquae ad mediam Graeciam remissiones efficiunt in nationibus sonorum scansione, item a medio in ordinem crescendo ad extremos septentriones sub altitudines caeli nationum spiritus sonitibus gravioribus a natura rerum exprimuntur. ita videtur mundi conceptio tota propter inclinationem consonantissime per solis temperaturam ad harmoniam esse composita.
passages.translation: Accordingly, the peoples who dwell in the space nearest the lower pole, in the southern regions measured from the line of the axis, produce a thin and very high-pitched sound of voice because of their small elevation in relation to the world, like the string nearest the angle of the instrument. Next to them, the other peoples, as far as central Greece, produce successive descents in the scale of sounds. Likewise, increasing in due order from the middle to the farthest north, beneath the heights of the sky, the breath of the peoples is uttered by nature in deeper tones. Thus the whole conception of the world, because of its inclination, appears to be composed in perfect consonance, through the tempering of the sun, according to harmony.

passages.latin: igitur quae nationes sunt inter axis meridiani cardinem ac septentrionalis medio positae, uti in diagrammate musico medianae vocis habent sonitum in sermone, quaeque progredientibus ad septentrionem sunt nationes, quod altiores habent distantias mundi, spiritus vocis habentes umore repulsos ad hypatas et proslambanomenon, a natura rerum sonitu graviore coguntur uti. eadem ratione e medio progredientibus ad meridiem gentes paranetarum <netarum> que acutissimam sonitus vocis perficiunt tenuitatem.
passages.translation: Therefore the peoples situated midway between the pole of the southern axis and that of the northern have in their speech the sound of the middle voice, as in the musical diagram; the peoples one meets advancing towards the north, because they lie at greater distances in relation to the world, have the breath of their voices driven back by moisture towards the hypatae and the proslambanomenos, and are compelled by nature to use a deeper sound; and by the same reasoning the peoples one meets advancing from the middle towards the south produce the extreme, high-pitched thinness of voice of the paranetae and the netae.

passages.latin: hoc autem verum esse, ex umidis naturae locis graviora fieri et ex fervidis acutiora, licet ita experiendo animadvertere. calices duo in una fornace aeque cocti aequoque pondere ad crepitumque uno sonitu sumantur. ex his unus in aquam demittatur, postea ex aqua eximatur, tunc utrique tangantur. cum enim ita factum fuerit, largiter inter eos sonitus discrepabit aequoque pondere non poterunt esse. ita et hominum corpora uno genere figurationis et una mundi coniunctione concepta alia propter regionis ardorem acutum spiritum aeris exprimunt acutum, alia propter umoris abundantiam gravissimas effundunt sonorum qualitates.
passages.translation: That this is true — that moist places by nature produce deeper sounds and hot places higher ones — may be observed by the following experiment. Take two cups fired equally in the same kiln, of equal weight and giving the same note when struck. Plunge one of them into water and then take it out; then strike both. When this has been done, the sound will differ widely between them, and they can no longer be of equal weight. In the same way the bodies of men, though conceived with one kind of form and under one conjunction of the heavens, emit in some cases a sharp breath because of the heat of the region, and in others, because of the abundance of moisture, pour out sounds of the deepest quality.

passages.latin: Item propter tenuitatem caeli meridianae nationes ex acuta fervore mente expeditius celeriusque moventur ad consiliorum cogitationes. septentrionales autem gentes infusae crassitudine caeli, propter obstantiam aeris umore refrigeratae stupentes habent mentes. hoc autem ita esse a serpentibus licet aspicere, quae per calorem cum exhaustam habent umoris refrigerationem, tunc acerrime moventur, per brumalia autem et hiberna tempora ab mutatione caeli refrigeratae, inmotae sunt stupore. ita non est mirandum, si acutiores efficit calidus aer hominum mentes, refrigeratus autem contra tardiores.
passages.translation: Moreover, owing to the thinness of the air, the southern peoples, their minds made keen by heat, are quicker and readier in devising counsel; whereas the northern peoples, steeped in a dense and humid air and their wits chilled by its resistance, are slow and dull. The like may be seen in serpents, which move most nimbly in the heat, when their moisture is drawn off, but in the cold of winter, numbed by the change of climate, lie torpid. It is no wonder, then, that warm air makes the mind keener, and cold air the duller.

passages.latin: cum sint autem meridiane nationes animis acutissimis infinitaque sollertia consiliorum, simul ut ad fortitudinem ingrediuntur ibi succumbunt, quod habent exsuctas ab sole animorum virtutes. qui vero refrigeratis nascuntur regionibus, ad armorum vehementiam paratiores sunt magnis virtutibus sine timore, sed tarditate animi sine considerantia inruentes sine sollertia suis consiliis refragantur. cum ergo haec ita sint ab natura rerum in mundo conlocata et omnes nationes inmoderatis mixtionibus disparatae, veros inter spatium totius orbis terrarum regionesque medio mundi populus Romanus possidet fines.
passages.translation: But although the southern nations have the keenest minds and boundless ingenuity in counsel, the moment they enter upon deeds of courage they fail, for the sun has drained the vigor from their spirits; whereas those born in colder regions are readier for the clash of arms and charge without fear in their great courage, yet, being slow of mind, they rush in without judgment and so thwart their own designs. Since nature has so ordered these things throughout the world, and all the nations differ in their unequal blendings, it is in the true mean, midway between the regions of the whole earth, that the Roman people hold their dominion.

passages.latin: namque temperatissimae ad utramque partem et corporum membris animorumque vigoribus pro fortitudine sunt in Italia gentes. quemadmodum enim Iovis stella inter Martis ferventissimam et Saturni frigidissimam media currens temperatur, eadem ratione Italia inter septentrionalem meridianamque ab utraque parte mixtionibus temperatas et invictas habet laudes. itaque consiliis refringit barbarorum virtutes, forti manu meridianorum cogitationes. ita divina mens civitatem populi Romani egregia temperataque regione conlocavit, uti orbis terrarum imperii potiretur.
passages.translation: For the races of Italy are the most temperate on either hand, alike in bodily frame and in strength of mind for valour. Just as the planet Jupiter, coursing between the burning heat of Mars and the icy cold of Saturn, is thereby tempered, so Italy, lying between north and south, is blended of both and holds praises unsurpassed: by counsel she breaks the courage of the barbarians, and by strength of hand the designs of the southern peoples. Thus the divine mind set the city of the Roman people in a region excellent and temperate, that it might win the empire of the whole earth.

passages.latin: quodsi ita est uti dissimiles regiones ab inclinationibus caeli variis generibus sint comparatae, ut etiam naturae gentium disparibus animis et corporum figuris qualitatibusque nascerentur, non dubitemus aedificiorum quoque rationes ad nationum gentiumque proprietates apte distribuere, cum habeamus ab ipsa rerum natura sollertem et expeditam monstrationem. Quoad potui summa ratione proprietates locorum ab natura rerum dispositas animadvertere exposui et quemadmodum ad solis cursum et inclinationes caeli oporteat ad gentium figuras constituere aedificiorum qualitates dixi. itaque nunc singulorum generum in aedificiis commensus symmetriarum et universos et separatos breviter explicabo.
passages.translation: But if it is so that dissimilar regions are arranged in various kinds by the inclinations of the sky, so that the natures of nations are born with dissimilar minds and shapes and qualities of bodies, let us not doubt that the proportions of buildings also are aptly distributed according to the properties of the nations, since we have a skilful and ready demonstration from the nature of things themselves. I have explained as far as I could observe the properties of places arranged by the nature of things with the greatest reason, and I have said how the qualities of buildings should be arranged according to the shapes of nations according to the course of the sun and the inclinations of the sky. Therefore I will now briefly explain the commensurate symmetries of each kind in buildings, both universal and separate.

passages.latin: Nulla architecto maior cura esse debet nisi uti proportionibus ratae partis habeant aedificia rationum exactiones. cum ergo constituta symmetriarum ratio fuerit et commensus ratiocinationibus explicati, tum etiam acuminis est proprium providere ad naturam loci aut usum aut speciem < detractionibus aut> adiectionibus temperaturas ⟨et⟩ efficere, cum de symmetria sit detractum aut adiectum, uti id videatur recte esse formatum in aspectuque nihil desideretur.
passages.translation: No architect should have greater care than that the buildings should have the exactitudes of the proportions of the approved part. Therefore, when the system of symmetries has been established and has been measured by explained reasoning, then it is also characteristic of acumen to provide for the nature of the place or the use or the appearance <and to effect tempers by deductions or> additions, when symmetry has been subtracted or added, so that it appears to be correctly formed and nothing is wanting in appearance.

passages.latin: alia enim ad manum species esse videtur, alia in excelso, non eadem in concluso, dissimilis in aperto, in quibus magni iudicii est opera quid tandem sit faciundum. non enim veros videtur habere visus effectus, sed fallitur saepius iudicio ab eo mens. quemadmodum etiam in scaenis pictis videntur columnarum proiecturae, mutulorum ecphorae, signorum figurae prominentes, cum sit tabula sine dubio ad regulam plana. similiter in navibus remi cum sint sub aqua directi, tamen oculis infracti videntur, et quatenus eorum partes tangunt summam planitiem liquoris, apparent uti sunt directi, cum vero sub aqua sunt demissi, per naturae perlucidam raritatem remittunt enatantes ab suis corporibus fluentes imagines ad summam aquae planitiem atque eae ibi commotae efficere videntur infractum remorum oculis aspectum.
passages.translation: For there seems to be one kind of appearance at hand, another in a lofty place, not the same in a confined place, unlike in an open place, in which it is a matter of great judgment what is to be done. For the sight does not seem to have true effects, but the mind is often deceived by its judgment. Just as in painted scenes the projections of columns, the eaves of the masts, the figures of signs are seen to be prominent, when the table is undoubtedly level to the rule. Similarly, in ships, when the oars are straight under water, they nevertheless appear to be broken to the eye, and insofar as their parts touch the highest level of the liquid, they appear to be straight, but when they are lowered under water, by the transparent rarity of nature, they send back floating images flowing from their bodies to the highest level of the water, and these, being moved there, seem to produce a broken appearance of the oars to the eye.

passages.latin: hoc autem sive simulacrorum inpulsu seu radiorum ex oculis effusionibus uti physicis placet videmus, utraque ratione videtur ita esse uti falsa iudicia oculorum habeat aspectus.
passages.translation: Now, whether we see this through the impact of images or through the effusions of rays from the eyes, as is pleasing to the physical, for both reasons it seems to be the case that the eyes have false judgments of appearance.

passages.latin: cum ergo quae sunt vera falsa videantur et nonnulla aliter quam sunt oculis probentur, non puto oportere esse dubium quin ad locorum naturas aut necessitates detractiones aut adiectiones fieri debeant sed ita uti nihil in his operibus desideretur. haec autem etiam ingeniorum acuminibus non solum doctrinis efficiuntur.
passages.translation: Therefore, since what is true is seen as false and is proved to the eye in some way than it is, I do not think there should be any doubt that deductions or additions should be made according to the nature or necessities of the place, so that nothing is wanting in these works. But these things are also accomplished by the acumen of genius, not only by doctrine.

passages.latin: igitur statuenda est primum ratio symmetriarum, a qua sumatur sine dubitatione commutatio. deinde explicetur operis futuri locorum imum spatium longitudinis <et latitudinis>, cuius cum semel constituta fuerit magnitudo, sequatur eam proportionis ad decorem apparatio, uti non sit considerantibus aspectus eurythmiae dubius. de qua quibus rationibus efficiatur est mihi pronuntiandum, primumque de cavis aedium uti fieri debeant dicam.
passages.translation: First establish the system of proportions [from which any modification can confidently be derived]. Then set out the fundamental length and width of the intended building. Once its dimensions have been fixed, arrange its proportions in accordance with decor, so that its eurythmy is clear to the observer. I must explain how this is achieved, beginning with the arrangement of the courts of houses.

passages.latin: Cava aedium quinque generibus sunt distincta, quorum ita figurae nominantur, tuscanicum, corinthium, tetrastylon, displuviatum, testudinatum. tuscanica sunt in quibus trabes in atrii latitudine traiectae habeant interpensiva et collicias ab angulis parietum ad angulos tignorum intercurrentes, item asseribus stillicidiorum in medium compluvium deiectus. in corinthiis isdem rationibus trabes et compluvia conlocantur, sed a parietibus trabes recedentes in circumitionis circa columnas componuntur. tetrastyla sunt quae subiectis sub trabibus angularibus columnis et utilitatem trabibus et firmitatem praestant, quod neque ipsae magnum impetum coguntur habere neque ab interpensivis onerantur.
passages.translation: The central courts of houses, or cava aedium, are divided into five types: Tuscan, Corinthian, tetrastyle, displuviate and testudinate. In the Tuscan type, beams spanning the width of the atrium carry the cross-members and valleys that run from the corners of the walls to the corners of the beams; the rafters direct the rain toward the central compluvium. In the Corinthian type, the beams and compluvium are arranged on the same principles, but the beams are set back from the walls and supported on columns around the opening. The tetrastyle type has columns beneath the beams at the corners, giving practical support and stability: the beams need neither span so great a distance nor bear the load of the intervening members unsupported.

passages.latin: displuviata autem sunt in quibus deliquiae arcam sustinentes stillicidia reiciunt. haec hibernaculis maxime praestant utilitates, quod compluvia eorum erecta non obstant luminibus tricliniorum. sed ea habent in refectionibus molestiam magnam, quod circa parietes stillicidia defluentia cum tument fistulae, quae non celeriter recipiunt ex canalibus aquam defluentem, itaque redundantes restagnant et intestinum et parietes in eis generibus aedificiorum corrumpunt. testudinata vero ibi fiunt, ubi non sunt impetus magni et in contignationibus supra spatiosae redduntur habitationes.
passages.translation: There are rain-pits in which the drops, supporting the ark, are rejected. These are of the greatest use to winter quarters, because their rain-pits, when erected, do not obstruct the lights of the dining rooms. But they are a great nuisance in the kitchens, because around the walls the dripping water is contained by pipes which do not quickly receive the water flowing from the channels, and therefore overflowing, it stagnates and corrupts the interior and walls of those types of buildings. But the vaulted ones are made where there are no great draughts and the dwellings are made spacious on the upper floors.

passages.latin: Atriorum vero latitudines ac longitudines tribus generibus formantur. et primum genus distribuitur uti longitudo cum in quinque partes divisa fuerit, tres partes latitudini dentur, alterum cum in tres partes dividatur, duae partes latitudini tribuantur, tertium uti latitudo in quadrato paribus lateribus describatur inque eo quadrato diagonios linea ducatur, et quantum spatium habuerit ea linea diagonii, tanta longitudo atrio detur.
passages.translation: The breadth and length of atria are determined by three types. The first is laid out so that, the length being divided into five parts, three are given to the breadth; the second, the length being divided into three parts, assigns two to the breadth; the third is set out by describing upon the breadth a square with equal sides, drawing a diagonal across that square, and giving the atrium a length equal to that diagonal.

passages.latin: Altitudo eorum, quanta longitudo fuerit quarta dempta, sub trabes extollatur; reliquum lacunariorum et arcae supra trabes spatio tribuatur. Alis dextra ac sinistra latitudinis ⟨spatium⟩, cum sit atrii longitudo ab XXX pedibus ad pedes XL, ex tertia parte eius constituatur. ab XL ad pedes L longitudo dividatur in partes tres ⟨semis⟩, ex his una pars alis detur. cum autem erit longitudo ab quinquaginta pedibus ad sexaginta, quarta pars longitudinis alis tribuatur. a pedibus LX ad LXXX longitudo dividatur in partes quattuor et dimidiam, ex his una pars fiat alarum latitudo. a pedibus octoginta ad pedes centum in quinque partes divisa longitudo iustam constituerit latitudinem alarum. trabes earum liminares ita altae ponantur, ut altitudines latitudinibus sint aequales. imagines cum suis ornamentis ad latitudinem alarum sint constitutae.
passages.translation: Raise the atrium to the underside of the beams to a height equal to its length less one-quarter; allow the remaining space for the coffering and structure above the beams. The widths of the alae on either side should be proportioned to the atrium’s length. For a length of thirty to forty feet, give them one-third; for forty to fifty feet, divide the length into three and a half parts and give them one; for fifty to sixty feet, give them one-quarter; for sixty to eighty feet, divide it into four and a half parts and give them one; for eighty to one hundred feet, divide it into five parts to establish their width. Set their lintel beams at a height equal to the width of the alae. Arrange the ancestral images and their ornaments in proportion to that width.

passages.latin: Tablinum, si latitudo atrii erit pedum viginti, dempta tertia eius spatio, reliquum tribuatur. si erit ab pedibus XXX ad XL, ex atrii latitudine tablino dimidium tribuatur. cum autem ab XL ad LX, latitudo dividatur in partes quinque, ex his duae tablino constituantur. non enim atria minora maioribus easdem possunt habere symmetriarum rationes. si enim maiorum symmetriis utemur in minoribus, neque tablina neque alae utilitatem poterunt habere, sin autem minorum in maioribus utemur, vasta et inmania in his ea erunt membra. itaque generatim magnitudinum rationes exquisitas et utilitati et aspectui conscribendas putavi.
passages.translation: For the tablinum, if the breadth of the atrium is twenty feet, a third part being deducted, the remainder is assigned to it; if from thirty to forty feet, half the breadth is given to the tablinum; and from forty to sixty, the breadth is divided into five parts, of which two are assigned to it. For the smaller atria cannot have the same proportions as the larger.

passages.latin: altitudo tablini ad trabem adiecta latitudinis octava constituatur. lacunaria eius tertia latitudinis ad altitudinem adiecta extollantur. fauces minoribus atriis e tablini latitudine dempta tertia, maioribus dimidia constituantur.. Latitudines ostiorum ad altitudinem si dorica erunt uti dorica, si ionica erunt uti ionica perficiantur, quemadmodum de thyromatis in quarto libro rationes symmetriarum sunt expositae. compluvii lumen latum latitudinis atrii ne minus quarta, ne plus tertia parte relinquatur, longitudo uti atrii pro rata parte fiat.
passages.translation: The height of the tabulin added to the beam is to be one-eighth of the width. Its ceilings are to be raised by one-third of the width added to the height. The openings for the smaller atriums are to be one-third deducted from the width of the tabulin, and for the larger ones, half. The images are also to be set high with their ornaments to the width of the wings. The widths of the forum to the height, if they are Doric, are to be completed as Doric, if they are Ionic, as Ionic, as the reasons for symmetry are explained in the fourth book of the Thyromata. The width of the floodlight is to be left no less than a quarter, no more than a third, the length is to be made as the proportion of the atrium.

passages.latin: Peristyla autem in transverso tertia parte longiora sint quam introrsus, columnae tam altae quam porticus latae fuerint. peristyliorum intercolumnia ne minus trium, ne plus quattuor columnarum crassitudine inter se distent. sin autem dorico more in peristylo columnae erunt faciundae, uti in quarto libro de doricis scripsi ita moduli sumantur et ad eos modulos triglyphorumque rationes disponantur.
passages.translation: Peristyles should be a third longer across than from front to back, and the columns as high as the porticoes are broad. The intercolumniations should be spaced not less than three nor more than four column-diameters apart. But if the columns of the peristyle are to be Doric, the modules are to be taken as I set down for the Doric order.

passages.latin: Tricliniorum quanta latitudo fuerit, bis tanta longitudo fieri debebit. altitudines omnium conclaviorum, quae oblonga fuerint, sic habere debent rationem uti longitudinis et latitudinis mensura componatur et ex ea summa dimidium sumatur et quantum fuerit tantum altitudini detur. sin autem exhedrae aut oeci quadrati fuerint, latitudinis dimidia addita altitudines educantur. pinacothecae uti exhedrae amplis magnitudinibus sunt constituendae. oeci corinthii tetrastylique quique Aegyptii vocantur latitudinis et longitudinis uti supra tricliniorum symmetriae scriptae sunt, ita habeant rationem, sed propter columnarum interpositiones spatiosiores constituantur.
passages.translation: Dining rooms should be twice as long as they are wide. For an oblong room, add its length and width and assign half that sum to its height. Square exedras or oeci should rise to one and a half times their width. Picture galleries, like exedras, should be generously dimensioned. Corinthian, tetrastyle and so-called Egyptian halls should follow the same length-to-width proportions as dining rooms, but their overall dimensions must be greater to allow for the intervening columns.

passages.latin: inter corinthios autem et aegyptios hoc erit discrimen. corinthii simplices habent columnas aut in podio positas aut in imo, supraque habent epistylia et coronas aut ex intestino opere aut albario, praeterea supra coronas curva lacunaria ad circinum delumbata. in aegyptiis autem supra columnas epistylia et ab epistyliis ad parietes qui sunt circa inponenda est contignatio, supra coaxationem, pavimentum, subdiu ut sit circumitus. deinde supra epistylium ad perpendiculum inferiorum columnarum inponendae sunt minores quarta parte columnae. supra earum epistylia et ornamenta lacunariis ornantur et inter columnas superiores fenestrae conlocantur. ita basilicarum ea similitudo, non corinthiorum tricliniorum, videtur esse.
passages.translation: Between the Corinthian and the Egyptian halls (oeci) there will be this difference. The Corinthian have a single tier of columns, set either upon a podium or upon the ground, and above them architraves and cornices, whether of joinery or of plaster, and over the cornices a vault rounded on the compass. In the Egyptian, above the lower columns an architrave is laid, and from it to the surrounding walls a floor is set, to make an open walk in the air; then, plumb above the lower columns and set back, a second tier, a fourth smaller, is raised; above their architraves and ornaments the ceiling is coffered, and windows are set between the upper columns. Thus they have the air not so much of Corinthian dining-rooms as of basilicas.

passages.latin: fiunt autem etiam non italicae consuetudinis oeci, quos Graeci cyzicenos appellant. hi conlocantur spectantes ad septentrionem et maxime viridia prospicientes, valvasque habent in medio ipsi autem sunt ita longi et lati uti duo triclinia cum circumitionibus inter se spectantia possint esse conlocata, habentque dextra ac sinistra lumina fenestrarum valvata, uti de lectis per spatia fenestrarum viridia prospiciantur. altitudines eorum dimidia latitudinis addita constituuntur.
passages.translation: There are also made halls (oeci) not in the Italian manner, which the Greeks call Cyzicene. These are set facing north and looking out, for choice, upon the gardens, with folding doors in the middle. They are so long and broad that two sets of dining-couches, facing one another, can be placed with room to pass around them; and they have windows opening on either hand upon the gardens, so that from the couches one may look out over the greenery.

passages.latin: In his aedificiorum generibus omnes sunt faciendae earum symmetriarum rationes quae sine inpeditione loci fieri poterunt, luminaque parietum altitudinibus si non obscurabuntur, faciliter erunt explicata, sin autem inpedientur ab angustiis aut aliis necessitatibus, tunc erit ut ingenio et acumine de symmetriis detractiones aut adiectiones fiant, uti non dissimiles veris symmetriis perficiantur venustates.
passages.translation: In all these kinds of building the schemes of symmetry are to be carried out so far as the site allows without hindrance; and the openings for light are easily contrived, provided they are not darkened by party-walls.

passages.latin: Nunc explicabimus quibus proprietatibus genera aedificiorum ad usum et caeli regiones aptas debeant spectare. hiberna triclinia et balnearia ad occidentem hibernum spectent, ideo quod vespertino lumine opus est uti, praeterea quod etiam sol occidens adversus habens splendorem, calorem remittens efficit vespertino tempore regionem tepidiorem. cubicula et bybliothecae ad orientem spectare debent, usus enim matutinum postulat lumen, item in bybliothecis libri non putrescent. nam quaecumque ad meridiem et occidentem spectant, ab tineis et umore libri vitiantur, quod venti umidi advenientes procreant eas et alunt infundentesque umidos spiritus pallore volumina corrumpunt.
passages.translation: We shall now explain with what properties the several kinds of building should be suited to their use and to the quarters of the sky they face. Winter dining-rooms and baths should look towards the winter sunset, because the evening light is needed, and because the setting sun, casting its glow full upon them, gives off a warmth that makes the quarter milder towards evening. Bedrooms and libraries should face the east, for their use demands the morning light, and in libraries the books will not rot; whereas in those rooms that face south and west the books are spoiled by worms and damp, since the moist winds that rise from those quarters breed and nourish the worms and, spreading their damp breath, corrupt the rolls with mold.

passages.latin: triclinia verna et autumnalia ad orientem. tum enim praetenta luminibus adversus solis impetus progrediens ad occidentem efficit ea temperata ad id tempus quo his solitum est uti. aestiva ad septentrionem, quod ea regio non ut reliquae per solstitium propter calorem efficiuntur aestuosae, eo quod est aversa a solis cursu semper refrigerata et salubritatem et voluptatem in usu praestat. non minus pinacothecae et plumariorum textrina pictorumque officinae, uti colores eorum in opere propter constantiam luminis inmutata permaneant qualitate.
passages.translation: Spring and autumn dining rooms east. For with the lights shining against the sun's attacks, advancing towards the west, it creates a temperature at the time when it is customary to use them. Summer north, because that region does not become sultry like the rest during the solstice due to heat, because it is turned away from the sun's course, it is always cooled and provides health and pleasure in use. No less are the galleries and the textile workshops of the painters, so that their colors in their work remain unchanged in quality due to the constancy of the light.

passages.latin: Cum ad regiones caeli ita ea fuerint disposita, tunc etiam animadvertendum est quibus rationibus privatis aedificiis propria loca patribus familiarum et quemadmodum communia cum extraneis aedificari debeant. namque ex his quae propria sunt, in ea non est potestas omnibus intro eundi nisi invitatis, quemadmodum sunt cubicula triclinia balneae ceteraque quae easdem habent usus rationes. communia autem sunt quibus etiam invocati suo iure de populo possunt venire, id est vestibula cava aedium, peristylia quaeque eundem habere possunt usum. igitur îs qui communi sunt fortuna, non necessaria magnifica vestibula nec tabulina neque atria, quod aliis officia praestant ambiundo neque ab aliis ambiuntur.
passages.translation: Since they have been so arranged for the regions of heaven, then it is also necessary to observe by what reasons private buildings should be built, the proper places for the fathers of families, and how common ones with strangers should be built. For of those things which are proper, there is no power for all to enter therein except those who are invited, as there are chambers, dining rooms, baths, and other things which have the same uses. But there are also common ones into which even those who are invited by their own right from the people can come, that is, vestibules, caves, peristyles, which can have the same use. Therefore, those who are in common fortune, do not need magnificent vestibules, nor small tables, nor courts, because they perform services to others by surrounding them rather than being surrounded by others.

passages.latin: qui autem fructibus rusticis serviunt, in eorum vestibulis stabula tabernae, in aedibus cryptae horrea apothecae ceteraque quae ad fructus servandos magis quam ad elegantiae decorem possunt esse, ita sunt facienda. item feneratoribus et publicanis commodiora et speciosiora et ab insidiis tuta, forensibus autem et disertis elegantiora et spatiosiora ad conventus excipiundos, nobilibus vero qui honores magistratusque gerundo praestare debent officia civibus, faciunda sunt vestibula regalia alta, atria et peristylia amplissima, silvae ambulationesque laxiores ad decorem maiestatis perfectae, praeterea bybliothecas, pinacothecas, basilicas non dissimili modo quam publicorum operum magnificentia ⟨habeant⟩ comparatas, quod in domibus eorum saepius et publica consilia et privata iudicia arbitriaque conficiuntur.
passages.translation: But those who live by the produce of the countryside should have, in their vestibules, stables and shops, and in the house itself cellars, granaries, storerooms and the like, contrived rather for keeping the produce than for elegance. For moneylenders and tax-farmers, houses more comfortable and handsome, and secure against intrigue; for advocates and men of eloquence, houses more elegant and roomy, to receive their callers; but for nobles, who in holding office and magistracies must render services to the citizens, there must be made lofty royal vestibules, the most ample atria and peristyles, with groves and broad walks finished in keeping with their dignity, and besides these, libraries and basilicas appointed with a magnificence not unlike that of public buildings — since in the houses of such men both public counsels and private suits and arbitrations are very often conducted.

passages.latin: ergo si his rationibus ad singulorum generum personas, uti in libro primo de decore est scriptum, ita disposita erunt aedificia, non erit quod reprehendatur. habebunt enim ad omnes res commodas et emendatas explicationes. earum autem rerum non solum erunt in urbe aedificiorum rationes, sed etiam ruri, praeterquam quod in urbe atria proxima ianuis solent esse, ruri ab pseudourbanis statim peristylia, deinde tunc atria habentia circum porticus pavimentatas spectantes ad palaestras et ambulationes. Quoad potui urbanas rationes aedificiorum summatim perscribere, proposui, nunc rusticorum expeditionum ⟨apparationes⟩ ut sint ad usum commodae quibusque rationibus conlocare oporteat eas dicam.
passages.translation: Therefore, if buildings are arranged in this way for each class of persons, as is written in the first book of the Decorum, there will be nothing to be criticized for. For they will have convenient and improved explanations for all things. Now there will be the rules for buildings not only in the city, but also in the country, besides the fact that in the city the atriums are usually close to the doors, but in the country the peristyle immediately after the pseudo-urban ones, then the atriums having paved porches around the porticoes facing the palaestras and the walks. As far as I could write down the urban rules for buildings in summary, I proposed, now I will tell you the expeditions of the countrymen so that they are convenient for use and in what ways it is necessary to place them.

passages.latin: primum de salubritatibus, uti in primo volumine de moenibus conlocandis scriptum est, regiones aspiciantur et ita villae conlocentur. magnitudines earum ad modum agri copiasque fructuum comparentur. chortes magnitudinesque earum ad pecorum numerum atque quot iuga boum opus fuerit ibi versari, ita finiantur. in chorte culina quam calidissimo loco designetur, coniuncta autem habeat bubilia, quorum praesepia ad focum et orientis caeli regionem spectent, ideo quod boves lumen et ignem spectando horridi non fiunt. item agricolae religione inpediti non putant oportere aliam regionem caeli boves spectare nisi ortum solis.
passages.translation: First of all, concerning health, as is written in the first volume on the placing of walls, let the regions be considered and the villages placed accordingly. Their sizes should be compared to the size of the field and the abundance of fruits. The cohorts and their sizes should be determined according to the number of cattle and how many yokes of oxen it will be necessary to turn there. In the cohort, the kitchen should be designated in the warmest place, and the cattle should be connected, the stalls of which should look at the hearth and the eastern sky, so that the oxen do not become horrified by looking at light and fire. Likewise, farmers who are inexperienced in the regions do not think that it is necessary for the oxen to look at any other sky region than the rising of the sun.

passages.latin: bubilium autem debent esse latitudines nec minores pedum denûm nec maiores quindenûm, longitudo uti singula iuga ne minus pedes occupent septenos. balnearia item coniuncta sint culinae, ita enim lavationi rusticae ministratio non erit longe. torcular item proximum sit culinae, ita enim ad molarios fructus commoda erit ministratio, habeatque coniunctam vinariam cellam habentem ab septentrione lumina fenestrarum. cum enim alia parte habuerit qua sol calfacere possit, vinum quod erit in ea cella confusum ab calore efficietur inbecillum.
passages.translation: The widths of the cattle pens should be neither less than ten feet nor more than fifteen, and the length should be such that each row does not occupy less than seven feet. The baths should also be connected to the kitchen, for thus the service of the country will not be far. The winepress should also be close to the kitchen, for thus the service of the olive trees will be convenient, and it should have a wine cellar connected to it, having windows facing north. For since it has another side from which the sun can warm it, the wine that will be in that cellar will be confused by the heat and become weak.

passages.latin: olearia autem ita est conlocanda ut habeat a meridie calidisque regionibus lumen. non enim debet oleum congelari sed tepore caloris extenuari. magnitudines autem earum ad fructuum rationem et numerum doliorum sunt faciundae, quae cum sint cullearia, per medium occupare debent pedes quaternos. ipsum autem torcular si non cocleis•torquetur sed vectibus et prelo premitur, ne minus longum pedes XL constituatur, ita enim erit vectiario spatium expeditum. latitudo eius ne minus pedum senûm denûm, nam sic erit ad prelum opus facientibus libera versatio et expedita. sin autem duobus prelis loco opus fuerit, quattuor et viginti pedes latitudini dentur.
passages.translation: The oil press should be placed so that it has light from the south and hot regions. For the oil should not be frozen but rather be weakened by the warmth of the heat. Their sizes should be made according to the quantity of fruit and the number of barrels, which, since they are spoon-shaped, should occupy four feet in the middle. But if the press itself is not turned with screws but is pressed with bars and a press, it should not be less than forty feet long, for in this way there will be an easy space for the transporter. Its width should not be less than ten feet, for in this way those doing the full work will have free and easy movement. But if two presses are needed instead, twenty-four feet should be given to the width.

passages.latin: Ovilia et caprilia ita sunt magna facienda uti singula pecora areae ne minus pedes quaternos et semipedem, ne plus senos possint habere. granaria sublimata et ad septentrionem aut aquilonem spectantia disponantur, ita enim frumenta non poterint cito concalescere, sed ab flatu refrigerata diu servantur. namque ceterae regiones procreant curculionem et reliquas bestiolas quae frumentis solent nocere. equilibus quae maxime in villa loca calidissima fuerint constituantur, dum ne ad focum spectent. cum enim iumenta proxime ignem stabulantur, horrida fiunt.
passages.translation: Oval and goat pens should be made so large that each herd of cattle cannot have less than four and a half feet, or more than six. Granaries should be elevated and arranged facing north or northeast, for in this way the grain will not be able to heat up quickly, but will be kept cool by the wind for a long time. For other regions breed weevils and other small animals that are accustomed to harm grain. For horses, the warmest places in the village should be placed, so that they do not look at the fire. For when cattle are stabled close to the fire, they become horrified.

passages.latin: item non sunt inutilia praesepia quae conlocantur extra culinam in aperto contra orientem. cum enim in hieme anni sereno caelo in ea traducuntur matutino boves, ad solem pabulum capientes fiunt nitidiores. horrea fenilia farraria pistrina extra villam facienda videntur, ut ab ignis periculo sint villae tutiores. si quid delicatius in villis faciundum fuerit, ex symmetriis quae in urbanis supra scriptis sunt constitutae ita struantur uti sine inpeditione rusticae utilitatis aedificentur.
passages.translation: Likewise, stables placed outside the kitchen in the open air facing east are not useless. For when in the winter of the year the oxen are brought there in the morning in a clear sky, they become brighter as they feed in the sun. Barns, barns, mills, and bakeries seem to be built outside the village, so that the villages are safer from the danger of fire. If anything more delicate is to be done in the villages, they should be constructed in such a way that they are built without hindering the rural utility, based on the symmetries established in urban buildings above.

passages.latin: Omniaque aedificia ut luminosa sint, oportet curari; sed quae sunt ad villas, faciliora videntur esse, ideo quod paries nullius vicini potest obstare, in urbe autem aut communium parietum altitudines aut angustiae loci inpediundo faciunt obscuritates. Itaque de ea re sic erit experiundum. Ex qua parte lumen oporteat sumere, linea tendatur ab altitudine parietis, qui videtur obstare, ad eum locum, quo oporteat inmittere, et si ab ea linea, in altitudinem cum prospiciatur, poterit spatium puri caeli amplum videri, in eo loco lumen erit sine inpeditione.
passages.translation: All buildings must be cared for so that they are luminous, but those that are near villages seem to be easier because no neighbor's wall can obstruct them, but in a city either the heights of the common walls or the narrowness of the place obstruct them and cause darkness. Therefore, this is what we should try about this matter. From which side the light should be let in, and if from that line, when looking up into the sky, a large space of pure sky can be seen, in that place there will be light without obstruction.

passages.latin: sin autem officient trabes ea lumina aut contignationes, de superioribus partibus aperiatur et ita inmittatur. et ad summam ita est gubernandum ut ex quibuscumque partibus caelum prospici poterit, per eas fenestrarum loca relinquantur, sic enim lucida erunt aedificia. cum autem in tricliniis ceterisque conclavibus maximus est usus luminum, tum etiam in itineribus clivis scalis, quod in his saepius alii aliis obviam venientes ferentes sarcinas solent incurrere. Quoad potui distributiones operum nostratium, ut sint aedificatoribus non obscurae, explicui. nunc etiam quemadmodum Graecorum consuetudinibus aedificia distribuantur, uti non sint ignota, summatim exponam.
passages.translation: But if the beams or lintels of the floors obstruct it, it should be opened from the upper parts and let in. And to sum up, it should be so governed that from whatever parts the sky can be seen, places for windows should be left through them, for in this way the buildings will be bright. But since in dining rooms and other rooms the greatest use is made of lights, then also in the paths of stairs, because in these people often encounter each other carrying loads. As far as I could, I have explained the distributions of our works, so that they may not be obscure to the builders. Now I will also briefly explain how buildings are distributed according to the customs of the Greeks, so that they may not be unknown.

passages.latin: Atriis Graeci quia non utuntur, neque aedificant, sed ab ianua introeuntibus itinera faciunt latitudinibus non spatiosis, et ex una parte equilia, ex altera ostiariis cellas, statimque ianuae interiores finiuntur. hic autem locus inter duas ianuas graece θυρωρεῖον appellatur. deinde est introitus in peristylon. id peristylum in tribus partibus habet porticus inque parte quae spectat ad meridiem duas antas inter se spatio amplo distantes in quibus trabes invehuntur, et quantum inter antas distat, ex eo tertia dempta spatium datur introrsus. hic locus apud non nullos prostas, apud alios pastas nominatur.
passages.translation: The Greeks do not use or build courts, but they make paths that are not very wide for those entering from the door, and on one side they have stalls, on the other the cells for the porters, and immediately the inner doors end. This place between the two doors is called in Greek θυρωρεῖον. Then there is the entrance into the peristyle. This peristyle has a portico on three sides, and on the side that faces south there are two antae, widely spaced apart from each other, upon which beams are carried, and the distance between the arches is taken from that, one third of the space is given inside. This place is called prostas by some, pastas by others.

passages.latin: in his locis introrsus constituuntur oeci magni, in quibus matres familiarum cum lanificis habent sessionem. in prostadis autem dextra ac sinistra cubicula sunt conlocata, quorum unum thalamos, alterum amphithalamos dicitur. circum autem in porticibus triclinia cotidiana, cubicula, etiam cellae familiaricae constituuntur. haec pars aedificii gynaeconitis appellatur.
passages.translation: Within these are set the great halls (oeci) where the mistresses of the household sit with the wool-workers. To right and left of the prostas are bedchambers, the one called the thalamos, the other the amphithalamos. Around the porticoes are the everyday dining-rooms, bedchambers, and servants’ rooms. This part of the house is called the gynaeconitis, the women’s quarters.

passages.latin: Coniunguntur autem his domus ampliores habentes lautiora peristylia, in quibus pares sunt quattuor porticus altitudinibus, aut una quae ad meridiem spectat excelsioribus columnis constituitur. id autem peristylum quod unam altiorem habet porticum, rhodiacum dicitur. habent autem eae domus vestibula egregia et ianuas proprias cum dignitate porticusque peristyliorum albariis et tectoriis et ex intestino opere lacunariis ornatas, et in porticibus quae ad septentrionem spectant triclinia cyzicena et pinacothecas, ad orientem autem bybliothecas, exhedras ad occidentem, ad meridiem vero spectantes oecos quadratos ita ampla magnitudine uti faciliter in eo quattuor tricliniis stratis ministrationum ludorumque operis locus possit esse spatiosus.
passages.translation: These houses are joined by larger ones, having more elaborate peristyles, in which there are four porticos of equal height, or one that faces south is built with higher columns. But that peristyle which has one higher portico is called Rhodian. These houses have excellent vestibules and doors of their own, and the porticos of the peristyles are adorned with dignity, with white walls and ceilings and with ceilings of internal work, and in the porticos that face north there are dining rooms and picture galleries, while to the east there are libraries, and to the west there are rooms facing south, and square courtyards of ample size, so that in those four dining rooms there can be easily a spacious place for serving meals and playing.

passages.latin: in his oecis fiunt virilia convivia. non enim fuerat institutum matres familiarum eorum moribus accumbere. haec autem peristylia domus andronitides dicuntur, quod in his viri sine interpellationibus mulierum versantur. praeterea dextra ac sinistra domunculae constituuntur habentes proprias ianuas triclinia et cubicula commoda, uti hospites advenientes non in peristylia sed in ea hospitalia recipiantur. nam cum fuerunt Graeci delicatiores et fortuna opulentiores, hospitibus advenientibus instruebant triclinia cubicula cum penu cellas primoque die ad cenam invitabant, postero mittebant pullos ova holera poma reliquasque res agrestes. ideo pictores ea quae mittebantur hospitibus picturis imitantes xenia appellaverunt. ita patres familiarum in hospitio non videbantur esse peregre, habentes secretam in his hospitalibus libertatem.
passages.translation: In these rooms, men's banquets are held. For it was not customary for mothers of families to sit down in their manners. But this peristyle of the house is called the Andronitides, because in it the men are occupied without the interruptions of women. Moreover, on the right and left are small houses built, having their own doors, dining rooms and comfortable bedrooms, so that guests arriving may not be received in the peristyle but in that hospital. For when the Greeks were more refined and more wealthy in fortune, they furnished dining rooms, bedrooms with pantry rooms for guests arriving, and on the first day they invited them to dinner, and on the second day they sent them chickens, eggs, vegetables, apples, and other country things. Therefore, painters, imitating the things that were sent to the guests in their paintings, called them xenia. Thus the fathers of families did not seem to be abroad in their hospitality, having a secret liberality in these hospitals.

passages.latin: inter duo autem peristylia et hospitalia itinera sunt quae mesauloe dicuntur, quod inter duas aulas media sunt interposita, nostri autem eas andronas appellant. Sed hoc valde est mirandum, nec enim graece nec latine potest id convenire. Graeci enim ἀνδρῶνας appellant oecus, ubi convivia virilia solent esse, quod eo mulieres non accedunt. item aliae res sunt similes, uti xystus prothyrum telamones et nonnulla alia eius modi.ξυστός enim est graeca appellatione porticus ampla latitudine, in qua athletae per hiberna tempora exercentur. nostri autem hypaethrus ambulationes xysta appellant, quas Graeci παραδρομίδας dicunt. item πρόθυρα graece dicuntur quae sunt ante ianuas vestibula, nos autem appellamus prothyra quae graece dicuntur διάθυρα.
passages.translation: Between the two peristyles and the guest apartments are passages called mesaulae, because they lie between two courts; our own people, however, call them andrones. Yet this is very strange, for the term agrees with neither Greek nor Latin usage: the Greeks call ἀνδρῶνας the halls where the men’s banquets are held, since women do not enter there. There are other terms of the same kind — xystus, prothyrum, telamones, and a few besides. The ξύστος, in Greek usage, is a portico of ample breadth in which athletes train during the winter season; our people, however, call open-air walks xysta, which the Greeks name παραδρομίδας. Likewise, what in Greek are called πρόθυρα are the vestibules before the doors; but we call prothyra what the Greeks call διάθυρα.
