passages.latin: item si qua virili figura signa mutulos aut coronas sustinent, nostri telamones appellant, cuius rationes quid ita aut quare dicantur ex historiis non inveniuntur, Graeci vero eos ἄτλαντας vocitant. Atlas enim formatur historia sustinens mundum, ideo quod is primum cursum solis et lunae siderumque omnium versationum rationes vigore animi sollertiaque curavit hominibus tradenda, eaque re a pictoribus et statuariis deformatur pro eo beneficio sustinens mundum, filiaeque eius Atlantides, quas nos vergilias, Graeci autem πλειάδας nominant, cum sideribus in mundo sunt dedicatae.
passages.translation: Likewise, if there are those who support the symbols of a man's figure with a mute or crown, ours call them Telamones, the reasons for which are not found in the histories, but the Greeks call them Atlases. For Atlas is formed by history as supporting the world, because he was the first to take care of the course of the sun and moon and the reasons for all the movements of the stars, by the vigor of his mind and skill, to be handed down to men, and for that reason he is deformed by painters and sculptors as supporting the world for his benefit, and his daughters, the Atlanteans, whom we call Vergilias, and the Greeks call Pleiades, are dedicated to the stars in the world.

passages.latin: nec tamen ego ut mutetur consuetudo nominationum aut sermonis, ideo haec proposui, sed uti non sint ignota philologis exponenda iudicavi. Quibus consuetudinibus aedificia italico more et Graecorum institutis conformantur exposui, et de symmetriis singulorum generum proportiones perscripsi. ergo quoniam de venustate decoreque ante est conscriptum, nunc exponemus de firmitate quemadmodum ea sine vitiis permanentia ad vetustatem conlocentur.
passages.translation: I have not set out these matters to alter established names or ordinary usage, but to make them known to those concerned with language. I have explained the customs according to which buildings are formed in the Italian manner and in the Greek tradition, and have described the proportions of each type. Having discussed beauty and propriety, I shall now turn to strength and explain how buildings can be constructed without defects for lasting service.

passages.latin: Aedificia quae plano pede instituuntur, si fundamenta eorum facta fuerint ita ut in prioribus libris de muro et theatris a nobis est expositum, ad vetustatem ea erunt sine dubitatione firma. sin autem hypogea concamarationesque instituentur, fundationes eorum fieri debent crassiores quam quae in superioribus aedificiis structurae sunt futurae, eorumque parietes pilae columnae ad perpendiculum inferiorum medio conlocentur, uti solido respondeant. nam si in pendentibus onera fuerint parietum aut columnarum, non poterint habere perpetuam firmitatem.
passages.translation: Buildings that are built on a flat base, if their foundations are made in such a way as we have explained in previous books on walls and theaters, will undoubtedly be strong for a long time. But if basements and chambers are built, their foundations should be made thicker than those that will be used in the structures of the upper buildings, and their walls, pillars, and columns should be placed perpendicular to the middle of the lower ones, so that they correspond to the solid. For if the loads of the walls or columns are on the overhangs, they will not be able to have permanent strength.

passages.latin: praeterea inter lumina secundum pilas et antas postes si supponentur, erunt non vitiosae. limina enim et trabes structuris cum sint oneratae, medio spatio pandantes frangunt sub lysi structuras. cum autem subiecti fuerint et subcuneati postes, non patiuntur insidere trabes neque eas laedere.
passages.translation: Furthermore, if placed between the openings, by piers and antae, they will not be defective. For thresholds and beams, when loaded with structures, break the suspended structures while they hang in half; but when the posts have been secured and wedged together, they do not allow the beams to rest on them or damage them.

passages.latin: item administrandum est uti levent onus parietum fornicationes cuneorum divisionibus et ad centrum respondentes earum conclusurae. cum enim extra trabes aut liminum capita arcus cuneis erunt conclusae, primum non pandabit materies levata onere, deinde si quod vetustate vitium ceperit, sine molitione fulturarum faciliter mutabitur.
passages.translation: It is also necessary to ensure that the load on the walls is relieved by the divisions of the wedges and their closures corresponding to the center. For when the outside beams or the capitals of the thresholds are closed with wedges, first the materials will not expand when the load is lifted, and then if they have developed any defect due to age, they can be easily replaced without the need for supports.

passages.latin: itemque quae pilatim aguntur aedificia, et cuneorum divisionibus coagmentis ad centrum respondentibus fornices concluduntur, extremae pilae in his latiores spatio sunt faciundae, uti vires eae habentes resistere possint, cum cunei ab oneribus parietum pressi per coagmenta ad centrum se prementes extruderent incumbas. itaque si angulares pilae erunt spatiosis magnitudinibus, continendo cuneos firmitatem operibus praestabunt.
passages.translation: Likewise, buildings carried up in piers, when the arches are closed by the divisions of the wedges corresponding to the joints at the center, the outer piers in these should be made wider in space, so that the forces they possess can resist, when the wedges, pressed by the loads of the walls, press themselves through the joints towards the center and extrude themselves. Therefore, if the corner piles are of spacious sizes, by containing the wedges they will provide stability to the works.

passages.latin: Cum in his rebus animadversum fuerit uti ea diligentia in his adhibeatur, non minus etiam observandum est uti omnes structurae perpendiculo respondeant neque habeant in ulla parte proclinationes. maxima autem esse debet cura substructionum, quod in his infinita vitia solet facere terrae congestio. ea enim non potest esse semper uno pondere quo solet esse per aestatem, sed hibernis temporibus recipiendo ex imbribus aquae multitudinem crescens et pondere et amplitudine disrumpit et extrudit structurarum saeptiones.
passages.translation: Since in these matters it has been observed that such diligence is applied, it is no less important to observe that all structures correspond to the perpendicular and have no inclinations in any part. The greatest care should be taken with the substructures, because in these the accumulation of earth tends to cause infinite defects. For it cannot always be with the same weight as it usually is during the summer, but in winter times, receiving a multitude of water from the rains, it increases in weight and size and bursts and pushes out the partitions of the structures.

passages.latin: itaque ut huic vitio medeatur. sic erit faciundum ut primum pro amplitudine congestionis crassitudo structurae constituatur, deinde in frontibus anterides, sive erismae sunt, una struantur, eaeque inter se distent tanto spatio quanta altitudo substructionis est futura, crassitudine eadem qua substructio. procurrat autem ab imo pro quam crassitudo constituta fuerit substructionis, deinde contrahatur gradatim ita uti summam habeat prominentiam quanta operis est crassitudo.
passages.translation: Therefore, to remedy this defect, the thickness of the structure should first be fixed in proportion to the mass of earth to be retained; then, on the face, buttresses (anterides, or in Greek erismae) are built, set apart from one another by as much space as the height of the substructure will be, and of the same thickness as the substructure itself. They are carried out from the bottom by as much as the thickness fixed for the structure, and then drawn in so that the part standing in the face is as thick as a fourth part of the height.

passages.latin: praeterea introrsus contra terrenum coniuncta muro serratim struantur, uti singuli dentes ab muro tantum distent quanta altitudo futura erit substructionis, crassitudines autem habeant dentium structurae uti muri. item in extremis angulis cum recessum fuerit ab interiore angulo spatio altitudinis substructionis, in utramque partem signetur et ab his signis diagonios structura conlocetur, et ab ea media altera coniuncta cum angulo muri. ita dentes et diagonioe structurae non patientur tota vi premere murum, sed dissipabunt retinendo impetum congestionis.
passages.translation: Furthermore, they are built inwards against the ground, connected to the wall, in a serrated manner, so that each tooth is as far from the wall as the future height of the substructure will be, and the thickness of the teeth should be as thick as the structure of the wall. Likewise, in the extreme corners, when there is a recess from the inner corner by the space of the height of the substructure, let diagonals be marked on both sides and from these marks the structure is placed, and from that the other side connected to the corner of the wall. Thus the teeth and diagonals of the structure will not be allowed to press the wall with all their force, but will dissipate the impact of the congestion by retaining it.

passages.latin: Quemadmodum sine vitiis opera constitui oporteat et uti caveatur incipientibus exposui. namque de tegulis aut tignis aut asseribus mutandis non est eadem cura quemadmodum de his, quod ea quamvis sunt vitiosa, faciliter mutantur. itaque nec solida quia non putantur esse, quibus rationibus haec poterint esse firma et quemadmodum instituantur exposui.
passages.translation: I have explained to beginners how works should be constructed without defects and how precautions should be taken. For there is not the same care in changing tiles or beams or planks as in these, which, although defective, are easily changed. Therefore, I have explained what are not even supposed to be solid, by what means these could be made firm and how they are constructed.

passages.latin: quibus autem copiarum generibus oporteat uti, non est architecti potestas, ideo quod non in omnibus locis omnia genera copiarum nascuntur, ut in primo volumine est expositum, praeterea in domini est potestate utrum latericio an caementicio an saxo quadrato velit aedificare. itaque omnium operum probationes tripertito considerantur, id est fabrili subtilitate et magnificentia et dispositione. cum magnificenter opus perfectum aspicietur, a domini potestate inpensae laudabuntur, cum subtiliter, officinatoris probabitur exactio, cum vero venuste proportionibus et symmetriis habuerit auctoritatem, tunc fuerit gloria architecti.
passages.translation: The choice of available materials is not entirely within the architect’s power, since not every kind is found in every place, as Book I explains. The owner also decides whether to build in brick, rubble masonry, or ashlar. A work is judged under three heads: craftsmanship, magnificence, and arrangement. When a finished building impresses by its magnificence, the owner’s expenditure earns praise; when by its precision, the workmanship is commended. When beauty acquires authority through proportion and commensurability, the credit belongs to the architect.

passages.latin: haec autem recte constituuntur, cum is et a fabris et ab idiotis patiatur accipere se consilia. namque omnes homines, non solum architecti, quod est bonum possunt probare, sed inter idiotas et eos hoc est discrimen quod idiota nisi factum viderit, non potest scire quid sit futurum, architectus autem simul animo constituerit, antequam inceperit et venustate et usu et decore quale sit futurum habet definitum. Quas res privatis aedificiis utiles putavi et quemadmodum sint faciundae quam apertissime potui perscripsi. de expolitionibus autem eorum uti sint elegantes et sine vitiis ad vetustatem <>, insequenti volumine exponam.
passages.translation: But these things are rightly established, since he allows himself to be advised by both craftsmen and laymen. For all men, not only architects, can approve what is good, but the difference between laymen and architects is this: a layman cannot know what will be until he sees it done, while an architect, having already established it in his mind, has defined before he begins what it will be in terms of beauty, use, and decorum. I have described as clearly as I could what things are useful for private buildings and how they should be made. But I will explain their refinements, so that they are elegant and without defects for old age, in the following volume.

passages.latin: Maiores cum sapienter tum etiam utiliter instituerunt, per commentariorum relationes cogitata tradere posteris, ut ea non interirent sed singulis aetatibus crescentia voluminibus edita gradatim pervenirent vetustatibus ad summam doctrinarum subtilitatem. itaque non mediocres sed infinitae sunt his agendae gratiae, quod non invidiose silentes praetermiserunt, sed omnium generum sensus conscriptionibus memoriae tradendos curaverunt.
passages.translation: The ancients, both wisely and usefully, instituted the transmission of their thoughts to posterity through the reports of their commentaries, so that they would not perish, but, published in increasing volumes in each age, would gradually reach the highest subtlety of their doctrines. Therefore, the merits of this work are not moderate but infinite, because they did not pass over it in envious silence, but took care to transmit to memory all kinds of thoughts in writings.

passages.latin: namque si non ita fecissent, non potuissemus scire quae res in Troia fuissent gestae, nec quid Thales Democritus Anaxagoras Xenophanes reliquique physici sensissent de rerum natura quasque Socrates Platon Aristoteles Zenon Epicurus aliique philosophi hominibus agendae vitae terminationes finissent seu Croesus Alexander Darius ceterique reges quas res aut quibus rationibus gessissent fuissent notae, nisi maiores praeceptorum comparationibus omnium memoriae ad posteritatem commentariis extulissent.
passages.translation: For if they had not done so, we would not have been able to know what things had been done in Troy, nor what Thales, Democritus, Anaxagoras, Xenophanes, and the other natural philosophers had thought about the nature of things, nor what Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Zeno, Epicurus, and other philosophers had concluded the ends of life for men, nor what things Croesus, Alexander, Darius, and the other kings had done, or for what reasons, would have been known, unless the elders had brought forth the memory of all things in their commentaries by comparisons of precepts for posterity.

passages.latin: itaque quemadmodum his gratiae sunt agendae, contra qui eorum scripta furantes pro suis praedicant sunt vituperandi, quique non propriis cogitationibus scriptorum nituntur, sed invidis moribus aliena violantes gloriantur, non modo sunt reprehendendi, sed etiam quia impio more vixerunt, poena condemnandi. nec tamen haec res non vindicatae curiosius ab antiquis esse memorantur. quorum exitus iudiciorum qui fuerint, non est alienum quemadmodum sint nobis traditi explicare.
passages.translation: Just as gratitude is owed to those who transmit their thoughts, so those who steal others’ writings and proclaim them their own deserve condemnation. Those who claim glory by violating the work of others, instead of relying on their own ideas, merit not merely reproach but punishment for acting dishonourably. Such offenses, it is reported, did not go unpunished among the ancients. It is therefore appropriate to recount the outcomes of those judgments as they have been handed down to us.

passages.latin: reges Attalici magnis philologiae dulcedinibus inducti cum egregiam bybliothecam Pergami ad communem delectationem instituissent, tunc item Ptolomaeus infinito zelo cupiditatisque incitatus studio non minoribus industriis ad eundem modum contenderat Alexandriae comparare. cum autem summa diligentia perfecisset, non putavit id satis esse nisi propagationibus inseminando curaret augendam. itaque Musis et Apollini ludos dedicavit et quemadmodum athletarum sic communium scriptorum victoribus praemia et honores constituit.
passages.translation: When the Attalic kings, led by the great delights of philology, had established an excellent library at Pergamum for the common enjoyment, then likewise Ptolemy, inspired by infinite zeal and desire, strove with no less diligence to furnish Alexandria with the same. But when he had accomplished it with the utmost diligence, he did not think that it was sufficient unless he took care to increase it by insemination. Accordingly he dedicated games to the Muses and Apollo, and, as he did to athletes, so he established prizes and honors for the victors of common writings.

passages.latin: his ita institutis cum ludi adessent, iudices litterati qui ea probarent erant legendi. rex cum iam sex civitatis lectos habuisset nec tam cito septumum idoneum inveniret, retulit ad eos qui supra bybliothecam fuerunt et quaesiit si quem novissent ad id expeditum. tunc ei dixerunt esse quendam Aristophanen, qui summo studio summaque diligentia cotidie omnes libros ex ordine perlegeret. itaque conventu ludorum cum secretae sedes iudicibus essent distributae, cum ceteris Aristophanes citatus quemadmodum fuerat locus ei designatus sedit.
passages.translation: As the games approached, learned judges had to be selected to assess them. The king had already chosen six men from the city but could not readily find a suitable seventh. He consulted those in charge of the library and asked whether they knew anyone qualified. They told him of a certain Aristophanes, who read through all the books in order each day with exceptional diligence and attention. When the games assembled and reserved seats had been assigned to the judges, Aristophanes was summoned with the others and took his appointed place.

passages.latin: primo poetarum ordine ad certationem inducto cum recitarentur scripta, populus cunctus significando monebat iudices quod probarent. itaque cum ab singulis sententiae sunt rogatae, sex una dixerunt et quem maxime animadverterunt multitudini placuisse, ei primum praemium, insequenti secundum tribuerunt. Aristophanes vero cum ab eo sententia rogaretur, eum primum renuntiari iussit qui minime populo placuisset.
passages.translation: When the first order of poets was brought to the competition, and their writings were recited, the whole people indicated by signs to the judges what they should approve. Accordingly, when each was asked for his opinion, the six gave one, and to him whom they observed had most pleased the multitude, they awarded the first prize, and to the next the second. But Aristophanes, when his opinion was asked of him, ordered that the one who had least pleased the people be dismissed first.

passages.latin: cum autem rex et universi vehementer indignarentur, surrexit et rogando impetravit ut paterentur se dicere. itaque silentio facto docuit unum ex his eum esse poetam, ceteros aliena recitavisse, oportere autem iudicantes non furta sed scripta probare. admirante populo et rege dubitante, fretus memoriae certis armariis infinita volumina eduxit et ea cum recitatis conferendo coegit ipsos furatos de se confiteri. itaque rex iussit cum his agi furti condemnatosque cum ignominia dimisit, Aristophanen vero amplissimis muneribus ornavit et supra bybliothecam constituit.
passages.translation: But when the king and all were greatly indignant, he rose and begged that they be allowed to speak. So, by making silence, he taught that one of them was a poet, and that the others had recited other people's works, but that they judged it necessary to prove that they were not stolen but written. With the people astonished and the king doubtful, he, relying on his memory, brought out an infinite number of volumes from certain cupboards and, comparing them with the ones recited, forced the thieves themselves to confess that they had stolen them. So the king ordered that these be tried and those convicted of theft were released with disgrace, but Aristophanes was adorned with the most magnificent gifts and placed over the library.

passages.latin: insequentibus annis a Macedonia Zoilus, qui adoptavit cognomen ut Homeromastix vocitaretur, Alexandriam venit suaque scripta contra Iliadem et Odyssean comparata regi recitavit. Ptolomaeus vero cum animadvertisset poetarum parentem philologiaeque omnis ducem absentem vexari et cuius ab cunctis gentibus scripta suspicerentur ab eo vituperari, indignans nullum ei dedit responsum. Zoilus autem cum diutius in regno fuisset, inopia pressus summisit ad regem postulans ut aliquid sibi tribueretur.
passages.translation: In the following years, Zoilus, who adopted the surname Homeromastix, came from Macedonia to Alexandria and read his writings against the Iliad and the Odyssey to the king, having prepared them. But Ptolemy, when he perceived that the father of poets and the leader of all philology was being harassed in his absence, and that his writings, whose writings were highly regarded by all nations, were being censured by him, became indignant and gave him no answer. But Zoilus, when he had been in the kingdom for a long time, was pressed by poverty and sent to the king, requesting that something be given to him.

passages.latin: rex vero respondisse dicitur Homerum, qui ante annos mille decessisset, aevo perpetuo multa milia hominum pascere, item debere qui meliore ingenio se profiteretur non modo unum sed etiam plures alere posse. et ad summam mors eius ut parricidii damnati varie memoratur. alii enim scripserunt a Philadelpho esse in crucem fixum, nonnulli Chii lapides esse coniectos, alii Zmyrnae vivum in pyram coniectum. quorum utrum ei acciderit, merenti digna constitit poena. non enim aliter videtur promereri qui citat eos quorum responsum, quid senserint scribentes, non potest coram indicari.
passages.translation: The king is said to have replied that Homer, who died a thousand years ago, would feed many thousands of men in perpetuity, and that he who would claim to be superior in genius should be able to feed not only one but also many. And to sum up, his death as a condemned parricide is variously recorded. For some have written that he was crucified at Philadelphia, some that he was stoned at Chios, others that he was thrown alive on a pyre at Smyrna. Whether any of these things happened to him, the punishment he deserved was decidedly worthy. For it does not seem that he deserves otherwise who quotes those whose response, what they thought when writing, cannot be stated in person.

passages.latin: ego vero, Caesar, neque alienis indicibus mutatis interposito nomine meo id profero corpus neque ullius cogitata vituperans institui ex eo me adprobare, sed omnibus scriptoribus infinitas ago gratias quod egregiis ingeniorum sollertiis ex aevo conlatis abundantes alius alio genere copias praeparaverunt, unde nos uti fontibus haurientes aquam et ad propria proposita traducentes facundiores et expeditiores habemus ad scribendum facultates talibusque confidentes auctoribus audemus institutiones novas comparare.
passages.translation: But I, Caesar, neither do I produce this body with my own name interposed, having altered the evidence of others, nor do I set out to approve myself by criticizing the thoughts of anyone, but I give infinite thanks to all writers, who, with the excellent skills of their geniuses, brought together from time immemorial, have prepared abundant resources of one kind or another, from which we, drawing water as from springs and translating it for our own purposes, have more eloquent and expeditious faculties for writing, and, trusting in such authors, we dare to compare new compositions.

passages.latin: Igitur tales ingressus eorum quia ad propositi mei rationes animadverti praeparatos, inde sumendo progredi coepi. namque primum Agatharchus Athenis Aeschylo docente tragoediam scaenam fecit et de ea commentarium reliquit. ex eo moniti Democritus et Anaxagoras de eadem re scripserunt, quemadmodum oporteat ad aciem oculorum radiorumque extentionem certo loco centro constituto lineas ratione naturali respondere, uti de certa re certae imagines aedificiorum in scaenarum picturis redderent speciem et quae in directis planisque frontibus sint figurata, alia abscedentia, alia prominentia esse videantur.
passages.translation: Therefore, such were their entrances, because I observed that the reasons for my purpose were prepared, and I proceeded from there with strength. For first Agatharchus, under the instruction of Aeschylus, staged a tragedy in Athens and left a commentary on it. From him, Democritus and Anaxagoras, advised, wrote on the same subject, how it is necessary for lines to correspond by natural reason to the line of sight and the extension of rays, with a center established at a certain place, so that from an uncertain thing certain images of buildings in stage paintings might give the appearance, and those which are figured on straight and flat fronts might seem to be otherwise absurdly prominent.

passages.latin: postea Silenus de symmetriis doricorum edidit volumen, de aede Iunonis quae est Sami dorica Theodorus, ionice Ephesi quae est Dianae Chersiphron et Metagenes, de fano Minervae quod est Priene ionicum Pytheos, item de aede Minervae dorice quae est Athenis in arce Ictinos et Carpion, Theodorus Phocaeus de tholo qui est Delphis, Philo de aedium sacrarum symmetriis et de armamentario quod fuerat Piraei portu, Hermogenes de aede Dianae ionice quae est Magnesia pseudodipteros et Liberi Patris Teo monopteros, item Arcesius de symmetriis corinthiis et ionico Trallibus Aesculapio quod etiam ipse sua manu dicitur fecisse, de Mausoleo Satyrus et Pytheos, quibus vero felicitas maximum summumque contulit munus.
passages.translation: Later Silenus published a volume on the symmetries of the Dorics, Theodorus on the temple of Juno, which is the Doric temple of Samos, and Metagenes on the Ionic temple of Ephesus, which is the temple of Diana, Chersiphron and Metagenes, on the temple of Minerva, which is the Ionic temple of Priene, Pytheos, likewise on the Doric temple of Minerva, which is in Athens in the citadel of Ictions and Carpion, Theodore Phocaeus on the tholos which is at Delphi, Philo on the symmetries of sacred buildings and on the armoury which he had made in the port of Piraeus, Hermogenes on the Ionic temple of Diana, which is the temple of Magnesia, and the Theomonopteros of Liberi Patris, Arcesius on the symmetries of Corinth and the Ionic temple of Aesculapius at Trallis, which he himself is said to have made with his own hand, and Satyrs and Pytheos on the Mausoleum, to which, however, fortune bestowed the greatest and most sublime gift.

passages.latin: quorum enim artes aevo perpetuo nobilissimas laudes et sempiterno florentes habere iudicantur, ei cogitatis egregias operas praestiterunt. namque singulis frontibus singuli artifices sumpserunt certatim partes ad ornandum et probandum Leochares Bryaxis Scopas Praxiteles, nonnulli etiam putant Timotheum, quorum artis eminens excellentia coegit ad septem spectaculorum eius operis pervenire famam.
passages.translation: For their arts are judged to have the most noble praises throughout the ages and to flourish for ever, and they have produced excellent works of design. For on each front, individual artists competed to adorn and prove Leochares, Bryaxis, Scopas, Praxiteles, and some even think Timotheus, whose eminent excellence of art forced the fame of his work to reach seven spectacles.

passages.latin: praeterea minus nobiles multi praecepta symmetriarum conscripserunt, uti Nexaris Theocydes Demophilos Pollis Leonidas Silanion Melampus Sarnacus Euphranor. non minus de machinationibus, uti Diades Archytas Archimedes Ctesibios Nymphodorus Philo Byzantius Diphilos Democles Charias Polyidos Pyrros Agesistratos. quorum ex commentariis quae utilia esse his rebus animadverti, collecta in unum coegi corpus, et ideo maxime, quod animadverti in ea re ab Graecis volumina plura edita, ab nostris oppido quam pauca. Fuficius enim nimirum de his rebus primus instituit edere volumen, item Terentius Varro de novem disciplinis unum de architectura, P. Septimius duo.
passages.translation: Moreover, many less noble men wrote precepts on symmetry, such as Theocides of Nexaris, Demophilus, Pollis, Leonidas, Silanion, Melampus, Sarnacus, Euphranor. No less on engineering, such as Diades, Archytas, Archimedes, Ctesibius, Nymphodorus, Philo, Byzantius, Diphilus, Democles, Charias, Polyides, Pyrrhus, Agesistratus. From whose commentaries I have observed to be useful in these matters, I have collected several volumes on this subject published by the Greeks, and more than a few by our own people. Fuficius was the first to undertake to publish a volume on these matters, as was Terentius Varro, one on the nine disciplines, on architecture, and Publius Septimius, two.

passages.latin: amplius vero in id genus scripturae adhuc nemo incubuisse videtur, cum fuissent et antiqui cives magni architecti, qui potuissent non minus eleganter scripta comparare. namque Athenis Antistates et Callaeschros et Antimachides et Porinos architecti Pisistrato aedem Iovi Olympio facienti fundamenta constituerunt, post mortem autem eius propter interpellationem reipublicae incepta reliquerunt. itaque circiter annis <quadringentis> post Antiochus rex cum in id opus inpensam esset pollicitus, cellae magnitudinem et columnarum circa dipteron conlocationem epistyliorumque et ceterorum ornamentorum ad symmetriam distributionem magna sollertia scientiaque summa civis Romanus Cossutius nobiliter est architectatus. id autem opus non modo vulgo sed etiam in paucis a magnificentia nominatur.
passages.translation: But no one seems to have yet devoted himself more to that kind of writing, since there were also great architects among the ancient citizens who could have produced writings no less elegantly. For at Athens the architects Antistates and Callaeschros and Antimachides and Phormus laid the foundations of the temple of Jupiter Olympias which Pisistratus was building, but after his death they abandoned the projects because of the interruption of the state. Accordingly, about four hundred years later, when King Antiochus had promised to spend on that work, the size of the room and the arrangement of the columns around the dipteron and the distribution of the epistyles and other ornaments in a symmetrical manner were nobly designed by the Roman citizen Cossutius with great skill and supreme knowledge. And that work is not only popularly but also in a few places by its magnificence.

passages.latin: nam quattuor locis sunt aedium sacrarum marmoreis operibus ornatae dispositiones, e quibus propriae de his nominationes clarissima fama nominantur. quorum excellentiae prudentesque cogitationum apparatus suspectus habent in deorum σημαντικοῖς. primumque aedes Ephesi Dianae ionico genere ab Chersiphrone Gnosio et filio eius Metagene est instituta, quam postea Demetrius ipsius Dianae servus et Paeonius Ephesius dicuntur perfecisse. Mileti Apollini item ionicis symmetriis ⟨aedem⟩ idem Paeonius Daphnisque Milesius instituerunt. Eleusine Cereris et Proserpinae cellam inmani magnitudine Ictinos dorico more sine exterioribus columnis ad laxamentum usus sacrificiorum pertexit.
passages.translation: For in four places there are arrangements of sacred buildings adorned with marble works, from which the most famous names are properly named. The excellences and prudent arrangements of which are suspected in the ceremony of the gods. The first temple of Diana at Ephesus was erected in the Ionic style by Chersiphron of Gnosius and his son Metagenes, which is said to have been completed afterwards by Demetrius, the servant of Diana herself, and Paeonius of Ephesus. The same was erected in the Ionic style by Paeonius and Daphnis of Miles. The cella of Ceres and Proserpina at Eleusis was built in the Doric style without exterior columns for the relaxation of sacrifices.

passages.latin: eam autem postea cum Demetrius Phalereus Athenis rerum potiretur, Philo ante templum in fronte columnis constitutis prostylon fecit. ita aucto vestibulo laxamentum initiantibus operique summam adiecit auctoritatem. in asty vero Olympium amplo modulorum comparatu corinthiis symmetriis et proportionibus, uti supra scriptum est, architectandum Cossutius suscepisse memoratur, cuius commentarium nullum est inventum. nec tamen a Cossutio solum de his rebus scripta sunt desideranda sed etiam a G. Mucio, qui magna scientia confisus aedis Honoris et Virtutis Marianae cellae columnarumque et epistyliorum symmetrias legitimis artis institutis perfecit. id vero si marmoreum fuisset, ut haberet quemadmodum ab arte subtilitatem sic ab magnificentia et inpensis auctoritatem, in primis et summis operibus nominaretur.
passages.translation: But later, when Demetrius Phalerum took possession of Athens, Philo built a prostylon in front of the temple with columns set in front. Having thus built the vestibule, he added a great deal of authority to the workmen who were beginning it. But in Asty, when the Olympos were compared in ample dimensions with the Corinthian symmetries and proportions, as has been written above, it is recorded that Cossutius undertook to design the architectur, of which no commentary has been found. And yet, not only Cossutius is to be missed in writings on these matters, but also Gaius Mucius, who, relying on great knowledge, completed the symmetry of the columns and epistyles of the temple of Honor and Virtue of Mariana, according to the legitimate rules of art. But if it had been made of marble, so that it would have authority from magnificence and expense, as well as from subtlety of art, it would have been named among the first and greatest works.

passages.latin: Cum ergo et antiqui nostri inveniantur non minus quam Graeci fuisse magni architecti et nostra memoria satis multi, et ex his pauci praecepta edidissent, non putavi silendum sed disposite singulis voluminibus de singulis exponere. rebus itaque quoniam sexto volumine privatorum aedificiorum rationes perscripsi, in hoc qui septimum tenet numerum de expolitionibus quibus rationibus et venustatem et firmitatem habere possint exponam.
passages.translation: Since, therefore, our ancients are found to have been no less great architects than the Greeks, and there are quite a few of them in our memory, and of these few have published precepts, I did not think it necessary to be silent, but to explain each one in order in each volume. Therefore, since in the sixth volume I have written down the methods of private buildings, in this, which contains the seventh volume, I will explain the refinements by which they can have both beauty and strength.

passages.latin: Primumque incipiam de ruderatione, quae principia tenet expolitionum, uti curiosius summaque providentia solidationis ratio habeatur. et si plano pede erit eruderandum, quaeratur solum si sit perpetuo solidum, et ita exaequetur, et inducatur cum statumine rudus. sin autem omnis aut ex parte congesticius locus fuerit, fistucationibus•cum magna cura solidetur. in contignationibus vero diligenter est animadvertendum ne qui paries qui non exeat ad summum, sit extructus sub pavimentum, sed potius relaxatus supra se pendentem habeat coaxationem. cum enim solidus exit, contignationibus arescentibus aut pandatione sidentibus, permanens structurae soliditate dextra ac sinistra secundum se facit in pavimentis necessario rimas.
passages.translation: Archaeological note — Bk. 7.1 (pavements). Vitruvius transmits the ancient recipe for the layered Roman floor, which archaeology confirms across the Empire (from Fishbourne in Britain to Lod in Israel, from Zippori to Braga). From the bottom up: the statumen (large stones forming the base and draining ground moisture); the rudus or ruderatio (a mortar of broken brick and lime, more than 20 cm thick, rammed down —three parts lime to one if fresh, five if recycled—); the nucleus (a fine layer of three parts crushed potsherd to one of lime, some 15 cm); and above it the setting bed where the tesserae of the pavimentum were fixed. On upper floors the whole is laid over the joists. A key material here is opus signinum (cocciopesto): lime with crushed terracotta, waterproof, of Punic North African origin, spread through Sicily and Italy and used both for floors and for cisterns. The Vitruvian stratigraphy remains the reference framework for the archaeometry of mosaics.

passages.latin: item danda est opera ne commisceantur axes aesculini querco, quod quercei simul umorem perceperunt se torquentes rimas faciunt in pavimentis. sin autem aesculus non erit et necessitas coegerit, propter inopiam querceis ⟨uti⟩ sic videtur esse faciundum ut secentur tenuiores. quo minus enim valuerint, eo facilius clavis fixi continebuntur deinde in singulis tignis extremis partibus axis bini clavi figantur, uti nulla ex parte possint se torquendo anguli excitare. namque de cerro aut fago seu farno nullus ad vestutatem potest permanere. coaxationibus factis si erit, filex, si non, palea substernatur, uti materies ab calcis vitiis defendatur.
passages.translation: Also, care must be taken not to mix the axes of the aesculinus with the oak, because the oaks, having perceived the moisture at the same time, twist themselves and make cracks in the floors. But if the aesculinus is not available and necessity compels, due to the scarcity of oaks it seems that it is necessary to cut them thinner. For the weaker they are, the more easily they will be held fixed with nails. Then the axes are fixed with two nails in each of the extreme parts of the beams, so that they cannot raise the corners by twisting from any side. For none of the fir, beech or fir can last for a long time. After the coaxings have been made, if there is one, it is covered with straw, if not, so that the materials are protected from the defects of lime.

passages.latin: tunc insuper statuminetur ne minore saxo quam qui possit manum implere. statuminationibus inductis rudus si novum erit, ad tres partes una calcis misceatur, si redivivum fuerit, quinque ad duo mixtionis habeant responsum. deinde rudus inducatur et vectibus ligneis, decuriis inductis, crebriter pistatione solidetur, et id non minus pinsum absolutum crassitudine sit dodrantis. insuper ex testa nucleus inducatur mixtionem habens ad tres partes unam calcis, ne minore crassitudine [pavimentum] digitorum senûm. supra nucleum ad regulam et libellam exacta pavimenta struantur sive sectilia seu tesseris.
passages.translation: Then, in addition, let it be determined that it should not be made with a smaller stone than can fill the hand. After the determinations, if the raw material is new, it should be mixed with one part lime to three parts, if it is recycled, five parts to two parts of the mixture should be the answer. Then, the raw material should be introduced and solidified with wooden bars, boards, and frequent pounding, and that the absolute paste should not be less than the thickness of the dodrant. In addition, a core of the shell should be introduced, containing one part lime to three parts, so that the thickness of the pavement is less than the fingers of the old man. On top of the core, floors should be built, using a rule and a level, whether it is made of tiles or tiles.

passages.latin: cum ea structa fuerint et fastigia sua ex structione habuerint, ita fricentur uti si sectilia sint, nulli gradus in scutulis aut trigonis aut quadratis seu favis extent, sed coagmentorum compositio planam habeat inter se directionem. si tesseris structum erit, ut eae omnes angulos habeant aequales. cum enim anguli non fuerint omnes aequaliter plani, non erit exacta ut oportet fricatura. item testacea spicata tiburtina sunt diligenter exigenda, ut ne habeant lacunas nec extantes tumulos, sed <sint> extenta et ad regulam perfricata. super fricaturam, levigationibus et polituris cum fuerint perfecta, incernatur marmor, et supra loricae ex calce et harena inducantur.
passages.translation: When they have been built, the peaks will have their own structure, and they will be rubbed so that if they are sectile, no steps in the scrolls or triangles or squares or honeycombs will extend, but the composition of the joints will have a flat direction between them. If it is built with tiles, it will be so that all of them have equal angles. For since the angles will not all be equally flat, the rubbing will not be as exact as it should be. Likewise, the spiked shells of Tiburtine must be carefully removed, so that they do not have gaps or protruding mounds, but <are> extended and rubbed to the rule. Marble is laid on top, and on top of them are placed armour plates made of lime and sand.

passages.latin: Subdiu vero maxime idonea faciunda sunt pavimenta, quod contignationes umore crescentes aut siccitate decrescentes seu pandationibus sidentes movendo se faciunt vitia pavimentis, praeterea gelicidia et pruinae non patiuntur integra permanere. itaque si necessitas coegerit, ut minime vitiosa fiant sic erit faciundum. cum coaxatum fuerit, super altera coaxatio transversa sternatur clavisque fixa duplicem praebeat contignationi loricationem. deinde ruderi novo tertia pars testae tunsae admisceatur calcisque duae partes ad quinque mortarii mixtionibus praestent responsum.
passages.translation: But the most suitable pavements should be made in the long term, because floors that increase with moisture or decrease with dryness or that sit on supports by moving themselves cause defects in the pavements, and furthermore frost and frost do not allow them to remain intact. Therefore, if necessity compels them, so that they become the least defective, this is what should be done. When it has been compacted, another compaction is laid across it and nails are fixed to provide a double location for the pavement. Then a third part of crushed stone is mixed with new rubble and two parts of lime to five parts of mortar are mixed to provide the answer.

passages.latin: statuminatione facta, rudus inducatur, idque pistum absolutum ne minus pede sit crassum. tunc autem nucleo inducto, uti supra scriptum est, pavimentum e tessera grandi circiter binûm digitûm caesa struatur fastigium habens in pedes denos digitos binos, quod si bene temperabitur et recte fricatum fuerit, ab omnibus vitiis erit tutum. uti autem inter coagmenta materies ab gelicidiis ne laboret, fracibus quotannis ante hiemem saturetur. ita non patietur in se recipere gelicidii pruinam.
passages.translation: Having made the determination, the rough is introduced, and the finished dough is not less than a foot thick. Then, after the core has been introduced, as is written above, a floor is built from a large tile cut about two inches thick, having a ridge of ten inches on each foot, which, if well tempered and properly rubbed, will be safe from all defects. But so that the materials between the joints do not suffer from frost, it is saturated with broken pieces every year before winter. In this way it will not be allowed to receive frost from the frost.

passages.latin: sin autem curiosius videbitur fieri oportere, tegulae bipedales inter se coagmentatae supra rudus substrata materia conlocentur habentes singulis coagmentorum frontibus excelsos canaliculos digitales. quibus iunctis inplicetur calx ex oleo subacta confricenturque inter se coagmenta compressa. ita calx quae erit haerens in canalibus durescendo contexteque solidescendo non patietur aquam neque aliam rem per coagmenta transire. cum ergo fuerit hoc ita perstratum, supra nucleus inducatur et virgis caedendo subigatur. supra autem sive ex tessera grandi sive ex spica testacea ⟨pavimenta⟩ struantur fastigiis quibus est supra scriptum, et cum sic erunt facta, non cito vitiabuntur.
passages.translation: If a more careful construction is required, lay closely jointed two-foot tiles over the prepared bedding on the rudus. Give the meeting edges finger-wide grooves. Work oil-tempered lime into these grooves and rub the joints together under pressure. As the lime hardens into a continuous bond, it prevents water or other matter from passing through. Spread the nucleus over the tiles and compact it by beating with rods. Above it, lay either large tesserae or a herringbone pavement of fired clay, with the falls prescribed earlier. A floor made in this way will not readily deteriorate.

passages.latin: Cum a pavimentorum cura discessum fuerit, tunc de albariis operibus est explicandum. id autem erit recte, si glaebae calcis optimae ante multo tempore quam opus fuerit macerabuntur, uti si qua glaeba parum fuerit in fornace cocta, in maceratione diuturna liquore defervere coacta uno tenore concoquatur. namque cum non penitus macerata sed recens sumitur, cum fuerit inducta habens latentes crudos calculos pustulas emittit. qui calculi in opere uno tenore cum permacerantur, dissolvunt et dissipant tectorii politiones.
passages.translation: After the construction of pavements, lime finishing must be explained. Soak the best lumps of lime well before they are needed. Any lump insufficiently burned in the kiln can then be thoroughly slaked by prolonged contact with water. Fresh lime used before it is fully soaked contains hidden unslaked particles that form blisters after application. As those particles finally slake within the work, they disrupt and break up the plaster finish.

passages.latin: cum autem habita erit ratio macerationis et id curiosius operi praeparatum erit, sumatur ascia et quemadmodum materia dolatur, sic calx in lacu macerata ascietur. si ad eam offenderint calculi, non erit temperata. cumque siccum et purum ferrum educetur, indicabit eam evanidam et siticulosam. cum vero pinguis fuerit et recte macerata, circa id ferramentum uti glutinum haerens omni ratione probabit se esse temperatam. tunc autem machinis comparatis camerarum dispositiones in conclavibus expediantur, nisi lacunariis ea fuerint ornata.
passages.translation: Once the soaking has been carefully completed, take an adze and test the lime in its pit as one would hew timber. If the tool strikes hard particles, the lime is not properly prepared. If the iron emerges dry and clean, the lime is lean and thirsty. If the lime is rich and thoroughly slaked, it clings to the tool like glue, showing that it is ready. Then prepare the supporting apparatus and set out the vaulted ceilings in the rooms, unless they are to have coffered ceilings.

passages.latin: Cum ergo camerarum postulabitur ratio, sic erit faciundum. asseres directi disponantur inter se ne plus spatium habentes pedes binos, et hi maxime cupressei, quod abiegnei ab carie et ab vetustate celeriter vitiantur, hique asseres cum ad formam circinationis fuerint distributi, catenis dispositis ad contignationes, sive tecta erunt, crebriter clavis ferreis fixi religentur, eaeque catenae ex ea materia comparentur cui nec
passages.translation: Where a vaulted ceiling is required, set straight wooden laths no more than two feet apart. Cypress is preferable, since fir is quickly damaged by decay and age. Arrange the laths to the curve of the vault and attach them to the floor or roof framing with closely fixed iron nails and wooden hangers. Choose wood for those hangers that is resistant to

passages.latin: asseribus dispositis tum tomice ex sparto hispanico harundines graecae tunsae ad eos uti forma postulat religentur. item supra cameram materies ex calce et harena mixta subinde inducatur, ut si quae stillae ex contignationibus aut tectis ceciderint sustineantur. sin autem harundinis graecae copia non erit, de paludibus tenues colligantur et mataxae tomice ad iustam longitudinem una crassitudine alligationibus temperentur, dum ne plus inter duos nodos [alligationibus] binos pedes distent, et hae ad asseres, uti supra scriptum est, tomice religentur cultellique lignei in eas configantur. cetera omnia uti supra scriptum est expediantur.
passages.translation: Once the laths are in place, bind crushed Greek reeds to them with cords of Spanish esparto, following the required curve. Apply a mixture of lime and sand above the vault to catch any drops falling from the floor or roof above. If Greek reeds are unavailable, gather slender marsh reeds and tie them into bundles of even thickness and suitable length, keeping the ties no more than two feet apart. Bind these bundles to the laths in the same manner and fix wooden slips into them. Complete the remaining work as described above.

passages.latin: Cameris dispositis et intextis, imum caelum earum trullissetur, deinde harena dirigatur, postea autem creta aut marmore poliatur. Cum camerae politae fuerint, sub eas coronae sunt subiciendae, quas maxime tenues et subtiles oportere fieri videbitur. cum enim grandes sunt, pondere deducuntur nec possunt se sustinere. in hisque minime gypsum debet admisceri, sed ex creto marmore uno tenore perduci, uti ne praecipiendo non patiatur uno tenore opus inarescere. etiamque cavendae sunt in cameris priscorum dispositiones, quod earum planitiae coronarum <> gravi pondere inpendentes sunt periculosae.
passages.translation: Once the vaults have been framed and woven, apply a rough coat to their undersides, level them with sand plaster, and finish with chalk or marble. Beneath the finished vaults, form cornices as thin and light as possible: large cornices are pulled down by their own weight and cannot support themselves. Mix no gypsum into them; use sifted marble throughout, so that premature setting does not prevent the work from drying uniformly. Avoid the old arrangements of vaulted ceilings, whose projecting cornices are dangerous because of their weight.

passages.latin: Coronarum autem sunt < figurae aliae purae> aliae caelatae. conclavibus autem ubi ignis aut plura lumina sunt ponenda, purae fieri debent, ut eo facilius extergeantur. in aestivis et exhedris, ubi minime fumus est nec fuligo potest nocere, ibi caelatae sunt faciendae, semper enim album opus propter superbiam candoris non modo ex propriis sed etiam alienis aedificiis concipit fumum.
passages.translation: Cornices may be ⟨plain or⟩ carved. In rooms where fires or many lamps will be used, make them plain so that they can be cleaned more easily. In summer rooms and exedras, where smoke and soot cause less harm, carved cornices are appropriate. The brilliance of white plaster makes smoke apparent, whether it comes from the building itself or from neighboring buildings.

passages.latin: Coronis explicatis parietes quam asperrime trullissentur, postea autem supra, trullissatione subarescente, deformentur directiones harenati, uti longitudines ad regulam et ad lineam, altitudines ad perpendiculum, anguli ad normam respondentes exigantur. namque sic emendata tectoriorum in picturis erit species. subarescente, iterum et tertio inducatur. ita cum fundatior erit ex harenato directura, eo firmior erit ad vetustatem soliditas tectorii.
passages.translation: After completing the cornices, give the walls a rough coat. As it begins to dry, apply and straighten the sand-plaster coat, checking horizontal lines with rule and string, verticals with the plumb line, and corners with the square. This improves the appearance of the painted finish. When the coat has partly dried, apply a second and a third. The more substantial this sand-plaster foundation, the more durable the finished plaster will be.

passages.latin: cum ab harena praeter trullissationem non minus tribus coriis fuerit deformatum, tunc e marmore graneo directiones sunt subigendae, dum ita materies temperetur uti cum subigatur non haereat ad rutrum, sed purum ferrum e mortario liberetur. grandi inducto et inarescente, alterum corium mediocre dirigatur. id cum subactum fuerit et bene fricatum, subtilius inducatur. ita cum tribus coriis harenae et item marmoris solidati parietes fuerint, neque rimas neque aliud vitium in se recipere poterunt.
passages.translation: After at least three sand-plaster coats have been applied in addition to the rough coat, work on a coat of coarse marble plaster. Mix it so that it does not cling to the trowel, but leaves the iron clean when lifted from the mixing vessel. When this coarse coat has been applied and has begun to dry, level on a medium-grained coat. After that has been worked and rubbed smooth, apply a finer one. Walls built up with three coats of sand plaster and three of marble plaster resist cracking and other defects.

passages.latin: sed et liaculorum subactionibus fundata soliditate marmorisque candore firmo levigata, coloribus cum politionibus inductis nitidos expriment splendores. colores autem, udo tectorio cum diligenter sunt inducti, ideo non remittunt sed sunt perpetuo permanentes, quod calx in fornacibus excocto liquore facta raritatibus evanida, ieiunitate coacta corripit in se quae res forte contigerunt, mixtionibusque ex aliis potestatibus conlatis seminibus seu principiis una solidescendo, in quibuscumque membris est formata cum fit arida redigitur uti sui generis proprias videatur habere qualitates.
passages.translation: Thorough working with the polishing tools gives the finish solidity, while the whiteness of the marble produces a smooth, bright surface. Colors applied as the finish is polished acquire a brilliant sheen. When carefully laid on wet plaster, they remain fast rather than fading. Vitruvius explains this by the lime’s porous, thirsty condition after its moisture has been driven out in the kiln: it draws in substances that come into contact with it. Their constituent principles combine as the material hardens, so that the dry surface seems to possess the colors as qualities of its own.

passages.latin: itaque tectoria quae recte sunt facta neque vetustatibus fiunt horrida, neque cum extergentur remittunt colores, nisi si parum diligenter et in arido fuerint inducti. cum ergo ita in parietibus tectoria facta fuerint uti supra scriptum est, et firmitatem et splendorem et ad vetustatem permanentem virtutem poterunt habere. cum vero unum corium harenae et unum minuti marmoris erit inductum, tenuitas eius minus valendo faciliter rumpitur nec splendorem politionibus propter inbecillitatem crassitudinis proprium obtinebit.
passages.translation: Properly made plaster does not roughen with age or lose its colors when wiped, unless the pigments were applied carelessly or to a dry surface. Walls finished by the method described above retain strength, brilliance, and lasting quality. If only one sand-plaster coat and one fine marble coat are used, the thin finish readily cracks and lacks the substance needed to acquire the brilliance of a well-polished surface.

passages.latin: quemadmodum enim speculum argenteum tenui lamella ductum incertas et sine viribus habet remissiones splendoris, quod autem e solida temperatura fuerit factum, recipiens in se firmis viribus politionem fulgentes in aspectu certasque considerantibus imagines reddet, sic tectoria quae ex tenui sunt ducta materia non modo sunt rimosa, sed etiam celeriter evanescunt, quae autem fundata harenationis et marmoris soliditate sunt crassitudine spissa, cum sunt politionibus crebris subacta, non modo sunt nitentia, sed etiam imagines expressas aspicientibus ex eo opere remittunt.
passages.translation: A silver mirror made from a thin sheet gives faint, uncertain reflections, whereas one of substantial material takes a firm polish and returns clear, brilliant images. Plaster is similar: a thin coating cracks and soon deteriorates. A thick finish founded on solid sand and marble coats, repeatedly worked and polished, not only shines but reflects distinct images to the viewer.

passages.latin: Graecorum vero tectores non solum his rationibus utendo faciunt opera firma, sed etiam mortario conlocato, calce et harena ibi confusa, decuria hominum inducta, ligneis vectibus pisant materiam, et ita ad certamen subacta tunc utuntur. itaque veteribus parietibus nonnulli crustas excidentes pro abacis•utuntur, ipsaque tectoria abacorum et speculorum divisionibus circa se prominentes habent expressiones.
passages.translation: Greek plasterers strengthen their work not only by these methods. They also mix lime and sand in a mixing vessel and set a gang of ten men to pound it with wooden rammers. After this vigorous working, they use the mixture. Some people cut panels from old walls and reuse them; their plaster surfaces carry raised moldings around divisions into panels and mirror-like fields.

passages.latin: Sin autem in craticiis tectoria erunt facienda, quibus necesse est in arrectariis et transversariis rimas fieri, ideo quod luto cum linuntur necessario recipiunt umorem, cum autem arescunt extenuati in tectoriis faciunt rimas, id ut non fiat haec erit ratio. cum paries totus luto inquinatus fuerit, tunc in eo opere cannae clavis muscariis perpetuae figantur, deinde iterum luto inducto si priores transversariis harundinibus fixae sunt, secundae erectis figantur et ita, uti supra scriptum est, harenatum et marmor et omne tectorium inducatur. ita cannarum duplex in parietibus harundinibus transversis fixa perpetuitas nec segmina nec rimam ullam fieri patietur.
passages.translation: Plaster applied to wattle partitions is liable to crack along the uprights and crosspieces. These absorb moisture when coated with clay and then shrink as they dry, splitting the finish. To prevent this, coat the whole wall with clay and fasten a continuous layer of reeds with broad-headed nails. Apply another clay coat and fix a second reed layer across the first: if the first reeds run horizontally, set the second vertically. Then apply the sand plaster, marble coats, and complete finish as described above. These two continuous layers of reeds, fixed across one another, prevent breaks and cracks.

passages.latin: Quibus rationibus siccis locis tectoria oporteat fieri dixi, nunc quemadmodum umidis locis politiones expediantur ut permanere possint sine vitiis, exponam. et primum conclavibus quae plano pede fuerint, in imo pavimento alte circiter pedibus tribus pro harenato testa trullissetur et dirigatur, uti eae partes tectoriorum ab umore ne vitientur. sin autem aliqui paries perpetuos habuerit umores, paululum ab eo recedatur et struatur alter tenuis distans ab eo quantum res patietur, et inter duos parietes canalis ducatur inferior quam libramentum conclavis fuerit, habens nares ad locum patentem. item cum in altitudinem perstructus fuerit, relinquantur spiramenta. si enim non per nares umor et in imo et in summo habuerit exitus, non minus in nova structura se dissipabit. his perfectis paries testa trullissetur et dirigatur et tunc tectorio poliatur.
passages.translation: I have explained how plaster finishes should be made in dry places. I shall now describe their treatment in damp places so that they remain sound. In ground-floor rooms, apply and level a crushed-tile plaster instead of sand plaster on the lower part of the wall, to about three feet above the floor. This protects the finish from moisture. Where a wall remains continuously damp, build a second, thin wall a short distance in front of it, as space permits. Between the walls, run a channel below floor level with vents to the open air, and leave ventilation openings at the top. Without outlets both below and above, moisture will spread through the new work as well. When these provisions are complete, rough-coat and level the wall with crushed-tile plaster, then apply the finish.

passages.latin: sin autem locus non patietur structuram fieri, canales fiant et nares exeant ad locum patentem. deinde tegulae bipedales ex una parte supra marginem canalis inponantur, ex altera parte besalibus <laterculis> pilae substruantur, in quibus duarum tegularum anguli sedere possint, et ita a pariete eae distent ut ne plus pateant palmum. deinde insuper erectae mammatae tegulae ab imo ad summum ad parietem figantur, quarum interiores partes curiosius picentur ut ab se respuant liquorem. item in imo et in summo supra camaram habeant spiramenta.
passages.translation: If there is not enough space to build another wall, make channels with vents opening to the outside. Lay two-foot tiles with one side resting on the channel’s edge; support the other side on piers of eight-inch bricks, so that the corners of two tiles can rest on each pier. Keep the tiles no more than a palm’s breadth from the wall. Above these, fix studded tiles upright against the wall from bottom to top, carefully coating their inner surfaces with pitch to repel moisture. Provide ventilation openings both at the bottom and at the top, above the vault.

passages.latin: tum autem calce ex aqua liquida dealbentur, uti trullissationem testaceam non respuant. namque propter ieiunitatem quae est a fornacibus excocta non possunt recipere nec sustinere, nisi calx subiecta utrasque res inter se conglutinet et cogat coire. trullissatione inducta pro harenato testa dirigatur, et cetera omnia uti supra scripta sunt in tectorii rationibus perficiantur.
passages.translation: Then they are whitened with lime from liquid water, so that they do not reject the earthenware trowel. For because of the fastness which is produced by the kilns, they cannot receive or withstand it, unless the lime applied adheres both things to each other and forces them to come together. The trowel is then applied instead of the sanded one, and all the other things are carried out as written above in the rules for roofers.

passages.latin: Ipsi autem politionibus eorum ornatus proprios debent habere ad decoris rationes, uti et ex locis aptas et generum discriminibus non alienas habeant dignitates. tricliniis hibernis non est utilis compositione nec megalographia nec camerarum coronario opere subtilis ornatus, quod ea et ab ignis fumo et ab luminum crebris fuliginibus corrumpuntur. in his vero supra podia abaci•ex atramento sunt subigendi et poliendi, cuneis silaceis seu miniaceis interpositis. et explicandae camerae pure politae, etiam pavimentorum non erit displicens, si qui animadvertere voluerit, Graecorum hibernaculorum usum minime sumptuosus et utilis apparatus.
passages.translation: But their decorations should have their own reasons for decoration, so that they may have dignities that are appropriate to the place and not alien to the differences of gender. In winter dining rooms, neither large-scale painting nor subtle decoration in the crowning work of the chambers is useful in composition, because they are corrupted by the smoke of the fire and by the frequent soot of the lights. In these, however, the above podiabaci are to be subjected and polished with ink, with wedges of siliceous or miniaceous interposed. The chamber, when explained, is clean and polished, and even the pavements will not be displeasing, if anyone wishes to observe, the least costly and useful equipment of the Greeks for the use of winter quarters.

passages.latin: foditur enim infra libramentum triclinii altitudo circiter pedum binûm, et solo festucato•inducitur aut rudus aut testaceum pavimentum ita fastigatum ut in canali habeat nares. deinde congestis et spisse calcatis carbonibus inducitur e sabulone et calce et favilla mixta materies crassitudine semipedali. ad regulam et libellam summo libramento cote despumato redditur species nigri pavimenti. ita conviviis eorum et quod poculis et pytismatis effunditur simul cadit siccescitque, quique versantur ibi ministrantes etsi nudis pedibus fuerint, non recipiunt frigus ab eius modi genere pavimenti.
passages.translation: For a pit is dug below the dining room level to a depth of about two feet, and on the ground is laid either a rough or earthen floor, so leveled that it has holes in the channel. Then, with heaped and thickly trodden coals, a mixture of sand, lime and ash is laid to a thickness of half a foot. With a ruler and a level, the appearance of a black floor is rendered by skimming the foam from the top of the level. Thus, at their banquets, whatever is poured into cups and bowls falls down and dries up at the same time, and those who are there serving, even if they are barefoot, do not receive the cold from that kind of floor.

passages.latin: Ceteris conclavibus id est vernis autumnalibus aestivis, etiam atriis et peristylis constitutae sunt ab antiquis ex certis rebus certae rationes picturarum. namque pictura imago fit eius quod est seu potest esse, uti homines, aedificia, naves reliquarumque rerum, e quibus, finitis certisque corporibus, figurata similitudine sumuntur exempla. ex eo antiqui qui initia expolitionibus instituerunt imitati sunt primum crustarum marmorearum varietates et conlocationes, deinde coronarum siliculorum cuneorum inter sese varias distributiones.
passages.translation: For other rooms, that is, for spring, autumn, and summer, and also for atriums and peristyles, the ancients established certain types of paintings from certain things. For painting is an image of what is or can be, such as a man, a building, a ship, and other things, from which, having finite and certain bodies, examples are gathered in figured likeness. From this the ancients, who began the refinements, imitated first the varieties and arrangements of marble crusts, then the various distributions of crowns and wedges of siliceous stone among themselves.

passages.latin: postea ingressi sunt ut etiam aedificiorum figuras, columnarum et fastigiorum eminentes proiecturas imitarentur, patentibus autem locis uti exhedris propter amplitudines parietum scaenarum frontes tragico more aut comico seu satyrico designarent, ambulationibus vero propter spatia longitudinis varietatibus topiorum ornarent ab certis locorum proprietatibus imagines exprimentes. pinguntur enim portus promunturia litora flumina fontes euripi fana luci montes pecora pastores, nonnulli loci item signorum megalographiam habent et deorum simulacra seu fabularum dispositas explicationes, non minus troianas pugnas seu Ulixis errationes per topia, ceteraque quae sunt eorum similibus rationibus ab rerum natura procreata.
passages.translation: Later, painters began to imitate the forms of buildings and the projecting members of columns and pediments. On the broad walls of open rooms such as exedras, they represented stage facades in the tragic, comic, or satyric manner. Along walks, whose length offered greater scope, they painted varied landscapes drawn from the distinctive features of particular places: harbors, promontories, shores, rivers, springs, canals, sanctuaries, groves, mountains, flocks, and shepherds. Some settings also contain large-scale figure paintings, images of gods, or ordered scenes from myths, including the battles at Troy and the wanderings of Ulysses through landscapes, together with other subjects drawn on similar principles from the natural world.

passages.latin: sed haec quae ex veris rebus exempla sumebantur, nunc iniquis moribus inprobantur. nam pinguntur tectoriis monstra potius quam ex rebus finitis imagines certae. pro columnis enim struuntur calami, striati cum crispis foliis et volutis, pro fastigiis appagineculi item candelabra aedicularum sustinentia figuras, supra fastigia eorum surgentes ex radicibus cum volutis <> teneri flores habentes in se sine ratione sedentia sigilla, non minus coliculi dimidiata habentes sigilla alia humanis alia bestiarum capitibus.
passages.translation: But these subjects, once drawn from real things, are now condemned by a depraved taste. For upon the plaster are painted monstrosities rather than truthful images of definite things: reeds are set up in place of columns; in place of pediments, fluted scrolls with curling leaves and volutes; candelabra bearing the figures of little shrines; and, above their pediments, springing from roots, a multitude of slender stalks with volutes, bearing for no reason little seated figures, and other stalks half-human and half-animal in their heads.

passages.latin: haec autem nec sunt nec fieri possunt nec fuerunt.. quemadmodum enim potest calamus vere sustinere tectum aut candelabrûm ornamenta fastigii seu coliculus tam tenuis et mollis sustinere sedens sigillum aut de radicibus et coliculis ex parte flores dimidiataque sigilla procreari? at haec falsa videntes homines non reprehendunt sed delectantur, neque animadvertunt si quid eorum fieri potest necne. ergo ita novi mores coegerunt, uti inertiae mali iudices convincerent artium virtutes. iudiciis autem infirmis obscuratae mentes non valent probare quod potest esse cum auctoritate et ratione decoris. neque enim picturae probari debent quae non sunt similes veritati, nec si factae sunt elegantes ab arte, ideo de his statim debet recte iudicari, nisi argumentationis certas rationes habuerint sine offensionibus explicatas.
passages.translation: Yet such things do not exist, cannot exist and have never existed. How can a reed truly support a roof, a candelabrum the ornaments of a pediment, or a stalk so slender and soft a seated figure? How can flowers and half-figures grow from roots and stalks? Yet people look at these falsehoods without criticism and take pleasure in them, never considering whether any of them could exist. New fashions have thus led bad judges to condemn artistic excellence as ineptitude. Minds obscured by unsound judgment cannot recognize what may properly exist in accordance with the principles of decor. Paintings that bear no resemblance to reality should not be approved; nor, merely because they are elegantly executed, should they immediately be judged sound unless their subjects can be explained by coherent reasoning without inconsistency.

passages.latin: etenim etiam Trallibus cum Apaturius Alabandeus eleganti manu finxisset scaenam in minusculo theatro, quod ἐκκλησιαστήριον apud eos vocitatur, in eaque fecisset columnas signa Centauros sustinentes epistylia, tholorum rotunda tecta, fastigiorum prominentes versuras, coronasque capitibus leoninis ornatas quae ora stillicidiorum e tectis habent rationem, praeterea supra ea nihilominus episcaenum, in qua tholi pronai semifastigia omnisque tecti varius picturis fuerat ornatus, itaque cum aspectus eius scaenae propter asperitatem eblandiretur omnium visus et iam id opus probare fuissent parati,
passages.translation: For even at Tralles, when Apaturius of Alabanda had painted with elegant hand the stage of the small theater which they call the ἐκκλησιαστήριον, and had set in it columns and statues — Centaurs upholding the architraves, the rounded roofs of domes, the projecting angles of pediments, and cornices ornamented with lions’ heads, all of which belong by rights to the eaves of a roof — men were already prepared to approve the work for its charm, when Licymnius the mathematician came forward.

passages.latin: tum Licymnius mathematicus prodiit et ait Alabandis satis acutos ad omnes res civiles haberi, sed propter non magnum vitium indecentiae insipientes eos esse iudicatos, quod in gymnasio eorum quae sunt statuae omnes sunt causas agentes, foro discos tenentes aut currentes seu pila ludentes. ita indecens inter locorum proprietates status signorum publice civitati vitium existimationis adiecit. videamus item nunc ne Apaturii scaena efficiat et nos Alabandis aut Abderitas. qui enim vestrum domos supra tegularum tecta potest habere aut columnas seu fastigiorum explicationes? haec enim supra contignationes ponuntur, non supra tegularum tecta. si ergo quae non possunt in veritate rationem habere facti in picturis probaverimus, accedemus et nos his civitatibus quae propter haec vitia insipientes sunt iudicatae.
passages.translation: Then Licymnius the mathematician came forward and said: “The Alabandians are reckoned shrewd enough in all civic affairs; yet for one small fault of impropriety they are held wanting in judgment, for in their gymnasium all the statues are of men pleading causes, while in the forum they hold the discus, or run, or play at ball. Thus the unfitness of the statues to the character of their settings fastened upon the city a public reputation for poor sense. Let us beware, then, lest this scene-painting make us too into Alabandians: for which of you can have, upon the tiled roof of his house, columns or the carved cornices of pediments? Such things rest upon floors, not upon roof-tiles. If, then, we approve in painting what can have no warrant in reality, we join those cities judged wanting in sense.

passages.latin: itaque Apaturius contra respondere non est ausus, sed sustulit scaenam et ad rationem veritatis commutatam postea correctam adprobavit. utinam dii inmortales fecissent uti Licymnius revivisceret et corrigeret hanc amentiam tectoriorumque errantia instituta. sed quare vincat veritatem ratio falsa, non erit alienum exponere. quod enim antiqui insumentes laborem et industriam probare contendebant artibus, id nunc coloribus et eorum eleganti specie consecuntur, et quam subtilitas artificis adiciebat operibus auctoritatem, nunc dominicus sumptus efficit ne desideretur.
passages.translation: Apaturius therefore dared not reply. He removed the stage painting, revised it in accordance with truth and subsequently secured approval for the corrected work. Would that the immortal gods might bring Licymnius back to life to correct this madness and these misguided practices of wall decoration. It is worth explaining why a false approach prevails over truth. What the ancients sought to commend through art, labor and diligence is now achieved through colors and their elegant appearance. The authority that the craftsman’s subtlety once gave to a work is now supplied by the owner’s expenditure, so that its absence goes unnoticed.

passages.latin: quis enim antiquorum non uti medicamento minio parce videtur usus esse? at nunc passim plerumque toti parietes inducuntur. accedit huc chrysocolla, ostrum, armenium. haec vero cum inducuntur etsi non ab arte sunt posita, fulgentes colorum reddunt visus, et ideo quod pretiosa sunt, legibus excipiuntur, ut ab domino non a redemptore repraesententur.
passages.translation: Which of the ancients does not seem to have used minium sparingly, as one would a medicine? Now, by contrast, whole walls are commonly coated with it. Chrysocolla, purple and Armenian blue are added as well. Even when applied without artistry, these colors give the eye a brilliant impression. Because they are expensive, contracts make a special provision that the owner, rather than the contractor, should supply them.

passages.latin: Quae commonefacere potui ut ab errore discedatur in opere tectorio satis exposui, nunc de apparitionibus ut succurrere potuerit dicam, et primum quoniam de calce initio est dictum, nunc de marmore ponam. Marmor non eodem genere omnibus regionibus procreatur, sed quibusdam locis glaebae ut salis micas perlucidas habentes nascuntur, quae contusae et molitae praestant operibus utilitatem. quibus autem locis eae copiae non sunt, caementa marmorea, sive assulae dicuntur, quae marmorarii ex operibus deiciunt, contunduntur et moluntur, <et cum> est subcretum in operibus utuntur. aliis locis, ut inter Magnesiae et Ephesi fines, sunt loca unde foditur ⟨farina⟩ parata quam nec molere nec cernere opus est, sed sic est subtilis quemadmodum si qua est manu contusa et subcreta.
passages.translation: I have said enough to warn against mistakes in plasterwork. I shall now discuss the materials, beginning with marble, since lime has already been treated. Marble does not occur in the same form in every region. In some places lumps containing translucent particles like grains of salt are found; crushed and ground, they are useful in building. Where such supplies are unavailable, the fragments or chips discarded by marble-workers are crushed, ground and, once sifted, used in the work. Elsewhere, as in the territory between Magnesia and Ephesus, a ready-made powder is quarried. It needs neither grinding nor sifting, being as fine as material crushed and sifted by hand.

passages.latin: Colores vero alii sunt qui per se certis locis procreantur et inde fodiuntur, nonnulli ex aliis rebus tractationibus aut mixtionum temperaturis compositi perficiuntur, uti praestent eandem in operibus utilitatem. primum autem exponemus quae per se nascentia fodiuntur, uti sil, quod graece ὤχρα dicitur. haec vero multis locis ut etiam in Italia invenitur, sed quae fuerat optima, attica ideo nunc non habetur quod Athenis argentifodinae cum habuerunt familias, tunc specus sub terra fodiebantur ad argentum inveniendum. cum ibi vena forte inveniretur, nihilominus uti argentum persequebantur, itaque antiqui egregia copia silis ad politionem operum sunt usi. item rubricae copiosae multis locis eximuntur, sed optimae paucis, uti Ponto Sinope, et Aegypto, in Hispania Balearibus, non minus etiam Lemno, cuius insulae vectigalia Atheniensibus senatus populusque Romanus concessit fruenda. paraetonium vero ex ipsis locis unde foditur habet nomen. eadem ratione melinum, quod eius metallum in sola cycladi Melo dicitur esse.
passages.translation: Some colors occur naturally in particular places and are mined there; others are produced by processing materials or adjusting mixtures to serve the same purpose in building. First I shall describe those extracted in their natural state, such as sil, called ὤχρα in Greek. It is found in many places, including Italy, but the Attic variety, once the best, is no longer available. When the Athenian silver mines employed slave gangs, underground galleries were driven in search of silver. If a vein of ochre was encountered, it was pursued as eagerly as silver, and the ancients consequently had an excellent supply for finishing their buildings. Red ochres are also extracted abundantly in many places, but the finest come from only a few: Sinope in Pontus, Egypt, the Balearic Islands in Hispania and Lemnos, whose revenues the Roman Senate and people granted to the Athenians. Paraetonium takes its name from the place where it is quarried; similarly, melinum is so called because its deposit is said to occur only on Melos in the Cyclades.
passages.scope_note: El DOCX reúne estas secciones en un solo bloque; se conserva íntegro.

passages.latin: creta viridis item pluribus locis nascitur, sed optima Zmyrnae. hanc autem Graeci θεοδοτεῖον vocant, quod Theodotus nomine fuerat cuius in fundo id genus cretae primum est inventum. auripigmentum, quod ἀρσενικόν graece dicitur, foditur Ponto. sandaraca item pluribus locis, sed optima Ponto proxime flumen Hypanim habet metallum.
passages.translation: Green earth also occurs in several places, but the best is found at Smyrna. The Greeks call it theodoteion after Theodotus, on whose estate that kind of earth was first discovered. Orpiment, called ἀρσενικόν in Greek, is mined in Pontus. Sandaraca occurs in several places too, but its finest deposit is in Pontus near the river Hypanis.
passages.scope_note: El DOCX reúne estas secciones en un solo bloque; se conserva íntegro.

passages.latin: Ingrediar nunc minii rationes explicare. id autem agris Ephesiorum Cilbianis primum esse memoratur inventum, cuius et res et ratio satis magnas habet admirationes. foditur enim glaeba quae dicitur, antequam tractationibus ad minium perveniant, vena uti ferrum, magis subrufo colore, habens circa se rubrum pulverem. cum id foditur, ex plagis ferramentorum crebras emittit lacrimas argenti vivi, quae a fossoribus statim colliguntur.
passages.translation: I shall now explain minium. It is said to have been discovered first in the Cilbian fields belonging to the Ephesians. Both the substance and its treatment are remarkable. Before processing yields minium, the material is extracted as a lump from a vein resembling iron ore, but more reddish in color and surrounded by red dust.
