When it is mined, the blows of the tools release frequent drops of quicksilver, which the miners immediately collect.

passages.latin: hae glaebae cum collectae sunt, in officina propter umoris plenitatem coiciuntur in fornacem ut interarescant, et is qui ex his ab ignis vapore fumus suscitatur cum resedit in solum furni, invenitur esse argentum vivum. exemptis glaebis guttae eae quae residebunt propter brevitates non possunt colligi, sed in vas aquae converruntur et ibi inter se congruunt et una confunduntur. id autem cum sint quattuor sextariorum, mensurae cum expenduntur, invenientur esse pondo centum.
passages.translation: Because these lumps contain much moisture, they are taken to the workshop and put into a furnace to dry. The fumes raised by the heat of the fire, when deposited on the furnace floor, prove to be quicksilver. After the lumps have been removed, the remaining droplets are too small to gather individually. They are swept into a vessel of water, where they unite into a single mass. When the quantity reaches four sextarii, it will be found on weighing to amount to one hundred pounds.

passages.latin: cum in aliquo vase est confusum, si supra id lapideum centenarium pondus inponatur, natat in summo neque eum liquorem potest onere suo premere nec elidere nec dissipare. centenario sublato si ibi auri scripulum inponatur, non natabit sed ad imum per se deprimetur. ita non amplitudine ponderis sed genere singularum rerum gravitatem esse non est negandum.
passages.translation: When a liquid is mixed in a vessel, if a hundred-year-old stone weight is placed on top of it, it floats on top and cannot press down on the liquid with its own weight, nor can it remove or dissipate it. If a gold coin is placed there after the hundred-year-old stone weight is removed, it will not float but will sink to the bottom by itself. Thus it cannot be denied that gravity is not due to the magnitude of the weight but to the nature of individual things.

passages.latin: id autem multis rebus est ad usum expeditum. neque enim argentum neque aes sine eo potest recte inaurari. cumque in veste intextum est aurum eaque vestis contrita propter vetustatem usum non habeat honestum, panni in fictilibus vasis inpositi supra ignem comburuntur. is cinis coicitur in aquam, et additur eo argentum vivum. id autem omnes micas auri corripit in se et cogit secum coire. aqua defusa cum id in pannum infunditur et ibi manibus premitur, argentum per panni raritates propter liquorem extra labitur, compressione coactum aurum intra purum invenitur.
passages.translation: But this is for many things for ready use. For neither silver nor brass can be properly gilded without it. When gold is woven into a garment, and that garment, worn out because of its age, is no longer fit for honest use, the cloths are placed in earthenware vessels and burned over a fire. The ashes are thrown into water, and quicksilver is added to it. This, however, seizes all the gold flakes in itself and forces them to coalesce. When the water is poured into the cloth and pressed there with the hands, the silver slides out through the rarefied nature of the cloth because of the liquid, while the gold, forced inside by compression, is found pure.

passages.latin: Revertar nunc ad minii temperaturam. ipsae enim glaebae cum sunt aridae, contunduntur pilis ferreis, et lotionibus et cocturis crebris relictis stercoribus efficiuntur ut adveniant colores. cum ergo emissae sint ex minio per argenti vivi relictionem quas in se naturales habuerat virtutes, efficitur tenera natura et viribus inbecillis.
passages.translation: I return now to the preparation of minium. Once dry, the lumps are crushed with iron pestles. Repeated washing and heating remove the impurities and bring out the color. When the separation of the quicksilver has deprived the minium of its inherent properties, however, it becomes delicate and weak.

passages.latin: itaque cum est in expolitionibus conclavium tectis inductum, permanet sine vitiis suo colore. apertis vero id est peristyliis aut exhedris aut ceteris eiusdem modi locis, quo sol et luna possit splendores et radios inmittere, cum ab his locus tangitur, vitiatur et amissa virtute coloris denigratur. itaque cum et alii multi tum etiam Faberius scriba cum in Aventino voluisset habere domum eleganter expolitam, peristyliis parietes omnes induxit minio, qui post dies XXX facti sunt invenusto varioque colore. itaque primo locavit inducendos alios colores.
passages.translation: Applied to the finished plaster of covered rooms, it therefore retains its color without deterioration. In open places, such as peristyles, exedrae and similar spaces, where sunlight and moonlight can reach it, exposure causes it to deteriorate and blacken as its color loses its strength. Among many others, Faberius the scribe, wishing to finish his house on the Aventine elegantly, coated all the walls of its peristyles with minium. Within thirty days they had become discoloured and uneven, and he promptly contracted for other colors to be applied over them.

passages.latin: at si qui subtilior fuerit et voluerit expolitionem miniaceam suum colorem retinere, cum paries expolitus et aridus fuerit, ceram ponticam igni liquefactam paulo oleo temperatam saeta inducat, deinde postea carbonibus in ferreo vase compositis eam ceram una cum pariete calfaciundo sudare cogat, atque ut peraequetur deinde tunc candela centunculisque puris subigat, uti signa marmorea nuda curantur. haec autem γάνωσις graece dicitur.
passages.translation: A more discerning owner who wishes a minium finish to retain its color should, once the wall is polished and dry, brush it with Pontic wax melted over a fire and mixed with a little oil. Then place coals in an iron vessel and heat the wax together with the wall, causing it to sweat and spread evenly. Finally work it with a wax taper and clean linen, as bare marble statues are treated. This process is called γάνωσις in Greek.

passages.latin: ita obstans cerae ponticae lorica non patitur nec lunae splendorem nec solis radios lambendo eripere ex his politionibus colorem. quae autem in Ephesiorum metallis fuerunt officinae, nunc traiectae sunt ideo Romam quod id genus venae postea est inventum Hispaniae regionibus, e quibus metallis glaebae portantur et per publicanos Romae curantur. eae autem officinae sunt inter aedem Florae et Quirini.
passages.translation: Thus the breastplate of Pontic wax, standing firm, does not suffer either the brilliance of the moon or the rays of the sun to lick away the color from these polishes. But the workshops which were in the metals of the Ephesians have now been transferred to Rome, because that kind of vein was later discovered in the regions of Spain, from which metals the slabs are brought and treated by the publicans in Rome. Now those workshops are between the temple of Flora and Quirinus.

passages.latin: Vitiatur minium admixta calce. itaque si qui velit experiri id sine vitio esse, sic erit faciendum. ferrea lamna sumatur, eo minium inponatur, ad ignem conlocetur donec lamna candescat. cum e candore color mutatus fuerit eritque ater, tollatur lamna ab igni et sic refrigeratum si restituatur in pristinum colorem, sine vitio esse probabitur, sin autem permanserit nigro colore, significabit se esse vitiatum.
passages.translation: Let the minium be tainted with lime. Therefore, if anyone wishes to test whether it is without taint, this is what must be done. Take an iron plate, put the minium on it, and place it over the fire until the plate becomes red-hot. When the color has changed from whiteness and become black, remove the plate from the fire and, having cooled it, if it is restored to its original color, it will be proven to be without taint, but if it remains black, it will indicate that it is tainted.

passages.latin: Quae succurrere potuerunt mihi de minio dixi. chrysocolla adportatur a Macedonia, foditur autem ex îs locis qui sunt proximi aerariis metallis. armenium et indicum nominibus ipsis indicatur quibus in locis procreatur.
passages.translation: I have spoken of those things which could have helped me concerning minium. Chrysocolla is brought from Macedonia, and is mined from those places which are nearest to the precious metals. Armenian and indigo are indicated by the very names in which they are produced.

passages.latin: Ingrediar nunc ad ea quae ex aliis generibus tractationum temperaturis commutata recipiunt colorum proprietates, et primum exponam de atramento, cuius usus in operibus magnas habet necessitates, ut sint notae quemadmodum praeparentur certis rationibus artificiorum ad id temperaturae.
passages.translation: I will now proceed to those things which receive the properties of colors when changed by other types of treatment temperatures, and I will first explain about ink, the use of which in works has great needs, so that it may be known how it is prepared by certain methods of artificers at that temperature.

passages.latin: namque aedificatur locus uti laconicum et expolitur marmore subtiliter et levigatur. ante id fit fornacula habens in laconicum nares, et eius praefurnium magna diligentia comprimitur ne flamma extra dissipetur. in fornace resina conlocatur. hanc autem ignis potestas urendo cogit emittere per nares intra laconicum fuliginem, quae circa parietem et camerae curvaturam adhaerescit. inde collecta partim componitur ex gummi subacta ad usum atramenti librarii, reliquum tectores glutinum admiscentes in parietibus utuntur.
passages.translation: Build a room like a Laconian hot room, finish its interior with fine marble plaster, and polish it smooth. In front of it, construct a small furnace with vents opening into the room, and seal the firing chamber carefully so that the flame cannot escape outside. Place resin in the furnace. As it burns, the fire drives soot through the vents into the room, where it adheres to the walls and the curved vault. Collect this soot: work part of it with gum to make writing ink; plasterers mix the remainder with glue for use on walls.

passages.latin: Si autem hae copiae non fuerint paratae, ita necessitatibus erit administrandum, ne expectatione morae res retineatur. sarmenta aut taedae schidiae comburantur, cum erunt carbones extinguantur, deinde in mortario cum glutino terantur.
passages.translation: But if these supplies are not ready, then the necessities must be managed in this way, so that the matter is not held up by the expectation of delay. The twigs or splinters of firewood are burned, when the coals are extinguished, they are then ground in a mortar with glue.

passages.latin: ita erit atramentum tectoribus non invenustum. non minus si faex vini arefacta et cocta in fornace fuerit et ea contrita cum glutino in opere inducetur, atramenti suavitatis superque efficiet colorem, et quo magis ex meliore vino parabitur, non modo atramenti sed etiam indici colorem dabit imitari.
passages.translation: Thus the ink will be not unattractive to the painters. No less so if the dregs of wine have been dried and cooked in a furnace and this crushed together with the glue are introduced into the work, on which it will produce a color of the sweetness of the ink, and the more it is prepared from the best wine, it will imitate not only the color of the ink but also of the indicator.

passages.latin: Caeruli temperationes Alexandriae primum sunt inventae, postea item Vestorius Puteolis instituit faciundum. ratio autem eius e quibus est inventa satis habet admirationis. harena enim cum nitri flore conteritur adeo subtiliter ut efficiatur quemadmodum farina, ea aes cyprum limis crassis uti scobis facta mixta conspargitur ut conglomeretur. deinde pilae manibus versando efficiuntur et ita conligantur ut inarescant. aridae componuntur in urceo fictili, urcei in fornace. ita aes et ea harena ab ignis vehementia confervescendo cum coaluerint, inter se dando et accipiendo sudores a proprietatibus discedunt suisque viribus per ignis vehementiam confectis caeruleo rediguntur colore.
passages.translation: Blue (caeruleum) was first compounded at Alexandria, and afterwards Vestorius set up its manufacture at Puteoli. The method of its discovery is well worth admiration. Sand is ground together with flowers of natron so finely that it becomes as it were flour; copper is filed with coarse files into shavings and sprinkled over it; the mixture is moistened, rolled by hand into balls, dried, and packed in an earthen jar, and the jars are placed in a furnace. So, when the copper and the sand grow incandescent together by the fierceness of the fire, by giving and receiving their properties from one another they take on a blue color.

passages.latin: usta vero, quae satis habet utilitatis in operibus tectoriis, sic temperatur. glaeba silis boni coquitur ut sit in igni candens. ea autem aceto extinguitur et efficitur purpureo colore.
passages.translation: But the burnt clay, which is quite useful in roofing works, is tempered in this way. A lump of good clay is cooked until it is glowing in the fire. Then it is extinguished with vinegar and becomes purple in color.

passages.latin: De cerussa aerugineque quam nostri aerucam vocitant non est alienum quemadmodum comparetur dicere. Rhodo enim doliis sarmenta conlocantes aceto suffuso supra sarmenta conlocant plumbeas massas, deinde ea operculis obturant ne spiramento obturatum emittatur. post certum tempus aperientes inveniunt e massis plumbeis cerussam. eadem ratione lamellas aereas conlocantes efficiunt aeruginem quae aeruca appellatur.
passages.translation: Of the lead rust which our people call aeruca, it is not strange to say how it is compared. For in Rhodes, placing vine shoots in barrels, they place lead masses on top of the vine shoots, suffused with vinegar, then close them with lids so that the air cannot escape. After a certain time, opening them, they find lead from the lead masses. In the same way, placing bronze plates, they produce a rust which is called aeruca.

passages.latin: cerussa vero cum in fornace coquitur, mutato colore ad ignem [incendi] efficitur sandaraca. id autem incendio facto ex casu didicerunt homines, et ea multo meliorem usum praestat quam quae de metallis per se nata foditur.
passages.translation: White lead (cerussa), when baked in a kiln, changes color in the fire and turns into sandarach (red lead). Men learned this by chance, from a fire, and this pigment renders far better service than the one extracted by digging, born of its own accord in the veins.

passages.latin: Incipiam nunc de ostro dicere, quod et carissimam et excellentissimam habet praeter hos colores aspectus suavitatem. id autem excipitur e conchylio marino, e quo purpura efficitur, cuius non minores sunt quam ceterarum <rerum> naturae considerantibus admirationes, quod habet non in omnibus locis quibus nascitur unius generis colorem, sed solis cursu naturaliter temperatur.
passages.translation: I shall now speak of sea-purple (ostrum), which, beyond all the other colors, has the costliest and most exquisite loveliness of aspect. It is obtained from a marine shellfish, from which the purple dye is made, and to the observer its nature holds wonders not less than those of any other thing; for it does not yield a color of one kind in all the places where it is gathered, but is tempered by the course of the sun.

passages.latin: itaque quod legitur Ponto et Gallia, quod hae regiones sunt proximae ad septentrionem, est atrum. progredientibus inter septentrionem et occidentem invenitur lividum. quod autem legitur ad aequinoctialem orientem et occidentem, invenitur violaceo colore. quod vero meridianis regionibus excipitur, rubra procreatur potestate, et ideo hoc Rhodo etiam insula creatur ceterisque eiusmodi regionibus quae proximae sunt solis cursui.
passages.translation: Therefore, what is read as Pontus and Gaul, because these regions are closest to the north, is black. As we proceed between the north and the west, it is found to be livid. But what is read as east and west of the equinoctial line is found to be of a violet color. But what is taken up in the southern regions is produced by red power, and therefore this island of Rhodes is also created and other such regions which are closest to the course of the sun.

passages.latin: ea conchylia cum sunt lecta, ferramentis circa scinduntur, e quibus plagis purpurea sanies uti lacrima profluens excussa in mortariis terendo comparatur, et quod ex concharum marinarum testis eximitur, ideo ostrum est vocitatum. id autem propter salsuginem cito fit siticulosum, nisi mel habeat circa fusum.
passages.translation: When these shells are picked, they are split open with tools, from which wounds a purple sap, like a tear, is obtained by grinding them in mortars, and the testicle taken from the seashells is therefore called oyster. But because of its saltiness it quickly becomes dry, unless it has honey mixed in it.

passages.latin: Fiunt etiam purpurei colores infecta creta rubiae radice et hysgino, non minus et ex floribus alii colores. itaque tectores cum volunt sil atticum imitari, violam aridam coicientes in vas cum aqua, confervefaciunt ad ignem, deinde cum est temperatum coiciunt in linteum, et inde manibus exprimentes recipiunt in mortarium aquam ex violis coloratam, et eo cretam infundentes et eam terentes efficiunt silis attici colorem.
passages.translation: Purple colors are made by infusing chalk with ruby root and hyssop, and no less other colors are made from flowers. Therefore, when painters wish to imitate Attic sil, they put dry violets in a vessel with water, heat them over the fire, then when it is lukewarm they pour them onto a cloth, and from there, squeezing them with their hands, they take the water colored from the violets into a mortar, and pouring chalk into it and grinding it, they produce the color of Attic sil.

passages.latin: eadem ratione vaccinium temperantes et lacte miscentes purpuram faciunt elegantem. item qui non possunt chrysocolla propter caritatem uti, herba quae luteum appellatur caeruleum inficiunt, et <> utuntur viridissimum colorem. haec autem infectiva appellatur. item propter inopiam coloris indici cretam selinusiam aut anulariam vitro, quod Graeci ἰσάτιν appellant, inficientes, imitationem faciunt indici coloris.
passages.translation: In the same way, those who temper cranberries and mix them with milk make an elegant purple. Likewise, those who cannot use chrysocolla because of charity, infuse the herb called yellow with blue, and <thus> use a very green color. This is called infective. Likewise, because of the lack of the color of the indicator, infusing selinous or annular chalk with glass, which the Greeks call ἴσατιν, they make an imitation of the color of the indicator.

passages.latin: Quibus rationibus et rebus ad dispositionem firmitates <> quibusque decoras oporteat fieri picturas, item quas habeant omnes colores in se potestates, ut mihi succurrere potuit in hoc libro perscripsi. itaque omnes aedificationum perfectiones quam habere debeant opportunitatem ratiocinationis, septem voluminibus sunt finitae, insequenti autem de aqua, si quibus locis non fuerit, quemadmodum inveniatur et qua ratione ducatur quibusque rebus si erit salubris et idonea probetur explicabo.
passages.translation: By what means and things the firmness of refinements is reached, and by what means beautiful pictures should be made, and likewise what powers all colors have in themselves, as could be of assistance to me, I have written down in this book. Therefore all the perfections of buildings, which they should have the opportunity of reasoning, are finished in seven volumes, but in the following I will explain about water, if in what places it is not, how it is found and by what means it is drawn, and for what purposes it will be proved wholesome and suitable.

passages.latin: De septem sapientibus Thales Milesius omnium rerum principium aquam est professus, Heraclitus ignem, Magorum sacerdotes aquam et ignem, Euripides, auditor Anaxagorae, quem philosophum Athenienses scaenicum appellaverunt, aera et terram, eamque e caelestium imbrium conceptionibus inseminatam fetus gentium et omnium animalium in mundo procreavisse, et quae ex ea essent prognata, cum dissolverentur temporum necessitate coacta in eandem redire, quaeque de aere nascerentur, item in caeli regiones reverti neque interitiones recipere et dissolutione mutata in eam recidere, in qua ante fuerant, proprietatem. Pythagoras vero, Empedocles, Epicharmos aliique physici et philosophi haec principia esse quattuor proposuerunt: aerem, ignem, terram, aquam, eorumque inter se cohaerentiam naturali figuratione e generum discriminibus efficere qualitates.
passages.translation: Among the Seven Sages, Thales of Miletus held that water was the first principle of all things; Heraclitus favored fire, and the priests of the Magi both water and fire. Euripides, a pupil of Anaxagoras whom the Athenians called “the philosopher of the stage”, proposed air and earth: the latter, fertilised by rain from the heavens, brought forth human beings and other living creatures. What arose from earth would return to it when dissolved by time, while what arose from air would return to the regions of the sky, not perishing but reverting through dissolution to its former nature. Pythagoras, Empedocles, Epicharmus and other natural philosophers proposed four principles — air, fire, earth and water — whose natural combination produces different qualities.

passages.latin: Animadvertimus vero non solum nascentia ex his esse procreata, sed etiam res omnes non ali sine eorum potestate neque crescere nec tueri. Namque corpora sine spiritus redundantia non possunt habere vitam, nisi aer influens cum incremento fecerit auctus et remissiones continenter. Caloris vero si non fuerit in corpore iusta comparatio, non erit spiritus animalis neque erectio firma, cibique vires non poterunt habere coctionis temperaturam. Item si non terrestri cibo membra corporis alantur, deficient et ita a terreni principii mixtione erunt deserta.
passages.translation: We observe that the elements not only produce living things: without their power nothing can be nourished, grow or be sustained. Bodies cannot live without a sufficient supply of breath, as incoming air maintains the continual expansion and contraction of breathing. Unless the body has the proper measure of heat, it lacks vitality and strength, and food cannot be digested at the necessary temperature. Unless its members are nourished by food from the earth, they fail, deprived of the contribution of the earthly element.

passages.latin: Animalia vero si fuerint sine umoris potestate, exsanguinata et exsucata [a principiorum liquore] interarescent. Igitur divina mens, quae proprie necessaria essent gentibus, non constituit difficilia et cara, uti sunt margaritae, aurum, argentum ceteraque, quae neque corpus nec natura desiderat, sed sine quibus mortalium vita non potest esse tuta, effudit ad manum parata per omnem mundum. Itaque ex his, si quid forte defit in corpore spiritus, ad restituendum aer adsignatus id praestat. Apparatus autem ad auxilia caloris solis impetus et ignis inventus tutiorem efficit vitam. Item terrenus fructus escarum praestans copiis supervacuis desiderationibus alit et nutrit animales pascendo continenter. Aqua vero non solum potus sed infinitas usu praebendo necessitates, gratas, quod est gratuita, praestat utilitates.
passages.translation: Animals deprived of moisture would likewise lose their blood and bodily fluids and dry up. The divine mind therefore did not make the necessities of human life difficult and costly to obtain, as are pearls, gold, silver and other things that neither the body nor nature requires. Instead, it made readily available throughout the world the things without which mortal life cannot be sustained. If the body lacks breath, air restores it. The warmth of the Sun and the use of fire provide the heat that makes life more secure. The produce of the earth supplies abundant food, continually feeding and sustaining living creatures. Water provides not only drink but countless other necessities, and its usefulness is all the more welcome because it is freely available.

passages.latin: Ex eo etiam qui sacerdotia gerunt moribus Aegyptiorum, ostendunt omnes res e liquoris potestate consistere. Itaque cum hydria aqua ad templum aedemque casta religione refertur, tunc in terra procumbentes manibus ad caelum sublatis inventionis gratias agunt divinae benignitati.
passages.translation: Those who hold priestly office according to Egyptian custom likewise show that all things depend on the power of water. When water is brought in a hydria to a temple or sanctuary with due reverence, they prostrate themselves on the ground and raise their hands to heaven, giving thanks to divine beneficence for its discovery.

passages.latin: Est enim maxime necessaria et ad vitam et ad delectationes, et ad usum cotidianum Ea autem erit facilior, si erunt fontes aperti et fluentes. Sin autem non profluent, quaerenda sub terra sunt capita et colligenda. Quae sic erunt experienda, uti procumbatur in dentes, antequam sol exortus fuerit, in locis, quibus erit quaerendum, et in terra mento conlocato et fulto prospiciantur eae regiones; sic enim non errabit excelsius quam oporteat visus, cum erit inmotum mentum, sed libratam altitudinem in regionibus certa finitione designabit. Tunc, in quibus locis videbuntur umores concrispantes et in aera surgentes, ibi fodiatur; non enim in sicco loco hoc potest signum fieri.
passages.translation: For water is most necessary both for life and for its pleasures, and for daily use. It will be the easier to obtain if there are open and flowing springs. But where none flow forth, the sources must be sought and gathered underground. The search is to be made thus: let a man lie face downward, before the sun has risen, in the places in which it is to be sought, and with the chin placed and supported on the ground, those regions are to be looked for; for in this way the sight will not err higher than it should be, when the chin is motionless, but will designate a balanced height in the regions with a certain boundary. Then, in those places where moistures are seen to be bubbling and rising into the air, there is to be dug; for this sign cannot be made in a dry place.

passages.latin: Item animadvertendum est quaerentibus aquam, quo genere sint loca; certa enim sunt, in quibus nascitur. In creta tenuis et exilis et non alta est copia; ea erit non optimo sapore. Item sabulone soluto tenuis, sed inferioris loci invenietur; ea erit limosa et insuavis. Terra autem nigra sudores et stillae exiles inveniuntur, quae ex hibernis tempestatibus collectae in spissis et solidis locis subsidunt; haec habent optimum saporem. Glarea vero mediocres et non certae venae reperiuntur; hae quoque sunt egregia suavitate. Item sabulone masculo harenaque carbunculo certiores [et stabiliores] sunt copiae; eaeque sunt bono sapore. Rubro saxo et bonae et copiosae, si non per intervenia dilabantur et liquescant. Sub radicibus autem montium et in saxis silicibus uberiores et affluentiores; eaeque frigidiores sunt et salubriores. Campestribus autem fontibus salsae, graves, tepidae, non suaves, nisi quae ex montibus sub terra submanantes erumpunt in medios campos ibique arborum umbris contectae praestant montanorum fontium suavitatem.
passages.translation: Those searching for water should also examine the nature of the ground, since different kinds occur in particular formations. In clay the supply is slight, shallow and poor in taste. In loose sand it is likewise scanty, though found at a greater depth, and it is muddy and unpleasant. In black earth, small seepages and droplets collect from winter rain and settle in dense, compact ground; these have an excellent taste. Gravel contains moderate and uncertain veins, also of excellent sweetness. In coarse sand and carbunculus, supplies are more reliable [and more constant], and their taste is good. In red rock the supply is abundant and good, provided that it does not escape and disperse through intervening fissures. Beneath mountain slopes and in siliceous rock it is more plentiful, colder and more wholesome. Springs in the plains, by contrast, are saline, heavy, lukewarm and unpleasant, except where water runs underground from the mountains and emerges in the middle of a plain: shaded there by trees, it retains the sweetness of mountain springs.

passages.latin: Signa autem, quibus terrarum generibus supra scriptum est, ea invenientur nascentia: tenuis iuncus, salix erratica, alnus, vitex, harundo, hedera aliaque, quae eiusmodi sunt, quae non possunt nasci per se sine umore. Solent autem eadem in lacunis nata esse, quae sidentes praeter reliquum agrum excipiunt ex imbribus et agris per hiemem propterque capacitatem diutius conservant umorem. Quibus non est credendum, sed quibus regionibus et terris, non lacunis, ea signa nascuntur, non sata, sed naturaliter per se procreata, ibi est quaerenda.
passages.translation: The signs, which are written above, will be found growing in the following types of land: the slender rush, the wandering willow, the alder, the vitex, the reed, the ivy, and other such plants, which cannot grow by themselves without moisture. But they are usually grown in lakes, which, when they sit in them, receive more moisture from the rains and fields than from the rest of the land, and because of their capacity, they retain moisture longer during the winter. We must not believe these, but we must seek in which regions and lands, not lakes, these signs grow, not sown, but naturally produced by themselves.

passages.latin: In quibus si eae significabuntur inventiones, sic erunt experiundae. Fodiatur quoquoversus locus latus ne minus pedes <tres, altus pedes> quinque, in eoque conlocetur circiter solis occasum scaphium aereum aut plumbeum aut pelvis. Ex his quod erit paratum, id intrinsecus oleo ungatur ponaturque inversum, et summa fossura operiatur harundinibus aut fronde, supra terra obruatur; tum postero die aperiatur, et si in vaso stillae sudoresque erunt, is locus habebit aquam.
passages.translation: Where these signs indicate water, test the ground as follows. Dig a pit at least three feet across in each direction and five feet deep. At about sunset place in it a bronze or lead vessel, or a basin, whichever is available, first coating its inner surface with oil and setting it upside down. Cover the opening of the pit with reeds or leaves and lay earth over them. Open it the following day: if droplets of condensation appear in the vessel, the place contains water.

passages.latin: Item si vasum ex creta factum non coctum in ea fossione eadem ratione opertum positum fuerit, si is locus aquam habuerit, cum apertum fuerit, vas umidum erit et iam dissolvetur ab umore. Vellusque lanae si conlocatum erit in ea fossura, insequenti autem die de eo aqua expressa erit, significabit eum locum habere copiam. Non minus si lucerna concinnata oleique plena et accensa in eo loco operta fuerit conlocata et postero die non erit exusta, sed habuerit reliquias olei et enlychnii ipsaque umida invenietur, indicabit eum locum habere aquam, ideo quod omnis tepor ad se ducit umores. Item in eo loco ignis factus si fuerit et percalefacta terra et adusta vaporem nebulosum ex se suscitaverit, is locus habebit aquam.
passages.translation: An unfired clay vessel placed in the pit and covered in the same way will, if water is present, be found damp and beginning to disintegrate. A fleece of wool from which water can be squeezed the following day likewise indicates an abundant supply. A lamp, prepared with oil and lit before being enclosed there, will indicate water if it has not burnt out by the next day, still contains oil and wick, and is found damp: warmth attracts moisture. Similarly, if a fire lit there heats the earth and causes a misty vapor to rise, water is present.

passages.latin: Cum haec ita erunt pertemptata et, qua supra scripta sunt, signa inventa, tum deprimendus est puteus in eo loco, et si erit caput aquae inventum, plures circa sunt fodiendi et per specus in unum locum omnes conducendi.
passages.translation: Once these tests have been made and the signs described above have been found, sink a well at that place. If a source of water is discovered, dig several more wells around it and connect them by underground galleries so that the water gathers at a single point.

passages.latin: Intervallaque montium maxime recipiunt imbres et propter silvarum crebritatem nives ab umbris arborum et montium ibi diutius conservantur, deinde liquatae per terrae venas percolantur et ita perveniunt ad infimas montium radices, ex quibus profluentes fontium erumpunt ructus. Campestribus autem locis contrario non possunt habere copias. Nam quaecumque sunt, non possunt habere salubritatem, quod solis vehemens impetus propter nullam obstantiam umbrarum eripit exhauriendo fervens ex planitie camporum umorem, et si quae sunt aquae apparentes, ex his, quod est levissimum tenuissimumque et subtili salubritate, aer avocans dissipat in impetum caeli, quaeque gravissimae duraeque et insuaves sunt partes, eae in fontibus campestribus relinquuntur.
passages.translation: The valleys between mountains receive the most rain. Dense woodland and the shade of trees and mountains preserve the snow there for longer; when it melts, it filters through veins in the earth and reaches the lowest mountain slopes, where it gushes out in springs. In the plains, by contrast, supplies cannot be abundant or wholesome. With no shade to obstruct it, the Sun’s fierce heat draws moisture from the exposed ground. Of any water that remains visible, the air carries away and disperses the lightest, finest and most wholesome parts, leaving the heaviest, hardest and least pleasant components in the springs of the plains.

passages.latin: Itaque, quae ex imbribus aqua colligitur, salubriores habet virtutes, quod eligitur ex omnibus fontibus levissimis subtilibusque tenuitatibus, deinde per aeris exercitationem percolata tempestatibus liquescendo pervenit ad terram. Etiamque non crebriter in campis confluunt imbres, sed in montibus aut ad ipsos montes, ideo quod umores ex terra matutino solis ortu moti cum sunt egressi, in quamcumque partem caeli sunt proclinati, trudunt aera; deinde, cum sunt moti, propter vacuitatem loci post se recipiunt aeris ruentis undas.
passages.translation: Therefore, the water that is collected from the rains has more salubrious virtues, because it is selected from all the lightest and most subtle springs, and then, filtered by the exercise of the air, it reaches the ground, liquefied by storms. Moreover, the rains do not often flow in the plains, but in the mountains or on the mountains themselves, for this reason that the moistures, when they have emerged from the earth at the morning sunrise, are moved by the air in whatever part of the sky they are inclined to; then, when they are moved, because of the emptiness of the place, they receive the waves of the rushing air behind them.

passages.latin: Aer autem, qui ruit, trudens quocumque umorem per vim spiritus impetus et undas crescentes facit ventorum. A ventis autem quocumque feruntur umores conglobati ex fontibus, et fluminibus et paludibus et pelago, cum tepores solis colligunt et exhauriunt et ita tollunt in altitudinem nubes. Deinde cum aeris unda nitentes, cum perventum ad montes, ab eorum offensa et procellis propter plenitatem et gravitatem liquescendo disparguntur et ita diffunditur in terras.
passages.translation: But the air, which rushes, pushing moisture wherever it is by the force of the breath, creates the gusts and rising waves of the winds. But wherever the winds carry the moisture gathered from springs, from rivers and marshes and the sea, they collect and drain it with the time of the sun and thus lift the clouds to a height. Then, shining with the wave of the air, when it reaches the mountains, it is dispersed by their impact and storms because of its fullness and gravity, melting and thus it is spread over the lands.

passages.latin: Vaporem autem et nebulas et umores ex terra nasci haec videtur efficere ratio, quod ea habet in se et calores fervidos et spiritus inmanes refrigerationesque et aquarum magnam multitudinem. Ex eo, cum refrigeratum noctu sol oriens impetu tangit orbem terrae et ventorum flatus oriuntur per tenebras, ab umidis locis egrediuntur in altitudinem nubes. Aer autem cur a sole percalefactus cum rationibus tollit ex terra umores, licet ex balineis exemplum capere.
passages.translation: The following explanation appears to account for the generation of vapor, mist and moisture from the earth: the earth contains intense heat, powerful currents of air, cold and great quantities of water. When the rising Sun strikes its surface, cooled during the night, and winds arise in the darkness, clouds rise from damp places into the air. The way air heated by the Sun lifts moisture from the earth may be understood by considering baths.

passages.latin: Nullae enim camerae, quae sunt caldariorum, supra se possunt habere fontes, sed caelum, quod est ibi ex praefurniis ab ignis vapore percalefactum, corripit ex pavimentis aquam et aufert secum in camararum curvaturas et sustinet, ideo quod semper vapor calidus in altitudinem se trudit. Et primo non remittit propter brevitatem, simul autem plus umoris habet congestum, non potest sustinere propter gravitatem, sed stillat supra lavantium capita. Item eadem ratione caelestis aer, cum ab sole percepit calorem, ex omnibus locis hauriendo tollit umores et congregat ad nubes. Ita enim terra fervore tacta eicit umores, ⟨ut⟩ etiam corpus hominis ex calore emittit sudores.
passages.translation: The vaults over the hot rooms of baths cannot have springs above them. Instead, the air inside, heated by the fire at the furnaces, draws water from the floors, carries it up into the curved vaults and holds it there, because hot vapor always rises. At first, while the quantity is small, it does not release the moisture. Once more has accumulated, however, it can no longer support the weight, and water drips onto the bathers’ heads. In the same way, atmospheric air warmed by the Sun draws moisture from every place and gathers it into clouds. Heat causes the earth to give off moisture just as it causes the human body to sweat.

passages.latin: Indices autem sunt eius rei venti, ex quibus qui a frigidissimis partibus veniunt procreati, septentrio et aquilo, extenuatos siccitatibus in aere flatus spirant; auster vero et reliqui, qui a solis cursu impetum faciunt, sunt umidissimi et semper adportant imbres, quod percalefacti ab regionibus fervidis adveniunt, et omnibus terris lambentes eripiunt umores et ita eos profundunt ad septentrionales regiones.
passages.translation: But the indications of this are the winds, which, when they come from the coldest parts, are born from the north and the north-east, and breathe in the air, weakened by the dryness; but the south and the others, which come from the course of the sun, are very humid and always bring rain, because they arrive very hot from the hot regions, and, sliding down, they snatch the moisture from all the lands and thus carry it deeper to the northern regions.

passages.latin: Haec autem sic fieri testimonio possunt esse capita fluminum, quae orbe terrarum chorographiis picta itemque scripta plurima maximaque inveniuntur egressa ad septentrionem. Primumque in India Ganges et Indus ab Caucaso monte oriuntur; Syria Tigris et Euphrates; Asiae item, Ponto Borysthenes, Hypanis, Tanais; Colchis Phasis; Gallia Rhodanus; Celtica Rhenus; citra Alpis Timavos et Padus; Italia Tiberis; Maurusia, quam nostri Mauretaniam appellant, ex monte Atlante Dyris, qui ortus ex septentrionali regione progreditur per occidentem ad lacum Eptagonum et mutato nomine dicitur Agger, deinde ex lacu Eptabolo sub montes desertos subterfluens per meridiana loca manat et influit in Paludem quae appellatur, circumcingit Meroen, quod est Aethiopum meridianorum regnum, ab hisque paludibus se circumagens per flumina Astansobam et Astoboam et alia plura pervenit per montes ad cataractam ab eoque se praecipitans per septentrionalem pervenit inter Elephantida et Syenen Thebaicosque in Aegyptum campos et ibi Nilus appellatur.
passages.translation: The river sources shown on maps and described in accounts of the world provide evidence for this explanation: many of the greatest rivers emerge in northern regions. In India the Ganges and Indus rise from the Caucasus; in Syria, the Tigris and Euphrates; in Asia, in the region of Pontus, the Borysthenes, Hypanis and Tanais; in Colchis, the Phasis; in Gaul, the Rhône; in Celtic territory, the Rhine; on this side of the Alps, the Timavus and Po; and in Italy, the Tiber. In Maurusia, which our people call Mauretania, the river Dyris rises from Mount Atlas, flows from the northern region westwards to Lake Eptagonus and changes its name to Agger. From Lake Eptabolus it passes beneath the desert mountains, flows through southern regions and enters the marshes that surround Meroë, the kingdom of the southern Ethiopians. From these marshes it winds through the Astansobas, Astoboa and several other rivers, crosses the mountains to the cataract, plunges down and flows northwards between Elephantine and Syene through the Theban plains into Egypt, where it is called the Nile.

passages.latin: Ex Mauretania autem caput Nili profluere ex eo maxime cognoscitur, quod ex altera parte montis Atlantis alia capita item profluentia ad occidentem Oceanum, ⟨petunt⟩ ibique nascuntur ichneumones, crocodili, aliae similes bestiarum pisciumque naturae praeter hippopotamos.
passages.translation: But it is best known that the head of the Nile flows from Mauretania, because from the other side of the mountain of Atlantis other heads also flow towards the western Ocean, and there are born ichneumons, crocodiles, and other similar animals and fish, besides hippopotamuses.

passages.latin: Ergo cum omnia flumina magnitudinibus in orbis terrarum descriptionibus a septentrione videantur profluere Afrique campi, qui sunt in meridianis partibus subiecti solis cursui, latentes penitus habeant umores nec fontes crebros amnesque raros, relinquitur, uti multo meliora inveniantur capita fontium, quae ad septentrionem aut aquilonem spectant, nisi si inciderint in sulphurosum locum aut aluminosum seu bituminosum. Tunc enim permutantur <et> aut calidae aquae aut frigidae odore malo et sapore profundunt fontes.
passages.translation: Therefore, since all rivers seem to flow from the north in their magnitudes in descriptions of the world, the plains of Africa, which are in the southern parts subject to the course of the sun, have completely hidden moisture, and neither frequent springs nor rare rivers, it remains that much better sources should be found which face the north or northeast, unless they fall into a sulphurous or aluminous or bituminous place. For then they are exchanged <and> either hot waters or cold ones deepen the springs with a bad smell and taste.

passages.latin: Neque enim calidae aquae est ulla proprietas, sed frigida aqua, cum incidit percurrens in ardentem locum, effervescit et percalefacta egreditur per venas extra terram. Ideo diutius non potest permanere, sed brevi spatio fit frigida. Namque si naturaliter esset calida, non refrigeraretur calor eius. Sapor autem et odor et color eius non restituitur, quod intinctus et commixtus est propter naturae raritatem.
passages.translation: For hot water has no property, but cold water, when it falls as it flows into a burning place, boils and, being very hot, comes out through the veins outside the earth. Therefore it cannot remain longer, but in a short space becomes cold. For if it were naturally hot, its heat would not be cooled. But its taste, smell and color are not restored, because it is mixed and mixed, due to the rarity of nature.

passages.latin: Sunt autem etiam nonnulli fontes calidi, ex quibus profluit aqua sapore optimo, quae in potione ita est suavis, uti nec fontalis ab Camenis nec Marcia saliens desideretur. Haec autem ab natura perficiuntur his rationibus. Cum in imo per alumen aut bitumen seu sulphur ignis excitatur, ardore percandefacit terram, quae est supra se; item fervidum emittit in superiora loca vaporem, et ita, si qui in îs locis, qui sunt supra, fontes dulcis aquae nascuntur, offensi eo vapore effervescunt inter venas et ita profluunt incorrupto sapore.
passages.translation: There are also some hot springs, from which flow water of excellent taste, which is so sweet in drink, that neither the spring of the Camenae nor the Marcian water (the Aqua Marcia) is desired. But these are accomplished by nature in these ways. When fire is excited at the bottom by alum or bitumen or sulphur, it scorches the earth above it with its heat; and it emits a hot vapor into the higher places, and so, if in any of these places, which are above, springs of sweet water arise, offended by that vapor they boil between the veins and thus flow forth without any corrupting taste.

passages.latin: Sunt etiam odore et sapore non bono frigidi fontes, qui ab inferioribus locis penitus orti per loca ardentia transeunt et ab eo per longum spatium terrae percurrentes refrigerati perveniunt supra terram sapore odore coloreque corrupto, uti in Tiburtina via flumen Albula et in Ardeatino fontes frigidi eodem odore, qui sulphurati dicuntur, et reliquis locis similibus. Hi autem, cum sunt frigidi, ideo videntur aspectu fervere, quod, cum in ardentem locum alte penitus inciderunt, umore et igni inter se congruentibus offensa vehementi fragore validos recipiunt in se spiritus, et ita inflati vi venti coacti bullientes crebre per fontes egrediuntur. Ex his autem qui non sunt aperti, sed ⟨grumis⟩ aut saxis continentur, per angustas venas vehementia spiritus extruduntur ad summos grumorum tumulos.
passages.translation: There are also cold springs with a bad smell and taste, which, rising from deep below, pass through burning places and from there, running over a long distance of land, reach the surface of the earth cooled with a spoiled smell and color, as in the Tiburtine road the river Albula and in the Ardeatine cold springs with the same smell, which are called sulphurous, and in other similar places. But these, when they are cold, seem to boil to the eye because, when they have fallen deeply into a burning place, the moisture and fire, which are in harmony with each other, are struck with a violent crash and receive strong spirits into themselves, and thus, being inflated by the force of the wind, they frequently come out bubbling through the springs. But from those which are not open, but are contained by rocks, the spirits are forced out through narrow veins to the highest mounds of the cairns by the force of the wind.

passages.latin: Itaque qui putant se altitudine, qua sunt grumi, capita fontium posse habere, cum aperiunt fossuras latius, decipiuntur. Namque uti aeneum vas non in summis labris plenum sed aquae mensurae suae capacitatis habens ⟨e⟩ tribus duas partes operculumque in eo conlocatum, cum ignis vehementi fervore tangatur, percalefieri cogit aquam, ea autem propter naturalem raritatem in se recipiens fervoris validam inflationem non modo implet vas, sed spiritibus extollens operculum et crescens abundat, sublato autem operculo emissis inflationibus in aere patenti rursus ad suum locum residit: ad eundem modum ea capita fontium cum sunt angustiis compressa, ruunt in summo spiritus aquae bullitus, simul autem sunt latius aperti, exanimati per raritates liquidae potestatis residunt et restituuntur in libramenti proprietatem.
passages.translation: Therefore, those who think that they can have the heads of springs from the height of the clods, when they open the trenches wider, are deceived. For as a brass vessel, not filled to the very brim, but having two-thirds of its capacity of water, and a lid placed in it, when the fire is touched with intense heat, forces the water to become very hot, but the water, due to its natural rarefaction, receiving within itself a strong inflation of heat, not only fills the vessel, but also lifts the lid with spirits and increases in abundance, but when the lid is lifted, the inflations are released and it returns to its place in the open air. In the same way, when those heads of springs are compressed by narrow spaces, the boiling spirits of the water rush in at the top, but at the same time they are opened wider, tested by the rarities of the liquid power, they settle and are restored to their property of balance.

passages.latin: Omnis autem aqua calida ideo [quod] est medicamentosa, quod in pravis rebus percocta aliam virtutem recipit ad usum. Namque sulphurosi fontes nervorum labores reficiunt percalefaciendo exurendoque caloribus e corporibus umores vitiosos. Aluminosi autem, cum dissoluta membra corporum paralysi aut aliqua vi morbi receperunt, fovendo per patentes venas refrigerationem contraria caloris vi reficiunt, et hoc continenter restituuntur in antiquam membrorum curationem. Bituminosi autem interioris corporis vitia potionibus purgando solent mederi.
passages.translation: But all hot water is medicinal because it receives its healing power for use in bad cases. For sulphurous springs relieve the labors of the nerves by heating them and burning away the foul humours from the bodies with their heat. But aluminous springs, when the limbs of the body have become weak due to paralysis or some disease, by warming them through the open veins they relieve the body by the opposite force of heat, and this continually restores the limbs to their former health. But bituminous springs are wont to cure the vices of the interior of the body by cleansing them with potions.

passages.latin: Est autem aquae frigidae genus nitrosum, uti Pinnae Vestinae, Cutiliis aliisque locis similibus, quae potionibus depurgat per alvumque transeundo etiam strumarum minuit tumores. Ubi vero aurum, argentum, ferrum, aes, plumbum reliquaeque res earum similes fodiuntur, fontes inveniuntur copiosi, sed hi maxime sunt vitiosi. Habent enim uti aquae calidae sulphur alumen bitumen, faecem, quae, per potiones cum in corpus iniit et per venas permanando nervos attingit et artus, eos durat inflando. Igitur nervi inflatione turgentes e longitudine contrahuntur et ita aut nervicos aut podagricos efficiunt homines, ideo quod ex durissimis et spissioribus rigidissimisque rebus intinctas habent venarum raritates.
passages.translation: There is also a kind of cold water, nitrous, as in Pinnae Vestinae, Cutilii, and other similar places, which purifies by drinking and, passing through the bowels, also reduces the swellings of the goiters. But where gold, silver, iron, copper, lead, and other similar things are mined, springs are found in abundance, but these are especially vitiated. For hot vitriolic waters contain sulphur, alum, and bitumen, and when these enter the body through drinks and continue through the veins, they reach the nerves and joints, hardening them by swelling them. Therefore, the nerves, swelling by swelling, contract in length and thus make men neurasthenic or gouty, because they have the rarefied veins soaked in the hardest and thickest and coldest things.

passages.latin: Aquae autem species est, quae cum habeat non satis perlucidas et ipsa uti flos natat in summo, colore similis vitri purpurei. Haec maxime considerantur Athenis. Ibi enim ex eiusmodi locis et fontibus in asty et ad portum Piraeum ducti sunt salientes, e quibus bibit nemo propter eam causam, sed lavationibus et reliquis rebus utuntur, bibunt autem ex puteis et ita vitant eorum vitia. Troezeni non potest id vitari, quod omnino aliud genus aquae non reperitur, nisi quod cibdeli habeant; itaque in ea civitate aut omnes aut maxima parte sunt pedibus vitiosi. Cilicia vero civitate Tarso flumen est nomine Cydnos, in quo podagrici crura macerantes levantur dolore.
passages.translation: But there is a kind of water which, though not sufficiently transparent, and which itself floats like a flower on the top, is of a color similar to purple glass. These are most highly regarded in Athens. For there, from such places and springs, springs have been brought to Asty and to the port of Piraeus, from which no one drinks for that reason, but they use washings and other things, but they drink from wells and thus avoid their vices. This cannot be avoided in the Troezen, for no other kind of water is found at all, except as many as they have; and therefore in that city either all or the greater part are defective in their feet. But in the Cilician city of Tarsus there is a river called Cydnus, in which gouty sufferers, soaking their legs, are relieved of their pain.

passages.latin: Sunt autem et alia multa genera, quae habent suas proprietates, ut in Sicilia flumen est Himeras, quod a fonte cum est progressum, dividitur in duas partes; quae pars profluit contra Etruriam, quod per terrae dulcem sucum percurrit, est infinita dulcedine, quae altera parte per eam terram currit, unde sal foditur, salsum habet saporem. Item Paraetonio et quod est iter ad Ammonem et Casio ad Aegyptum lacus sunt palustres, qui ita sunt salsi, ut habeant insuper se salem congelatum. Sunt autem et aliis pluribus locis et fontes et flumina <et> lacus, qui per salifodinas percurrentes necessario salsi perficiuntur.
passages.translation: But there are also many other kinds, which have their own properties, as in Sicily there is a river called Himeras, which, when it has advanced from its source, is divided into two parts; the part which flows towards Etruria, which runs through the sweet juice of the land, is of infinite sweetness, while the other part which runs through that land, from which salt is mined, has a salty taste. Likewise, in Paraetonium and on the road to Ammon and Cassius in Egypt there are marshy lakes, which are so salty that they have frozen salt on top of them. But there are also in many other places springs and rivers <and> lakes, which, running through salt mines, are necessarily made salty.

passages.latin: Alii autem per pingues terrae venas profluentes uncti oleo fontes erumpunt, uti Solis, quod oppidum est Ciliciae, flumen nomine Liparis, in quo natantes aut lavantes ab ipsa aqua unguntur. Similiter Aethiopiae lacus est, qui unctos homines efficit, qui in eo nataverint, et India, qui sereno caelo emittit olei magnam multitudinem, item Carthagini fons, in quo natat insuper oleum, odore uti scobe citreo; quo oleo etiam pecora solent ungere. Zacyntho et circa Dyrrachium et Apolloniam fontes sunt, qui picis magnam multitudinem cum aqua evomunt. Babylone lacus amplissima magnitudine, qui λίμνη ἀσφάλτιτις appellatur, habet supra natans liquidum bitumen; quo bitumine et latere testaceo structum murum Samiramis circumdedit Babyloni. Item Iope in Syria Arabiaque Nomadum lacus sunt inmani magnitudine, qui emittunt bituminis maximas moles, quas diripiunt qui habitant circa.
passages.translation: But others, flowing through the veins of the earth, burst forth with oil-anointed springs, as at Solis, a town in Cilicia, a river called Liparis, in which those who swim or wash are anointed by it. Similarly, there is a lake in Ethiopia which makes men anointed who swim in it, and India, which, when the sky is clear, emits a great quantity of oil, as well as a spring in Carthage, in which oil also floats, with a smell like that of lemon grass; with which oil they also anoint cattle. At Zacynthus and around Dyrrachium and Apollonia there are springs which spew out a great quantity of pitch with water. At Babylon a lake of very large size, which is called λίμνη ἀσφαλτῖτις, has liquid bitumen floating on it; with which bitumen and earthenware brick wall was built at Sameramis surrounding Babylon. Likewise at Joppa in Syria and Arabia there are lakes of the Numidians of enormous size, which emit the greatest quantities of bitumen, which those who live around plunder.

passages.latin: Id autem non est mirandum; nam crebrae sunt ibi lapidicinae bituminis duri. Cum ergo per bituminosam terram vis erumpit aquae, secum extrahit et, cum sit egressa extra terram, secernitur et ita reicit ab se bitumen. Etiamque est in Cappadocia in itinere, quod est inter Mazaca et Tyana, lacus amplus, in quem lacum pars sive harundinis sive alii generis si demissa fuerit et postero die exempta, ea pars, quae fuerit exempta, invenietur lapidea, quae autem pars extra aquam manserit, permanet in sua proprietate.
passages.translation: But this is not to be wondered at; for there are frequent stony deposits of hard bitumen there. Therefore, when the force of the water bursts through bituminous soil, it draws it with it, and when it has gone out of the ground, it is separated and thus throws the bitumen from itself. And there is also in Cappadocia, on the road, which is between Mazaca and Tyana, a large lake, into which lake if a piece of reed or of some other kind is dropped and taken out the next day, that part which was taken out will be found to be stony, but the part which remained outside remains in its own right.

passages.latin: Ad eundem modum Hierapoli Phrygiae effervet aquae calidae multitudo, e quibus circum hortos et vineas fossis ductis inmittitur; haec autem efficitur post annum crusta lapidea. Ita quotannis dextra ac sinistra margines ex terra faciundo inducunt eam et efficiunt his crustis in agris saepta. Hoc autem ita videtur naturaliter fieri, quod in îs locis et ea terra, quibus is nascitur, sucus subest coaguli naturae similis; deinde cum commixta vis egreditur per fontes extra terram, a solis et aeris calore cogitur congelari, ut etiam in areis salinarum videtur.
passages.translation: In the same way, at Hierapolis in Phrygia, a multitude of hot waters boil, from which they are let in through ditches around the gardens and vineyards; but this becomes a crust of stone after a year. Thus every year on the right and left they introduce it by making the edges of the earth and make fences in the fields in these crusts. But this seems to happen naturally, because in these places and the land in which it is born, the juice is under the nature of a clot; then when the mixed force comes out of the earth through springs, it is forced to freeze by the heat of the sun and the air, as is also seen in the air of salt lakes.

passages.latin: Item sunt ex amaro suco terrae fontes exeuntes vehementer amari, ut in Ponto est flumen Hypanis. ⟨is⟩ A capite profluit circiter milia XL sapore dulcissimo; deinde, cum pervenit ad locum, qui est ab ostio ad milia CLX, admiscetur ei fonticulus oppido quam parvulus. Is cum in eum influit, tunc tantam magnitudinem fluminis facit amaram, ideo quod per id genus terrae et venas, unde sandaracam fodiunt, ea aqua manando perficitur amara.
passages.translation: Likewise, there are springs issuing from the bitter juice of the earth, which are exceedingly bitter, as in Pontus is the river Hypanus. From its head it flows about 40 miles with a very sweet taste; then, when it reaches a place which is 160 miles from the mouth, a small spring is mixed with it, which is very small. When it flows into it, then by the greatness of the river it becomes bitter, for this reason, because through that kind of earth and the veins from which they dig sandaraca, the water is made bitter by flowing.

passages.latin: Haec autem dissimilibus saporibus a terrae proprietate perficiuntur, uti etiam in fructibus videtur. Si enim radices arborum aut vitium aut reliquorum seminum non ex terrae proprietatibus sucum capiendo ederent fructus, uno genere essent in omnibus locis et regionibus omnium sapores. Sed animadvertimus insula Lesbo vinum protropum, Maeonia Catacecaumeniten, Lydia Tmoliten, Sicilia Mamertinum, Campania Falernum, Terracina et Fundis Caecubum reliquisque locis pluribus innumerabili multitudine genera vini virtutesque procreari. Quae non aliter possunt fieri, nisi, cum terrenus umor suis proprietatibus saporis in radicibus sit infusus, enutrit materiam per quam egrediens ad cacumen profundat proprium loci et generis sui ⟨in⟩ fructus saporem.
passages.translation: But these are perfected with dissimilar flavors by the properties of the earth, as is also seen in fruits. For if the roots of trees or vines or other seeds did not produce fruit by drawing juices from the properties of the earth, the flavors of all would be of one kind in all places and regions. But we observe that the island of Lesbos produces protropous wine, Maeonia Catacecaumene, Lydia Tmolite, Sicily Mamertine, Campania Falerno, in Terracina and Fundis Caecubus and many other places in an innumerable multitude, kinds of wine and virtues are produced. Which cannot be done otherwise, unless, when the earthly moisture is infused with its properties of flavor in the roots, it nourishes the matter through which, rising to the top, it deepens the flavor proper to the place and kind of fruit.

passages.latin: Quodsi terra generibus umorum non esset dissimilis et disparata, non tantum in Syria et Arabia in harundinibus et iuncis herbisque omnibus essent odores, neque arbores turiferae, neque piperis darent bacas, nec murrae glaebulae, nec Cyrenis in ferulis laser nasceretur, sed in omni terra regionibus eodem genere omnia procrearentur. Has autem varietates terrae umoris qualitatis regionibus et locis inclinatio mundi et solis impetus propius aut longius cursum faciendo tales efficit nec solum in his rebus, sed etiam in pecoribus et armentis haec non ita similiter efficerentur, nisi proprietates singularum terrarum ⟨umorum⟩ in regionibus ad solis potestatem temperarentur.
passages.translation: But if the earth were not dissimilar and disparate in the kinds of moisture, not only would there be odours in the reeds and rushes and all the herbs in Syria and Arabia, nor would frankincense trees, nor peppercorns yield berries, nor myrrh clusters, nor would Cyrene produce a laser in its canes, but in every region of the earth everything would be produced in the same kind. Now these varieties in regions and places are produced by the inclination of the world and by the influence of the sun, by making its course nearer or farther, such are the qualities of the earth and the moisture, and not only in these things, but also in cattle and herds, these would not be produced in such a similar way, unless the properties of the individual lands in the regions were tempered to the power of the sun.

passages.latin: Sunt enim Boeotiae flumina Cephisos et Melas, Lucanis Crathis, Troia Xanthus inque agris Clazomeniorum et Erythraeorum et Laodicensium fontes. Ad ⟨ea⟩ flumina cum pecora suis temporibus anni parantur ad conceptionem partus, per id tempus adiguntur eo cotidie potum, ex eoque, quamvis sint alba, procreant aliis locis leucophaea, aliis locis pulla, aliis coracino colore. Ita proprietas liquoris, cum inît in corpus, proseminat intinctam sui cuiusque generis qualitatem. Igitur quod in campis Troianis proxime flumen armenta rufa et pecora leucophaea nascuntur, ideo id flumen Ilienses Xanthum appellavisse dicuntur.
passages.translation: For the rivers of Boeotia are Cephisos and Melas, of Lucania Crathis, of Troy Xanthus, and in the fields of the Clazomenians and Erythraeans and Laodiceans springs. At the rivers with their cattle at their proper times of the year they are prepared for conception and birth, during that time they are driven to drink it daily, and from it, although they are white, in some places they produce white, in others a fawn, in others a raven-colored. Thus the property of the liquid, when it is in the body, reveals the inherent quality of each of its kinds. Therefore, because in the Trojan plains red cattle and white cattle are born near the river, the Ilians are said to have called that river Xanthus.

passages.latin: Etiamque inveniuntur aquae genera mortifera, quae per maleficum sucum terrae percurrentia recipiunt in se vim venenatam, uti fuisse dicitur Terracinae fons, qui vocabatur Neptunius, ex quo qui biberant inprudentes, vita privabantur; quapropter antiqui eum obstruxisse dicuntur. Et Chrobsi Thracia lacus ex quo non solum qui biberint, moriuntur, sed etiam qui laverint. Item in Thessalia fons est profluens, ex quo fonte nec pecus ullum gustat nec bestiarum genus ullum propius accedit; ad quem fontem proxime est arbor florens purpureo colore.
passages.translation: And there are also found kinds of waters that are deadly, which, flowing through the earth through the malefic juice, receive within themselves a poisonous force, as is said to have been the fountain of Terracina, which was called Neptune, from which those who drank unwisely were deprived of life; for which reason the ancients are said to have blocked it. And the lake of Chrobsi in Thrace, from which not only those who drank die, but also those who washed. Likewise in Thessaly there is a spring flowing, from which no cattle taste nor does any kind of beast approach; near which spring is a tree flowering with a purple color.

passages.latin: Non minus in Macedonia quo loci sepultus est Euripides, dextra ac sinistra monumenti advenientes duo rivi concurrunt. In unum, e quibus ad unum accumbentes viatores pransitare solent propter aquae bonitatem, ad rivum autem, qui est ex altera parte monumenti, nemo accedit, quod mortiferam aquam dicitur habere. Item est in Arcadia Nonacris nominata terrae regio, quae habet in montibus ex saxo stillantes frigidissimos umores. Haec autem aqua Στυγός ὕδωρ nominatur, quam neque argenteum neque aeneum nec ferreum vas potest sustinere, sed dissilit et dissipatur. Conservare autem eam et continere nihil aliud potest nisi mulina ungula, qua etiam memoratur ab Antipatro in provinciam ubi erat Alexander, per Iollam filium perlata esse et ab eo ea aqua regem esse necatum.
passages.translation: No less in Macedonia, where Euripides is buried, two streams meet on the right and left of the monument. In one, travelers are accustomed to dine because of the goodness of the water, but no one approaches the stream that is on the other side of the monument, because it is said to have deadly water. Likewise, in Arcadia there is a region of land called Nonacris, which has very cold waters dripping from the rocks on the mountains. This water is called Stygian water, which neither silver nor bronze nor iron vessels can hold, but breaks and is dissipated. But nothing else can preserve and contain it except a hoof mill, which is also mentioned to have been carried by Antipater to the province where Alexander was, by his son Iollas, and by him the king was killed by the water.

passages.latin: Item Alpibus in Cottii regno est aqua; ex qua qui gustant, statim concidunt. Agro autem Falisco via Campana in campo Corneto est lucus, in quo fons oritur; ibique avium et lacertarum reliquarumque serpentium ossa iacentia apparent.
passages.translation: Likewise, in the Alps, in the kingdom of Cottus, there is water; those who taste it immediately fall to their deaths. But in the Faliscan country, on the Campanian road, in the plain of Cornetus, there is a grove in which a spring rises; everywhere the bones of birds and lizards and other serpents are seen lying.

passages.latin: Fieri autem hoc naturaliter ideo videtur, quod acer et acidus sucus subest in ea terra, per quam egredientes venae intinguntur acritudine, et ita, cum in corpus inierunt, dissipant quae ex aquarum subsidentia in corporibus et concrescentia offenderunt. Quare autem discutiantur ex acidis eae res, sic possumus animadvertere. Ovum in aceto si diutius positum fuerit, cortex eius mollescet et dissolvetur. Item plumbum, quod est lentissimum et gravissimum, si in vase conlocatum fuerit et in eo acetum suffusum, id autem opertum et oblitum erit, efficietur, uti plumbum dissolvatur, et fiat cerussa.
passages.translation: This seems to happen naturally because there is a sharp and acidic juice in the earth, through which the veins that emerge are dipped in the sharpness, and thus, when they enter the body, they disperse what they have encountered from the subsidence of the waters in the bodies and their concretion. But why these things are dispersed by acids, we can observe in this way. If an egg is left in vinegar for a long time, its shell will soften and dissolve. Likewise, lead, which is very slow and heavy, if it is placed in a vessel and vinegar is poured into it, but this is covered and forgotten, it will be made to dissolve like lead, and become lead.

passages.latin: Eisdem rationibus aes, quod etiam solidiore est natura, similiter curatum si fuerit, dissipabitur et fiet aerugo. Item margarita. Non minus saxa silicea, quae neque ferrum neque ignis potest per se dissolvere, cum ab igni sunt percalefacta, aceto sparso dissiliunt et dissolvuntur. Ergo cum has res ante oculos ita fieri videamus, ratiocinemur isdem rationibus ex acidis propter acritudinem suci etiam calculosos e natura rerum similiter posse curari.
passages.translation: By the same reasoning, if bronze, which is also more solid by nature, is similarly cured, it will disintegrate and become rust. Likewise pearl. No less do flint stones, which neither iron nor fire can dissolve by themselves, when they are heated by fire, disintegrate and dissolve when sprinkled with vinegar. Therefore, since we see these things happening before our eyes, let us reason by the same reasoning that stones that are naturally calcified can also be cured by acids because of the acridity of the juice.

passages.latin: Sunt autem etiam fontes uti vino mixti, quemadmodum est unus Paphlagoniae, ex quo eam aquam sine vino potantes fiunt temulenti. Aequiculis autem in Italia et in Alpibus natione Medullorum est genus aquae, quam qui bibunt, efficiuntur turgidis gutturibus.
passages.translation: There are also springs mixed with wine, as is the case in Paphlagonia, from which those who drink it without wine become intoxicated. But among the Aequi in Italy and in the Alps, among the Medullae, there is a kind of water, which makes those who drink it swell up in their throats.

passages.latin: Arcadia vero civitas est non ignota Clitor, in cuius agris est spelunca profluens aqua, e qua qui biberint, fiunt abstemii. Ad eum autem fontem epigramma est in lapide inscriptum: hac sententia versibus graecis: eam non esse idoneam ad lavandum, sed etiam inimicam vitibus, quod apud eum fontem Melampus sacrificiis purgavisset rabiem Proeti filiarum restituissetque earum virginum mentes in pristinam sanitatem. epigramma autem est id, quod est subscriptum:
passages.translation: In Arcadia lies the well-known city of Clitor, in whose territory a cave gives forth water that makes those who drink it abstain from wine. Beside the spring a Greek epigram is inscribed on stone. It says that the water is unsuitable for bathing and hostile to vines, because at this spring Melampus had purified the madness of the daughters of Proetus through sacrifices and restored the maidens’ minds to their former health. The epigram reads:

passages.latin: Item est in insula Cia fons e quo qui inprudentes biberint, fiunt insipientes, et ibi est epigramma insculptum ea sententia: iucundam eam esse potionem fontis eius, sed qui biberit, saxeos habiturum sensus. Sunt autem versus hi:
passages.translation: On the island of Ceos there is also a spring whose water makes those who drink it unwittingly lose their reason. An inscribed epigram says that the water is pleasant to drink, but that whoever drinks it will acquire the senses of a stone. The verses run:

passages.latin: Susis autem, in qua civitate est regnum Persarum, fonticulus est ex quo qui biberint amittunt dentes. Item in eo est scriptum epigramma quod significat hanc sententiam: egregiam esse aquam ad lavandum, sed ea si bibatur, excutere e radicibus dentes. Et huius epigrammatos sunt versus graece:
passages.translation: At Susa, the city of the Persian kings, there is a small spring whose water causes those who drink it to lose their teeth. Its epigram says that the water is excellent for washing, but drinking it dislodges the teeth by their roots. Its Greek verses run:

passages.latin: Sunt etiam nonnullis locis fontium proprietates, quae procreant qui ibi nascuntur egregiis vocibus ad cantandum, uti Tarso, Magnesiae, aliis eiusmodi regionibus. Etiamque Zama est civitas Afrorum, cuius moenia rex Iuba duplici muro saepsit ibique regiam domum sibi constituit. Ab ea milia passus XX est oppidum Ismuc, cuius agrorum regiones incredibili finitae sunt terminatione. Cum esset enim Africa parens et nutrix ferarum bestiarum, maxime serpentium, in eius agris oppidi nulla nascitur, et si quando adlata ibi ponatur, statim moritur; neque id solum, sed etiam terra ex his locis si alio translata fuerit, et ibi. Id genus terrae etiam Balearibus dicitur esse. Sed aliam mirabiliorem virtutem ea habet terra, quam ego sic accepi.
passages.translation: In some places the properties of springs are also said to give those born there exceptionally fine singing voices, as at Tarsus, Magnesia and similar regions. Zama is an African city which King Juba enclosed with a double wall and made the site of his royal residence. Twenty miles away lies Ismuc, whose territory has a remarkable natural boundary. Although Africa breeds and sustains wild creatures, especially snakes, none of these snakes is born in the town’s territory; if one is brought there, it dies at once. Moreover, soil carried from that district is said to have the same effect elsewhere. Such soil is also reported in the Balearic Islands. The district has another, still more remarkable property, which I learned as follows.

passages.latin: Gaius Iulius Masinissae filius, cuius erant totius oppidi agrorum possessiones, cum patre Caesare militavit. is hospitio meo est usus. Ita cotidiano convictu necesse fuerat de philologia disputare. Interim cum esset inter nos de aquae potestate et eius virtutibus sermo, exposuit esse in ea terra eiusmodi fontes, ut, qui ibi procrearentur, voces ad cantandum egregias haberent, ideoque semper transmarinos catlastros emere formosos et puellas maturas eosque coniungere, ut, qui nascerentur ex his, non solum voce egregia sed etiam forma essent non invenusta.
passages.translation: Gaius Julius, the son of Masinissa, who owned the entire land of the town, served with his father Caesar. He enjoyed my hospitality. Thus, during our daily conversation, it was necessary to discuss philology. Meanwhile, when we were discussing the power of water and its virtues, he explained that there were such springs in that land that those who were born there had excellent singing voices, and therefore they always bought beautiful seamen from overseas and mated them with mature girls, so that those born of them would not only have excellent voices but also be not unattractive in appearance.

passages.latin: Cum haec tanta varietas sit disparibus rebus natura distributa quod humanum corpus est ex aliqua parte terrenum, in eo autem multa genera sunt umorum, uti sanguinis, lactis, sudoris, urinae, lacrimarum: ergo si in parva particula terreni tanta discrepantia invenitur saporum, non est mirandum, si tanta in magnitudine terrae innumerabiles sucorum reperientur varietates, per quarum venas aquae vis percurrens tincta pervenit ad fontium egressus, et ita ex eo dispares variique perficiuntur in propriis generibus fontes propter locorum discrepantiam et regionum qualitates terrarumque dissimiles proprietates.
passages.translation: Since such great variety is distributed by nature to disparate things, that the human body is in some part earthly, and in it there are many kinds of fluids, such as blood, milk, sweat, urine, tears: therefore if such a discrepancy of flavors is found in a small particle of earth, it is not surprising if in such a large earth innumerable varieties of juices are found, through whose veins the water force, flowing, reaches the outlets of springs, and thus from this disparate and various springs are perfected in their own kinds, because of the discrepancy of places and the qualities of regions and the dissimilar properties of lands.

passages.latin: Ex his autem rebus sunt nonnulla, quae ego per me perspexi, cetera in libris graecis scripta inveni, quorum scriptorum hi sunt auctores: Theophrastos, Timaeus, Posidonios, Hegesias, Herodotus, Aristides, Metrodorus, qui magna vigilantia et infinito studio locorum proprietates, regionum qualitates aquarum virtutes ab inclinatione caeli ita esse distributas scriptis dedicaverunt. Quorum secutus ingressus in hoc libro perscripsi quae satis esse putavi de aquae varietatibus, quo facilius ex his praescriptionibus eligant homines aquae fontes, quibus ad usum salientes possint ad civitates municipiaque perducere.
passages.translation: Of these things, however, there are some which I have observed for myself, the rest I have found written in Greek books, the authors of which are: Theophrastus, Timaeus, Posidonius, Hegesias, Herodotus, Aristides, Metrodorus, who with great vigilance and untiring diligence have dedicated their writings to the properties of the waters, the powers of the waters according to the inclination of the heavens, and the qualities of the regions, as they are thus distributed. Following their introduction, I have written in this book what I thought was sufficient about the varieties of water, so that people may more easily choose from these prescriptions the sources of water which, when they rise, they may bring to cities and towns for use.

passages.latin: Nulla enim ex omnibus rebus tantas habere videtur ad usum necessitates, quantas aqua, ideo quod omnium animalium natura, si frumenti fructu privata fuerit, arbustivo aut carne aut piscatu aut etiam qualibet ex his reliquis rebus escarum utendo poterit tueri vitam, sine aqua vero nec corpus animalium nec ulla cibi virtus potest nasci nec tueri nec parari. Quare magna diligentia industriaque quaerendi sunt et eligendi fontes ad humanae vitae salubritatem.
passages.translation: For of all things, none seems to have such great necessities for use as water, for the reason that the nature of all animals, if deprived of the fruit of grain, will be able to maintain life by using trees or meat or fishing or any of these other things for food, but without water neither the body of animals nor any of the virtues of food can be born, maintained or prepared. Therefore, great care and industry must be used to seek and choose sources for the health of human life.

passages.latin: Expertiones autem et probationes eorum sic sunt providendae. Si erunt profluentes et aperti, antequam duci incipiantur, aspiciantur animoque advertantur, qua membratura sint qui circa eos fontes habitant homines; et si erunt corporibus valentibus, coloribus nitidis, cruribus non vitiosis, non lippis oculis, erunt probatissimi. Item si fons novus fossus fuerit, et in vas corinthium sive alterius generis, quod erit ex aere bono, ea aqua sparsa maculam non fecerit, optima est. Itemque in aeneo si ea aqua defervefacta et postea requieta et defusa fuerit, neque in eius aenei fundo harena aut limus invenietur, ea aqua erit item probata.
passages.translation: But their tests and proofs are to be provided in this way. If they are flowing and open, before they begin to be led, let them be observed and noted in their minds, what kind of members the people who live around those springs are; and if they are of strong bodies, bright colors, legs not defective, and eyes not flawed, they will be most approved. Likewise, if a new spring has been dug, and in a Corinthian vessel or another kind, which will be of good brass, the water does not stain when poured, it is the best.
