Likewise, in a bronze one, if the water has been boiled and then rested and poured out, and neither sand nor silt is found in its bronze bottom, the water will also be approved.

passages.latin: Item si legumina in vas cum ea aqua coniecta ad ignem posita celeriter percocta fuerint, indicabunt aquam esse bonam et salubrem. Non etiam minus ipsa aqua, quae erit in fonte, si fuerit limpida et perlucida, quoque pervenerit aut profluxerit, muscus non nascetur neque iuncus, neque inquinatus ab aliquo inquinamento is locus fuerit, sed puram habuerit speciem, in⟨dica⟩bitur his signis esse tenuis et summa salubritate.
passages.translation: Likewise, if vegetables are placed in a vessel with water and quickly boiled over a fire, they will indicate that the water is good and wholesome. Not least, if the water itself, which is in a spring, is clear and transparent, and if it flows or flows, and if moss or rushes do not grow, and if the place is not polluted by any pollution, but has a pure appearance, these signs indicate that it is pure and in the highest health.

passages.latin: Nunc de perductionibus ad habitationes moeniaque, ut fieri oporteat, explicabo. Cuius ratio est prima perlibratio. Libratur autem dioptris aut libris aquariis aut chorobate, sed diligentius efficitur per chorobaten, quod dioptrae libraeque fallunt. Chorobates autem est regula longa circiter pedum viginti. Ea habet ancones in capitibus extremis aequali modo perfectos inque regulae capitibus ad normam coagmentatos, et inter regulam et ancones a cardinibus compacta transversaria, quae habent lineas ad perpendiculum recte descriptas pendentiaque ex regula perpendicula in singulis partibus singula, quae, cum regula est conlocata, aeque, tangendo aeque ac pariter lineas descriptionis, indicant libratam conlocationem.
passages.translation: Now I will explain the measurements to be made for dwellings and walls, as they should be. The reason for this is the first balancing. It is balanced with diopters or water scales or a chorobate, but it is more carefully done with a chorobate, because diopters and scales are misleading. A chorobate is a rule about twenty feet long. It has ancones at the extreme ends, equally perfect, and cemented together according to the rule's heads, and between the rule and the ancones are transverse hinges, which have lines correctly described perpendicularly and hanging from the rule perpendicularly in each part, which, when the rule is placed, those that touch the lines of description equally and equally indicate a balanced placement.

passages.latin: Sin autem ventus interpellaverit et motionibus lineae non potuerint certam significationem facere, tunc habeat in superiore parte canalem longum pedes V, latum digitum, altum sesquidigitum, eoque aqua infundatur, et si aequaliter aqua canalis summa labra tanget, scietur esse libratum. item eo chorobate cum perlibratum ita fuerit, scietur, quantum habuerit fastigii.
passages.translation: But if the wind has interrupted it and the movements of the lines cannot make a certain sign, then let it have in the upper part a channel five feet long, a finger wide, and a half-finger deep, and water be poured into it, and if the water touches the upper lip of the channel evenly, it will be known that it is level. Thus, when the chorobate has been leveled in this way, it will be known how much height it has.

passages.latin: Fortasse, qui Archimedis libros legit, dicet non posse fieri veram ex aqua librationem, quod ei placet aquam non esse libratam, sed sphaeroides habere schema et ibi habere centrum, quo loci habet orbis terrarum. Hoc autem, sive plana est aqua seu sphaeroides, necesse est: <ad> extrema capita dextra ac sinistra, cum librata regula erit pariter sustinere regulam aquam; sin autem proclinatum habuerit regulae canalem erit ex una parte, quae erit altior, non in summis labris aqua. Necesse est enim, quocumque aqua sit infusa, in medio inflationem curvaturamque habere, sed capita dextra ac sinistra inter se librata esse. Exemplar autem chorobati erit in extremo volumine descriptum. Et si erit fastigium magnum, facilior erit decursus aquae; sin autem intervalla erunt lacunosa, substructionibus erit succurrendum.
passages.translation: Perhaps someone who reads Archimedes' books will say that true balance cannot be achieved from water, because he likes the water not to be balanced, but to have a spheroidal scheme, but to have a center there, where the world has its place. Now, whether the water is flat or spheroidal, this is necessary: <to> the extreme heads of the rule should equally support the water of the rule; but if it is inclined on one side, which will be higher, the channel of the rule will not have water on the upper lips. For it is necessary, wherever the water is poured, to have swelling and curvature in the middle, but that the heads on the right and left should be balanced with each other. Now the model of the chorobate will be described in the outer volume. And if there is a large peak, the flow of the water will be easier; but if the intervals are gaping, assistance will have to be provided by substructures.

passages.latin: Ductus autem aquae fiunt generibus tribus: rivis per canales structiles, aut fistulis plumbeis, seu tubulis fictilibus. Quorum hae sunt rationes. Si canalibus, ut structura fiat quam solidissima, solumque rivi libramenta habeat fastigata ne minus in centenos pedes sicilico eaeque structurae confornicentur, ut minime sol aquam tangat. Cumque venerit ad moenia, efficiatur castellum et castello coniunctum ad recipiendam aquam triplex inmissarium, conlocenturque in castello tres fistulae aequaliter divisae intra receptacula coniuncta, uti, cum abundaverit ab extremis, in medium receptaculum redundet.
passages.translation: Archaeological note — Bk. 8.6 (the Roman aqueducts). The chapter on conduits is illuminated by the archaeology of the greatest hydraulic system of antiquity. Rome came to have eleven aqueducts: the first was the Aqua Appia (312 BCE, of Appius Claudius the Blind), mostly underground; there followed the Anio Vetus, the Aqua Marcia (144 BCE) —the longest and famed for its purity— the Aqua Claudia and the Anio Novus, whose arches still cross the Roman campagna. The chief ancient source is the De aquaeductu of Sextus Julius Frontinus, curator aquarum under Nerva and Trajan, half a century after Vitruvius. The three methods Vitruvius describes are verified in the remains: masonry channels (specus) in the great aqueducts, lead pipes (fistulae, stamped by the plumbarius) in the urban distribution, and terracotta pipes. Surviving monuments such as the Pont du Gard (Nîmes) and the aqueduct of Segovia, and the network of Ostia, confirm the gentle gradient and the engineering that Book VIII theorizes.

passages.latin: Ita in medio ponentur fistulae in omnes lacus et salientes, ex altero in balneas vectigal quotannis populo praestent, ex quibus tertio in domus privatas, ne desit in publico; non enim poterint avertere, cum habuerint a capitibus proprias ductiones. Haec autem quare divisa constituerim, hae sunt causae, uti qui privatim ducent in domos vectigalibus tueantur per publicanos aquarum ductus.
passages.translation: Thus pipes will be placed in the middle for all the lakes and springs, from one they will pay a yearly tax to the people for the baths, from which a third will go to private houses, so that there will be no shortage in the public; for they will not be able to divert it, since they will have their own conduits from the capitals. But the reasons why I have made these divisions are these, so that those who conduct water privately into their houses may be protected by the publicans by means of surveillance.

passages.latin: Sin autem medii montes erunt inter moenia et caput fontis, sic erit faciendum, uti specus fodiantur sub terra librenturque ad fastigium, quod supra scriptum est. Et si tofus erit aut saxum, in suo sibi canalis excidatur, sin autem terrenum aut harenosum erit, solum et parietes cum camara in specu struantur et ita perducatur. Puteique ita sint facti, uti inter duos sit actus.
passages.translation: But if there are mountains between the walls and the head of the spring, it will be necessary to do this, that caves be dug underground and leveled to the summit, as written above. And if it is tofu or rock, a channel should be cut out in its own right, but if it is earth or sandy, the soil and walls with a chamber should be built in the cave and so brought in. And the wells should be made so that there is a passage between the two.

passages.latin: Sin autem fistulis plumbeis ducetur, primum castellum ad caput struatur, deinde ad copiam aquae lumen fistularum constituatur, eaeque fistulae ⟨e⟩ castello conlocentur ad castellum, quod erit in moenibus. Fistulae ne minus longae pedum denûm fundantur. Quae si centenariae erunt, pondus habeant in singulas pondo MCC; si octogenariae, pondo DCCCCLX; si quinquagenariae, pondo DC; quadragenariae pondo CCCCLXXX; tricenariae pondo CCCLX; vicenariae pondo CCXL; quinûm denûm pondo CLXXX; denûm pondo CXX; octonûm pondo C; quinariae pondo LX. E latitudine autem lamnarum, quot digitos habuerint, antequam in rotundationem flectantur, magnitudinum ita nomina concipiunt fistulae. Namque quae lamna fuerit digitorum quinquaginta, cum fistula perficietur ex ea lamna vocabitur quinquagenaria similiterque reliquae.
passages.translation: If the water is to be conveyed in lead pipes, first build a reservoir at the source and determine the bore of the pipes according to the volume of water. Lay them from this reservoir to the distribution tank within the city walls. Cast each pipe at least ten feet long. A hundred-finger pipe should weigh 1,200 Roman pounds; an eighty-finger pipe, 960; a fifty-finger pipe, 600; a forty-finger pipe, 480; a thirty-finger pipe, 360; a twenty-finger pipe, 240; a fifteen-finger pipe, 180; a ten-finger pipe, 120; an eight-finger pipe, 100; and a five-finger pipe, 60. The names of the sizes derive from the width, measured in fingers, of the lead sheets before they are bent into a cylinder. Thus a pipe made from a sheet fifty fingers wide is called a fifty-finger pipe, and the other sizes are named in the same way.

passages.latin: Ea autem ductio, quae per fistulas plumbeas est futura, hanc habebit expeditionem. Quodsi caput habeat libramenta ad moenia montesque medii non fuerint altiores, ut possint interpellare, sed intervalla, necesse est substruere ad libramenta, quemadmodum in rivis et canalibus. Sin autem non longa erit circumitio, circumductionibus, sin autem valles erunt perpetuae, in declinato loco cursus dirigentur. Cum venerint ad imum, non alte substruitur, ut sit libramentum quam longissimum; hoc autem erit venter, quod Graeci appellant κοιλίαν. Deinde cum venerit adversus clivum, ex longo spatio ventris leniter tumescit; ⟨ut⟩ exprimatur in altitudinem summi clivi.
passages.translation: A water supply carried through lead pipes should be arranged as follows. If the source stands high enough above the city and no intervening mountains rise high enough to obstruct the route, but only valleys intervene, build supports to maintain the gradient, as with open channels and conduits. A short detour may instead be taken around them. Where valleys extend too far for this, direct the pipes down the slope. At the bottom provide low supports to form the longest possible level reach: this is the venter, called κοιλία in Greek. On meeting the opposite slope, the pipe rises gently from that long level reach, allowing the water to be forced up to the summit.

passages.latin: Quodsi non venter in vallibus factus fuerit nec substructum ad libram factum, sed geniculus erit, erumpet et dissolvet fistularum commissuras. Etiam in ventre colliquiaria sunt facienda, per quae vis spiritus relaxetur. Ita per fistulas plumbeas aquam qui ducent, his rationibus bellissime poterunt efficere, quod et decursus et circumductiones et ventres et expressus hac ratione possunt fieri, cum habebunt a capitibus ad moenia fastigii libramenta.
passages.translation: If no venter is provided in the valley and the pipe is not supported on a level base, but instead turns through an abrupt elbow, the pressure will burst the pipe joints. Colliquiaria must also be provided in the venter to relieve the force of the air. With these arrangements, a supply through lead pipes can be carried successfully down slopes, around detours, through low level reaches and up rising sections, provided that the necessary difference in level is maintained between the source and the city.

passages.latin: Item inter actus ducentos non est inutile castella conlocari, ut, si quando vitium aliqui locus fecerit, non totum omneque opus contundatur et, in quibus locis sit factum, facilius inveniatur; sed ea castella neque in decursu neque in ventris planitia neque in expressionibus neque omnino in vallibus, sed in perpetua ⟨fiant⟩ aequalitate.
passages.translation: It is also useful to place tanks at intervals of two hundred actus, so that, if a fault occurs at any point, the entire installation need not be dismantled and the damaged section can be located more easily. These tanks should stand on continuously level ground, not on descents, along the level bottom of a siphon, on rising sections or anywhere in valleys.

passages.latin: Sin autem minore sumptu voluerimus, sic est faciendum. Tubuli crasso corio ne minus duorum digitorum fiant, sed ita hi tubuli ex una parte sint lingulati, ut alius in alium inire convenireque possint. coagmenta autem eorum calce viva ex oleo subacta sunt inlinienda, et in declinationibus libramenti ventris lapis est ex saxo rubro in ipso geniculo conlocandus isque perterebratus, uti ex decursu tubulus novissimus in lapide coagmentetur et primus ex librati ventris; ad eundem modum adversum clivum et novissimus librati ventris in cavo saxi rubri haereat et primus expressionis ad eundem modum coagmentetur.
passages.translation: If a less costly method is preferred, make earthenware pipes with walls at least two fingers thick. Give each pipe a projecting tongue at one end so that it fits into the next. Coat their joints with quicklime worked with oil. At the bend where the descending line meets the level section of the siphon, place a bored block of red stone into which the last pipe of the descent and the first pipe of the level section are jointed. At the opposite rise, join the last pipe of the level section and the first rising pipe in the same way in a bored block of red stone.

passages.latin: Ita librata planitia tubulorum ad decursus et expressiones non extolletur. Namque vehemens spiritus in aquae ductione solet nasci, ita ut etiam saxa perrumpat, nisi primum leniter et parce a capite aqua inmittatur et in geniculis aut versuris alligationibus aut pondere saburra contineatur. Reliqua omnia uti fistulis plumbeis ita sunt conlocanda. Item cum primo aqua a capite inmittitur, ante favilla inmittetur, uti coagmenta, si qua sunt non satis oblita, favilla oblinantur.
passages.translation: Thus the level of the tubes, when leveled, should not be exaggerated for the purpose of running and expressing. For a strong spirit is wont to arise in the conveyance of water, so that it even breaks through rocks, unless first the water is let in gently and sparingly from the head, and the ballast is held in place by means of ligatures or sluices, or by weight. All the rest should be placed in the same way as lead pipes. Likewise, when the water is first let in from the head, ashes should be let in first, so that the agglomerations, if any, are not sufficiently removed, are covered with ashes.

passages.latin: Habent autem tubulorum ductiones ea commoda. Primum in opere quod si quod vitium factum fuerit, quilibet id potest reficere. Etiamque multo salubrior est ex tubulis aqua quam per fistulas, quod plumbum videtur esse ideo vitiosum, quod ex eo cerussa nascitur; haec autem dicitur esse nocens corporibus humanis. Ita quod ex eo procreatur, <si> id est vitiosum, non est dubium, quin ipsum quoque non sit salubre.
passages.translation: Earthenware conduits have these advantages. First, if a fault occurs during use, anyone can repair it. Moreover, water conveyed through earthenware is much more wholesome than water carried through lead pipes. Lead is considered harmful because white lead is produced from it, and white lead is said to injure the human body. If what is produced from lead is harmful, there can be no doubt that lead itself is unwholesome.

passages.latin: Exemplar autem ab artificibus plumbariis possumus accipere, quod palloribus occupatos habent corporis colores. Namque cum fundendo plumbum flatur, vapor ex eo insidens corporis artus et in diem exurens eripit ex membris eorum sanguinis virtutes. Itaque minime fistulis plumbeis aqua duci videtur, si volumus eam habere salubrem. Saporemque meliorem ex tubulis esse cotidianus potest indicare victus, quod omnes, et structas cum habeant vasorum argenteorum mensas, tamen propter saporis integritatem fictilibus utuntur.
passages.translation: The pallor of lead-workers provides an example. When lead is melted, the vapor it gives off settles on the limbs and, progressively burning them, deprives the blood of its vitality. If we wish our water to be wholesome, therefore, it should certainly not be conveyed through lead pipes. Everyday practice also shows that water tastes better from earthenware: even people whose tables are furnished with silver vessels use pottery to preserve the purity of its taste.

passages.latin: Sin autem fontes, ⟨non sunt⟩ unde ductiones aquarum, faciamus, necesse est puteos fodere. In puteorum autem fossionibus non est contemnenda ratio, sed acuminibus sollertiaque magna naturales rerum rationes considerandae, quod habet multa variaque terra in se genera. Est enim uti reliquae res ex quattuor principiis composita. Et primum est ipsa terrena; habetque ex umore aquae fontes; item calores, unde etiam sulphur, alumen, bitumen nascitur; aerisque spiritus inmanes, qui, cum graves per intervenia fistulosa terrae perveniunt ad fossionem puteorum et ibi homines offendunt fodientes, vi naturali vaporis obturant eorum naribus spiritus animales; ita, qui non celerius inde effugiunt, ibi interimuntur.
passages.translation: If there are no springs from which we can bring in water, wells must be dug. Their excavation demands careful judgment: the natural properties of the ground must be considered with considerable skill and ingenuity, since the earth contains many different substances. Like everything else, it is composed of four elements. First comes earth itself; it also contains springs arising from watery moisture, heat from which sulfur, alum, and bitumen are produced, and powerful currents of air. When these heavy exhalations pass through the earth’s tubular openings into a well shaft and encounter the diggers, the force of the vapor obstructs their breathing. Anyone who fails to escape quickly is killed there.

passages.latin: Hoc autem quibus rationibus caveatur, sic erit faciendum. Lucerna accensa demittatur; quae si permanserit ardens, sine periculo descendetur. Sin autem eripietur lumen a vi vaporis, tunc secundum puteum dextra ac sinistra defodiantur aestuaria; ita quemadmodum per nares spiritus ex aestu <ariis> dissipabuntur. Cum haec sic explicata fuerint et ad aquam erit perventum, tunc saepiatur as⟨sa⟩ structura, ne obturentur venae.
passages.translation: The following precautions are prescribed. Lower a lit lamp into the well; if it continues to burn, a person may descend without danger. If the vapor extinguishes the flame, dig ventilation shafts to the right and left beside the well, so that the air can escape through them as through nostrils. Once these arrangements have been made and water has been reached, line the well with open-jointed masonry so that the water-bearing veins are not blocked.

passages.latin: Sin autem loca dura erunt aut nimium venae penitus fuerint, tunc signinis operibus ex tectis aut superioribus locis excipiendae sunt copiae. In signinis autem operibus haec sunt facienda. Uti harena primum purissima asperrimaque paretur, caementum de silice frangatur ne gravius quam librarium, calx quam vehementissima mortario mixta, ita ut quinque partes harenae ad duas respondeant. Eorum fossa ad libramentum altitudinis, quod est futurum, calcetur vectibus ligneis ferratis.
passages.translation: If the ground is hard or the water-bearing veins lie too deep, collect supplies from roofs or higher ground in cisterns built in opus signinum. Prepare very clean, coarse sand, and break flint into pieces weighing no more than a pound each. Mix very strong lime in the mixing vessel, using five parts sand to two of lime. Ram the material into the trenches to the intended wall height with iron-shod wooden rammers.

passages.latin: Parietibus calcatis, in medio quod erit terrenum, exinaniatur ad libramentum infimum parietum. Hoc exaequato solum calcetur ad crassitudinem, quae constituta fuerit. Ea autem si duplicia aut triplicia facta fuerint, uti percolationibus transmutari possint, multo salubriorem [et suaviorem] aquae usum efficient; limus enim cum habuerit, quo subsidat, limpidior fiet et sine odoribus conservabit saporem. Si non, salem addi necesse erit et extenuari.
passages.translation: After the walls have been rammed, remove the earth between them down to their lowest level. Level the bottom and ram the floor to the prescribed thickness. Two or three connected cisterns, allowing water to pass through successive stages of filtration, make the supply much healthier [and sweeter]. When the silt has somewhere to settle, the water becomes clearer and retains its taste without an offensive smell. Otherwise, salt must be added to refine it.

passages.latin: Nobilibus athletis, qui Olympia, Pythia Isthmia, Nemea vicissent, Graecorum maiores ita magnos honores constituerunt, uti non modo in conventu stantes cum palma et corona ferant laudes, sed etiam, cum revertantur in suas civitates cum victoria, triumphantes quadrigis in moenia et in patrias invehantur e reque publica perpetua vita constitutis vectigalibus fruantur. Cum ergo id animadvertam, admiror, quid ita non scriptoribus eidem honores etiamque maiores sint tributi, qui infinitas utilitates aevo perpetuo omnibus gentibus praestant. Id enim magis erat institui dignum, quod athletae sua corpora exercitationibus efficiunt fortiora, scriptores non solum suos sensus, sed etiam omnium, <cum> libris ad discendum et animos exacuendos praeparant praecepta.
passages.translation: The Greeks established such great honors for the noble athletes who had won Olympia, Isthmia, and Nemea, that they should not only stand in the assembly and bear praise with a palm and a crown, but also, when they returned to their cities with victory, be carried triumphantly in chariots into the walls and into their homelands, and enjoy the fruits established by the state for life. Therefore, when I observe this, I wonder why even greater honors should not be paid to writers, who have provided infinite benefits to all nations throughout all ages. For it was more worthy of being established that athletes make their bodies stronger by exercise, writers prepare not only their own senses, but also the precepts of all, <with> books for learning and sharpening the minds.

passages.latin: Quid enim Milo Crotoniates, quod fuit invictus, prodest hominibus aut ceteri, qui eo genere fuerunt victores, nisi quod, dum vixerunt ipsi, inter suos cives habuerunt nobilitatem. Pythagorae vero praecepta, Democriti, Platonis, Aristotelis ceterorumque sapientium cotidiana perpetuis industriis culta non solum suis civibus, sed etiam omnibus gentibus recentes et floridos edunt fructus. E quibus qui a teneris aetatibus doctrinarum abundantia satiantur, optimos habent sapientiae sensus, instituunt civitatibus humanitatis mores, aequa iura, leges, quibus absentibus nulla potest esse civitas incolumis.
passages.translation: For what does Milo of Croton, who was undefeated, do to men or to others who were victors of that kind, except that, while they lived, they enjoyed nobility among their citizens? But the precepts of Pythagoras, the daily cultivation of Democritus, Plato, Aristotle, and other wise men by the constant industry, bear fresh and flourishing fruits not only to their own citizens, but also to all nations. From which those who are satisfied from an early age with the abundance of learning, have the best of wise sense, and establish in their cities the morals of humanity, just rights, and laws, without which no city can be safe.

passages.latin: Cum ergo tanta munera ab scriptorum prudentia privatim publiceque fuerint hominibus praeparata, non solum arbitror palmas et coronas his tribui oportere, sed etiam decerni triumphos et inter deorum sedes eos dedicandos iudicari.
passages.translation: Therefore, since such great gifts have been prepared for men by the prudence of writers, both privately and publicly, I think that not only should palms and crowns be awarded to them, but also that triumphs should be decreed and that they should be judged by being dedicated among the seats of the gods.

passages.latin: Et primum Platonis e multis ratiocinationibus utilissimis unam, quemadmodum ab eo explicata sit, ponam. Locus aut ager paribus lateribus si erit quadratus eumque oportuerit duplicare, quod opus fuerit genere numeri, quod multiplicationibus non invenitur, eo descriptionibus linearum emendatius reperitur. Est autem eius rei haec demonstratio. Quadratus locus, qui erit longus et latus pedes denos, efficit areae pedes C. Si ergo opus fuerit eum duplicare, id est pedum CC, item e paribus lateribus facere, quaerendum erit, quam magnum latus eius quadrati fiat, ut ex eo CC pedes duplicationibus areae respondeant. Id autem numero nemo potest invenire. Namque si XIIII constituentur, erunt multiplicati pedes CXCVI, si XV, pedes CCXXV.
passages.translation: First I shall set out one of Plato’s many valuable demonstrations, as he himself expounded it. If a place or field is square, with equal sides, and it must be doubled, this cannot be achieved by any number through multiplication, but is obtained instead by the correct drawing of lines. And this is a demonstration of this. A square place, which is ten feet long and ten feet wide, makes an area of 100 feet. Therefore, if it is necessary to double it, to make it 200 feet, and also with equal sides, it will be necessary to find how large the side of its square is made, so that from it 200 feet correspond to the doublings of the area. But no one can find this numerically. For if 14 are formed, the multiplied feet will be 196, if 15, 225 feet.

passages.latin: Ergo quoniam id non explicatur numero, in eo quadrato, longo et lato pedes X quod fuerit, linea ab angulo ad angulum diagonios perducatur, uti dividantur duo trigona aequa magnitudine, singula areae pedum quinquagenûm, ad eiusque lineae diagonalis longitudinem locus quadratus paribus lateribus describatur. Ita quam magna duo trigona in minore quadrato quinquagenûm pedum linea diagonio fuerint designata, eadem magnitudine et eodem pedum numero quattuor in maiore erunt effecta. Hac ratione duplicatio grammicis rationibus ab Platone, uti schema subscriptum est in ima pagina, explicata est.
passages.translation: Since the result cannot be expressed as a whole-number measure, draw a diagonal from corner to corner of the square ten feet long and ten feet wide. This divides it into two equal triangles, each of fifty square feet. Construct a square with equal sides on the length of that diagonal. The smaller square contains two triangles of fifty square feet; the larger contains four of the same size and area. Plato thus explained the doubling by geometrical construction, as shown in the diagram drawn at the foot of the page.

passages.latin: Item Pythagoras normam sine artificis fabricationibus inventam ostendit, et quod magno labore fabri normam facientes vix ad verum perducere possunt, id rationibus et methodis emendatum ex eius praeceptis explicatur. Namque si sumantur regulae tres, e quibus una sit pedes III, altera pedes IIII, tertia pedes V, eaeque regulae inter se compositae tangant alia aliam suis cacuminibus extremis schema habentes trigoni, deformabunt normam emendatam. Ad eas autem regularum singularum longitudines si singula quadrata paribus lateribus describantur, quod erit trium latus, areae habebit pedes VIIII, quod IIII, XVI quod V erit, XXV.
passages.translation: Pythagoras also showed how to construct a right angle without relying on a craftsman’s square. His principles provide by reason and method the accuracy that craftsmen can scarcely achieve even with great labor. Take three rules, three, four and five feet long, and join their ends to form a triangle: they will define an accurate right angle. If a square is drawn on each rule, the square on the three-foot side has an area of nine square feet, that on the four-foot side sixteen, and that on the five-foot side twenty-five.

passages.latin: Ita quantum areae pedum numerum duo quadrata ex tribus pedibus longitudinis laterum et quattuor efficiunt, aeque tantum numerum reddit id unum ex quinque descriptum. Id Pythagoras cum invenisset, non dubitans a Musis se in ea inventione monitum, maximas gratias agens hostias dicitur his immolavisse. Ea autem ratio, quemadmodum in multis rebus et mensuris est utilis, etiam in aedificiis scalarum aedificationibus, uti temperatas habeant graduum librationes, est expedita.
passages.translation: The combined area of the squares on the three-foot and four-foot sides therefore equals the area of the square on the five-foot side. When Pythagoras discovered this, he believed that the Muses had guided him and is said to have offered sacrifices to them in gratitude. The same principle is useful in many calculations and measurements, and also in setting out staircases so that their steps have a convenient inclination.

passages.latin: Si enim altitudo contignationis ab summa coaxatione ad imum libramentum divisa fuerit in partes tres, erit earum quinque in scalis scaporum iusta longitudine inclinatio. ⟨quare⟩ Quam magnae fuerint inter contignationem et imum libramentum altitudinis partes tres, quattuor a perpendiculo recedant et ibi conlocentur inferiores calces scaporum. Ita si erunt temperatae; ⟨libratae⟩ et graduum ipsarum scalarum erunt conlocationes. Item eius rei erit subscripta forma.
passages.translation: For if the height of the floor from the highest point to the lowest platform is divided into three parts, five of them will be the right length of inclination in the ladders of the rungs. However great the three parts of the height between the floor and the lowest platform, four will recede from the perpendicular and there the lower steps of the rungs will be placed. Thus they will be moderate; and the placements of the steps themselves will be. Likewise the form of this matter will be as follows.

passages.latin: Archimedis vero cum multa miranda inventa et varia fuerint, ex omnibus etiam infinita sollertia id, quod exponam, videtur esse expressum. nimirum Hiero enim Syracusis auctus regia potestate, rebus bene gestis cum auream coronam votivam diis inmortalibus in quodam fano constituisset ponendam, manupretio locavit faciendam et aurum ad sacomam adpendit redemptori. Is ad tempus opus manu factum subtiliter regi adprobavit et ad sacomam pondus coronae visus est praestitisse.
passages.translation: Among Archimedes’s many remarkable inventions, the one I shall now describe seems to show extraordinary ingenuity. When Hiero had acquired royal power at Syracuse and his affairs had prospered, he decided to dedicate a golden crown to the immortal gods in a temple. He contracted for its manufacture and weighed out the gold to the craftsman on a balance. The completed work was presented to the king at the appointed time, delicately finished, and the crown appeared to match the weight of gold supplied.

passages.latin: Posteaquam indicium est factum dempto auro tantundem argenti in id coronarium opus admixtum esse, indignatus Hiero se contemptum esse neque inveniens, qua ratione id furtum reprehenderet, rogavit Archimeden, uti in se sumeret sibi de eo cogitationem. Tunc is, cum haberet eius rei curam, casu venit in balineum, ibique cum in solium descenderet, animadvertit, quantum corporis sui in eo insideret, tantum aquae extra solium effluere. idque cum eius rei rationem explicationis ostendisset, non est moratus, sed exsiluit gaudio motus de solio et nudus vadens domum ⟨uni⟩versis significabat clara voce invenisse, quod quaereret; nam currens identidem graece clamabat: εὕρηκα, εὕρηκα.
passages.translation: Later it was reported that some gold had been removed and an equal weight of silver mixed into the crown. Indignant at the deception, but unable to find a way of exposing the theft, Hiero asked Archimedes to investigate. While considering the problem, Archimedes happened to enter a bath. As he lowered himself into the tub, he noticed that the water flowing over its edge corresponded to the volume of his body submerged in it. Realizing that this suggested a way to solve the problem, he immediately leapt from the tub in delight and went home naked, proclaiming aloud that he had found what he sought. As he ran he repeatedly cried in Greek, εὕρηκα, εὕρηκα, “I have found it, I have found it”.

passages.latin: Tum vero ex eo inventionis ingressu duas fecisse dicitur massas aequo pondere, quo etiam fuerat corona, unam ex auro et alteram ex argento. Cum ita fecisset, vas amplum ad summa labra implevit aquae, in quo demisit argenteam massam. Cuius quanta magnitudo in vasum depressa est, tantum aquae effluxit. Ita exempta massa quanto minus factum fuerat, refudit sextario mensus, ut eodem modo, quo prius fuerat, ad labra aequaretur. Ita ex eo invenit, quantum pondus argenti ad certam aquae mensuram responderet.
passages.translation: Following this discovery, he is said to have made two masses equal in weight to the crown, one of gold and the other of silver. He filled a large vessel to its brim with water and lowered the silver mass into it. The water that overflowed corresponded to the volume of the immersed mass. After removing it, he measured in sextarii the water needed to restore the former level at the brim. In this way he established how a given weight of silver corresponded to a particular volume of water.

passages.latin: Cum id expertus esset, tum auream massam similiter pleno vaso demisit et ea exempta, eadem ratione mensura addita invenit ex aquae numero sextantum: minore quanto minus magno corpore eodem pondere auri massa esset quam argenti. Postea vero repleto vaso in eadem aqua ipsa corona demissa invenit plus aquae defluxisse in corona quam in aurea eodem pondere massa, et ita ex eo, quod fuerat plus aquae in corona quam in massa, ratiocinatus reprehendit argenti in auro mixtionem et manifestum furtum redemptoris.
passages.translation: He then lowered the gold mass into the full vessel and, after removing it, measured in the same way how much water was needed to refill it. The quantity was smaller: at equal weight, gold occupied less volume than silver. Finally he refilled the vessel and immersed the crown itself. More water overflowed than when the equal weight of gold had been immersed. From this greater displacement he demonstrated the mixture of silver with the gold and exposed the craftsman’s theft.

passages.latin: Transferatur mens ad Archytae Tarentini et Eratosthenis Cyrenaei cogitata; hi enim multa et grata a mathematicis rebus hominibus invenerunt. Itaque cum in ceteris inventionibus fuerint grati, in eius rei cogitationibus maxime sunt suspecti. Alius enim alia ratione explicaverunt, quod Delo imperaverat responsis Apollo, uti arae eius, quantum haberent pedum quadratorum, id duplicarentur, et ita fore uti, qui essent in ea insula, tunc religione liberarentur.
passages.translation: Let us turn to the discoveries of Archytas of Tarentum and Eratosthenes of Cyrene, who made many contributions in mathematics of benefit to humanity. Their other inventions earned them gratitude, but they are held in particular esteem for their treatment of the following problem. Each explained in a different way how to carry out Apollo’s command, given by an oracle at Delos, that his altars should be doubled in size, and how the people of the island might thus be released from their religious obligation.

passages.latin: Itaque Archytas cylindrorum descriptionibus, Eratosthenes organica mesolabi ratione idem explicaverunt. Cum haec sint tam magnis doctrinarum iucunditatibus animadversa et cogamur naturaliter inventionibus singularum rerum considerantes effectus moveri, multas res attendens admiror etiam Democriti de rerum natura volumina et eius commentarium, quod inscribitur Χειροκμήτων; †in quo etiam utebatur anulo signaretur amolcie est expertus†.
passages.translation: Archytas explained the problem by constructions involving cylinders, and Eratosthenes by the mechanical method of the mesolabe. Such achievements reveal the great pleasures of learning, and reflection on the effects of individual discoveries naturally moves us to admiration. Among many other works, I also admire Democritus’s writings on nature and his treatise entitled Χειροκμήτων. [The following clause, which refers to the use of a ring, is corrupt in the adopted Latin text and cannot be translated securely.]

passages.latin: Ergo eorum virorum cogitata non solum ad mores corrigendos, sed etiam ad omnium utilitatem perpetuo sunt praeparata, athletarum autem nobilitates brevi spatio cum suis corporibus senescunt; [itaque neque cum maxime sunt] florentes neque posteritati hi, quemadmodum sapientium cogitata hominum vitae, prodesse possunt.
passages.translation: The discoveries of these men are therefore directed not only towards improving conduct but also towards the lasting benefit of everyone. The renown of athletes, by contrast, ages quickly with their bodies. [Thus, even when at the height of their powers,] they cannot benefit posterity as the discoveries of the wise benefit human life.

passages.latin: Cum vero neque moribus neque institutis scriptorum praestantibus tribuantur honores, ipsae autem per se mentes aeris altiora prospicientes memoriarum gradibus ad caelum elatae aevo inmortali non modo sententias sed etiam figuras eorum posteris cogunt esse notas. Itaque, qui litterarum iucunditatibus instinctas habent mentes, non possunt non in suis pectoribus dedicatum habere, sicuti deorum, sic Ennii poetae simulacrum; Accii autem carminibus qui studiose delectantur, non modo verborum virtutes sed etiam figuram eius videntur secum habere praesentem esse.
passages.translation: But since honors are not bestowed on the excellent character or institution of writers, but their minds themselves, looking higher than the air, and raised to the heavens by the steps of their memories, compel posterity to know not only their opinions but also their figures. Therefore, those whose minds are innately inclined to the delights of literature cannot help but have in their hearts, as in the case of the gods, the image of the poet Ennis; while those who delight in the study of Accius' poems seem to have present with them not only the virtues of words but also his figure.

passages.latin: Item plures post nostram memoriam nascentes cum Lucretio videbuntur velut coram de rerum natura disputare, de arte vero rhetorica cum Cicerone, multi posterorum cum Varrone conferent sermonem de lingua latina, non minus etiam plures philologi cum Graecorum sapientibus multa deliberantes secretos cum his videbuntur habere sermones, et ad summam sapientium scriptorum sententiae corporibus absentibus vetustate florentes cum insunt inter consilia et disputationes, maiores habent, quam praesentium sunt, auctoritates omnes.
passages.translation: Likewise, many who were born after our memory will be seen to be discussing with Lucretius, as if in person, about the nature of things, and with Cicero, about the art of rhetoric; many of posterity will converse with Varro about the Latin language; no less will many philologists be seen to be deliberating much with the wise Greeks, having secret conversations with them; and, to sum up, the opinions of wise writers, absent from their bodies, flourishing in antiquity, when they are present in the midst of counsels and discussions, have all greater authority than those of the present.

passages.latin: Itaque, Caesar, his auctoribus fretus sensibus eorum adhibitis et consiliis ea volumina conscripsi, et prioribus septem de aedificiis, octavo de aquis, in hoc de gnomonicis rationibus, quemadmodum de radiis solis in mundo sunt per umbras gnomonis inventae quibusque rationibus dilatentur aut contrahantur, explicabo.
passages.translation: Relying on these authors, Caesar, and drawing on their ideas and counsel, I have written these books. In the first seven I treated buildings, in the eighth water, and in this one I shall explain gnomonics: how the Sun’s rays are traced through the shadows of gnomons, and by what principles those shadows lengthen or shorten.

passages.latin: Ea autem sunt divina mente comparata habentque admirationem magnam considerantibus, quod umbra gnomonis aequinoctialis alia magnitudine est Athenis, alia Alexandriae, alia Romae, non eadem Placentiae ceterisque orbis terrarum locis. Itaque longe aliter distant descriptiones horologiorum locorum mutationibus. Umbrarum enim aequinoctialium magnitudinibus designantur analemmatorum formae, e quibus perficiuntur ad rationem locorum et umbrae gnomonum horarum descriptiones. ἀνάλημμα est ratio conquisita solis cursu et umbrae crescentis ad brumam observatione inventa, e qua per rationes architectonicas circinique descriptiones est inventus effectus in mundo.
passages.translation: These things are ordained by the divine mind and excite great wonder in those who consider that the shadow of the equinoctial gnomon is of one size in Athens, another in Alexandria, another in Rome, not the same in Placentia and other parts of the world. Therefore, they differ greatly from the descriptions of the clocks of places. For the sizes of the equinoctial shadows are designated by the forms of the analemmas, from which the descriptions of the places and the shadows of the gnomons of the hours are completed according to the ratio. ἀνάλημμα is a ratio acquired by observing the course of the sun and the shadow growing towards winter, from which the effect in the world is found by architectonic ratios and descriptions of the compass.

passages.latin: Mundus autem est omnium naturae rerum conceptio summa caelumque sideribus et stellarum cursibus conformatum. Id volvitur continenter circum terram atque mare per axis cardines extremos. Namque in his locis naturalis potestas ita architectata est conlocavitque cardines tamquam centra, unum a terra inmani ⟨spatio⟩ in summo mundo ac post ipsas stellas septentrionum, alterum trans contra sub terra in meridianis partibus, ibique circum eos cardines orbiculos circum centra uti in torno perfecit, qui graece πόλοι nominantur, per quos pervolitat sempiterno caelum. Ita media terra cum mari centri loco naturaliter est conlocata.
passages.translation: Now the world is the conception of all things in nature, the highest heaven and the stars formed. It revolves continuously around the earth and the sea by the extreme pivots of the axis. For in these places the natural power has been architected and placed pivots as centers, one from the earth in the highest world and behind the very stars of the north, the other on the other side under the earth in the southern parts, and there around those pivots it has completed small orbs around the centers as in a wheel, which in Greek are called poles, through which the eternal heaven flies. Thus the earth is naturally placed in the middle with the sea as the center.

passages.latin: His natura dispositis ita, uti septentrionali parte a terra excelsius habeat altitudinem centrum, in meridiana autem parte in inferioribus locis subiectum a terra obscuretur, tunc etiam per medium transversa et inclinata in meridiem [circuli de] lata zona XII signis est conformata. Eorum species stellis dispositis XII partibus peraequatis exprimit depictam ab natura figurationem. Itaque lucentia cum mundo reliquisque sideribus ornatu circum terram mareque pervolantia cursus perficiunt ad caeli rotunditatem.
passages.translation: These are so arranged by nature that on the northern side the center has a height higher than the earth, on the southern side it is obscured by the earth in lower places, then also through the middle a zone transverse and inclined to the south of the circle is brought in twelve signs and shaped. Which appearance of them expresses the figure depicted by nature with the stars arranged in twelve equal parts. Therefore, shining with the world and the other stars, flying around the earth and sea in their adornment, they complete their courses to the roundness of the sky.

passages.latin: Omnia autem visitata et invisitata temporum necessitate sunt constituta. Ex quis sex signa numero supra terram cum caelo pervagantur, cetera sub terram subeuntia ab eius umbra obscurantur. Sex autem ex his semper supra terram nituntur. Quanta pars enim novissimi signi depressione coacta versatione subiens sub terram occultatur, tantundem eius contraria e conversationis necessitate suppressa rotatione circumacta trans locis patentibus ex obscuris egreditur ad lucem; namque vis una et necessitas utrimque simul orientem et occidentem perficit.
passages.translation: But all things visited and unvisited are established by the necessity of time. Of which six signs in number wander above the earth with the sky, the rest are obscured by its shadow, coming under the earth. But six of these are always founded above the earth. For as much of the last sign is hidden under the earth by depression, forced by its turning, so much of its opposite, by the necessity of its conversation, suppressed by rotation, goes out from the dark places to the light; for one force and necessity perfects both east and west at the same time.

passages.latin: Ea autem signa cum sint numero XII partesque duodecumas singula possideant mundi versenturque ab oriente ad occidentem continenter, tunc per ea signa contrario cursu luna, stella Mercurii, Veneris, ipse sol itemque Martis et Iovis et Saturni ut per graduum ascensionem percurrentes alius alia circumitionis magnitudine ab occidente ad orientem in mundo pervagantur. Luna die octavo et vicesimo et amplius circiter hora caeli circumitionem percurrens, ex quo signo coeperit ire, ad id signum revertendo perficit lunarem mensem.
passages.translation: Now since the signs are twelve in number and each occupies a twelfth part of the world and moves continuously from east to west, then through those signs the moon, the stars Mercury, Venus, the sun itself, as well as Mars, Jupiter and Saturn, travel in the opposite direction, as if by ascending degrees, each with a different magnitude of circuit from west to east, and they wander through the world. On the twenty-eighth day and more, the moon, having completed a circuit of the heavens for about an hour, from which it began to go, returns to that sign and completes the lunar month.

passages.latin: Sol autem signi spatium, quod est duodecuma pars mundi, mense vertente vadens transit; ita XII mensibus XII signorum intervalla pervagando cum redit ad id signum, unde coeperit, perficit spatium vertentis anni. Ex eo, quem circulum luna terdecies in XII mensibus percurrit, eum sol eisdem mensibus semel permetitur. Mercurii autem et Veneris stellae circa solis radios uti per centrum eum itineribus coronantes regressus retrorsus et retardationes faciunt, etiam stationibus propter eam circinationem morantur in spatiis signorum.
passages.translation: Now the sun passes through the space of a sign, which is the twelfth part of the world, as it moves through the space of a month; thus, in twelve months, by wandering through the intervals of twelve signs, when it returns to the sign from which it began, it completes the space of a year. Of that which the moon traverses thirteen times in twelve months, the sun is permitted to pass through that circle once in the same months. But the stars of Mercury and Venus, as they circle the rays of the sun through the center, make a backward and retarded return, and even at stations, because of that circumambulation, they remain in the spaces of the signs.

passages.latin: Id autem ita esse maxime cognoscitur ex Veneris stella, quod ea, cum solem sequatur, post occasum eius apparens in caelo clarissimeque lucens vesperugo vocitatur, aliis autem temporibus eum antecurrens et oriens ante lucem lucifer appellatur. Ex eoque nonnumquam plures dies in ⟨uno⟩ signo commorantur, alias celerius ingrediuntur in alterum signum. Itaque quod non aeque peragunt numerum dierum in singulis signis, quantum sunt moratae prius, transiliendo celerioribus itineribus perficiunt [iustum cursum. Ita efficitur], uti, quod demorentur in nonnullis signis, nihilominus, cum eripiant se ab necessitate morae, celeriter consequantur iustam circumitionem.
passages.translation: This is especially evident from the star Venus, which, when it follows the sun, appears in the sky after its setting and shines most brightly, and is called the evening star, but at other times, when it precedes it and rises before dawn, it is called the morning star. From this it sometimes remains in a sign for several days, at other times it enters another sign more quickly. Therefore, since they do not complete the same number of days in each sign as they have previously spent, they complete [the correct course] by skipping over it in more rapid courses. This is done so that, although they remain in some signs, nevertheless, when they escape the necessity of delay, they quickly complete their correct circuit.

passages.latin: Iter autem in mundo Mercurii stella ita pervolitat, uti trecentesimo et sexagensimo die per signorum spatia currens perveniat ad id signum, ex quo priore circumlatione coepit facere cursum, et ita peraequatur eius iter ut circiter tricenos dies in singulis signis habeat numeri rationem.
passages.translation: The journey of the star Mercury in the world is such that on the three hundred and sixty-sixth day, running through the spaces of the signs, it reaches the sign from which it began its course in the previous circulation, and its journey is so equalized that it has about thirty days in each sign.

passages.latin: Veneris autem, cum est liberata ab inpeditione radiorum solis, XXX diebus percurrit signi spatium. quod minus quadragenos dies in singulis signis patitur, cum stationem fecerit, restituit eam summam numeri in uno signo morata. Ergo totam circinationem in caelo quadringentesimo et octogensimo et quinto die permensa iterum init signum, ex quo signo prius iter facere coepit.
passages.translation: When Venus is free from the obstruction of the Sun’s rays, she passes through a sign in thirty days. Whatever falls short of forty days in each sign is made up when she remains stationary in one of them. Having thus completed the whole circuit of the heavens on the four hundred and eighty-fifth day, she returns to the sign from which her previous course began.

passages.latin: Martis vero circiter sexcentesimo octogensimo tertio siderum spatia pervagando pervenit eo, ex quo initium faciendo cursum fecerat ante, et in quibus signis celerius percurrit, cum stationem fecit, explet dierum numeri rationem. Iovis autem placidioribus gradibus scandens contra mundi versationem, circiter CCCLX diebus singula signa permetitur, et consistit post annum XI et dies CCCXIII et redit in id signum, in quo ante XII annos fuerat. Saturni vero, mensibus undetriginta et amplius paucis diebus pervadens per signi spatium, anno nono et vicensimo et circiter diebus CLX, in quo ante tricensimo fuerat anno, in id restituitur, ex eoque, quo minus ab extremo distat mundo, tanto maiorem circinationem rotae percurrendo tardior videtur esse.
passages.translation: Mars travels through the zodiac and returns to the point from which its previous course began in about 683 days; where it passes through a sign more rapidly, its stationary period makes up the required number of days. Jupiter advances more slowly against the rotation of the heavens, taking about 360 days to pass through each sign. After eleven years and 313 days it returns to the sign it occupied nearly twelve years earlier. Saturn takes twenty-nine months and a few additional days to cross a sign, returning in twenty-nine years and about 160 days to the sign it occupied nearly thirty years before. Being nearer the outermost part of the universe, it travels a larger circuit and therefore appears slower.

passages.latin: Ei autem, qui supra solis iter circinationes peragunt, maxime cum in trigono fuerint, quod is inierit, tum non progrediuntur, sed regressus facientes morantur doneque cum idem sol de eo trigono in aliud signum transitionem fecerit. Id autem nonnullis sic fieri placet, quod aiunt solem, cum longius absit abstantia quadam, non lucidis itineribus errantia per ea sidera obscuritatis morationibus inpedire. Nobis vero id non videtur. Solis enim splendor perspicibilis et patens sine ullis obscurationibus est per omnem mundum, ut etiam nobis appareant, cum faciant eae stellae regressus et morationes. Ergo si tantis intervallis nostra species potest id animadvertere, quid ita divinitatibus splendoribusque astrorum iudicamus obscuritates obici posse?
passages.translation: But those who make their rounds above the sun's path, especially when they are in a trine that it has entered, then they do not advance, but make returns and remain, and finally when the same sun has made a transition from that trine to another sign. But some people like to do this in this way, which they say that the sun, when it is farther away by a certain absence, does not hinder the stars wandering through it on their bright paths with delays of darkness. But to us this does not seem to be the case. For the brightness of the sun is perceptible and open without any obscurations throughout the whole world, so that it also appears to us when those stars make returns and stays. Therefore, if our species can observe this at such intervals, why do we judge that the divinations and splendors of the stars can be so much objected to as obscurity?

passages.latin: Ergo potius ea ratio nobis constabit, quod, fervor quemadmodum omnes res evocat et ad se ducit, ut etiam fructus e terra surgentes in altitudinem per calorem videmus, non minus aquae vapores a fontibus ad nubes per arcus excitari, eadem ratione solis impetus vehemens radiis trigoni forma porrectis insequentes stellas ad se perducit et ante currentes veluti refrenando retinendoque non patitur progredi, sed ad se regredi, in alterius trigoni signum esse.
passages.translation: Therefore, we will rather understand this reason, that just as heat evokes and draws all things to itself, as we also see fruits rising from the earth to a height through heat, and no less water vapors are raised from springs to the clouds by arcs, so by the same reason the vehement force of the sun, with its rays extended in the form of a triangle, draws the following stars to itself, and as if restraining and holding them back, it does not allow them to advance, but to return to itself, being in the sign of another triangle.

passages.latin: Fortasse desiderabitur, quid ita sol quinto a se signo potius quam secundo aut tertio, quae sunt propiora, facit in his fervoribus retentiones. Ergo, quemadmodum id fieri videatur, exponam. Eius radii in mundo uti trigoni paribus lateribus formae lineationibus extenduntur. Id autem nec plus nec minus est ad quintum ab eo signo. Igitur si radii per omnem mundum fusi circinationibus vagarentur neque extentionibus porrecti ad trigoni formam linearentur, propiora flagrarent. Id autem etiam Euripides, Graecorum poeta, animadvertisse videtur. Ait enim, quae longius a sole essent, haec vehementius ardere, propiora vero eum temperata habere. Itaque scribit in fabula Phaethonte sic: καίει τὰ πόρρω, τἄγγυθεν δ’ εὔκρατ’ ἔχει.
passages.translation: Perhaps it will be wondered why the sun, in the fifth sign from itself rather than the second or third, which are nearer, causes retentions in these fervors. Therefore, I will explain how this seems to be done. Its rays in the world are extended in the form of a triangle with equal sides, by lines. But this is neither more nor less than the fifth sign from that sign. Therefore, if the rays were to wander through the whole world in circles, nor were they to be extended in the form of a triangle, by lines, the nearer things would burn. And Euripides, the Greek poet, seems to have noticed this also. For he says that those things which were farther from the sun burn more vehemently, but those which were nearer he keeps in moderation. Therefore he writes in the fable of Phaethon thus: καῖε τὰ πόρρω, τἀγγύθεν δ' εὔκρατ' ἔχει.

passages.latin: Si ergo res et ratio et testimonium poetae veteris id ostendit, non puto aliter oportere iudicari, nisi quemadmodum de ea re supra scriptum habemus.
passages.translation: Therefore, if the fact and reason and the testimony of the ancient poet show this, I do not think it should be judged otherwise than in the way we have written about that matter above.

passages.latin: Quemadmodum, si in rota, qua figuli utuntur, inpositae fuerint septem formicae canalesque totidem in rota facti sint circum centrum imo adcrescentes ad extremum, in quibus hae cogantur circinationem facere, verseturque rota in alteram partem, necesse erit eas contra rotae versationem nihilominus adversus itinera perficere, et quae proximum centrum habuerit, celerius pervagari, quaeque extremum orbem rotae peragat, etiamsi aeque celeriter ambulet, propter magnitudinem circinationis multo tardius perficere cursum: similiter astra nitentia contra mundi cursum suis itineribus perficiunt circumitum, sed caeli versatione redundationibus referuntur cotidiana temporis circumlatione.
passages.translation: Just as if seven ants were placed on a wheel used by potters, and as many channels were made in the wheel around the center at the bottom, increasing towards the end, in which these are forced to make a circuit, and the wheel is turned in the other direction, it will be necessary for them to complete their journeys no less in opposition to the rotation of the wheel, and the one that has the nearest center will travel more quickly, and the one that completes the outer circle of the wheel, even if it walks equally quickly, will complete its course much more slowly because of the magnitude of the circuit: in the same way the shining stars complete their circuit in their journeys against the course of the world, but the rotation of the heavens is referred to by the daily circulation of time.

passages.latin: Esse autem alias stellas temperatas, alias ferventes, etiamque frigidas haec esse causa videtur, quod omnis ignis in superiora loca habet scandentem flammam. Ergo sol aethera, qui est supra se, radiis exurens efficit candentem, in quibus locis habet cursum Martis stella; itaque fervens ab ardore solis efficitur. Saturni autem, quod est proxima extremo mundo tangit ⟨que⟩ congelatas caeli regiones; vehementer est frigida. Ex eo Iovis, cum inter utriusque circumitiones habeat cursum, a refrigeratione caloreque earum medio convenientes temperatissimosque habere videtur effectus.
passages.translation: But the reason why there are other stars that are temperate, others that are boiling, and also that are cold seems to be that all fire has a flame that rises to higher places. Therefore the sun, burning the aether, which is above it, with its rays, has made it red-hot, in which places the star Mars has its course; therefore it is made hot by the heat of the sun. But Saturn, which is nearest to the outermost world, touches the frozen regions of the sky; it is extremely cold. Hence Jupiter, since it has its course between the orbits of both, seems to have effects that are appropriate and most temperate from the cooling and heat of them.

passages.latin: Berosus, qui ab Chaldaeorum civitate sive natione progressus in Asia etiam disciplinam Chaldaicam patefecit, ita est professus:
passages.translation: Pilam esse ex dimidia parte candentem, reliqua habere caeruleo colore. Cum autem cursum itineris sui peragens subierit sub orbem solis, tunc eam radiis et impetu caloris corripi convertique candentem propter eius proprietatem luminis ad lumen. Cum autem ea vocata ab solis orbi superiora spectent, tunc inferiorem partem eius, quod candens non sit, propter aeris similitudinem obscuram videri. Cum ad perpendiculum ea sit ad eius radios, totum lumen ad superiorem speciem retineri, et tunc eam vocari primam.

passages.latin: Cum praeteriens vadat ad orientis caeli partes, relaxari ab impetu solis extremamque eius partem candentiae oppido quam tenui linea ad terram mittere splendorem, et ita ex eo eam secundam vocari. cotidiana autem versationis remissione tertiam, quartam in dies numerari. Septimo die, ⟨cum⟩ sol sit ad occidentem, [luna autem inter orientem et occidentem] medias caeli teneat regiones, quod dimidia parte caeli spatio distet a sole, item dimidiam candentiae conversam habere ad terram. Inter solem vero et lunam cum distet totum mundi spatium et lunae orienti sol trans contra sit ad occidentem, eam, quo longius absit, a radiis remissam XIIII die plena rota totius orbis mittere splendorem, reliquosque dies decrescentia cotidiana ad perfectionem lunaris mensis versationibus et cursu a sole revocationibus subire sub rotam radiosque eius et ita menstruas dierum efficere rationes.
passages.translation: When passing by it goes to the eastern parts of the sky, it is relaxed from the force of the sun and the outer part of its brightness is as thin as a line to the earth, and so from that it is called the second. The daily rotation is reduced to the third, the fourth to the days. On the seventh day, the sun is to the west, [the moon between east and west] it occupies the middle regions of the sky, because it is distant from the sun by half the space of the sky, and also has half of its brightness turned towards the earth. But between the sun and the moon, since the whole space of the world is distant and the sun is on the other side of the moon to the west, it, the farther it burns, is relaxed from the rays and on the fourteenth day it sends out a full wheel of the whole world, and on the remaining days it decreases daily and the perfection of the lunar month by rotations and reversions from the sun, it undergoes under the wheel and its rays and now makes the monthly days.

passages.latin: Uti autem Aristarchus Samius mathematicus vigore magno rationes varietatis disciplinis de eadem ⟨re⟩ reliquit, exponam. Non enim latet lunam ⟨non⟩ suum propriumque habere lumen, sed esse uti speculum et ab solis impetu recipere splendorem. Namque luna de septem astris circulum proximum terrae in cursibus minimum pervagatur. Ita quot mensibus sub rotam solis radiosque uno die, antequam praeterit, latens obscuratur. Cum est cum sole, nova vocatur. Postero autem die, quo numeratur secunda, praeteriens ab sole visitationem facit tenuem extremae rotundationis. Cum triduum recessit ab sole, crescit et plus inluminatur. Cotidie vero discedens cum pervenit ad diem septimum, distans a sole occidente circiter medias caeli regiones, dimidia lucet, et eius quae ad solem pars spectat, ea est inluminata.
passages.translation: But as Aristarchus the Samian mathematician has vigorously left reasons for the variety of disciplines concerning the same, I will explain. For it is not hidden that the moon does not have its own light, but is like a mirror and receives its brightness from the sun's impact. For the moon travels the nearest circle of the earth in the shortest of the seven stars. Thus, as many months pass under the wheel and rays of the sun, on one day, before it passes, it is hidden and darkened. When it is with the sun, it is called a new day. But on the next day, which is counted as the second, passing by the sun, it makes a thin visitation of extreme roundness. When it has been away from the sun for three days, it grows and becomes more illuminated. But descending daily, when it reaches the seventh day, distant from the sun in the west about half the regions of the sky, half the light, and that part of it which looks towards the sun is illuminated.

passages.latin: Quarto autem decumo die, cum in diametro spatio totius mundi absit ab sole, perficitur plena et oritur, cum sol sit ad occidentem, ideo quod totum spatium mundi distans consistit contra et impetu solis totius orbis in se recipit splendorem. Septumo decumo die cum sol oriatur, ea pressa est ad occidentem. Vicensimo et altero die cum sol est exortus, luna tenet circiter caeli medias regiones, et id quod spectat ad solem, id habet lucidum reliquis obscura. Item cotidie cursum faciendo circiter octavo et vicensimo die subit sub radios solis, et ita menstruas perficit rationes.
passages.translation: But on the fourteenth day, when it is far from the sun in the diameter of the whole world, it is completed full and rises, since the sun is to the west, for this reason that the whole distant space of the world stands against it and receives the brightness of the whole world by the force of the sun. On the seventeenth day, when the sun rises, it is pressed to the west. On the twenty-second day, when the sun has risen, the moon occupies approximately the middle regions of the sky, and that which looks towards the sun has light, the rest is dark. Likewise, making its daily course, on about the twenty-eighth day it comes under the rays of the sun, and thus completes the monthly calculations.

passages.latin: Namque cum arietis signum iniit et partem octavam pervagatur, perficit aequinoctium vernum. Cum progreditur ad caudam tauri sidusque vergiliarum, e quibus eminet dimidia pars prior tauri, in maius spatium mundi quam dimidium procurrit procedens ad septentrionalem partem. E tauro cum ingreditur in geminos exorientibus vergiliis, magis crescit supra terram et auget spatia dierum. Deinde <e> geminis cum iniit ad cancrum, qui brevissimum tenet caeli spatium, cum pervenit in partem octavam, perficit solstitiale tempus, et peragens pervenit ad caput et pectus leonis, quod eae partes cancro sunt attributae.
passages.translation: For when it enters the sign of Aries and travels through an eighth part, it completes the vernal equinox. When it advances to the tail of Taurus and the constellation of Vergil, from which the first half of Taurus stands out, it extends over a greater space of the world than half, proceeding towards the northern part. When it enters from Taurus into the rising Gemini, Vergil, it grows more above the earth and increases the lengths of the days. Then, when it enters from Gemini to Cancer, which occupies the shortest space of the sky, when it reaches an eighth part, it completes the solstitial time, and in doing so it reaches the head and breast of the lion, because those parts are attributed to Cancer.

passages.latin: E pectore autem leonis et finibus cancri solis exitus percurrens reliquas partes leonis inminuit diei magnitudinem et circinationis reditque in geminorum aequalem cursum. Tunc vero a leone transiens in virginem progrediensque ad sinum vestis eius contrahit circinationem et aequat ad eam, quam taurus habet, cursus rationem. E virgine autem progrediens per sinum, qui sinus librae partes habet primas, in librae parte VIII perficit aequinoctium autumnale; qui cursus aequat eam circinationem, quae fuerat in arietis signo.
passages.translation: But the sun's exit from the lion's chest and the ends of Cancer, passing through the remaining parts of the lion, diminishes the magnitude of the day and the circumference and returns to the equal course of the twins. Then, passing from the lion into the virgin and advancing to the bosom, its garment contracts the circumference and equalizes the ratio of the course to that which the bull has. But proceeding from the virgin through the bosom, which bosom has the first parts of Libra, in the eighth part of Libra it completes the autumnal equinox; which course equalizes the circumference which had been in the sign of Aries.

passages.latin: Scorpionem autem cum sol ingressus fuerit occidentibus vergiliis, minuit progrediens meridianas partes longitudines dierum. E scorpione cum percurrendo init in sagittarium ad <femina> eius, contractiorem diurnum pervolat cursum. Cum autem incipit a <feminibus> sagittarii, quae pars est attributa capricorno, ad partem octavam, brevissimum caeli percurrit spatium. Ex eo a brevitate diurna bruma ac dies brumales appellantur. E capricorno autem transiens in aquarium adauget et aequat sagittarii longitudine diei spatium. Ab aquario cum ingressus est in pisces favonio flante, scorpionis comparat aequalem cursum. Ita sol ea signa circum pervagando certis temporibus auget aut minuit dierum et horarum spatia.
passages.translation: But when the sun enters Scorpio with the setting of the Vergils, it shortens the length of the days as it progresses towards the meridian parts. When it travels from Scorpio to Sagittarius, it flies through a shorter daily course. But when it begins at the thighs of Sagittarius, which is the part assigned to Capricorn, it travels through an eighth part of the sky, covering the shortest distance. From this, from the shortness of the day, the winter days are called Brumac. But when it passes from Capricorn into Aquarius, it increases and equals the length of the day in Sagittarius. When it enters Pisces from Aquarius with the blowing of the Favonius, it equals the course of Scorpio. Thus, as the sun travels around those signs, it increases or decreases the distances of days and hours at certain times.

passages.latin: Namque septentrio, quem Graeci nominant ἄρκτον sive ἑλίκην, habet post se conlocatum custodem. ab eo Non longe conformata est virgo, cuius supra umerum dextrum lucidissima stella nititur, quam nostri provindemiatorem, Graeci προτρυγητήν vocant; candens autem magis spica eius est colorata. Item alia contra est stella media genuorum custodis arcti: qui arcturus dicitur est ibi dedicatus.
passages.translation: For the north, which the Greeks call ἄρκτον or ἑλίκην, has a guardian placed behind it. Not far away is a virgin, over whose right shoulder shines a very bright star, which ours call the providential, the Greeks call προτρυγητήν; but its spike is colored more brightly. Likewise, on the other side is another star between the knees of the guardian of the arc: he who is called Arcturus is there delicate.

passages.latin: E regione capitis septentrionis transversus ad pedes geminorum auriga stat in summo cornu tauri -- ita quae in summo cornu laevo est, aurigae pedis una tenet partem stella -- et adplicantur aurigae manui haedi, capra laevo umero. Tauri quidem et arietis insuper Perseus -- dexterioribus subter currentis basem vergiliis, at sinisterioribus caput arietis -- et manu dextra innitens Cassiepiae simulacro, laeva supra tauri tenet gorgoneum ad summum caput, subiciens Andromedae pedibus.
passages.translation: Opposite the head of the Bear, and extending across toward the feet of the Twins, stands the Charioteer at the tip of the Bull’s horn: a single star marks both the tip of the Bull’s left horn and part of the Charioteer’s foot. The Kids lie by his hand, and the Goat is on his left shoulder. Above the Bull and the Ram is Perseus, with the Pleiades beneath his right side and the Ram’s head beneath his left. His right hand rests against the figure of Cassiopeia; with his left he holds the Gorgon’s head above the top of the Bull’s head, placing it beneath Andromeda’s feet.

passages.latin: Item pisces supra Andromedam, ex aequis ventris ex aequisque sunt supra spinam equi, cuius ventris lucidissima stella finit ventrem equi et caput Andromedae. Manus Andromedae dextra supra Cassiepiae simulacrum est constituta, laeva ⟨supra⟩ aquilonalem piscem. Item aquarii supra equi caput est. Equi ungulae attingunt aquarii ⟨e regione volucrem. inter Cepheum et Andromedae⟩ genua; Cassiepia media est dedicata. Capricorni supra in altitudinem aquila et delphinus. Secundum eos est sagitta. Ab ea autem ⟨non longe⟩ volucris, cuius pinna dextra Cephei manum attingit et sceptrum, laeva supra Cassiepiae innititur. Sub avis cauda pedes equi sunt subiecti.
passages.translation: Likewise, the fish are above Andromeda, and her belly and horse are above the spine of the equine, whose belly the brightest star ends the belly of the horse and the head of Andromeda. The right hand of Andromeda is placed above the image of Cassiopeia, the left a northern fish. Likewise, the aquarius is above the horse's head. The horse's hooves touch the knees of the aquarius; Cassiopeia is dedicated in the middle. Above Capricorn in height is an eagle and a dolphin. Next to them is an arrow. From the eautem birds, whose right wing touches the hand of Cepheus and rests on the scepter, the left one rests above Cassiopeia. Under the bird's tail the horse's feet are covered.

passages.latin: Inde sagittarii, scorpionis, librae insuper serpens summo rostro coronam tangit. eum medium ophiuchos in manibus tenet serpentem, laevo pede calcans mediam frontem scorpionis. A parte ophiuchi capitis non longe positum est caput eius, qui dicitur nisus in genibus. eorum Autem faciliores sunt capitum vertices ad cognoscendum, quod non obscuris stellis sunt conformati.
passages.translation: Then the serpent touches the crown of Sagittarius, Scorpio, and Libra with the top of its beak. In the middle of it, Ophiuchus holds a serpent in his hands, stepping on the middle forehead of the Scorpion with his left foot. Not far from the head of Ophiuchus is his head, which is said to be bent on its knees. But the tops of their heads are easier to recognize, because they are not shaped like dark stars.

passages.latin: Pes ingeniculati adit fulcitve capitis tempus serpentis, cuius per vipereos flexus minor arctorum, qui septentriones dicuntur, inplicatur. delphinum; contra volucris rostro est proposita lyra. Inter umeros custodis et geniculati corona est ordinata. In septentrionali vero circulo duae positae sunt arctoe scapularum ⟨e regione⟩ dorsis inter se compositae et pectoribus aversae. E quibus minor κυνόσουρα, maior ἑλίκη a Graecis appellatur. Earumque capita inter se dispicientia sunt constituta, caudae capitibus earum adversae contra dispositae figurantur; utrarumque enim superando eminent.
passages.translation: The kneeling man's foot is supported by the head of a serpent, whose arcs, which are called the north, are entwined. A dolphin is bent slightly by them; a lyre is placed with its beak against the birds. A crown is arranged between the shoulders of the guard and the kneeling man. In the northern circle, however, two arcs are placed, the backs of the shoulder blades being placed together and the breasts facing away. Of these, the smaller is called κυνόσουρα, the larger ἑλίκη by the Greeks. Their heads are placed opposite each other, and their tails are depicted as arranged opposite their heads; for they both stand out by overcoming each other.

passages.latin: In summo per caudas earum esse dicitur. Item serpens est porrecta, e qua stella quae dicitur polus elucet contra caput maioris septentrionis; namque qua est proxume draconem, circum ⟨polum⟩ caput eius involvitur. ima vero circum cynosurae caput iniecta est flexu porrectaque proxime eius pedes. Haec autem intorta replicataque se attollens reflectitur a capite minoris ad maiorem, circa rostrum et capitis tempus dextrum. Item supra caudam minoris pedes sunt Cephei, ibique ad summum cacumen facientes stellae sunt trigonum paribus lateribus, insuper arietis signum. Septentrionis autem minoris et Cassiepiae simulacri complures sunt stellae confusae.
passages.translation: At the top it is said to be by their tails. Likewise, a serpent is stretched out, from which a star called the pole shines around the head of the greater North; for that which is nearest the dragon is wrapped around its head. But one is thrown around the head of the Cynosura by a stream and stretched out near its feet. But this, twisted and folded with the head of the lesser to the greater, around the beak and the right side of the head. Likewise, above the tail of the lesser are the feet of Cepheus, and there at the highest peak are stars forming a triangle with equal sides, and above it the sign of Aries. But the images of the lesser North and Cassiopeia are several confused stars.

passages.latin: Primum sub capricorno subiectus piscis austrinus caudam prospiciens ceti. Ab eo ad sagittarium locus est inanis. Turibulum sub scorpionis aculeo. Centauri priores partes proximae sunt librae et scorpioni. Tenet in manibus simulacrum, id quod bestiam astrorum periti nominaverunt. virginem et leonem et cancrum anguis porrigens agmen stellarum intortus succingit, regione cancri erigens rostrum, ad leonem medioque corpore sustinens craterem ad manumque virginis caudam subiciens in qua inest corvus; quae sunt autem supra scapulas, peraeque sunt lucentia.
passages.translation: First, under Capricorn, a southern fish is placed, looking towards the tail of a whale. From there to Sagittarius, there is an empty space. A censer is placed under the sting of a scorpion. The front parts of the centaur are close to Libra and Scorpio. He holds in his hands an image of what the experts in the stars have called the beast. To the Virgin, the Lion, and the Crab, a serpent stretches out a coiled array of stars, raising its beak in the region of the Crab, to the Lion, and in the middle of the body, he holds a bowl, and to the hand of the Virgin, he places the tail in which are ravens; but those which are above the shoulders are equally luminous.

passages.latin: Ad anguis inferius ventris, sub caudam subiectus est centaurus. Iuxta cratera et leonem navis est, quae nominatur Argo, cuius prora obscuratur, sed malus et quae sunt circa gubernacula eminentia videntur, ipsaque navicula et puppis per summam caudam cani iungitur. Geminos autem minusculus canis sequitur contra anguis caput. Maior item sequitur minorem. Orion vero transversus est subiectus, pressus ungula tauri, manu laeva ⟨pellem⟩ tenens, clavam altera ad geminos tollens.
passages.translation: At the lower corners of the belly, under the tail, is a centaur. Next to the bowl and the lion is a ship, which is called Argo, the prow of which is obscured, but the mast and what is around the rudders are seen to be prominent, and the ship itself and the stern are joined by the top of the dog's tail. But the smaller dog follows the twins with its head turned. The larger one follows the smaller one. Orion, however, is placed across, pressed by the bull's hoof, holding with his left hand, and lifting the twins with his other hand.

passages.latin: Apud eius vero basim canis parvo intervallo insequens leporem. Arieti et piscibus cetus est subiectus, a cuius crista ordinate utrisque piscibus disposita est tenuis fusio stellarum, quae graece vocitantur ἁρπεδόναι. Magnoque intervallo introrsus pressus nodus serentium, attingit summam ceti cristam. Esse fuit per speciem stellarum flumen. Profluit initium fontis capiens a laevo pede Orionis. Quae vero ab aquario fundi memoratur aqua, profluit inter piscis austrini caput et caudam ceti.
passages.translation: At its base, however, a dog pursues a hare at a great distance.
